spelling no real CLI produces, so every test standing on it -- the whole
of `tests/e2e` included -- exercised a shape that existed only in the
harness. The fake now emits the qualified name and calls the registry
with the bare one, which is what a real run does, so `tests/e2e`'s
propose-then-approve test covers the path an agent actually takes.

`TrackedPullRequest` (`model.PullRequestRef`/`model.PrHealth`/
`model.TrackedPullRequest`, `pkg/model/pullrequest.go`) turned out not to
need a table of its own: `model.Task`'s existing `LinkFixes` link already
records which PR a task's push produced, `task_observation` already
records completion/closure, and `Store.OpenPullRequestLinks` is the one
new read `pkg/orchestrator/sync.go`'s `SyncPullRequests` needed against
those two tables — a `TrackedPullRequest` value is assembled fresh from a
`GetPullRequest`/`ListCheckRuns` read each cycle rather than cached
anywhere, which is what its own `ObservedAt` field is for. Folders are
still unbuilt; nothing here needed them.

`orchestrator`'s own directive parser (`ParseDirectives`) is deliberately
narrower than `grain/automation/directives.py`: `/repo`, `/base`,
`/auto-merge` and `/reads` only (bwsalmon/agents#352 added the last —
repeatable, adding a repo to `Task.Reads` per line rather than replacing
it, per docs/data-model.md's "One write target, many read targets"; a
`Reads` entry is cloned read-only alongside the target and mentioned in
`BuildPrompt`'s own prompt, but grants nothing — `gitproxy`'s authorizer,
not this package, is what actually refuses a push to one). `/pr`
(continue an existing PR), `/review` (post a
review instead of pushing) and `/depends` (cross-task ordering) all need a
dispatch shape `RunDispatch`/`BuildPrompt` don't build yet — every task
today is `IntentImplement`, fresh branch, no continuation — and are listed
in `directives.go`'s own doc comment as exactly that, not silently
dropped. `add_review_comment` calls from a run are read off the same seam
(`agent.Result.ToolCalls`, where `ProcessResult` already finds
`ask_question`/`comment_on_issue`/`propose_task`) and turned into a real
`CreateReview` call whenever the run has a pull request behind it — which
a review task's does, through the task it reviews
(`relayReviewFeedback`). `propose_task`'s `depends_on` is
resolved now: `relayProposedTasks` files each entry as a real
`model.LinkDependsOn`, against an existing task id (the proposing task's
own included, which is what a piece split out of the work in hand names)
or the local `id` of an *earlier* `propose_task` call in the same run —
earlier, not any, since a batch resolved in call order cannot contain a
cycle, and a `depends-on` cycle is two tasks neither of which is ever
dispatchable again. An entry naming neither is kept in the proposal's own
body for a human instead of filed as a link: `task_blocked` and
`model.IsBlocked` both count a blocking link as open until its target's
observation says closed, so a dangling target — one that names no task at
all — blocks forever (deliberately: it fails closed), and a proposal
blocked by something that does not exist has nothing that could ever
unblock it.

An entry naming a task that *does* exist and will never finish is refused
for the same reason, and it had to be learnt the expensive way
(grain/task-487). `BuildPrompt` told every run to name "task N itself"
when the follow-up only makes sense once this task's change has landed,
which is right for every task that lands a change and ends, and wrong for
the one kind that does not: a standing console session is by definition a
task that is never finished, and a blocking link is released only by its
target closing (`task_blocked` counts a target whose `closed_at` is
null). The director followed the sentence. Eight tasks were filed with
`depends_on: ["450"]` in a day, every one of them undispatchable, two
more reached `main` only because an operator bumped them by hand — and
nothing in the UI said the queue was holding anything, because a blocked
task and a task waiting its turn both read `queued`. `model.LinkContinues`
had already carried the finding in its own doc comment ("it must never be
made to block ... the session would be dead the moment somebody split
it"); the code took care not to make a session a blocking target and the
prompt then asked an agent to do it by hand.

Three things answer it, and the order matters: the prompt is the
etiquette, the refusal is the mechanism, and the row is what makes the
next one a thirty-second diagnosis. `model.NeverCompletes` names the
property rather than the kind — a task that never reaches a terminal
state — so the next never-ending thing grain grows adds itself in one
place instead of at every call site; today it is read off the console
session tag, the only record of that association. `Store.
DependencyNeverSatisfiable` pairs it with the task's state, because a
session's *closed* task is a dependency already met and a perfectly good
thing to wait on: only the live one is a link with nothing on the other
end. Both filing paths refuse such a link and say so in the body
(`model.NeverEndingDependencyNote`, the bargain `unresolvedDependencyNote`
already strikes — the run said something about ordering and the approver
should see that it was dropped and why), while a person attaching one in
the picker gets a validation error instead, since there is somebody there
to tell. And `list_grain_tasks` now carries `blocked on <ids>` on the row,
off the `BlockedBy` the UI's own chip already draws: the state cannot say
it, by design — blocked is an annotation on queued and not a state — so
the one place a reader could tell the two apart was a tooltip in a
browser nobody had open.

Resolving it is half of it; an agent has to be told to write one at all,
and told the two facts it needs to. `propose_task`'s description now asks
for `depends_on` in so many words — a proposal that names nothing is
unblocked as soon as it is queued, which for most proposals is the moment
a human approves them and for some is at once, and can be dispatched
beside the work it was meant to follow — and `BuildPrompt` names the running task's
own id, which an agent otherwise could only reverse out of its branch
name. The same schema carries `auto_merge`: a proposal inherits the
proposing task's setting as before (bwsalmon/agents#345), an explicit
`false` opts a proposal out of that inheritance for work an agent judges
deserves its own review, and an explicit `true` is still capped at what
the proposing task itself holds (`proposedAutoMerge`) — a run that could
mark its own proposals auto-merge would be granting itself the unreviewed
merge a human withheld. `BuildPrompt` mentions `auto_merge` only to a task
that is itself an auto-merge job, since there is nothing another task
could do with it.

An auto-merge job's proposal is now filed *approved* as well, not only
auto-merge (`model.AutoSubmits`, grain/task-112). The gate is the one
auto-merge inheritance already passes through and not a looser one:
`parent.AutoMerge`, `GrantsSubsetOf` so the child asks for no capability
its parent lacked, and `LandsWhereGranted` so it lands on the branch — or
the declared write target's branch — the same human already opened to
unreviewed commits. A child whose `reads` name a repository its parent
could not fetch (`model.UngrantedReads`) is filed proposed too, with a
note naming them, since the git proxy would otherwise let it clone that
repository with nobody having agreed to it. The argument is that the gate was not buying
anything: a task whose own commits merge with nobody reading them could
have written the follow-up itself and merged that, so making it wait for
a click on work of the same shape on the same branch costs a round trip
through a person with no decision left to make. Everything outside that
shape still waits: a proposal onto another branch, into a repository
nobody declared, or asking for a capability the parent never held is
filed `PROPOSED` like any other, and so is every proposal from a task
that does not auto-merge. `auto_merge: false` is *not* an opt-out of it —
whether a pull request is read and whether the work is queued are
different questions, and a run that judged a proposal worth reviewing has
said nothing about the second. The approval it carries is
`model.AutoSubmitPrincipal`, an automation actor on nobody's behalf,
which is docs/data-model.md's own shape for an approval made by policy
rather than by a person.

Both paths that file a proposal apply it, since a proposal can be filed
twice over: `relayProposedTasks` at the end of a run, and
`ui.Client.CreateTask` for one filed live while the run is still going
(`daemonProposalFiler`, whose `ProposedBy` is what `CreateTask` reads the
parent off). That second path used to decide auto-merge on the daemon
side from the repo alone, which quietly let an auto-merge task with a
`/base` of its own pass auto-merge to a proposal filed against the
default branch; the daemon now sends what the run asked for and
`CreateTask` caps both answers against `model.AutoSubmits`. The MCP tool
says which of the two happened in its result (`mcp.FiledProposal.Queued`)
rather than telling every run its proposal is unapproved, and
`BuildPrompt` tells an auto-merge job the same thing up front, because
the fact changes what a run has to write: `depends_on` is now the only
thing holding a proposal behind work it has to follow.

The other permission that queues a proposal without a click is a standing
console session whose deployment has ticked `TasksApproved`, and for a
while only one of those two paths applied it (grain/task-311). The replay
read the setting; `CreateTask` had never heard of sessions and fell
through to `model.AutoSubmits`, which can never say yes for a session — it
holds no auto-merge and no branch to land on. Since a session's runs have
a daemon to file through, *every* proposal it makes went down the path
that ignored the permission, while the prompt grain writes for it said in
so many words that its tasks were filed approved. The director filed four
tasks under that belief and told an operator they were "set going"; all
four sat `proposed`. The permission is one predicate now
(`model.ConsoleSession.QueuesProposals`) and the prompt sentence, the
live gate and the replay gate are each written from it, so a change to
one cannot leave the others disagreeing. The live path applies it exactly
as the replay does: approved as `ConsoleSessionPrincipal`, outside
`AutoSubmitLimits` (a session's permission is a person sitting in front
of the chat, not a run's inherited one, so a cap on it would be a cap on
how much a human may ask for in a day — what that work goes on to queue
for *itself* is bounded as usual, through `model.SelfApproved`), and
passing on no auto-merge. That call also used to attribute what it filed
to whoever the client acts as, so a proposal read back as `Filed by:
operator (human)` on work no operator had seen; a request naming
`ProposedBy` is now attributed as the replay attributes it, grain on
behalf of the task that proposed it.

What that permission alone did not bound is the tree it can grow
(grain/task-120). A proposal filed approved inherits its parent's
auto-merge too, so it may auto-submit in turn, and one approval could
grow a self-approved tree of any size with nobody in the loop after the
first. Each step still needs an agent to call `propose_task` and every
task in such a tree is confined to the branch and the capabilities that
first human granted, so this is a looping agent rather than an
escalation of privilege — and it is still the failure
docs/data-model.md says is cheapest to catch at creation.
`model.AutoSubmitLimits` catches it in two halves, both read from the
store per proposal by `Store.ExceededAutoSubmitLimit`. *Depth* walks
`LinkProposedBy` up from the proposing task and counts the unbroken run
of ancestors that were themselves queued with nobody looking
(`model.SelfApproved`, which is an `AutoSubmitPrincipal` or
`ConsoleSessionPrincipal` approval and deliberately not every
automation-on-nobody's-behalf one: a schedule's firing and a review task
are approved by policy too, but nobody proposed them). A human approval
ends the walk, so the guarantee is "at most `Depth` levels of
self-approved work between one human decision and the next" rather than
a ceiling on how deep a tree can ever be. *Fan-out* counts how many
proposals the proposing task has already had queued that way — per task
over its whole life, not per run: a proposal carries no run identity,
and counting from the store is the one measure both filing paths can
agree on. Because each path writes a proposal before deciding the next,
the count already includes the siblings filed a moment ago in the same
run, so neither path keeps a tally of its own.

Hitting a limit costs a click and never the work: the proposal is filed
unapproved, with `model.AutoSubmitLimitNote` appended to its body naming
the bound and saying that whoever is reading it is now the decision —
`otherBranchAutoMergeNote`'s own reason, one silent downgrade further on.
The withholding is of the approval alone; `auto_merge` on the child is
still decided by the permission, since who reads a pull request and who
queues the work are different questions. Both filing paths apply it, for
the reason they both apply `AutoSubmits`. A standing console session is
outside the bound and the tasks below it are inside it: its permission is
a person in front of the chat rather than a run's inherited one, so a cap
on its proposals would cap how much a human may ask for in a day, while
what that human cannot see is what the work they asked for queues for
itself. The pair is deployment configuration
(`grain_config.max_auto_submit_depth` and `max_auto_submit_fan_out`,
defaults 2 and 5, settable through `PUT /api/settings`, `grain sync` and
the Settings pane) because deployment-wide is the only configuration
surface there is; docs/data-model.md argues per-folder is the granularity
anyone actually wants, and that tree is unbuilt. A stored zero reads as
"nobody chose" and resolves to the default, so a deployment upgrading
across those columns gains the bounds rather than a pair of zeroes that
would read as none.

`proposalSection` says the bound exists to the runs it affects, without
saying where they stand in it — nothing in `BuildPrompt` can know that
without a store read, and it would not change what a run should do. What
it does change is what a proposal's body is written for: a run told flatly
that its proposals are never read writes them for nobody, and the one
past the limit is exactly the one a person has to read.

That schema now carries a `repo` as well, which is how a task reaches
more than one repository (grain/task-54). `model.Task.Writes` is any
number of extra write targets — a repo and the base branch work goes on
*there*, one row each in `task_write`, picked in the new-task form and on
a task's detail panel, or given as `grain create -write
owner/name[@branch]`. docs/data-model.md's "exactly one write target per
task" invariant is intact where it matters, which is the run: a sandbox
is one checkout, its branch is `grain/task-<id>` in the task's own
`Target`, and `gitproxy` still refuses a push to anything else — a
`Writes` entry reaches the proxy through `GitScope` as one more repo the
run may *fetch*, beside its `Reads`. What it buys is the route to the
second repository. `BuildPrompt` names those repos and their branches and
says the change over there is made by calling `propose_task` with `repo`
set to one of them; `relayProposedTasks` files that proposal against that
repo, on that branch, and `model.LandsWhereGranted` — `SameBranch`
widened by exactly the declared write targets, and by nothing else — lets
it inherit the parent's auto-merge, because that repo and that branch are
precisely what a human wrote on the task. So a two-repo change is two
pull requests against two bases, each reviewable on its own, rather than
one run holding two checkouts whose merges would have to be ordered by
something nothing in the model can say.

`repo` is not limited to those declared targets, though (grain/task-144).
A proposal may name any repository this deployment works in, and is filed
there on that repository's default branch — `model.Store.WorksInRepo` is
the gate: `targetRepos` alone where a deployment restricts its repos,
since a task filed off that list is parked before it ever dispatches, and
otherwise the repos it has demonstrably worked in (a repo some task
targets, one some task declares as a write target, one carrying a
`repo_config` row of its own — the same union the frontend's `knownRepos`
builds its dropdowns from). Restricting it to the declared targets made
the argument wrong most of the time it mattered: a run reading a week of
this deployment's own history in its state repository, asked which
agent-ergonomics work was worth doing, proposed eight tasks of which
seven were changes to grain's own code — and all eight were filed against
the state repository, where a Go change cannot land, leaving a human to
retarget seven by hand. Nobody had declared a write target because nobody
knew in advance what the findings would be about. What such a proposal
does *not* get is any of the parent's auto-merge: it lands on a branch
nobody granted, `LandsWhereGranted` says no, and
`otherBranchAutoMergeNote` says so on the proposal — which is the
remaining difference between naming a declared write target and naming
one of the deployment's other repos, and the reason declaring one still
means something. A proposal naming a repo nothing here has ever worked in
is still filed — against the parent's own repo, with a note saying what
was asked for — on `unresolvedDependencyNote`'s reasoning: losing an
agent's work over an argument nobody would ever see is worse than filing
it in the wrong place and saying so. The other half is that an agent has
to know the argument exists at all: `propose_task`'s description says
where a proposal lands by default and asks for `repo` on work that
belongs elsewhere, and `BuildPrompt` names the repository a proposal
would otherwise be filed against, since the default is a fact about grain
rather than about the work in front of the run.

The three things that file a task on somebody's behalf declare them too
(grain/task-86): a template, a schedule, and the suites built on
templates. `schedule_write` and `template_write` sit beside the
`schedule_read`/`template_read` pair those rows already carry, offered by
the same picker the new-task form uses, and every path that turns that
content into a task copies them — a schedule's firing, a suite pass, a
qualification run, the review a template files. Without that, a recurring
job spanning two repos had to be filed by hand every time, which is the
thing this feature exists to stop. A repo off `targetRepos` is refused
where the template or the schedule is saved, not where it fires, so the
argument happens in front of the person having it rather than at three in
the morning; a write target naming the repo a firing turns out to be
filed *against* is dropped instead (`model.WritesBesides`), since an
unbound template cannot know which repo its callers will target and the
task's own `Target` already grants strictly more.

The one path that files a task from another *task* rather than from
reusable content carries them too (grain/task-110): a backport inherits
its parent's `Writes` alongside its `Reads` and `Grants`, whole, with the
base each was declared on. A change that needed a second repository on
`rel.latest` needs the same second repository on the branches it is
backported to, and a backport filed without them can neither clone that
repo nor propose a task for it. The bases are not rewritten for the
release branch the backport is aimed at, because only the parent repo's
branch is changing: a `Writes` base is a standing declaration about
*another* repository, which knows nothing about this one's release train.
A second repository with release branches of its own is left to the run
doing the backport to notice and say in the task it proposes, rather than
guessed at filing time.

Repairing a PR that goes red is built now (bwsalmon/agents#283):
`SyncPullRequests` runs a merge queue, one per target repo, over every
task that asked for `/auto-merge` and still has a PR open. Only the
queue's head — whichever of a repo's waiting tasks sits first in the
backlog — is ever acted on in a
cycle; a repair started for the second task while the first is still
being repaired would likely need starting over the moment the first
merges and changes what the second is based against, so everything behind
the head just waits. Nothing merges while CI is still
running: a check run GitHub has not finished reads `PrHealth.PENDING`
(`healthFrom`), which is neither clean nor failing, so the head simply
holds its place and the next cycle asks again — a queue that merged on
"no failure reported yet" would land changes before their tests had said
anything about them. Pending outranks failing on purpose, so a red job
alongside a still-running one waits too: the queue asks for exactly one
automatic repair per pull request, and it is worth a cycle to ask for
that one against CI's whole verdict rather than against whichever job
went red first. A check GitHub concluded `cancelled` reads `PENDING`
too, and for the same reason: it finished without judging anything, so
calling it clean merges on a suite that never reported, while calling it
failing would send an agent at a job nobody thinks is broken and would
have a merge queue's own "cancelled, will retry" check block a pull
request. That is the one place the ordering inverts — a check that
actually failed outranks a cancelled one, since a cancelled check will
never say anything more on its own — which keeps a fail-fast matrix, one
job red and its siblings cancelled with it, on the repair path instead
of the two-hour one. Nor does it merge before CI has said *anything*: an empty check
list is read `PENDING` too, until the head commit has carried it for
`defaultCheckRegistrationWindow` (two minutes). GitHub creates a
workflow run's check runs asynchronously after processing a push, so a
sync landing in the gap between the push and that sees nothing — and
nothing is also what a repo with no CI configured answers, forever, with
no way to tell the two apart from the Checks API. The window is the only
thing that can, and a deployment with genuinely no CI pays it once per
head commit. On a repository holding the `grain-ci` capability there is a
second verdict in the same judgement: grain's own CI, read off the task's
record rather than out of GitHub (`withGrainCI`), red and pending exactly
as a check is — with the difference that having nothing recorded about a
commit is never read as a failure, since a CI engine that is off or
restarting is the commonest reason for it. And all of that is reasoning about one *commit*, so the
cycle names it at every step rather than letting any of them mean
"whatever the branch points at now": the check runs are read for the head
sha off the pull-request read (a branch-scoped read answers for a commit
the cycle never saw), the window above is keyed on it, and the merge
carries it in GitHub's own `sha` parameter, which refuses with `409` if
the branch has moved since. That closes the gap a push landing mid-cycle
would otherwise walk through — a human's own "push a fix by hand", a
repair run pushing to the branch it was sent to fix, a redispatched task
pushing again — and costs one cycle when it happens: the task keeps its queue
position and the commit that landed is judged next cycle on its own CI.
Nor does it wait for CI that is never coming: a head that
has read `PENDING` for longer than `defaultCheckStallDeadline` (two
hours, timed per head commit over one unbroken run of pending reads) is
given up on — a comment naming the checks that never finished,
`Observation.MergeQueueBlockedAt` set, the queue moved on — since a
workflow waiting on an approval nobody gives, or a provider that posted
"queued" and went away, would otherwise hold its repo's whole queue for
the life of the deployment with nothing said to anyone. No repair is
asked for on that one: nothing has failed, and a check that never
finishes is usually waiting on something outside the pull request, so
there may be nothing in it to repair. The comment says which of the two
waits it is giving up on, since a cancelled check is not stuck on
anything — it is finished, and only a re-run will get a verdict out of
it, which is a different thing to go and do. A conflicted or failing head is not taken at
its word, either. Before anything is filed for it, `refreshStaleHead`
asks GitHub to merge the pull request's own base branch into its head
branch (`POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/merges`, `Client.MergeBranch`) —
because the common shape of a broken head is not a broken change but a
stale one: its checks last ran against a `main` that has since moved, so
either GitHub can no longer compute a merge ref and every
`on: pull_request` job dies at checkout (which reads as *failing*, not as
a conflict), or the verdict that did report is about a tree nobody would
ever merge. The queue does not try to tell those apart before acting —
`mergeable_state` reports `blocked` rather than `behind` for exactly this
case, and a check run names no base — it asks for the merge and lets the
answer classify: `201` means it was behind and is not now, so CI re-runs,
the head holds its queue position while it does, and the *next* cycle
decides on a fresh verdict; `204` means the branch already contained its
base, so the failure is genuine and the repair is asked for as it always
was; `409` means it genuinely conflicts, which is the case a repair is
really for, asked for immediately and now naming the conflict the queue
watched GitHub refuse rather than one inferred from a `Mergeable` flag.
That is one API call in place of a full agent run for what has been the
majority of this deployment's automatic fixes — every one of them
resolved by a plain `git merge origin/main` an agent booted a sandbox to
type. It happens once per *repair round* — once before the repair is
asked for and once after it has run (`Observation.MergeQueueRefreshedAt`
read against `MergeQueueRepairAt`, both persisted for the same reason the
CI clocks are not: losing one would cost a repeated write to GitHub
rather than another window of waiting), only for the queue head, and
never for a branch the queue is not steering or one it has given up on. It is a
merge, never a rebase: nothing force-pushes a branch an agent may still
hold a clone of.

A conflicted or failing head that survives all that is **sent back to an
agent on its own branch** (grain/task-271). The queue comments on the
task saying what is broken, which branch to push to, and what CI printed
if a job went red; clears `Observation.CompletedAt`, which is what makes
`StateOf` read the task `queued` again; and stamps
`Observation.MergeQueueRepairAt`. The next `dispatch.Cycle` picks it up
through the ordinary path, the run continues the branch the pull request
is already open from, and GitHub re-runs that one pull request's checks
once. Until grain/task-271 the queue filed a *separate* task instead —
pre-approved, `/base` the broken branch, `/auto-merge true`, stacked and
merged back once green, which is `core.py`'s own `_suggest_fix` trick
minus the human approval step bwsalmon/agents#283 asked to remove. It
worked, and it cost two full rounds of CI for one resolution: the fix
branch's own before it could merge, and the head branch's afterward, with
the queue waiting out both and a second pull request left behind. A
conflict resolved on the branch that has the conflict needs neither.
`LinkFixTask` is still defined and such a task still merges if a database
holds one in flight; nothing writes a new one.

`MergeQueueRepairAt` is the whole record of a repair, and four things
read it: the queue waits on it rather than on another task's state, it
will not merge a branch an agent is still pushing to, the store spends
the capacity `Limits.Mergers` keeps back on the repair run (`mergerTaskSQL`,
which used to be the `ReasonFix` column alone), and never clearing it is
what holds the deployment to one automatic repair per pull request. If
the repair finishes and the PR is still broken, the refresh above is
offered once more before anyone is troubled — the base has been moving
under that branch the whole time the repair ran, since the queue passes a
head being repaired over and keeps merging the changes behind it, so a
resolution that was right when it was pushed can be merely *behind* by
the time it is read, and a merge is what nearly all of them turn out to
need. If that merge lands, the next cycle judges the fresh verdict. If
GitHub says the branch was not behind, or that it conflicts for real,
`SyncPullRequests` gives up automatically rather than asking for a second
repair: it comments explaining why, and saying which of those two answers
it got, sets `Observation.MergeQueueBlockedAt`, and the queue moves on to
the next task in that repo — a blocked task still merges the moment a human's
own push makes it clean, it just stops being anyone's queue head, so it
can no longer hold up what's behind it. It judges that a cycle *after*
the one the repair completed on, since dispatch runs before sync inside a
tick and the verdict read on that tick describes the branch as it was
before the repair pushed to it.

The task goes visibly back to working while this happens, which is what
a person watching the queue should see — so the frontend says which kind
of work it is: `ui.Task.Repairing` carries it, a repairing row's grain
mark animates in green rather than the accent's gold, and its badge reads
"Repairing" instead of "Running". A row that has gone back to running has
not gone back to the beginning.

Giving up is one round, not the end of the road (grain/task-301). Every
one of those three exits is the queue saying "this needs a person", and
what a person mostly does about it is the thing the comment asked for —
push the fix, prod whatever the checks were waiting on, merge the base in
by hand — after which they want the queue to have another go. Until this
there was no way to ask: `MergeQueueBlockedAt` was written once and
cleared by nothing, so the only two ways out were a pull request that
happened to read *clean* on some later cycle (the blocked arm merges it
with no queue position involved) and closing the task. A conflict a
person resolved by hand, or checks they unstuck, still had to be merged
on GitHub by that same hand. So the detail pane grows a **Retry merge**
button on exactly the tasks that have been given up on, `grain
retry-merge <id>` is the same ask from a shell, and both are
`ui.Client.RetryMerge` over `POST /api/tasks/{id}/retry-merge`.

A retry is a whole fresh round rather than a nudge, because the queue's
memory of having tried is three stamps and any one of them left standing
would make the next cycle give up again on the spot: `MergeQueueBlockedAt`
(which is what keeps the task out of `isQueueMember`),
`MergeQueueRepairAt` (one repair for the life of the pull request) and
`MergeQueueRefreshedAt` (one base-branch merge per repair round). All
three go back to nil together, and the task is a queue entry again on the
next cycle — read the checks afresh, merge the base in if the branch has
fallen behind, send it back to an agent once more if that is not enough,
and give up again, once, if that round fails too. Nothing here goes to
GitHub and nothing merges: a retry cannot land a change whose CI the
queue has not read, it can only put the change back in front of the
thing that reads it. It refuses a task with no pull request (there is no
queue entry without one) and a closed task (no cycle looks at one at all
— reopen it first), and it says what it did in the task's own thread,
under the person who clicked it, since three fields going back to nil is
otherwise invisible.

The one part of the queue's state a retry cannot clear is the stall clock,
which is in memory and keyed by pull request (`pendingChecks`) rather than
stored on the task — so instead the clock stops being kept for a pull
request the queue has given up on: `escalateStalledChecks` drops the
sighting as it blocks, and `queueEntry.observe` declines to time a blocked
entry at all. The clock measures how long the queue has been *waiting* on
CI, and it is not waiting on one it has stopped driving. Without that, a
task blocked for checks that never finished would come back from a retry
with a clock already reading the whole deadline and be given up on again
on the very next cycle; with it, a retry buys another full wait — and
still a bounded one, since the new clock starts from the first cycle after
the retry and ends the same way the first did.

No new record was needed for the
queue itself: `queueOrder` derives the whole queue from `Task.AutoMerge`,
`Origin.Reason` and `MergeQueueBlockedAt` fresh every cycle, and
`queueHeads` takes each repo's first entry from it — the same "derive it,
don't store it" discipline `TaskState` already holds to.

What the queue does write down is where it is. Every cycle,
`showQueueAtFrontOfBacklog` moves the tasks waiting to land to the front
of the backlog in the order they will land (`Store.MoveToFrontOfBacklog`)
— so a task list answers "what is grain about to finish, and in what
order" without anyone opening a task, and so a repair, being the head
task itself going back to work, is dispatched ahead of new work without
anything having to file it there. It is the same order in both
directions: `queueOrder` reads position back off the backlog rather than
comparing `Task.CreatedAt` behind everyone's back, so dragging one
waiting pull request above another really does change which merges first,
and `Store.Ready` needs no carve-out for the merge queue's own work any
more — being at the head of the list is what dispatches it first, which
is a thing a human can see and, if they disagree, undo.

That head is now the top of the list rather than its far end
(grain/task-201). `ui.Client.ListTasks` used to hand a UI or CLI the
*reverse* of the store's order unless `model.Config.NewestFirst` was set,
a newest-first display inherited from when a task's position was just its
age — so the paragraph above was only true if you read the list bottom
upwards, and the tasks about to merge sat furthest from where anyone
looks first. The flip is gone: a list reads top-to-bottom in the order
grain will work through it, merges at the very top, and `NewestFirst` now
only decides which end of that list a newly filed task joins (the bottom
by default, behind everything already queued; the top when it is on).

And that end is now chosen where the task is filed, not in Settings
(grain/task-202). The new-task form carries an "Add to backlog" picker —
front, so it runs next, or end, behind everything already queued — and
`grain create -position front|end` is the same choice from a shell;
`ui.CreateTaskRequest.AtFront` carries it, and a request that names an
end wins over whatever is stored. Naming one also *stores* it
(`Store.SetNewestFirst`, which writes `grain_config.newest_first` alone
rather than replacing the row the way a settings save does), so the next
task filed with no opinion joins the same end and the form opens on the
choice the last one made (`GET /api/config`'s `newestFirst`). That is the
whole of the remembering: `NewestFirst` was always "where new work joins
the backlog", and the only thing that changed is that filing a run of
urgent work at the front no longer means opening Settings first and
remembering to put it back. A filing that names no end changes nothing —
a schedule, a proposal or a script cannot quietly reset what a human
picked — and an interactive session is unaffected either way, since it
dispatches ahead of the backlog regardless of what any of this says.

The git proxy has moved, though (`gitproxy/`, above) — it is the one
piece of "actually dispatching" v2 now owns outright, credential ladder
and sandbox-token identity included. `grain/proxy`'s
`SandboxCredentialOverrides` (bwsalmon/agents#52's per-task
`grain-github-<name>` label) is a `Task.Grants` entry here instead of a
second sandbox-keyed file: `model.GitCredentialGrant` is the Grant the
label produces, `Store.GitCredentialOverride` resolves a sandbox's live
task down to the name it names, and `GitProxy.Handle` uses that name
against `CredentialSet.Get` in place of the owner/repo ladder whenever
one is present — no override outlives the task, because it is stored
with every other Grant the task carries rather than written and cleared
around dispatch. `dispatch.Cycle` also mints no leases yet — a run's
`Leases` field exists in the schema and `gitproxy` never reads it; the
git proxy authorizes straight off `Task.Target`/`Reads` instead, which
serves the same fail-closed purpose without depending on that field being
populated first.

The GitHub client has moved too (`pkg/github/`, above) — a straight port
of `grain/automation/github.py`'s `GitHubClient`: every method (list/get/
close/reopen an issue, add/remove a label, branch existence and its head
commit, create/find a pull request, `default_branch`, review comments,
check runs, the plain comment thread, `create_comment`, and
`create_review`'s always-draft PR review) behind the same `Transport`
seam the Python version uses, so `github_test.go` proves the same path
building, pagination, and status handling against `FakeTransport` a unit
test would. (A `DryRunClient` wrapper -- reads pass through, mutations
print -- backed the CLI's and UI's `-dry-run` flags until those stopped
talking to GitHub at all; it has since been deleted.) `pkg/github/githubsim/`
is the "replicate v1's simulator" half: a port of
`tests/test_live_issue_to_pr.py`'s `RealGitHubMock` as a stateful
`github.Transport`, so a live end-to-end test gets the same trick that
file's own docstring describes — every real `GitHubClient` behaviour
(path building, JSON field extraction) still runs, with only the network
call underneath swapped for an in-memory stand-in — and `BranchExists`
answers from a real bare git repo via `git show-ref` rather than its own
bookkeeping, since that check is the one a live test can't afford to
fake. `pkg/orchestrator` decides when to call any of it: it dispatches a
task through `dispatch.Cycle`, opens or reuses a pull request once a run
pushes, and closes one out once GitHub reports it merged or closed. Its
`live_test.go` drives the same two scenarios
`tests/e2e/e2e_test.go` already proved by hand (a push that becomes a
merged, closed PR; a question that parks a task and a reply that
resumes it) through
`orchestrator.RunCycle` and a real `github.Client` against `githubsim`
instead — starting, since the inversion, from a task filed through
`pkg/ui.Client` the way a person at the CLI files one. This absorbed a second, independently-built
package that once did a narrower version of the same job — see "What this
does not have yet" below.

The capability provider contract exists now too (`pkg/model/capability.go`),
though nothing here ported it — `docs/data-model.md`'s design was never
built in v1 either. `CapabilityProvider`'s four methods — `Resolve`,
`Materialize`, `PromptSection`, `Revoke` — plus `Placement`, the
vocabulary a provider returns rather than performs so material moves
declaratively and never through a shell or a prompt. A provider here is
handed no Runner at all, unlike the Python contract `docs/data-model.md`
describes — v2 has no host adapter yet for one to run commands against,
so starting from the declarative-only half of that design (the half a
containerised provider is restricted to) costs nothing now and stays
correct once a Runner exists. `ResolveGrants`, `MaterializeGrants` and
`PromptSections` walk a task's `Grant`s against a `CapabilityRegistry`
in registration order, honouring `docs/data-model.md`'s rule that a
half-materialized capability is never described to the agent as
present.

`capability/geminikey/` is now a real `MINT` provider
(bwsalmon/agents#239), porting `grain/automation/gemini_keys.py`'s
`gemini-key` capability: it mints a Gemini API key scoped to the
Generative Language API, places it at `/home/debian/.gemini-api-key`,
and revokes it, calling the API Keys API directly through its Go client
library rather than shelling out to `gcloud` the way the Python version
has to — one of the two things `google.golang.org/api` was expected to
correct, per "Two things the port corrected" above. `Reap` (and
`DeleteExpired` beneath it) is the "clean up after 24 hours if leaked"
safety net, mirroring `delete_expired_keys`.

`gcpkey.Provider` (`pkg/capability/gcpkey/`) is now a real `MINT` provider too —
`gcp-key`, ported from `grain/automation/gcp_keys.py` but talking to the
IAM API directly rather than shelling to `gcloud`, and authenticated
through `CapabilityContext.Credentials` rather than a Runner, so it needed
no controller of its own to build. `model.Reaper` (`pkg/model/capability.go`)
is new alongside it: an optional interface for a provider whose minted
resource can outlive the `Lease` that recorded it, matching
`docs/data-model.md`'s description of `gcp_keys.py`'s own
`delete_expired_keys` as a backstop independent of any task record —
`gcpkey.Provider.Reap` implements it by asking GCP's own key listing for
the answer, not grain's store. `geminikey.Capability.Reap` plays the same
backstop role for Gemini keys, and is a `model.Reaper` too as of
grain/task-140 — it was a free function (`DeleteExpired`, still there for
a caller-chosen cutoff) that no binary called until then, which meant a
Gemini key minted for a run whose controller died between the mint and
the store write was never deleted by anything: `revokeAll` covers only
the leases grain still has a record of, and a lost record is precisely
what the backstop exists for.

Its one asymmetry with `gcpkey.Provider.Reap` is worth an operator
knowing: an API key carries no service account of its own for a
`ListKeys` call to scope to, so the sweep is **project-wide** and the
`grain-` display-name prefix is all that separates grain's keys from
anyone else's. Two grain deployments minting into one GCP project reap
each other's *leaked* keys — never each other's live ones (nothing under
24 hours old is touched) and never either daemon's own operating key
(`geminikey.OperatingKeyDisplayName`, exempted by exact name). Give each
deployment its own GCP project if that matters, the same way deployments
that must not reap each other's VMs get separate `-granule-state-dir`
values.

Both providers can now point at the same standing credential —
`geminikey.Capability.Credential` and `gcpkey.Provider.Config.
MinterCredential` are each just a name resolved through
`CapabilityContext.Credentials`, so an operator wires them to the same
one to get bwsalmon/agents#239's "This can share the same account from
the gcp capability" — the daemon is now the executor that does that
wiring (`-gcp-project`/`-gcp-agent-service-account`, bwsalmon/agents#254,
now driving `pkg/orchestrator.RunDispatch` rather than the original
`pkg/orchestrate` package it shipped against, per bwsalmon/agents#263):
it constructs a real `CapabilityContext` per dispatch, applies every
`SideSandbox` `Placement` under the dispatch's sandbox root, and calls
`Revoke` once the run finishes. `Reap` is called too, now: `cmd/grain`'s
`reapCapabilities` sweeps every registered provider implementing
`model.Reaper` once an hour from the same reconcile loop, which is what
makes "clean up after 24 hours if leaked" hold within roughly that bound
rather than "eventually" — a standalone sweep independent of any one
dispatch, matching `gcp_keys.py`'s own `delete_expired_keys` cron job,
just on grain's own timer rather than cron's.

`CapabilityContext.Credentials` (`model.CredentialResolver`) had no
production implementation until `pkg/secrets/`: a `Store` reading a
directory shaped like a Kubernetes Secret volume mount, so
`gcp-key`'s minter credential (and any future capability's) resolves
against real material rather than only the fakes `gcpkey_test.go` and
`model/capability_test.go` supply. `CapabilitySpec` grew a `Requires`
field alongside it -- the names, never the values, a capability
resolves through that resolver -- which `gcpkey.Provider.Spec()` and
`geminikey.Capability.Spec()` both set now, and which
`docs/data-model.md`'s new "secret store is a folder, not a table"
section is the checked-in listing of, per capability.

`agent/antigravity` can run an agent end to end against `mcp/`'s tools today,
and the daemon now calls it for real from `pkg/orchestrator`'s dispatch
loop rather than only from a test — `orchestrator.HostSandboxes` is the
only other thing `dispatch.Cycle`'s own dispatch path drives, and
neither
hands it more than a local directory to confine itself to yet
(`mcp.ConfigureGitCredentials` sets that directory's git credentials up
the same way v1's `configure_git_credentials` sets a real sandbox's up,
once per slot at daemon startup). The `mcpserver` subcommand itself can
now be pointed at a real remote VM instead — `-granule-vm` resolves a
bwsalmon/granule-managed VM's SSH endpoint (`pkg/granule`: the external port
granule persisted at `granule vm create` time, plus the pod IP that port
answers on, asked of containerd via `crictl` since granule has no
apiserver to have recorded it anywhere itself), `mcp.NewSSHSandboxTools`
runs the same four tools — `run_command`/`read_file`/`edit_file`/
`write_file` — against it instead of a local directory (`grain mcpserver`
can already be pointed at one by hand via `-granule-vm`,
bwsalmon/agents#256), and `orchestrator.GranuleSandboxes`
(bwsalmon/agents#262) is `Deps.Sandboxes`' real alternative to
`HostSandboxes`: one granule VM per dispatch slot, created via
`granule.Create` on first use and reused across cycles the same way
`HostSandboxes` reuses its directories, torn down by nothing here (see
that type's own doc comment). A granule VM's own image is still expected to
arrive already carrying the operator's SSH key and a running sshd, the
same assumption v1's sandbox image build stood in for — `../scripts/granule/`
is now that successor (bwsalmon/agents#267): a Packer template producing
a qcow2 pre-baked with the operator's SSH key, a running sshd, and the
same package list `provision/sandbox.sh` gives v1's own sandbox base —
see that directory's README.md for why the key and sshd are baked in at
build time rather than injected per-VM the way `LibvirtAdapter.create()`
does it for v1, and for what's still unresolved there (the exact `granule
vm create` flag a deployment's own `GranuleConfig.CreateArgs` above would
pass the built image's location through as, owned by bwsalmon/granule's
own CLI and still not confirmed from this repo — bwsalmon/agents#274).
The daemon still defaults `Deps.Sandboxes` to `HostSandboxes`, but
`-granule-sandboxes` (and the rest of its `-granule-*`/
`-cri-runtime-endpoint` flags, see "What this does not have yet" above)
now opts a real deployment into `GranuleSandboxes` instead — the flag that
picks the image lives in `-granule-create-arg`, repeated once per
`granule vm create` flag/value pair a deployment's own `granule vm create
-h` calls for, rather than a name this repo guesses at.

A real `github.RESTClient` exists and is wired into the daemon too, driving
every call `pkg/orchestrator` makes (issue listing/labelling, branch and
pull-request state, check runs, comments) — but not the agent's own
`ask_question`/`request_secret`/`comment_on_issue`/`propose_task`/
`add_review_comment`
calls: a run's own MCP server still wires those to a `mcp.MockSink` it
builds and discards internally on every call, so nothing happens at the
moment the agent makes one. `ProcessResult` only sees them after the
fact, through the `agent.Result` `Run` returns, not while the run is
live — and then relays a question, a secret request, a closing comment
and a proposal into the store for real, and a review comment onto the
pull request under review (or, failing one, into the task's own
conversation). Giving
`Framework.Run` (or its caller) a way to inject a real sink, so the
effect could happen while the run is still going, is still open.

`tests/e2e/` is that whole chain driven by hand, in a test, rather than
by `dispatch.Cycle` itself: it calls `dispatch.Cycle` to decide what runs,
then
drives `agent/antigravity` (scripted in most tests; the real `agy`
binary in `live_test.go`, gated on `GEMINI_API_KEY` and an installed
`agy`) through a sandbox-stand-in
directory against a real `gitproxy` in front of a local git server, and
plays the part of "the PR opened," "the PR merged" and "a human replied"
with the same `store.Observe` calls a real GitHub-sync component would
make. It proves the pieces already built compose correctly; it does not
close the gap above, since nothing there is wired to run on its own yet.

`self-debug` and `self-repair` (bwsalmon/agents#540, "configuration
mode") went from `ui.OfferedCapabilities` names with nothing behind them
to real `model.CapabilityProvider`s -- `pkg/capability/selfdebug` and
`pkg/capability/selfrepair` -- but what each one grants is not material
in a sandbox or text in a prompt, `model.CapabilityProvider`'s only two
channels; it is tools. `orchestrator.Config.GrantTools` is the new,
narrow seam that adds: a capability name to a function building extra
`mcp.Tool`s, consulted by `runOne` only for an `Interactive` task, and
kept as a caller-supplied map rather than a fifth `CapabilityProvider`
method on purpose, so `model/capability.go`'s own "a provider is handed
no Runner" stays true of the package itself even though a deployment can
now wire one in from outside it. `selfdebug.SourceTools` is read-only --
`read_grain_source`/`list_grain_source`, confined to whatever directory
a deployment's `-upgrade-src-dir` already names, needing no confirmation
of any kind, since nothing it exposes can change anything.
`selfrepair.HostCommandTools`' `run_host_command` is the opposite: it
runs a shell command directly against the same host `grain daemon`
itself runs on -- no sandbox, no adapter, the real machine -- so every
call posts the command into the task's own chat and blocks
(`selfrepair.Confirm`, polling `Store.Comments`) until a human replies
there with approve or deny, or a timeout refuses it for them. That block
is a real synchronous wait inside one tool call, unlike every other
human-in-the-loop primitive here (`ask_question` parks the whole run and
picks a reply up on the next dispatch) -- it only works if the tools run
in the same OS process as the store the reply lands on.

**Nothing satisfies that any more.** It held while the default framework
was the home-grown in-process Gemini runtime, which registered a run's
tools in-process and so already held that `*model.Store` connection.
Every framework that remains (`agent/antigravity`, `agent/claude`,
`agent/codex`) forks a CLI that manages its own MCP connection and
ignores `RunConfig.Tools` entirely, because there is no in-process
registry to hand a forked process. `Config.GrantTools` still assembles these tools and
`RunDispatch` still passes them, but no `Framework` consumes them, so
`selfrepair`'s host tool reaches no running agent today.

`self-debug` and `bootstrap-playbooks` are the halves that no longer
depend on any of that, because everything they offer is read-only and so
needs no route back into a live run's own conversation. `grain mcpserver`
takes `-grant <name>`, once per grant, and a `Framework` passes one pair
for each grant on the run's own task — `RunDispatch` reads them off the
task's `Grants` into `agent.RunConfig.Grants`, and `agent.GrantArgs` is
the one translation from "what this run may do" to "what that process is
told", shared by all three frameworks the way `RunDeadlineArgs` already
is. A repeated name rather than a flag per capability deliberately: which
tools a name turns on is `mcpserver`'s business alone, so a fourth
capability wanting this treatment is a name at either end and no new flag,
no new field and no framework change in between.

`-grant bootstrap-playbooks` is the simpler of the two: `bootstrap.
PlaybookTools`' `list_bootstrap_playbooks` and `read_bootstrap_playbook`
read markdown runbooks embedded in the grain binary itself, so the
subprocess is already holding everything they serve and needs no hop of
any kind. That matters because `Config.GrantTools` was the only thing
assembling them until this flag existed, and no CLI-driving `Framework`
consumes that map — a task granted `bootstrap-playbooks` was told about
tools that were on no run's roster.

`-grant self-debug` turns on `selfdebug.SourceTools`'
`read_grain_source`/`list_grain_source`, which answer what grain is
*built* to do. They refuse politely rather than disappearing when a
deployment has no source checkout (`-grain-src-dir` unset), so a run's
tool roster is a property of the grants it holds rather than of one
deployment's configuration.

#### grain-src/: the baked-in copy, never a clone

A self-debug run's `grain-src/` is the same tree those tools read: the
deployment's baked-in copy of its own source (the image's
`/usr/local/share/grain/src`, the host-mode copy installed beside the
binary, or `-upgrade-src-dir`). `orchestrator.placeGrainSource` puts it
in the sandbox read-only by the cheapest route the backend has: a
symlink in a host directory when this process cannot write the tree,
an extracted copy in a host directory otherwise, and a gzipped archive
(built once per process and revision) streamed into a container,
granule VM or pod. Nothing clones bwsalmon/grain and the git proxy
grants self-debug no read of it, so `self-debug` implies no repository
(`model.CapabilityRepos`) and a local policy never refuses it over
grain. A deployment with no baked copy runs the task anyway, without
`grain-src/`, and the prompt says why.

The copy carries a shallow `.git` when the build baked one
(`scripts/export-source.sh`, `GRAIN_SOURCE_HISTORY_DEPTH`, the
Dockerfile's `SOURCE_HISTORY_DEPTH` build arg): the newest N commits by
date with every object of each, HEAD detached at the build revision, no
other refs, no hooks or reflog, and a config written from scratch whose
`origin` can be neither fetched nor pushed. The `.git` of a tree is
placed only when it carries the `grain-baked-history` marker that script
writes, so an operator's own checkout never hands its `.git` to a
sandbox. Host-mode installs that stage their own checkout
(`GRAIN_HOST_SOURCE_DIR`) get 500 commits of it by default; those that
copy the image's tree get whatever the image baked. Because history
ships in every published image, deleted files included, an image build
that bakes any runs gitleaks over exactly that history and fails on a
finding (`GRAIN_SOURCE_SECRET_SCAN=require`). The image default is 0
until the findings over the 500-commit window are signed off (task
4337).

#### A checkout that is there and cannot be read

Those two tools answered `permission denied` for every path below the
checkout's root for days at a time, twice (grain/task-160,
grain/task-250): `list_grain_source` with no path listed the top level,
and everything under it failed. The cause is one shape repeated in three
places. Each path that stages that tree creates its *root* itself, with a
mode of its own — `scripts/export-source.sh`'s `mkdir -p`, `setup.sh`'s
`install -d -m0755` — and then fills it with content whose modes come
from somewhere else: a `git ls-files` tar that copies each file's mode out
of the build host's checkout verbatim, the `cp -a` fallback that brings
the directories' modes too (and which the release build takes routinely,
since git inside a build container often refuses the `.git` the context
copies in — `scripts/buildvcs.sh`'s own list), and the `docker cp` host
mode re-runs on every daemon start. So the root lists and nothing in it
opens.

It is worth stating why nobody saw it. The account that reads that tree is
never the one that staged it — container mode is a `docker run --user
<host uid>:<gid>` against an image whose files belong to root, host mode
is the unprivileged service account reading a tree root installed — so
the tree has to be *world*-readable, and every check anyone had written
asked whether the path existed, as root, which ignores the mode bits
entirely. `test -f <root>/go.mod` passed throughout.

Both halves are now explicit. The staging sets modes rather than
inheriting them (directories 0755, files 0644, keeping the exec bit git
records) and `export-source.sh` fails the build over a path an
unprivileged account could not use; the checks ask as that account and
below the root, and sweep the tree with `find -readable`/`-executable`
rather than naming one file, since the failure mode is "one level down,
everything". `selfdebug.CheckSourceReadable` is that question as Go —
read the root, then one directory below it — and the daemon logs it at
startup, because the alternative is finding out from an agent's tool call
weeks later. A permission error from either tool now reports the
*checkout* rather than the path: an errno per path reads as a path that is
not there, so a run tries another, and another, and concludes the file it
wanted is gone rather than that its capability is broken.

### Reading the journal the check is asked about

`-grant grain-log` (`pkg/capability/grainlog`) turns on one more
read-only tool, `read_grain_log`, which returns a bounded slice of this
host's own systemd journal through `pkg/systemlog` — the same source the
UI's System pane already serves.

It exists because of a failure that actually happened. grain files a
check task after every self-upgrade (`orchestrator.reconcileUpgradeCheck`),
and the first one this deployment ran was asked whether anything in the
daemon's log was new since the upgrade. The run could not read the log,
so it answered out of the state repository dump — evidence *about* the
log rather than the log — and reported clean. A panic a reconciler
recovers from, or an error repeating every tick without stopping
anything, leaves no trace in that dump. The question was taken out of the
check's body rather than left unanswerable; this is what puts it back,
naming the tool that answers it.

**It is its own capability, not part of `self-debug`.** "Read the source
this host runs" and "read everything anything on this host has ever
logged" are different things to hand an agent: the journal carries
whatever the daemon and every agent wrote to it, including material
quoted into error messages and other tasks' text. Folding it into
`self-debug` would have widened every existing `self-debug` task
silently. The upgrade check holds both grants; every other `self-debug`
task keeps only the source.

What a run reads leaves the host twice over — into a model's context, and
into a sandbox whose outbound network is *not* restricted (sandboxes here
are isolated from the host, not from the internet). Network isolation is
not the containment story, so three other things are:

- **Redaction on the host, in the `mcpserver` process, before the answer
  is built.** Known values, read from grain's own secret store and the
  git proxy's credential ladder (`-grain-secrets-dir`, passed by
  `agent.GrantArgs` beside its own grant the way `-grain-src-dir` is
  beside `self-debug`'s), catch a secret with no particular shape — a
  webhook secret, a pasted password. Patterns catch what this host cannot
  enumerate: `Authorization:` headers, bearer tokens, `ghp_`/
  `github_pat_`/`ghs_` and API-key prefixes, JWTs, credentials in a URL's
  userinfo, PEM headers. Doing this in the sandbox would be theatre —
  material redacted there has already arrived. A process that cannot
  build that list refuses every call rather than serving a journal it
  could not clean: an unread journal costs a run one answer, an
  unredacted one cannot be recalled.
- **A fixed surface.** The logs readable are an allowlist of two
  (`grain-daemon.service` and `dmesg`); every bound is a typed parameter
  — RFC3339 times, a priority off journald's own list, a line cap, a
  plain case-insensitive substring matched on the host rather than handed
  to journalctl's regex engine; and `systemlog.Query.args` is the only
  thing that composes journalctl's arguments, so no caller-supplied
  string reaches its argument surface. No shell anywhere near it.
- **Loud truncation, and an audit line per call.** Every cap reports
  itself, above the lines rather than after them, because a cap that
  silently drops the rest reproduces the exact false clean this exists to
  fix — a run that saw two hundred lines of a window holding thousands
  and could not tell that from a window holding two hundred. An empty
  answer says outright that it *is* an answer. And each call writes the
  task, the parameters and the line count to the `mcpserver`'s stderr,
  which the daemon collects into the very journal being read.

An excerpt in the check task's body was the cheaper alternative and was
rejected on the window: the question is "anything new *since this
upgrade*", which is `[upgrade, when the check runs]`, and a body is built
at filing time (`fileUpgradeCheck` stores `upgradeCheckBody`'s string on
the task), so an excerpt would cover `[upgrade, filing]` — close to empty
for a check filed at upgrade — and answer the question with a snapshot
taken before anything had happened. It also cannot be followed up: seeing
one panic, the next thing you want is the surrounding lines and whether
it repeats.

The other half of that question — what this deployment actually *did* —
used to be four more tools on the same grant (`mcp.NewTaskTools`'
`list_grain_tasks`, `read_grain_task`, `read_grain_task_prompt` and
`read_grain_task_transcript`, reading another task's record, its
attempts, the prompt its agent was really handed and its session
transcript through `cmd/grain/mcpserver.go`'s `daemonTasks` over the
daemon's REST API). They are gone, and the state repository is why: the
rows they rendered are files in it now (`tables/task.json`,
`tables/task_comment.json`, `tables/task_run.json`, prompts and
transcripts included — see "The store is a git repository again"), so a
task that needs to read what this deployment did is given read access to
that repository, and reads it with `read_file` and `run_command` like
any other checkout. Four tools, a `TaskReader` interface, an adapter in
`cmd/grain` and two `ui.HTTPClient` methods, all to render what a clone
already hands over. What that trades away is freshness: `task_run` is a
churn-tier table (below), so an attempt's transcript reaches the
repository on `ChurnInterval` rather than immediately, and a
still-running attempt's transcript-in-progress — which the daemon did
serve, from `Config.LiveTranscripts` — is not in a clone at all.

Those four tools are back, and the same trade is why. The export stopped
holding the rows: `staterepo.ExportConfig` writes the settings tables and
the two memory ones and deletes every other file under `tables/`, so
`task`, `task_run`, `task_comment` and `task_observation` are in SQLite
on the server and nowhere else until a backup mechanism of its own
exists. `cmd/grain/mcpserver.go` registers `mcp.NewTaskTools` for a run
holding `self-debug` again, and the state repository answers the other
question — what this deployment is configured to do, and what its memory
says. Prompts that had learned to send a run to `tables/task.json`
outlived the change by a few days and cost the runs that believed them a
clone and a directory listing each; the memory agent's body, the
director's, the upgrade check's and `stateRepoSection` all say the split
out loud now, and `pkg/model/staterepo_prompt_test.go` is what keeps them
saying it.

What a task record did not say, until `grain/task-212`, was anything the
merge queue had written about it: `Observation.MergeQueueState`, its
note, `MergeQueueStateAt`, `MergeQueueBlockedAt`, and the task's own
activity line. Those are the fields an operator asks about most — three
rounds of the same conversation in two days, one of which ("which tasks
are showing *can't read the pull request*?") could not be answered at
all, and one of which was answered only because the operator pasted the
words "behind task 149" back into the chat. The task's *state* does not
cover it: a change sits at `completed` for the whole of its journey
through the queue, and every wait that matters after the run is over is
in those columns. So `read_grain_task` renders them, in
`ui/src/state.js`'s own `MERGE_QUEUE_PHRASES` wording with the raw state
beside it — an agent and the operator reading their screen describe the
same row in the same words, and the raw name is what the logs are
written in. The section is absent, not empty, for a task the queue never
drove, which is nearly every task there is. Two deliberate divergences
from the browser: a state this build has no phrase for is printed by its
raw name rather than dropped (silence reads as "the queue is doing
nothing", which is the one wrong answer here), and a merge-queue
observation that outlived its pull request is still reported on a closed
task, with a sentence saying that the row itself shows none of it — the
record is evidence, and an agent quoting "Merging" about a row showing
nothing is the confusion this section is meant to end. The queue's note is
cut at `maxMergeQueueNoteBytes` with the cut stated, so one long field
near the top cannot push the attempts and the conversation out of the
head of a capped answer.

`list_grain_tasks` carries the state and nothing else of it — not the
note, not the age. "Which rows are stuck?" is asked of the whole lane at
once and was costing one `read_grain_task` per row; a phrase of a few
words on the handful of tasks the queue is actually driving answers it.
The note and the age answer the *next* question, which is about one row,
and belong where the reader has already chosen which task they are
asking about.

### Reading this deployment's own census

Those five tools are five because `read_grain_metrics` joined them
(`grain/task-237`). The record they render is what happened to one task;
the question grain kept dispatching work about is *how often* — "re-size
`mcp.maxToolResultBytes` from the tool-use census" was one such task, and
it had no way to read a census even in principle. `grain metrics` is a
client command against `GET /api/metrics` and a sandbox holds a git
credential and nothing else: no deployment address, no token, so building
the CLI from the checkout buys nothing. Nothing else in the roster
reported telemetry either. What was left was an operator pasting a report
into the task conversation before dispatch — which works, once, at
whatever window they chose, with no way to ask a second question of it.

The tool is the same report, behind the same grant, read-only like the
rest of it: every number in it is already on a page anyone with the UI
open can read, so the gate stays the grant a human attached rather than a
confirmation per call. It takes the question the endpoint takes — a
window, or an absolute `since`/`until` span, and a `repo`/`author` scope —
plus one argument the endpoint has no need of: `section`, one of the
report's ten parts (`mcp.MetricsSections`). A page of tables is more than
a tool result can carry whole, and "what does the census say" is nearly
always the question rather than "print everything", so `section: "tools"`
is the narrow call and the whole report is the wide one. The window and
the scope print above whichever section is asked for: a census quoted
without them is a number waiting to be attached to the wrong question.

The renderer is the CLI's, not a second one. `cmd/grain/metrics.go`'s
printer now writes to an `io.Writer` and is split into named sections
(`metricsSections`), `printer.metrics` passes `os.Stdout` and no section,
and `mcpserver.go`'s `daemonMetrics` asks the daemon over the same
`ui.HTTPClient` the task readers use and renders the answer into a
string. That direction is forced as well as cheap: `pkg/ui` owns the
report shape and imports `pkg/mcp` by way of `pkg/capability/selfdebug`,
so `pkg/mcp` can hold the *question* and an interface, and the rendering
has to happen in the one process that imports both. It is also why
`MetricsQuery`'s span fields are the words the caller wrote rather than
parsed values — `daemonMetrics` builds its request through the same
`metricsRequest` as `cmdMetrics`, so a window nobody can parse is refused
with the sentence an operator would have got. `cmd/grain`'s tests hold
`metricsSections` and `mcp.MetricsSections` to each other, since a
section on one side only is either a name that renders nothing or a table
no tool can ask for.

`Tool.ElisionAdvice` names the two questions that actually shorten a
report — one section, or a narrower window — rather than the generic
"call it again for less", which a report cannot act on: its length is ten
tables, not one long string.

Closing `selfrepair`'s own gap — a tool that blocks mid-call on a human's
reply in the task's chat — means giving the `mcpserver` subcommand a
route back to the store, which is a design question rather than a missing flag: the
isolation that makes the subprocess frameworks safe is exactly that it
holds no store handle. What it does hold is deliberately narrow and
deliberately not that: a read-only GitHub client scoped to one branch
and the branch it merges into
(`-data-dir`/`-pr-repo`/`-pr-branch`/`-pr-base`, for
`pull_request_status` and `base_branch_status` -- see "Letting a run
watch its own CI" and "Telling whose failure it is", below), and a REST
client of the daemon aimed at one endpoint about one task id
(`-server`/`-task`, for `open_pull_request` -- see "A run can open its
own pull request"). Neither is a store handle, and neither can answer
`selfrepair.Confirm`'s blocking read of `Store.Comments`.

bwsalmon/agents#621 once turned that pair of capabilities into an
explicit "configuration agent": an overlay button the frontend kept
reachable in the bottom-right corner of the screen, which filed a task
with nothing but `{"configuration": true}` and opened its chat the moment
it existed. One field on the task (`model.Task.Configuration`, a column
of its own) expanded server-side into `Interactive` forced true, the
`self-debug`/`self-repair`/`bootstrap-playbooks` grants, a default title
and a prompt about helping with a problem, a question or grain's own
configuration -- and `dispatch.Cycle` started every such task
unconditionally, ahead of the capacity-gated loop, so it could get a
sandbox even at the worker limit.

**It is gone.** What it was for was changing this deployment's
configuration, and configuration is not something to change by talking to
a chat agent about it any more: it is the state repository (see "The
store is a git repository again"). Settings, repo configuration, prompt
extensions, schedules and suites are files an ordinary task can be
dispatched at, edit, and open a pull request against, reviewed and merged
like any other change, with `grain state check` validating it before it
lands. A one-click chat that could reach into the running deployment
instead was a second, unreviewed way to do the same thing.

Nothing it was built out of goes with it. `self-debug`, `self-repair` and
`bootstrap-playbooks` are still capabilities, still grantable from the
new-task form or a deployment's defaults, and still reach a run the same
way (`grain mcpserver -grant <name>`) -- what is removed is the bundle,
the button, the field, the column and the exemption from the concurrency
limit, not the tools. A deployment that wants what the button offered
files an interactive task and ticks those grants, which is what the
button was assembling for it. Removing the special dispatch path costs
nothing that the state repository does not already answer: an interactive
task filed to debug a saturated deployment waits its turn like everything
else, and a deployment saturated badly enough for that to matter has a
`MaxWorkers` a person can raise -- through the state repository, or
through Settings.

## The agent runtime is a CLI now, not our own turn loop

grain used to drive the model itself. `pkg/agent/gemini` held a
hand-written turn loop: call the Gemini API's function calling, translate
each `mcp.ToolInfo` into a `genai.FunctionDeclaration`, execute whatever
`FunctionCall` came back against an in-process `pkg/mcp` registry, append
the results, go round again. It worked, and it was ours to maintain --
the schema translation, the turn accounting, the thought/text split, the
partial-result-on-failure rule, all of it code in this repo tracking an
API that moves.

`pkg/agent/antigravity` replaces it with Google's Antigravity CLI, the
`agy` binary that replaced Gemini CLI. The loop is agy's now. What is
left here is the shape `pkg/agent/claude` already settled on for driving
a real CLI: build the arguments, hand it a prompt, parse the transcript
it streams back -- the shape `pkg/agent/codex` follows too. Every
framework a deployment can pick between is a subprocess driver now, and
`agent.Framework` is the seam that makes them interchangeable.

**Debugging a generic AGY failure.** Open the failed task and click its
attempt to read the transcript. Grain now passes `--log-file` to each AGY
exec and appends an **AGY exec N diagnostics** section when that exec
fails, including failures with no stdout. This captures provider errors
that AGY replaces with “Agent execution terminated due to error.” in its
JSON stream. No deployment setting or debug flag is needed.

The excerpt contains at most 40 complete glog records and 16 KiB of log
text, selected from the final 64 KiB of that exec's log. Known AGY API
credentials (including URL/JSON encodings) and recognized credential
shapes are redacted before the excerpt reaches either the live transcript
or the stored transcript. Unprefixed continuation lines are omitted;
unrecognized, arbitrary secrets are not guaranteed to be recognized.
Raw log files are private (0600), live only in that run's temporary HOME,
and are deleted with it. Each retry gets a separate file; successful
execs add no diagnostics. This is diagnostic capture, not a change to
quota/capacity classification or retry policy.

**A generic AGY failure is now resumed before it is reported.** The two
endings a failed agy dispatch usually has -- `model turn exceeded 1m40s`,
grain's own deadline cancelling a turn that went quiet, and `run ended in
status ERROR: Agent execution terminated due to error.`, agy's
all-purpose sentence for a run it could not finish -- are neither of them
a verdict on the task, and both used to end the dispatch on the spot. The
task came back around minutes later in a *fresh* sandbox with an empty
conversation, having thrown away every model turn and every uncommitted
file of the attempt before it. `Framework.Run` now execs agy again
instead, on the same conversation in the same sandbox, with a turn that
says it was interrupted rather than that the task should start over
(`agent.InterruptedPrompt`). The bounds are the ones a capacity refusal
already had and are shared with it: two extra execs per run, 30 then 60
seconds of backoff, nothing once the run's own deadline is inside
`agent.MinimumRetryRuntime`. A turn cap that tripped, a quota refusal,
and agy's `FAILURE` status -- the one a classified provider refusal
arrives under, and so the one that might be a real verdict -- are
terminal as before, as is any interruption with no conversation to
resume -- or one agy will not accept `--conversation` for, which costs a
single exec that spends no model turn and then the ending the run would
have had anyway. `pkg/agent/antigravity/resume.go` carries the argument;
`agent/retry.go` carries the policy the three frameworks share, and
antigravity is so far the only one that resumes more than a refusal.

Four things about agy shaped the port, none of them cosmetic.

**It has no `--mcp-config`.** agy registers MCP servers per *user* --
`agy mcp add` writes them into `~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json`, and
caches each server's tool manifests under
`~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/mcp/<server>/`. A per-user
registration cannot express what grain needs, which is a per-*run*
binding: two runs dispatched concurrently against two different sandboxes
would share one registration, and whichever wrote it last would decide
where both runs' tools landed. So `Framework.Run` gives each run its own
private `HOME` -- a temp directory holding nothing but the config file
naming that run's own `mcpserver` server, and the settings file
authentication needs (below) -- and deletes it as the run returns. That has the same effect `claude`'s `--strict-mcp-config` has
there: the only MCP server a run can see is its own, because there is no
other config file in the `HOME` it was given to find one in.

**It caps a single MCP tool call, and has no `MCP_TOOL_TIMEOUT`.** agy
abandons a tool call after three minutes when nothing says otherwise;
the knob is a `timeoutSeconds` key on the server's own entry in that
same config file, where a positive value is seconds and a negative one
means no cap at all. Three minutes is far short of `wait_for_checks`,
which blocks for as long as CI takes, up to
`mcp.MaxWaitForChecksTimeout` (an hour) -- so a run that deliberately
asked to wait out a slow build would have the call killed under it and
be told the tool failed, which is neither true nor useful. `Run` writes
the key out past `mcp.MaxBlockingToolWait` -- that maximum, or a `chat`
turn's, whichever is longer -- for the reason `agent/claude` raises
`MCP_TOOL_TIMEOUT`: the deadline that ends the wait should be grain's,
whose expiry produces a report, not the CLI's, whose expiry produces a
tool failure.

**It has no `--max-turns`.** `RunConfig.MaxTurns` is therefore enforced
here rather than by the binary, and enforced on the live stream rather
than on the finished capture -- a cap applied after the process exits
would report a runaway run without ever having stopped one. A small
`io.Writer` spliced into agy's stdout counts completed `agent_response`
steps as they stream past and cancels the run's context at the cap;
`procgroup.Prepare` is what turns that into a kill of agy *and* its MCP
child rather than an orphan.

**It has no way to empty its native tool roster.** `claude` takes
`--tools ''`, which is how `agent/claude` guarantees a run reaches the
sandbox only through grain's own MCP tools, and `codex` gets no local
execution environment (see [Codex isolation](codex-isolation.md)). agy takes neither,
so a run always sees agy's `run_command`, `view_file`, `write_to_file` and
the rest beside grain's, and those execute wherever agy does -- on the
controller. Three things stand in for the switch. The private `HOME` holds
exactly one MCP server, so grain's tools are the only MCP tools there are.
They are registered eagerly, so the model sees them rather than having to
go looking. And the run's prompt opens by naming *both* rosters: which
`mcp_grain-sandbox_*` tools reach the sandbox, which of agy's own to treat
as unavailable, and the fact that the two rosters share names -- so a
model reaching for "run\_command" picks a tool by its prefix rather than by
its verb, which is the mistake the bare rule ("use grain's tools") leaves
available. `verifyToolRoster` then notes, on the run itself, a roster with
no route to grain at all. And a fourth thing does more than stand in for
the switch: a `PreToolUse` hook refuses the call outright, which a live
model has been watched running into (the next-but-one paragraph). A
