comparisons, `multiple` making it a set, an enum's options being both
its vocabulary and its rank, and every custom attribute able to be
empty. The declarations already ride on `GET /api/config`, which
`HTTPClient.CustomFields` reads, and it is read *only* when the command
line names an attribute the built-ins do not have: an ordinary listing
costs no extra round trip, and a name nothing declares is refused with
the attributes this deployment really has rather than with the built-in
list alone. `grain list -h` prints the same declarations under a heading
of their own, since a terminal has nowhere else to find out that this
deployment has a `custom.priority`. The one comparison that had to
change on this side is the date: a field holds a calendar day, so a
value is read in the deployment's own zone, by filters and orders alike
— which is the reading the browser gives it, and the two have to agree
or a list is sorted into an order its own filter disputes.

**And the same tasks left out of it (grain/task-98).** The one thing the
two surfaces still disagreed about was what a listing is *about*: the
frontend hides closed and deferred tasks unless somebody asks for them
(`state.js`'s `HIDDEN_BY_DEFAULT`, and the deployment's own
`showClosedByDefault` behind the checkbox), while `grain list` printed
every row the API answered with -- so `grain defer`'s own help ("deferred
tasks are hidden from task lists until asked for") described a UI the CLI
did not share, and on a deployment with a year of history behind it most
of what the command printed was closed. It hides the same two states
now, by the same rule: naming a state is asking to see it (`-state
closed`, or the `state:any:closed` it stands for), `-closed`/`-deferred`
are the checkboxes as flags (tri-state, so `-closed=false` leaves them
out of a deployment that shows them by default), and with neither the
deployment's own setting decides -- one `GET /api/settings`, and only
when the answer is actually needed. What was left out is said on stderr
rather than left as an absence, so a listing stays a listing: `grain
list | wc -l` counts tasks and `-json` still emits JSON and nothing else.

**...and on the frontend they are a filter like any other
(grain/task-186).** The two checkboxes above -- "Show closed tasks",
"Show deferred tasks" -- were the last thing in the toolbar that was not
a condition. They sat at the end of the row a filter editor had just been
built for, with a branch of their own inside `TaskList`, a per-list
override no link could carry, and no chip anywhere saying what the list
was leaving out. So what a list was about was two questions asked in two
places, and the one the URL and the chips described was not the one doing
most of the hiding.

They are one ordinary condition now: `State is none of Deferred, Closed`,
which every task view opens narrowed by (`taskFilters.js`'s
`defaultFilters`, built from `state.js`'s `SET_ASIDE_STATES` and from
`showClosedByDefault`, which is still what decides whether the closed
half is in it). It is a chip like any other, editable in the same editor,
deletable in one click, and it combines with everything else rather than
sitting beside it -- "closed tasks in `acme/widgets` created this week"
is now one narrowing rather than a checkbox plus two conditions.
`TaskList` is left asking one question about state instead of two, and
the "(closed tasks are hidden)" footnote an empty list used to carry is
gone, because the chip above the list already says it.

Three consequences worth naming. A list nobody has narrowed still lives
at `/`, and the deployment decides what that means when it is opened --
but from the first change onwards the query says the whole of what the
list is narrowed by, that condition included, so a link reopens the list
it was copied from rather than one narrowed by whatever the default has
become since (and a link that leaves the condition out is a link asking
for a list without it). `Clear` puts the toolbar back to what the view
opened asking rather than to nothing at all, since clearing to nothing
would fill the list with closed tasks and leave no gesture for undoing
it; a saved board opens on its own stored question, and a board that
stores none opens on this same default (grain/task-309 below), which is
what `Clear` puts a dashboard back to. And the rail's state entries
re-answer the condition
rather than intersecting with it (`App.jsx`'s `selectStateFilter`):
picking "Closed" there takes any `State` condition out of the narrowing,
because a list narrowed to "none of Deferred, Closed" and then asked for
"Closed" would otherwise be empty -- which is exactly the exemption the
checkboxes used to need, now written once where the two questions meet.
Conditions on every other attribute survive it, so walking down the
states keeps the repo you were looking at.

**What a link written before that change now means (grain/task-260).**
It means what it says, and what it says has no condition about state in
it. `/?q=ci`, `/?repo=acme/widgets`, a bookmark, a URL pasted into a
task: each still opens the list it names -- `paths.js` reads the old
toolbar's spelling and always will -- but the narrowing it parses to
carries no `State` clause, and `App.jsx` takes `askedNarrowing ||
defaultNarrowing(config)`, so nothing puts one back. Such a link opens
showing closed and deferred tasks where the same link used to hide them.
That is the answer chosen, not merely the one that happened. The
alternative -- folding the default in whenever a parsed narrowing names
no state -- would make "this list, closed ones included" unsayable in a
link, since that list is spelt by *not* carrying the condition, and it
would leave one query string meaning two different things depending on
which build wrote it. What the reader gets instead is on screen and one
gesture wide: an old link opens with no `State` chip above the list,
which is the list saying what it is and is not narrowed by, and `Clear`
puts it back on the deployment's own default. `ui/src/taskFilters.test.js`
pins all three -- the list an old-spelling URL produces, the list a URL
narrowing nothing produces, and the list `Clear` produces from the first
-- so the next person through here changes this on purpose or not at all.

**What a board that says nothing means (grain/task-309).** The same
thing, read the same way, because it is the same query: a board's
`query` is the address bar's own encoding, and `boards.js`'s
`boardNarrowing` reads it with the address bar's own parser
(`paths.js`). So a board that names a question asks the whole of that
question, closed tasks and all -- a panel carrying `q=test` and the list
its "Open" link opens both find the same 88 tasks -- and a board that
names nothing has asked nothing, which the deployment's default answers
for, exactly as it answers for `/`.

It used to mean "every task", and that was the one place where a view
and the link out of it were narrowed by two different questions. A
dashboard's panels inherit what the dashboard is asking (`panels.js`'s
`panelNarrowing`), so on a deployment holding 929 tasks of which 918
were closed, a panel header counted 929, the eight rows under it were
eight tasks that had merged weeks before, the state counts put 918 "in
no column", and the "Open" link beside all of it opened a list of 11.
Both numbers were right for their own view, which is how fourteen unit
cases and two end-to-end specs passed over it: on demo data one task in
twelve is closed and there is nothing to see
(`docs/hand-runs/2026-09-07-panel-dashboard.md`, section 2).

Two of the five kinds of board take that default, and the other three
are not an exception to the rule but the rule itself: the default is the
answer for a view with no answer of its own about which tasks to leave
out. A list board and a dashboard have none. A Kanban board says which
states it is about in its columns -- the same thing the rail's state
entries say, and narrowing one away from a column it draws would leave
that column empty with nothing but a chip to explain it. A timeline is a
chart of when work happened, and most work that happened has finished. A
report is not a view of tasks at all: it counts every task whatever its
state, so the condition would change none of its numbers and only add a
"not in force" line under its heading. A *panel* of any of those kinds
does inherit the dashboard's question, since that is what a panel with
no query of its own is for and since every one of them links back to the
list.

The cost is the paragraph above's, in the same shape: "a dashboard of
every task, closed ones included" is no longer said by leaving the query
empty. It is said the way a link says it, by naming a question with no
state condition in it -- `sort=created:desc` is the shortest. Two
smaller consequences of a dashboard now opening narrowed: its toolbar's
`Clear` goes back to that default rather than to nothing at all, since
"nothing at all" is the one narrowing no link can carry and a panel's
"Open" would stop landing on what the panel shows; and "New board",
"Edit board" and "Add panel" carry the narrowing that has been *asked*
rather than the one in force, so a reader who has narrowed nothing does
not file a task asking for a panel narrowed to
`f=state:none:deferred|closed`.

`ui/src/App.tasks.test.jsx` and `ui/e2e/boards.spec.js` pin the
agreement rather than either number -- what a panel shows and counts,
against the rows in the list its own "Open" link opens, for a dashboard
that asks nothing and for a panel that asks its own question -- so the
two cannot drift apart again without a test saying so.

**A flag after the argument it belongs to (grain/task-98).** Every usage
line here is written the way people type these commands -- `grain update
<id> [flags]`, `grain repo capabilities [-set a,b] <owner/name>` -- and
`flag.FlagSet.Parse` stops at the first word that is not a flag, so the
first of those forms did nothing at all: the id ended the parse, `-title`
sat among the leftover arguments, `fs.Visit` saw no flag set, and the
command sent an empty request and printed the unchanged task as though it
had worked. Exit status 0, output that looks like an edit, no edit.
`grain repo capabilities acme/widgets -set self-debug` printed the repo's
capabilities instead of replacing them, the same way. `parseArgs`
(`cmd/grain/main.go`) is Parse again on what is left after each
positional word -- GNU-style permutation, without the dependency -- so a
flag counts wherever it is written, the arguments come back in the order
they were typed, and a bare `--` still ends the flags for a value that
starts with a dash. `grain comment <id> <body...>` deliberately keeps out
of it: its body is free text, and a body word that happens to name a flag
has to stay a body word, which is what `misplacedFlag` says out loud
instead of guessing.

The vocabulary itself is a Go table (`cmd/grain/taskattributes.go`)
mirroring `taskAttributes.js`, rather than one table in Go the frontend
reads off the API. Most of a descriptor is a *function* -- how to read
the attribute off a task, what to call a value, which glyph its menu row
wears -- and none of that crosses an API; what could be sent is the ids,
the types and the labels, which is the small half. And the frontend
narrows a list it already holds, on every keystroke with no round trip
in it, so it would carry the table either way: serving it would leave
the same functions written on both sides *plus* a wire format between
them. So it is written twice and checked once --
`TestTaskAttributesMatchTheFrontend` and `TestOperatorsMatchTheFrontend`
read the two JS files off disk and fail when either side grows an
attribute, a type or a comparison the other has not. (Which is the
answer for as long as the vocabulary is fixed at build time. The
deployment-defined attributes `attributesFor(config)` is the seam for
would change that: those arrive from a config the CLI would have to be
told about, and that is when a served table starts earning its wire
format.)

Two things differ on purpose. The frontend drops a clause it cannot
answer, so a stale link opens the list it names rather than an error;
the CLI refuses one, with the words that work, because a flag is typed
rather than followed and a filter that was quietly ignored prints a
listing that reads like a deployment with no such tasks. And a bare day
(`created:after:2026-09-01`) is read in the deployment's own wall clock
in both places -- which the browser gets from `GET /api/config` and the
CLI asks the settings endpoint for, only when a listing actually names a
day, falling back to the default zone rather than refusing to print if
that call fails.

The search box itself carries an `×` at its right-hand end while there
is anything in it (`ListPrimitives.jsx`'s `ListSearchField`, grain/
task-62), which clears it in a click and leaves the cursor in the box
ready for the next search. Backspacing a phrase away was the only way
out of one before, which is a dozen keystrokes for the gesture every
other search box on the machine does in one; the toolbar `Clear`
described above is not the same thing, since it throws the filters away
too, and the four non-task list pages (repos, templates, schedules,
suites) share this box without having a `Clear` at all.

**A deployment's own fields are attributes like any other
(grain/task-53, grain/task-64).** A deployment has facts about its work
that grain cannot know and should not guess — which customer a task is
for, how urgent it is, when it is due — and until `model.CustomField`
the only place to put one was prose in the body, where nothing can sort
by it. A *custom field* is a name, a label, a type (`text`, `number`,
`enum` with its options, `date`, `boolean`), whether it holds one value
or a set (`multiple`), whether it belongs on the rows that list a task
(`show_on_row`), a description, a default and a position; the
values a task carries for them are on the task, a `{name: value}` map,
and nothing else about them is stored twice.

Where a declaration lives was the decision worth making, and it is
settings: one row per field in `custom_field`, which is on
`staterepo.SettingsTables`, so declaring one is a pull request against
`tables/custom_field.json` that `grain state check` validates before a
human merges it — and no pane and no endpoint writes one. That is the
opposite of the usual "let an operator add a column from the UI", on
purpose: the set of fields a deployment has is exactly the kind of thing
that should be a reviewed diff rather than a form somebody filled in and
forgot, and it is a change an agent can propose like any other. Values,
by contrast, are ordinary task data: the new-task form, the detail pane
and the bulk edit form offer an input per declaration
(`CustomFields.jsx`), `POST`/`PATCH
/api/tasks` take a `customFields` map and normalise it against the
declarations (a name nothing declares is an error; an *empty* one is
allowed, since that is how a value whose field has since been deleted is
cleared), and a `/new` link can carry them so "the same customer, the
same priority as that one" is one click. No field is required — the
tasks filed before it existed, and everything grain files itself, would
otherwise all be invalid — and a declared default is what the form
offers, never what the store applies. `orchestrator.BuildPrompt` puts
whatever a task carries into its run's prompt, which is most of the
point: the field says in a structured way what the body would otherwise
have to say in prose.

**A declaration that changes under stored values grandfathers them
(grain/task-64).** The declarations are a reviewed diff, which means
they move: an enum option is retired, a field stops holding a set. What
that leaves is values on tasks the declaration would no longer produce,
and every form here renders every declared field and so restates every
declared field — so refusing them, which is what the store did, meant a
task carrying one could not be edited at all. Editing its title sent the
retired option back and `PATCH` refused it; the bulk pane restated the
first value of a stranded set and silently deleted the others; the
single-valued select drew an empty box over a value that was still
there, so the box said "none" while the store said "critical".

`model.NormalizeCustomFieldValuesFrom` is the policy, and it is
deliberately the third of three. Not walking the tasks when a
declaration merges, because a merged pull request should not silently
rewrite task data and putting the option back would not bring the values
back. Not refusing them, for the paragraph above. Grandfathering: a
value already stored may be restated as it stands, cleared, or replaced
with one the declaration accepts, and a single-valued field left holding
a set may be pared down a value at a time, because every step of that
states a subset of what was there — while introducing a legacy value
onto something that was not already carrying it is the error it always
was, so one can never spread. Task, template and schedule edits all go
through it, normalising inside the store's own update closure where
what the row holds now can be read; a *filing* has nothing stored to
grandfather against and goes through the unchanged gate.

The forms' half is to show such a value rather than hide it, since the
migration is then something a human does a value at a time while
looking at the task: a row of its own in the picker marked "no longer
offered", a plain box where `<input type="date">` could not have held
it, warning-coloured chips in a multi-valued box, and — for a field
that has stopped being `multiple` — chips that can be removed one by
one and turn back into the ordinary control the moment one is left. The
new-task form goes the other way and drops them
(`fileableFieldValues`), because a "file a task with these fields" link
copied off a task carrying one would otherwise fail the create.

**And they can be found (grain/task-201).** Grandfathering answers what
happens to a stranded value and says nothing about where they are:
somebody retiring an enum option, or taking `multiple` off a field, had
no answer to "which tasks are still carrying the old value?" short of
reading the store. `-filter custom.priority:any:critical` works only if
you already know which value to ask about, and the narrowing bar's menus
offer the values the tasks in view carry, so a retired option was
findable by eye on a small backlog and not otherwise.

So "is a legacy value" sits beside "is empty" and "is set", in the
toolbar and in `grain list -filter custom.priority:legacy` — the first
comparison offered by an *attribute* rather than by its type, since only
a field the deployment declares has a vocabulary that can change under a
value already stored. The predicate behind it is
`model.CustomField.Offers`/`LegacyValues`, which is the Go twin of the
`isOffered`/`legacyValues` the forms already draw their notices from;
those moved out of `components/CustomFields.jsx` into
`taskAttributes.js`, because a filter may not depend on a view and that
file is already where a declaration becomes something a list can be
narrowed by.

Settings says the same thing where the declarations are listed: a line
under a field that reads "3 tasks still carry a value this field no
longer offers", which opens the list narrowed to exactly those tasks.
That one needs no endpoint at all -- the tab already holds every task
(`/api/tasks`) and now holds the predicate too, so it is a walk of a
list in memory. The link drops the default narrowing rather than adding
to it, because that one sets the closed and deferred tasks aside and the
count does not: a closed task carrying a retired option is still
carrying it.

The count, rather than the list, is what the *decision* wants, and the
moment to have it is while the change to `tables/custom_field.json` is
still a diff. `Store.LegacyCustomFieldUses` answers that for any set of
declarations — deliberately a parameter, so the question can be asked of
one nobody has merged — and `grain state check` prints it as a warning
per field: how many tasks carry each retired value, and which tasks they
are. A warning and not a failure, for the reason the other two custom
field warnings there are warnings: nothing is broken, grandfathering is
the designed behaviour, and failing would make retiring an option
impossible without clearing every task carrying it in the same pull
request — the coupling grandfathering exists to avoid. It sees the tasks
the dump carries, so a repository exporting the whole database answers
in full and a config-only one (settings and memory alone, which is what
this deployment's own `grain/config` is) has no task rows to count; the
running deployment is where that question is asked with the filter
instead.

**And everything that files a task can set one (grain/task-105).** A
human at a form was the only writer for as long as a declared field was
only a thing to read, which stopped being harmless once a field became
something to filter and sort by: a good half of what grain files, it
files itself, so the column was empty on exactly those tasks. A schedule
and a template now carry values of their own — settings like the rest of
those declarations, on `schedule_custom_field` and
`template_custom_field`, applied afresh at every firing rather than
resolved once, so "weekly dependency bump" can say `team: infra` on
every task it ever files — and `propose_task` takes a `custom_fields`
argument, so a run splitting work out of a job for one customer files it
as being for that customer. Values from an automation go through exactly
the gate a human's do; what differs is only what happens to one that
will not pass. An API request is refused, because somebody is waiting
who can fix it. A firing, or a proposal relayed after its run is over,
drops that value and carries on — a schedule must not stop running
because somebody retired a declaration months after it was written, and
a batch of proposals must not be lost over one argument, which is why
the proposal says in its body what could not be set.

**Including a shell (grain/task-167).** The last writer without a way to
say one was the CLI: `grain list` could narrow and sort by a declared
field, `POST`/`PATCH /api/tasks` had taken a `customFields` map all
along, and nothing typed at a terminal could set one — so a task filed
by hand, or by a scripted triage pass, said nothing about the very
columns its deployment reads its backlog by. `grain create -field
priority=high` and `grain update 12 -field areas=ui,daemon` are that,
spelt the way this CLI spells a flag with two halves in it (`-write
owner/name@branch`), repeatable, and cut on commas only for a field
whose declaration says it holds a set — so `-field customer='Acme,
Inc.'` stays one customer. The `=` is required, which is what makes
`-field priority=` the way to clear a value rather than a `-clear-field`
of its own: an empty value is already "empty this one" everywhere else
here, and it is the one thing sayable about a field whose declaration
has since been deleted. Everything is checked against `GET
/api/config`'s declarations before the request, through the same
`NormalizeValues` the server would use, so a name nothing declares or a
value an enum does not offer comes back with the names and the options
that work; `grain create -h` and `grain update -h` list them, the way
`grain list -h` already lists them as attributes. The one subtlety is
that `PATCH` *replaces* a task's values, because the pane that edits
them renders every field at once — so an edit naming one field reads the
task and re-states the others, a value whose declaration has changed
under it since (an enum option retired) included. That used to stop the
edit, with a message about a field the command line had never mentioned;
since grain/task-64 the server takes a restatement of what a task
already holds as saying nothing new about it, so the value rides along
untouched and `-field priority=` is still how it goes.

The narrowing bar then needed nothing new to declare. The declarations
already ride on `GET /api/config` and the values on every task in the
list, which is the vocabulary-and-a-way-to-read-one-task that
`attributesFor` wants, so a declared field *is* a custom attribute:
`custom.<name>`, namespaced so a field called `repo` gets a menu of its
own rather than shadowing the built-in, with the declared type deciding
its comparisons (a boolean is an enum of two values written Yes and No;
a type this build has never heard of is compared as text rather than
dropped). Every one of them can be empty and says so, since no field is
required, so "is empty"/"is set" are offered and each value menu carries
a "Not set" row. The one comparison that had to change was the date: a
field holds a calendar day and the editor names one too, so both are now
read in the deployment's own time zone — read as UTC, a task due on the
4th answered "no" to "is after the 4th" everywhere west of it. `grain
list` asks the same question of the same declarations (grain/task-99,
above): `-filter custom.priority:any:critical` is that menu typed rather
than picked, out of the same `GET /api/config` and under the same ids.

The same field is a *sort key* as well, which is the half a filter
cannot stand in for: "the tasks that are urgent" is a narrowing, and
"the backlog, most urgent first" is an order. This is where an enum
earns its declaration over the free text it would otherwise be. Its
options are its rank, so `Priority first to last` puts the low ones at
the top and the critical ones at the bottom, rather than the `high, low,
medium` that ordering the words alphabetically would get; a value the
field no longer declares ranks after every value it does, rather than
ahead of them, so dropping an option from `tables/custom_field.json`
does not silently promote every task still carrying it. A date orders by
the day it names, in the same zone the filter reads it in — the two have
to agree, or a list could be sorted into an order its own filter
disputes — and a number orders as a number, so 9 comes before 10. The
direction is worded from the declared type, the way every built-in of
that type is worded (`Oldest first` for a date, `Lowest first` for a
number, `A–Z` for text), and the tasks nobody filled the field in on go
last whichever way the order points, so reversing an order never buries
the list under the tasks it says nothing about. A field holding a set
(below) is the one kind there is no sensible order for, since its values
are unordered by construction; it is offered like any other and ranks on
whichever of its values comes first, which is a tie for most of the list
rather than a wrong answer.

**A field can hold a set (grain/task-106).** `multiple` on a
declaration, rather than a type of its own: how many values a field
holds and what one value looks like are separate questions, and an enum
of one option and an enum of several offer the same choices and check
them the same way. It is allowed on `text` and `enum` — a boolean set is
a set of at most two values nobody wants, and neither a number nor a
date has an obvious input or meaning as one. The values are a set, so
duplicates collapse and order is not kept, which is exactly what the
comparisons for one ask about: such a field is a `TYPE_TAGS` attribute
in the narrowing bar, with "is any of", "is none of" and "has all of"
— the vocabulary the built-in `Capability` has used all along, with
nothing able to declare into it until now. Storing several put the value
in `task_custom_field`'s primary key, a row per value the way `task_tag`
holds a task's tags; that is the one change here `CREATE TABLE IF NOT
EXISTS` cannot make to an existing database, so
`Store.ensureTaskCustomFieldValueKey` rebuilds that one table on the
first start after the upgrade rather than a `SchemaVersion` bump costing
every deployment its store. On the wire a value is a string or an array
of strings, one value marshalling as the bare string it always was, so
every reader written against the single-valued API stays right. The form
offers a box of chips for one, and a `/new` link carries it as the
parameter repeated (`?field.areas=ui&field.areas=daemon`).

A schedule, a template and a proposing agent write a set the same way
they write anything else (above): `schedule_custom_field` and
`template_custom_field` key on the value as `task_custom_field` does,
and `propose_task`'s `custom_fields` takes a string or an array of them
per field, exactly as the task API does.

**And the value is on the rows, not only in the pane (grain/task-100).**
A list can be narrowed and sorted by a declared field, but until now the
rows said nothing about one: sorting a backlog by `priority` reordered it
into an order the reader could not see, and the value lived in the task's
own detail pane and nowhere else. Two things put one on a row now, and
they answer two different questions. The *narrowing* answers "what is
this list in the order of": a list or a board sorted by a field shows
that field, every field the sort names, first among the row's chips —
which is the one case where the row genuinely cannot be read without the
value. The *declaration* answers "what does this deployment read its
backlog by": `show_on_row` puts a field on every row, every card and
every panel whether or not anything is being asked about it. A filter
adds nothing, deliberately — the toolbar's chip already says "Priority is
any of high", and every row that survived it answers the same, so
repeating that down the list is the one thing on a row a reader could
have worked out without reading it.

The row's width budget is the frontend's rather than the declaration's:
a row is one line that does not wrap and already carries state, number,
title, live status, repo, base, capabilities and origin, so
`ROW_FIELD_LIMIT` (three) is how many field values it will take, sorted
fields first so the limit never drops the one explaining the order.
A deployment that flags six fields is stating a preference the row
honours as far as it fits, not making a mistake `grain state check`
should fail — which is why `show_on_row` is a plain flag with no count
and no ordering of its own beside `position`. A field the task says
nothing about gets no chip at all, since "nobody said" is the ordinary
answer and a row of blanks would cost the title its width to say
nothing. The board's cards follow the same rule, which is what keeps a
task reading the same in a list, on a board and in a dashboard panel.

**What a narrowed list is *for* is doing something to all of it
(grain/task-47).** Every row carries a checkbox, and a selection raises
the batch actions bar (`BatchActionsBar.jsx`) along the bottom of the
window: Approve, Submit, Defer, Undefer, Close, Reopen and the
capability toggles, each fired once per selected task. Most of those
endpoints already no-op on a task they do not apply to, so a mixed
selection is safe to run one at; `Defer` is the exception that refuses
rather than no-ops, and is offered anyway because putting a stack of
proposals aside is what deferring is mostly for. A batch collects its
failures instead of stopping at the first (`App.jsx`'s `actBatch`) and
leaves the selection standing unless every call landed, so a partial
failure is retried on the rows still ticked rather than re-picked. The
board's cards carry the same checkbox and feed the same selection, so
"select a whole column and run it" is one gesture.

`Bulk edit…` is the same widening for the half of a task that is a value
rather than a verb: repo, base branch, auto-merge, agent framework,
review and prompt extension, on the whole selection at once
(`BulkEditOverlay.jsx`). Those are the fields that go wrong in batches
-- a pass filed against a base branch that has since been deleted, a
review nobody wants on twenty proposals, an auto-merge flag set the
wrong way on a suite run -- each of them one decision the operator has
already made and would otherwise re-type once per task pane. Every field
is behind its own "change this" tick and only a ticked one is sent,
which is what makes a mixed selection safe to edit: `PATCH
/api/tasks/{id}` leaves out what a request does not name, so a selection
spanning four repos can have its review detached without any of the four
being touched, and an emptied box stays the real edit it is ("no base",
"no review", "clear the override") rather than being guessed at as a
field nobody meant to change. What the selection already agrees on is
pre-filled; where it disagrees the control opens empty and says so,
since there is no value there that would be an honest default. Title and
description are deliberately not offered: they are what tells one task
from another, and they are also the two fields an edit re-sends to a
running agent as an addendum, which is a conversation with one run
rather than a property of a batch.

**The fields a deployment declares are in that form too
(grain/task-273).** They were the shape bulk edit exists for and the one
thing it could not do: a deployment declaring `priority`, `customer`,
`teams` and `due` had them on the new-task form, on the task pane and
under `grain create -field`, and "these six are all for Globex" was
still eight panes or eight `grain update` calls. Each declaration now
gets a row under **Fields**, behind the same tick as everything else and
rendered by the same control the other two forms use
(`CustomFields.jsx`), so a deployment that declares nothing sees the
form exactly as it was. Two readings are settled rather than left to be
inferred. A ticked field left empty *clears* the value on every selected
task, as an emptied base branch does and as `-field name=` does on the
CLI. And a `multiple` field replaces the set each task holds rather than
adding to it, which is what every other row here does and the only
reading under which a bulk edit can take a value *off* a selection. The
body is where the care is: `PATCH /api/tasks/{id}` reads `customFields`
as the task's whole answer about its declared fields, so each request
carries that task's own values for the fields nobody ticked alongside
the ones somebody did — a body naming only `priority` would set a
priority on six tasks and wipe the customer off all six.

**The same tasks as a Kanban board, with the operator's own columns
(grain/task-287).** The flat list answers "what is the backlog, in
order". The other question asked of a deployment all day -- "where is
everything right now" -- is answered by scrolling one list and reading
eight different state badges off it. So `TaskBoard.jsx` lays the same
tasks out in columns, one card each.

It was a fixed destination on the rail with a path of its own for most of
its life, and it is a **saved dashboard** now (the section on those is a
few paragraphs down): `kanban` is one of the layouts a board can be, so
the columns are opened by name from the Boards section of the rail rather
than from one entry above it, and a deployment has as many of them as
somebody has made rather than one for everybody (grain/task-162). What
changed is only how it is reached and what it is asked -- a board carries
its own query, where the fixed one was always every task -- and a kept
link to `/board` lands on the task list, which is the fallback any
unrecognized path here gets.

Two things make it a board rather than a second list. The columns are
the operator's: `BoardColumnsOverlay.jsx` names them, says which states
each collects and what order they run in, and a state in no column is
off the board altogether -- which is how closed tasks stay out of the
way by default, and how "which tasks show up" is answered without a
second vocabulary. And the toolbar over it is the list's own, moved out
to `taskFilters.js` (and to `NarrowingBar.jsx` once it became an editor,
above) so both views narrow by the same attributes with the same wording
rather than growing two drifting copies of one toolbar; the
menus are built from the tasks the columns admit, so a board with no
Closed column never offers a repo only closed tasks carry.

The layout lives in `localStorage`, next to the theme mode
(`ThemeModeContext.jsx`), for the same reason: this is how one person
wants to look at the deployment, not a fact about it -- nothing behind
`/api/config` changes when a column is renamed, and it keeps the whole
feature a frontend change with no settings key or migration behind it.
`board.js` is what makes that safe to read back: a stored layout naming
a state this build has never heard of, claiming one state in two
columns, or holding something that isn't a board at all is normalized or
dropped on the way in rather than rendered.

What the board deliberately does not do is let a card be dragged into
another column. A task's state is derived by the daemon from what has
actually happened to it (`model.StateOf`, `docs/data-model.md`), not
stored as a field the UI could set, so there is no write behind "drop
this in Running"; the gestures that really move a task between these
columns are the ones on the task itself, which is why a card opens the
task. Dragging *within* a column is real, and is the list's own drag --
`Store.Reorder`, in the same "between these two neighbours" terms, and
offered only under backlog order. Cards carry the list's checkbox and
feed the same selection, so the batch-actions bar works from either
view: select a whole column and run it.

**And the third question: what is waiting on *me* (grain/task-20).** The
list answers "what is the backlog", the board answers "where is
everything". Neither answers the one an operator actually opens grain to
ask, which is what grain cannot get on with until they do something.
Five kinds of task are stopped on a person: one parked on an
`ask_question` call, one whose pull request nobody has submitted, one
the merge queue has given up on, one that has burnt through its retries,
and a proposal nobody has approved. They are scattered down a list
ordered by what grain is about to run next, wearing five different
badges, and a deployment left alone for a day accumulates all five.

`Inbox` is the first entry on the rail, above the backlog itself,
carrying a count of exactly those (`state.js`'s `waitsOnUser`, which the
page and the count in the rail share so the number and the page cannot
disagree). `/inbox` groups them by the answer each one needs rather than
by state -- "Answer a question", "Submit for merge", "Unblock a merge",
"Retry or close", "Approve a proposal" -- in the order of how stuck each
kind of wait is, with proposals last because "not now" is so often the
honest answer to one and a backlog of them should not stand between a
reader and a run parked mid-sentence. That answer is a button there too
(`Defer`, grain/task-21, described at the top of this section): a deferred proposal
reads as deferred rather than as a proposal, so saying "not now" is what
takes the row off this page.

What makes it more than a saved filter is that the answer is on the row.
A filtered list still costs an opened pane per task to find out what that
task wants -- Approve lives on one, Submit on another, and a question
needs the timeline at the bottom of a third -- which is a lot of clicking
for the tasks that by definition nobody has got round to. So each row
carries the responses that apply to its own wait, they fire in place and
refresh the list, and none of them opens anything (`App.jsx`'s
`inboxAct`, which is `act` minus the pane it would put over the list
somebody is working down). A parked question opens a reply box under its
own row, with the question it is answering above it.

The one row that gets no reply box is the one that most looks like it
should have one. A run parked on `request_secret` is in the same state
as a run parked on a question, and a reply is a comment -- stored in the
conversation, and handed to the next run in its prompt. A box there
invites somebody to paste a credential into exactly the place grain
promises never to put one, so the inbox reads the task's own detail when
the box is opened, and a task with a `pendingSecret` gets the sentence
saying what was asked for and a way through to the write-only field on
its own pane instead (see "Write-only secrets access when colocated"
below).

**And the fourth question: *when* (grain/task-55).** The list answers
"what is the backlog", the board "where is everything", the inbox "what
is waiting on me". None of them answers the question somebody asks with a
calendar already open — what ran last night, what has been sitting in the
queue since Tuesday, whether those four tasks on one repo actually
overlapped or only look like they did in a list sorted by id. Every one
of those is a *length*, and a badge cannot be a length.

So `GanttChart.jsx` lays the same tasks out as bars against a clock. Like
the board above it, the chart was a fixed destination on the rail and is
a kind of saved dashboard now (`gantt`, grain/task-162), opened by name
from the Boards section. A bar runs from when a task was filed to when it
stopped being work in progress, with the moment it was first dispatched
drawn inside it, so the wait and the work
are two visibly different stretches of one length. A bar with no end is
still going: it reaches the "now" line and fades out there rather than
stopping square, because a bar that ends at the right-hand edge because
the task finished and one that ends there because it has not are opposite
facts. The axis is anchored to midnight in the *deployment's* zone, like
every other timestamp in the UI (`time.js`, grain/task-368), and what
falls outside the chosen range is counted under the toolbar rather than
quietly dropped.

The two settings over it are the operator's, and they are this browser's:
how far back to look (the same four windows Metrics offers, plus
"Everything", which sizes itself to the tasks) and what to group the rows
into (nothing, repo, state or author). They live in `localStorage` beside
the board's columns and for the same reason — this is how one person
wants to look at the deployment, not a fact about it — with `gantt.js`
normalizing whatever is read back, so a range this build has dropped
falls back without taking the lane choice with it. The toolbar over the
chart is the shared one (`NarrowingBar.jsx`), so the chart is narrowed by
the same attributes with the same wording as the list, and
`/boards/board-3?f=repo:any:acme/widgets` is a link somebody can send. A
repo's own page offers the chart as a third switch position beside List
and Board, reading the same one stored choice (`board.js`'s
`loadRepoView`).

What made this a change to the *server* as well is that two of those
three instants were nowhere a list could see them. A task row carried
`createdAt` and a state; when a task was first picked up and when it
ended were in `TaskDetail`'s attempts and observation, one request per
task, which is no way to draw a hundred bars. `model.TaskSpan` names the
pair, `Store.TaskSpans` reads one for every task in a single query
alongside the whole-store reads `ListTasks` already makes, and `ui.Task`
carries them as `startedAt`/`endedAt` on every shape a task is read back
through. The rule for what counts as an ending lives in that one type:
the earlier of a completion and a closure, and *absent* while neither has
happened — a failed attempt is not an ending, because a task whose
attempt failed is still open and its bar has not stopped.

The chart is one of the kinds a **saved dashboard** can be
(grain/task-48), and since grain/task-162 that is the only way to reach
one. A board is a row in the store naming a layout and a query, and
`gantt` is a third value for that layout beside `list` and
`kanban`: `/boards/board-3` opens the chart, asking that board's own
question, and the row that does it is the word `gantt` in
`tables/board.json` and nothing else. That is what the kind field was for
— `model.BoardKinds` is the one list of them, so the API's own "kind must
be…" reply names whatever this build can actually render rather than a
sentence somebody has to remember to update. What a board does *not*
carry is the range and the grouping: those stay this browser's, the same
way a Kanban board with no columns of its own falls back to the columns
its reader has chosen. And `New board` clicked while reading a timeline
asks for a timeline (`boards.js`'s `kindForView`), since the narrowing is
only half of what is on screen and the layout is the other half; clicked
anywhere else it offers the list a board is by default and names every
kind in the prompt, which is how somebody asks for a Kanban board now
that there is no fixed one to stand on.

**A dashboard an operator assembles out of panels** (grain/task-88) is
the fourth kind, and the one that is not a single view filling the pane.
A `panels` board is several of the views above at once — a timeline, the
state counts, a throughput sparkline, a list narrowed to what is waiting
on somebody — each panel a row in `board_panel` carrying its own kind,
heading, query, range and width. `/boards/board-4` draws them
(`ui/src/components/PanelBoard.jsx`); `panels.js` holds the vocabulary
and the falling back.

*Where a layout lives* was the question to settle before any of it was
written, because the two answers were both already in the codebase. The
Kanban columns and the timeline's range are `localStorage` keys, on the
argument that they are how one person is reading the deployment rather
than a fact about it. A board is a row in the store, on the argument that
it is asked for by name and meant to be there tomorrow. A panel layout
takes the second answer, for the reason `model.Board`'s own doc comment
gives about the board it hangs off: a dashboard is the first thing here
anybody wants to *share* — "open my dashboard" as a link, or one
dashboard a deployment agrees on — and the thing usually asked to build
one is an agent, which has a checkout and a git remote and no way at all
into a browser's storage. So the panels are settings rows, exported to
the state repository with everything else, and assembling a dashboard is
the same pull request that creating a board already is. What stays in the
browser is what was already there: a timeline panel's lanes and the
columns the state counts are grouped into are still the reader's own.

Nothing about a panel is drawn twice. Each one asks its own narrowing of
the tasks the page already holds, through the same `taskFilters.js` code
every task view uses; the timeline panel is `GanttChart` with its heading
and narrowing bar turned off (its `embedded` prop), the state counts are
`board.js`'s own grouping with the cards left off, the list is the list's
own `TaskRow`, and the throughput panel asks `/api/metrics` for the
report the Metrics pane prints, scoped to what the panel is asking. A
panel with no query of its own asks the dashboard's — the two are not
combined, since two conditions on one attribute intersect and "either
repo" narrowed by "the other repo" is nothing at all, so a panel that
means both says both.

*Nor is it asked twice.* Each panel drawing its own answer meant N sorts
and N filters of the same list on every three-second poll, which on a
store of 929 tasks was a main thread with nothing left over
(`docs/hand-runs/2026-09-07-panel-dashboard.md`, section 5, has the
numbers). `taskFilters.js`'s `narrowTasks` is the resolve/sort/match
every task view does, memoised on the identity of the task list and the
question asked of it: the panels that inherit the dashboard's narrowing
share one answer between them, two panels asking different things in the
same order share one sorted array, and a poll that changed nothing
computes none of it (which is what makes the list's identity worth
keeping — `poll.js`, "And it refreshes itself" below). The one question
never kept is one the clock is part of, since `within the last N days` is
answered against `Date.now()` and an answer to it stops being true on its
own. `PanelBoard.test.jsx` holds the bound as a test: six panels must
cost what one costs.

*A panel is a window onto a view, and draws like one* (grain/task-311).
The list panel has always shown its first eight rows and left the count
on its heading to say how many there are; the timeline panel had no such
budget, on the assumption that its range was one. It is not. A range
decides which tasks have a bar at all — a task whose span does not
overlap the window is off the chart, and the note under the axis says how
many are — but it cannot decide how many that leaves, and on a deployment
whose last seven days hold nine hundred tasks the answer is nine hundred
bars: a 400px panel with 14,000px of rows inside it, scrolled within a
page that also scrolls, and 42 times its own height at a phone's width
(`docs/hand-runs/2026-09-07-panel-dashboard.md`, sections 5 and 6). So
`GanttChart` takes a `maxRows` the panel sets and the full view leaves at
zero, applied to what the range already admitted and in the narrowing's
own order, and the chart says both things it is not showing in one line:
`Showing 10 of 904 in this range. 25 tasks outside this range.` They are
counted apart because they want different gestures — one is a range too
narrow, the other is a range too full for a panel. Ten rows because that
is what the box holds: `.panel-body` is 22rem, a `.gantt-row` is 1.65rem,
and the axis, the padding and that note come to about 4rem between them.
Which is the general shape of the thing: how many rows fit is a property
of the panel, not of the calendar.

*The dashboard's question is one the reader can change* (grain/task-111).
The panel grid carries the same `NarrowingBar` every task view does, over
the same narrowing `App` holds for all of them — so "this dashboard, but
only `acme/widgets`, just for a minute" is a gesture rather than an edit
to the rows in `board_panel`. What the toolbar narrows is the *fallback*:
a panel with no query follows it, a panel that carries its own question
is left asking it (narrowing that one further is the intersection above,
which would silently empty it), and the throughput panel follows both
rules like the rest (grain/task-317). That last one was the exception
until the endpoint behind it took a scope (a report board's own section,
below): it now sends the narrowing it is asking to `GET /api/metrics` as
`metrics.Scope` through the same `report.js` a report board uses, so a
dashboard narrowed to `acme/widgets` narrows its sparkline too, and a
panel that has said what it measures goes on measuring that. The span
follows the same rule as the question — the panel's own `range` if it
names one, otherwise whatever date range the narrowing names, which a
report reads as the window to measure over rather than as a filter on
filing dates. What a report cannot use (a search, a state) is dropped,
and the panel says so in its tooltip, which is where a page of two counts
and two sparklines has room for the line `ReportBoard` prints. A
dashboard still opens on its board's own query — `openBoard` seeds the
narrowing from the row — so nothing about a dashboard nobody touches
changed; what changed is that it can be narrowed from there. (A board
whose query names nothing has asked nothing, and opens on the
deployment's own default rather than over every task, which is what keeps
a panel and the list its "Open" link opens about the same tasks — "What a
board that says nothing means", above.)

*A scoped panel's heading leads to the report it is drawing
(grain/task-379).* The throughput panel used to be the one heading that
linked to `/metrics`, carrying nothing, on the argument that the report
took no filter and a link pretending to carry one would lie. Scoping the
panel turned that around — `/metrics` was the deployment-wide report and
that pane had no way to be told otherwise, so the link there from a panel
about `acme/widgets` became the one that lies — and for a while the
heading went to the task list instead, which is what the timeline and the
state counts got when `/gantt` and `/board` stopped existing. That was
honest but adjacent: a list is the panel's *question* rather than the
report's window (a `created` range means filing dates to a list and the
span to measure to a report), and the panel's own `range` was not in that
URL at all. The Metrics pane takes a scope now — "The Metrics pane takes
a scope of its own", below — so the heading goes back to `/metrics`
carrying both halves: the panel's narrowing as the pane's scope, and the
panel's range as the `created` condition a report reads as its window.
The other three headings still lead to the list, and `panels.js`'s
`panelDestination` is the one place that decides which is which, so the
`href` a reader copies and the click that opens without a page load are
one decision rather than two.

Two things fall out of it, and they are half of why it is worth having.
`Add panel` carries the question the reader composed rather than the
board's own — and, when the toolbar is still showing exactly the board's
question, carries none at all, since the row for "a panel of this
dashboard" is a row with an empty query rather than one frozen to the
query the dashboard has today. And the narrowing rides in the URL the way
every other task view's does (`paths.js` already writes one onto
`/boards/<id>`), so a dashboard somebody has narrowed is a link they can
send.

Every panel's heading is a link to the full view it is a small copy of,
asking the same question (`paths.js`), and so is every state count: a
dashboard is for noticing something, the view behind it is for doing
something about it, and a URL is what makes those the same place rather
than two that have to be re-narrowed by hand. `Add panel` opens a
pre-written task against the state repository carrying the narrowing on
screen, exactly as `New board` and `Edit board` do, and for the reason
`boards.js` gives at length: a form here would be a second way of writing
rows an agent already writes, to be kept in step with the first.

*Keeping a narrowing on the panel it was made on* (grain/task-313) is the
step between those two that neither was taking. Getting a panel's own
query right is iterative — learning that one word finds eighty-eight
tasks and another fifty-six is something a reader finds out by trying, in
the toolbar, in seconds — and until this, keeping the answer meant
describing the narrowing on screen a second time in prose, in a task
about a panel that already exists. So a panel showing a narrowing its
reader made carries a `Keep` beside its `Open`, and it opens the same
pre-written task with that query already in it, pointed at that one panel
(`boards.js`'s `keepPanelQueryTask`). It is the road every other change
to a board takes, filled in rather than left blank — not a panel form.
The control appears only where keeping something would mean something:
the dashboard must be narrowed away from what it *opens* on (its board's
stored question, or the deployment's own default where the board names
none, so the state condition already on an untouched dashboard's toolbar
is not read as one this reader composed, and `Clear` keeps nothing — the
reading `Add panel` already took of the same toolbar, now shared as
`keptQuery`), the panel must not carry a query of its own — one that
does is not following the toolbar, so it is not showing this narrowing,
and replacing its question is an edit to say in words — and the narrowing
must be one that panel would actually be showing. That last is a question
only the throughput panel can answer no to, and only sometimes: it reads
a query as a scope rather than as a filter (grain/task-317), so a
dashboard narrowed to a search term is one it is not narrowed by and
keeping that there would write a query changing nothing, while a
dashboard narrowed to a repo is one it *is* showing, and it offers the
same word the other three do. The
prompt says which row it means (the panel's `order_key`, the only field
naming a row nobody gave an id) and says out loud what the reader cannot
see from the gesture: a panel that carries its own query stops following
the toolbar for good. The query it carries is the whole of what is on
screen, the deployment's default condition on state included, and both
dashboard prompts say why a condition nobody typed is in there — a panel
with a query of its own is read exactly as written and given no default,
so dropping it would keep a panel wider than the one being pointed at. On
a phone `Keep` takes the same 44px target `Open` has, since it is the
same word at the same size in the same header and the one of the two that
writes something rather than navigating.

*A panel is dragged into its place* (grain/task-368), which is the other
half of what that hand run found and the one edit to a dashboard that is
not a task at all. Boards have been draggable into their folders and
their order since grain/task-81, on the argument that a board's *place*
is not content: it is a preference with no words in it, worth nothing
once said out loud, and checkable only by looking at the list again.
Every word of that is true of a panel, and on a phone its place is the
whole layout — every panel is full width and stacked in the board's own
order — so a dashboard whose panels could only be reordered by pull
request was one that kept whatever order the rows creating it happened to
take. `panelOrder.js` is `boardOrder.js` one level down: a place is
"immediately above that panel" or the end of the dashboard, and a drop
becomes an order key halfway between its new neighbours', or a renumber
of the board on even spacing when there is no gap left to halve.

Two decisions in it are worth reading. *The write is the whole `panels`
array*, through the `PATCH /api/boards/{id}` that already exists, rather
than a narrower endpoint for one row — because a narrower one would buy
nothing. `PutBoard` deletes and re-inserts every `board_panel` row of the
board whatever changed, so each row's autoincrement `id` moves and the
state repository's next dump rewrites every panel of that dashboard under
a one-field write exactly as under this one; the churn is the store's,
not the API's, and what is left is honest last-writer-wins over a handful
of rows. That is lossless because `normalizePanel` now keeps the row it
came from beside the row it drew: a panel whose kind this build has never
heard of is *drawn* as a list and must not be *written* as one, and since
the server refuses a kind it does not know, an older build reordering
such a dashboard fails visibly rather than flattening a panel a newer one
wrote. *And every key it writes is above zero*, which is not cosmetic:
`PutBoard` reads an order key of 0 as "this row was not numbered" and
substitutes the panel's position, so a genuine 0 is only safe on the
first row — a panel dropped at the head of a dashboard whose first panel
sits at 0 therefore renumbers the board rather than writing a negative
key. A dashboard hand-numbered 10/20/30 in the state repository still
survives; nothing renumbers it until a drag needs room it has not got.

The gesture is the shared one (`ReorderPickup.jsx`). A mouse drags a
panel by its header — a panel is a box with a body somebody scrolls,
selects text in and clicks rows inside, which a row in a list is not —
and the panel a drop would land above wears the rule down its *leading*
edge, since the grid wraps left to right and then down and a horizontal
rule would point at the wrong gap half the time. A finger or a keyboard
picks the panel up on the handle in its header, and picking one up stacks
the dashboard: every panel full width with its body closed, which is
neither a mode invented for the gesture nor a compromise — it is the
phone's own layout, which is the order itself with nothing else in the
way. It is also what makes the drop targets choosable: six panels of real
history are 2,500px of scrolling with their bodies open
(`docs/hand-runs/2026-09-07-panel-dashboard.md`, section 6), and slots
three screens apart are not a choice anybody can make. A panel has no id
anybody named, so what is dragged is named by its position — which is why
the move is written and then read back rather than applied optimistically:
the panel that moved is called something else the moment it lands, and
the server is the only thing that knows what.

**A report board** (grain/task-83) is the fifth kind and the first that
is not a view of the backlog at all. A `report` board draws grain's own
measurement report — throughput, latency, how attempts ended, what is
still waiting — over the tasks its query names, and `ReportBoard.jsx`
renders it (the same component the Metrics pane is now, with a board row
behind it rather than none — "The Metrics pane takes a scope of its
own", below). It is the case that tested whether `model.BoardKind`'s claim
holds for a kind sharing none of the machinery: it did, and what the kind
needed instead was two decisions.

*What a query means to a report.* A board's query is one kind-agnostic
field, so the question is what a set of conditions on tasks can honestly
say about a report over those tasks. Three of them can: `repo`, `author`
and a date range on `created` become `metrics.Scope` and the report's own
window, sent as `?repo=`, `?author=`, `?since=` and `?until=`, and the
daemon narrows the rows before it measures anything. That is the other
half of this change and the larger one: `GET /api/metrics` had only ever
answered "what did this whole deployment deliver", which is why the
throughput panel on a dashboard was the one panel that ignored the
dashboard's narrowing until grain/task-317 taught it to ask. `metrics.Scope` is applied once at the top of
`Compute`, before a number is taken, so a scoped report cannot come out
with its throughput over one set of tasks and its tool census over
another — and two inputs are deliberately left unscoped, because a
`RunCycle` tick belongs to the deployment rather than to any set of
tasks, and so does the concurrency ceiling utilization is a fraction of.

Everything else in the query — a search, a state, a sort — has nothing to
narrow in a distribution, and is dropped *visibly*: the page prints one
line naming the conditions it could not use. A board saved off a narrowed
list will usually carry one, and of the two dishonest options — refusing
to render, or pretending — neither is as useful as saying so. The date
reading is the one that is not literal and the page says which one it
took: `created:within:30` on a task list means "tasks filed in the last
thirty days", and as a report's window it means "measure the last thirty
days", which is a different set of tasks because a window bounds
measurements rather than rows. It is still the reading somebody asking
for it meant — the alternative reports a month's throughput with most of
that month's completions missing.

*Where a setting belonging to one kind lives.* Already answered twice:
`board_column` and `board_panel` are child tables because those rows are
what an agent edits in the state repository's dump and a column of
escaped JSON is not something anybody edits correctly. So the sections a
report board prints are `board_section`, and the precedent is a rule
rather than a coincidence. A board with no rows there prints the whole
report, which is `board_column`'s own fallback and what "a report board
for `acme/widgets`" should produce without inventing a layout.

Nothing on the page is drawn twice, for the reason the panels are not:
every section is the component the Metrics pane draws
(`MetricsSections.jsx`, which is where they moved to the day this page
was written), so a section improved in one place improves in both —
and since grain/task-379 the page around them is shared too. And
the toolbar over it is the same `NarrowingBar`, which here re-asks the
endpoint rather than filtering anything on screen — "this report, but
only `acme/widgets`, just for a minute" is a scope the daemon computes,
which is the gesture grain/task-111 gave every other view and the one
that needed a server change to reach this one.

What the chart deliberately does not do is draw dependency arrows or let
a bar be dragged. Both are what a planning tool's Gantt is for, and
neither means anything here: these dates are a record of what dispatch
did, not a plan somebody set, so there is no write behind "start this on
Thursday" — the same argument that keeps a card from being dragged
between the board's columns.

**`grain demo` (bwsalmon/agents#276, folded into its own subcommand by
#363) for trying out the frontend on its own.** A real `grain daemon`
needs a real Gemini key, a real store, and a real deployment's tasks to
look at anything. `grain demo` opens a throwaway embedded store in a
fresh temp directory instead and seeds it with fake tasks, one in each
`model.State` (`cmd/grain/demo.go`), through the same `ui.Client`/
`model.Store` writes a human clicking through the UI would make — no fake
`Store` standing in, matching the "real embedded SQLite, not a fake"
discipline every test in this repo already holds to
(`pkg/ui/client_test.go`). That makes it a real server exercising the real
frontend code, with fake data as the only difference from a real
deployment — useful for checking a frontend change renders every state
correctly without an orchestrator, a sandbox, a Gemini key, a real store,
or a git repo anywhere behind it. It seeds a handful of custom fields for
the same reason (`demoCustomFields`, grain/task-274): the fields a
deployment declares for itself are the one part of a task that is not
built in, so a demo declaring none shows a new-task form with no Fields
block, rows with no chips and a narrowing bar whose menus stop at the
built-ins. Six of them, one per control the form renders, plus one
declared and immediately retired so that the row a task keeps for a
withdrawn field has something behind it — and no more than that, because
the demo's forms are also what somebody opens to see what grain is. It
takes no `-data-dir` of its own —
there is no real store to point it at by mistake, only the throwaway one
it creates and seeds itself.

**Freshness, not a cache.** Every mutation in the frontend
(`ui/src/App.jsx`'s `act`) re-fetches the task afterward rather than
assuming its own optimistic update is now true, matching the direction
document's "it shows freshness for anything" — read live from the store
rather than presenting a stale value as current. There is nowhere here
for staleness to hide since nothing is ever cached across one request.

**And it refreshes itself.** A task changes state when `graind`
dispatches it, when a run finishes, and when a pull request merges —
none of which the browser is told about, so without a poll the screen
only moves when somebody clicks. `App.jsx` re-reads every three seconds,
skipping the tick entirely while the tab is hidden and never overlapping
itself.

Two details keep that useful rather than annoying. React's own
reconciliation already skips DOM writes for output that hasn't actually
changed, so an idle screen polled every three seconds never flickers,
loses focus, or resets its scroll — the vanilla-JS frontend this
replaced had to do that by hand, diffing a poll's JSON against
`lastList`/`lastDetail` before deciding whether to re-render at all, and
nothing about *that* needs it. And when the open task does change, an
unsent comment survives the re-render because `DetailOverlay.jsx`'s
comment box is an uncontrolled input: React never touches a `<textarea>`'s own DOM
value on a re-render, only on mount, so a reply someone is halfway
through typing is untouched by newer comments arriving underneath it.
Both behaviors were checked by driving the real UI in a browser.

**A diff against the last answer came back anyway, for a different
reason.** Not flicker — cost. `await api(...)` parses fresh JSON every
time, so a tick that learned nothing still handed every view a brand new
object graph: a re-render of everything holding it, and a miss in every
memo keyed on its identity. That is invisible on a demo store and it is
the whole cost of a quiet tab on a real one. Measured on 929 tasks, a
six-panel dashboard spent 1.0–1.2s of script on *every* three-second
tick and a ten-panel one 2.1–2.3s — a saturated main thread on a
deployment where nothing was happening
(`docs/hand-runs/2026-09-07-panel-dashboard.md`, section 5). So the four
things polled on every tick — the task list, the config, the live
sessions and an open task's detail — keep the value already in state when
the new one says the same thing (`ui/src/poll.js`'s `keepIfSame`, one
structural comparison of data already parsed). React bails out of the
re-render, and identity-keyed memos hold across ticks instead of missing
on every one.

The clock is what that costs, and it is paid back explicitly: the poll
used to double as a repaint timer, and everything reading `Date.now()` as
it drew — a running task's "as of 2m ago", the timeline's now-line — rode
along on it. `App.jsx` now ticks a clock of its own every thirty seconds
(`CLOCK_INTERVAL_MS`), which is half a step of the coarsest elapsed-time
label on screen, at a twentieth of the renders.

Polling rather than a change feed is deliberate, and unlike when this
store ran on Dolt, there is no longer a substrate underneath it to
decline: SQLite gives grain no commit log and no ready-made diff to build
a watch on (see "Grain no longer keeps a commit history" above), so a
real feed would mean building one from scratch — a diff joined across
six tables to answer "what changed about this task" (a capability toggle
changes `task_grant`, a comment changes `task_comment`), a story for
history that grows without bound, and handling for a cursor that has
aged out. That is a real feature; polling is fifteen lines with nothing
to get wrong, and for one operator watching a handful of tasks on the
same machine the two are indistinguishable.

## The store is a git repository again

grain's settings -- templates, suites, per-repo configuration, prompt
extensions, schedules -- are exactly the kind of thing a task is forever
asking to change, and until now the only way to change one was a human
editing it through the UI. A row in a SQLite file is not something an
agent can propose a diff to, so the mechanism grain already has for
changing anything else (a branch, a pull request, a review, a merge) was
the one mechanism that could not reach grain's own configuration.

So the database is a git repository now: `pkg/staterepo`, a working tree
under `<data-dir>/state-repo` holding every table as
`tables/<name>.json`. The store itself is unchanged -- it is still the
embedded SQLite database `pkg/model/sqlite` opens, and every query in
`pkg/model` is untouched. What changed is that the database is a
materialisation of the repository rather than the thing itself.

Rows are sorted by primary key and columns emitted in the table's own
declared order, so exporting an unchanged database twice produces
byte-identical files. That is not tidiness. The daemon exports on a
timer, and a dump whose row order wandered would commit and push on
every cycle forever, burying the changes that matter.

### One writer, so no merges

grain is the only writer of these files while it runs -- the UI and the
CLI reach the daemon over REST rather than opening the store, which is
what makes that claim true -- so a sync is a commit and a push and never
a resolve, and a pull is fast-forward only. Divergence means something
this model does not describe, and failing loudly beats resolving a
conflict in a database dump by guesswork.

A change an agent makes arrives the other way: a pull request against
the state repository, reviewed and merged like any other, which the
daemon pulls on the same thirty-second timer it exports on. What it does
with what arrives is asymmetric, and deliberately so. Only the settings
tables are imported (`staterepo.SettingsTables`: the deployment's config
row, repo configuration, templates, suites, schedules, qualification
plans), and they are imported wholesale, so a merged deletion of a
template really does delete it. Those are the tables an agent proposes
changes to and the tables grain does not write for itself, which is what
makes them safe to replace live. A merged change to a task or a run is
not applied, and the next export writes the database's own version of it
back out: the database is authoritative for what grain itself did.

A restart imports exactly the same tables, and that is worth saying
because it did not use to. `Load` read "HEAD is not the commit this host
recorded" as "a merge arrived" and replaced the whole state tier --
`task`, `task_comment`, `task_attachment`, `branch`, `release`, every
table but the three churn ones -- from the dump. The dump is whatever the
last export wrote, so that deleted every row grain had written since:
half a minute of them in the ordinary case, and an operator lands in that
window by habit rather than by accident, merging a settings pull request
and restarting grain to make it take effect. Nothing was gained by it
either, since a merged edit to `task` only ever survived if the process
happened to restart before the next tick pulled the same commit down and
recorded it as loaded. The import a restart does is now the import a tick
does.

The whole-database import -- every table, churn included -- is left with
the cases that need it, and what they have in common is that there is no
database ahead of the dump to protect. A working tree with no marker is
one: a clone onto a host that has never loaded it, which is the restore
case, and what makes a clone a whole deployment rather than a settings
file. A database with nothing in it is the other, and it is the same case
reached from the other side -- a store deleted, a volume restored from a
backup that did not include it, `sqlite.Open` handed a path that has
never held one -- where the working tree survived and the marker with it.

That second one used to be the one shape of this that lost data rather
than recovering from it. The marker answers "has the repository moved
since this host last agreed with it" and knows nothing about the
database, so a host whose store was gone read `marker == HEAD`, imported
nothing, came up empty, and the next sync exported that empty database
over the dump, committed it and pushed it -- with nothing further out to
object, because the remote was not ahead: this host really had written
the commit under it. The repository that exists to be the off-host copy
of the deployment was deleted by the deployment. (The paired case was
already handled: `scripts/setup.sh` moves the working tree aside
alongside the store on a schema bump, so the daemon re-seeds -- or, where
there is a remote to clone the tree back from, reformats the repository
over it, which is a few paragraphs below. It was the unpaired one --
store gone, tree kept -- that had no answer.) An empty
database now takes the whole repository, which costs nothing by
definition and is the restore an operator wanted, and the export in that
direction is refused outright and reported in the State pane rather than
committed (`staterepo.ErrDatabaseEmpty`) -- because a database that goes
away underneath a daemon that is already running cannot be restored on
the spot: an import that replaces every row is not something to do with
runs in flight holding the ids, so it waits for a restart. "Nothing in
it" means no row in any table, bar the schema stamp every database has
from the moment it is created; a database with a single task in it is one
this host is responsible for and takes the ordinary path.

If a pull arrives that cannot be applied -- a dump stamped with a schema
this build does not know, or rows that will not insert -- the daemon
stops exporting until it can. Writing the database over those files
would commit a revert of somebody's merged pull request and push it,
which is a worse answer than sitting still with the failure named in the
bootstrap pane.

Schema changes are destructive here, deliberately. A dump this build
cannot read is no more importable than a database it cannot open, so
`staterepo.Load` refuses an older or newer stamp outright rather than
guessing at a migration, and `scripts/setup.sh` moves the working tree
aside alongside the store on a schema bump. The encrypted secrets file is
carried across rather than archived with it: it is the one thing in there
that cannot be regenerated.

Archiving the tree is the whole answer for a deployment with no remote:
the daemon finds nothing, seeds a repository from its fresh database, and
carries on. For one with a remote it was not an answer at all, and said
it was — the next start's first act is to clone the archived tree back
down, dump, schema stamp and all, `Load` refuses it, `fatalStateRepoLoad`
stops the process, and systemd restarts it into the identical failure for
as long as anybody leaves it running. Every part of that loop is
behaving correctly, which is why it went unnoticed until somebody read
for it (grain/task-44).

So the schema bump says what it did, since it is the step that decided
those rows were not worth keeping when it moved the store holding them
aside. It leaves `<data-dir>/state-repo.reformat` — in the data
directory, which outlives both the store and the tree it has just
archived — and the next start reads it: `staterepo.Reformat` exports the
fresh database over the dump it cannot read, in one commit naming the
schema it left and the one it arrived at, pushes that, and removes the
note, so it authorises the schema change that wrote it and no later one.
The rows that were there stay in the history and stop being the tip; a
restore from that point on gives the deployment back as it is now, which
is the same thing the archived store means on the host.

It is asked rather than inferred. "A dump this build cannot read, and an
empty database" is also exactly what a restore looks like — a repository
cloned onto a new machine by an operator who wants its contents back —
and re-seeding on that would delete the only copy of a deployment whose
real answer is "run the build that wrote it". A schema mismatch with no
note behind it therefore still stops the process, with a journal line
that names both readings. `grain state reformat` writes the same note by
hand, for the deployments `setup.sh` never runs on: a binary replaced by
hand, an image pinned in the unit file. It needs neither the store, which
on a host in that state is usually one this build cannot open, nor the
network.

Destructive is what a schema change is when nobody carried the rows
across, and that is a statement about the *path*, not about schema
changes as such. `setup.sh` moves the store aside before the new build
ever opens it, so by the time anything can decide, the rows are gone and
all that is left is to say so. The UI's Upgrade button is on the other
side of that line: the build being replaced is still running, still has
the database open, and can write it out — so it does, and the deployment
comes back on its own rows (grain/task-59, "A schema change the button
can survive", below). The two answers meet in the same place, `pkg/staterepo`'s
`rewrite`, and differ in exactly one thing: the commit message. `Reformat`
commits "the rows this replaces are not coming back", which is true of
the first; `Migrated` commits "these are the same rows", which is true of
the second. The diffs are indistinguishable — every table rewritten at
once — so the sentence is the only thing a reader six months later has to
tell them apart, which is why there are two.

Not reaching the remote is a different fact, and the daemon treats it as
one. "The repository holds something this build must not overwrite" --
a schema stamp it cannot read, rows that will not import, a history that
diverged and is somebody's to resolve -- stops the process, because
