  which `hostStats` asks about the daemon's own `-data-dir` rather than
  about `/`: the daemon runs in a container whose root filesystem is an
  image layer nobody's runs fill, while the data directory is on the host
  volume that holds the store *and* every VM's disk overlay. That is the
  disk a deployment actually runs out of.

Both report 0/0 when there is no reading to be had, which the pane shows
as a dash and the trend charts skip rather than plotting as an empty
disk — the same "unavailable is not zero" treatment memory already got.

## Measuring throughput and latency

The previous section ends with "worth measuring before reaching for
either," and grain could not. Every moment needed to answer *how much is
this deployment getting done, and where does a task's day actually go?*
has been in the store since tasks became rows — filed, approved,
dispatched, finished, completed, closed — and nothing ever read them
together. `pkg/metrics` does, `GET /api/metrics` serves it, and `grain
metrics` prints it:

```console
$ grain metrics -window 7d
window: 2026-08-27T00:00:00Z -> 2026-09-03T00:00:00Z (168h0m0s)

throughput
  tasks filed                  42  (6.0/day)
  tasks completed              38  (5.4/day)
  tasks closed                  3
  attempts started             61
  attempts finished            60  (8.6/day)
  attempt outcomes         succeeded=45 failed=14 cancelled=1
  attempts per completion    1.58

capacity
  mean concurrent runs       0.42 of 3  (14% of the limit)
  live now                      2

latency (stages that ended inside the window)
  stage                                        n        p50        p90        max
  filed -> approved                           12      4m12s     1h2m0s    3h10m0s
  approved -> attempt started                 38        31s      2m10s       9m0s
  attempt started -> agent's first turn       57      3m20s      6m41s      11m2s
  agent's first turn -> attempt finished      57      9m11s     21m30s      48m0s
  one whole attempt                           60     12m48s     26m10s      52m0s
  attempt finished -> next attempt started     8       2m0s       4m0s       6m0s
  first attempt started -> completed          38      9m10s      22m0s      48m0s
  filed -> completed                          38      12m0s      50m0s    3h10m0s

backlog (right now, not over the window)
  awaiting_reply=1  proposed=1  queued=4  running=2
  oldest queued: task 51, waiting 2h14m0s
```

**A window bounds measurements; a scope bounds which tasks they are
about.** The window is the span a sample has to have *ended* inside — a
task completed this morning contributes its whole lead time even if it
was filed last month, which is what makes a report answer "what did this
deployment deliver during these dates" rather than "what happened
entirely within them". The scope (`metrics.Scope`, grain/task-83) is the
other question and a later one: a report about a repo, or about one
person's work, which `GET /api/metrics` takes as repeatable `?repo=` and
`?author=` parameters, a report board carries in its query, and `grain
metrics` takes as repeatable `-repo` and `-author` flags beside the span:

```console
$ grain metrics -since 2026-08-01 -until 2026-09-01 -repo acme/widgets -author ada
window: 2026-08-01T00:00:00Z -> 2026-09-01T00:00:00Z (744h0m0s)
scope:  tasks in acme/widgets, by ada

throughput
  tasks filed                  19  (0.6/day)
  tasks completed              17  (0.5/day)
  ...
```

**The span is said one of two ways and the scope is printed back.**
`-window` is a length ending now, which is the everyday reading;
`-since`/`-until` are actual dates, which is what "how did acme/widgets
go last month" needs and what no window can say (either takes a date like
`2026-08-01` or a full RFC 3339 timestamp, and a bare date is midnight
UTC so a report's boundaries do not move with a deployment's timezone
setting). Both are parsed by the command before it asks, so a typo is a
sentence from the command the operator ran rather than a 400 relayed back
from a daemon. The `scope:` line is the scope the daemon says it computed
under, echoed back by the endpoint and printed for the same reason the
report board prints it under the board's name: the printout is what ends
up pasted into a pull request comment or a weekly note, and a scoped
number under a bare `window:` header is one somebody will quote at the
wrong question. A report over every task prints no such line, which is
what a report has always been.

It is applied once, at the top of `Compute`, before a single number is
taken, and that is the whole of why it lives in `pkg/metrics` rather than
in the caller: a report is computed from five slices — the tasks, their
runs, the states the backlog is read off, and the two census tables the
tool and CI sections come from — and narrowing them by five separate
rules is how a report comes out with its throughput over one set of tasks
and its tool census over another. Two inputs are deliberately left alone.
A `RunCycle` tick belongs to the deployment rather than to any set of
tasks, so the cycles section says what it always says; and the
concurrency ceiling is the deployment's, which makes a scoped
`utilization` readable as "the share of capacity these tasks took" —
a real question, and not the same one as "was the deployment full".

**Nothing is stored, and nothing is counted on a hot path.** A report is
derived from the rows every time it is asked for, the same way
`task_state` is a view rather than a column
(`docs/data-model.md`: "anything derivable is derived, never stored").
There is no counter to increment, nothing to reset, and no way for a
metric to drift from the task it describes — retry a task, close it,
edit it, and every report from then on says what the record now says.
The cost is a full scan of `task` and `task_run` per report, which is
what a single-operator deployment can afford and what a much larger one
would have to revisit.

**With one deliberate exception: what sandboxes have cost is a counter
(grain/task-315).** "How many sandboxes, agent and CI, have we used so
far?" is not derivable from any row grain keeps. A sandbox exists for
the life of a run and is destroyed with it; the System pane reports the
ones that are up *now*; and nothing anywhere remembered the ones that
are gone, so the only route to an answer was counting job-start lines in
the journal — a floor rather than a figure, and unobtainable for any
stretch the log reader's ceiling could not reach back past. `task_run`
is close but not the same fact (a run's row says nothing about how long
a *machine* was held, and CI's sandboxes are not runs at all), and
`ci_job` is bounded by a retention sweep, so a count over it *goes down*
on the day the sweep runs. So `sandbox_usage` holds two rows of
counters, one per kind, bumped when a sandbox is asked for and again
when it is released: how many were attempted, how many came up, how many
were seen to stop, and how long those lived. They are in the store
rather than in the daemon because the deployment this was written for
had three upgrade shutdowns and a 52-restart crash loop in one day, and
a counter that resets on any of those reads zero at exactly the moments
somebody wants the number.

Three things it says about itself rather than leaving to a reader.
Sandbox-*hours* are the figure that matters and are counted beside the
count: a 36-minute image build and a 40-second lint are not the same
sandbox in any sense an operator cares about. A sandbox that was asked
for and never came up is counted as attempted and not as created, since
it spent something too, and a retry is a second attempt because it is a
second sandbox. And one whose daemon stopped while it was live is
counted as created and never as finished, which makes the missing time
readable — `created - finished` is exactly what grain did not see stop —
rather than guessed at. It is per kind and nothing finer; the
per-repository and per-job breakdown that answers "what does granule cost
against grain" is the next step, and is why these are aggregates rather
than a row per sandbox that would need a retention bound of its own.

It reaches a reader in two places: the System pane, under the live
sandboxes it is the history of — which is also what `read_deployment_health`
hands an agent — and the report, as a section that says in its own
heading that it is *not* over the window above it. `grain metrics`
prints the same:

```console
sandboxes (since 2026-09-05T04:08:00Z, NOT over the window above)
  kind          built     failed      hours      mean each  unaccounted
  agent            46          0        3.0          3m55s            0
  ci             2367          3     1201.0         30m29s            3
  all            2413          3     1204.0         29m59s            3
```

Costing a change is that read twice, before and after — which is exactly
what the two open tasks on CI job keying and a buildx cache backend each
ask somebody to hand-measure today.

**One moment had to start being recorded: `task_run.agent_started_at`.**
A run's `started_at` is stamped by dispatch, before any sandbox exists
(`Store.SetRunSandbox`), so `finished_at - started_at` is a VM boot, a
clone, a capability mint *and* the agent's own work, fused into one
number that cannot answer the question the previous section asks.
`RunDispatch` now records the moment it hands the run to
`agent.Framework.Run`, which splits that in two: **attempt started ->
agent's first turn** is the setup a golden image or a warm spare would
cut, and **agent's first turn -> attempt finished** is what the agent
framework spent, which grain does not control. Writing it can never cost
a run — a failure there is logged and the dispatch proceeds — and it is a
nullable column added by an ordinary `ensure*Column` migration, so an
existing store keeps working and its older runs simply report no split.

**A window bounds measurements, not rows.** A sample belongs to a window
when the moment it *ended* falls inside it, so a task filed last month
and completed this morning contributes its whole lead time. That makes
the report answer "what did this deployment deliver during these dates"
rather than "what happened entirely within them," which nothing ever
asks.

**A missing moment is skipped, never guessed**, which is why every stage
carries its own `n` and two stages of one report legitimately disagree
about how many samples they have. A run that failed in setup never
reached an agent, so it has no setup or agent sample — but it was still
an attempt, and still took time, so it is in `one whole attempt`. A task
a human filed directly was approved in the instant it was filed, so it is
left out of `filed -> approved` rather than counted as a zero that would
drag the percentile of the proposals that really did wait.

**The stages do not sum to the lead time,** and are not meant to. A task
can sit in `awaiting_reply` for a day, back off between attempts, or wait
on a dependency, and none of those is a stage anything records the start
of. Each stage is measured on its own; the lead time is what somebody who
filed a task actually waited, and the rest are answers to why it is what
it is.

**Throughput alone cannot say whether a deployment is fast enough,** so
the report carries the two gauges it has to be read against: the backlog
(by `task_state`'s own vocabulary, since "not finished" covers queued,
blocked, awaiting a reply and failed, which are four different problems —
and counting only the unfinished states, since every task whose run is
over, submitted or not, is a census rather than a queue), and occupancy
as a fraction of
`max_concurrent`. Idle capacity next to a
deep queue is a scheduling problem; saturated capacity next to a deep
queue is a capacity one. They are the first two numbers any optimization
here should have to move.

**The UI reads the same report,** in a pane of its own at `/metrics`,
reached from the sidebar beside Settings and System. (It was a tab of
the System pane until grain/task-173 — see "Metrics is its own
destination on the sidebar" above for why it left.) The window picker sends the same
strings `-window` takes, the throughput
buckets are drawn as sparklines, and the two presentation rules above
are enforced rather than described: the latency stages are a table of
independent distributions and never a stacked bar, which would draw a
claim about them adding up that the numbers do not make, and the backlog
is a section of its own headed "right now, not over the window". Each
stage's `n` sits beside its percentiles, and a percentile with too few
samples behind it to mean what its name says — fewer than 10 for a p90,
100 for a p99 — is dimmed and footnoted rather than shown as if it were
one. Unlike the System pane's own panels there is no poll: a report costs
a full scan every time it is asked for, so it loads once and reloads
when the window changes or Refresh is clicked.

**The Metrics pane takes a scope of its own (grain/task-379),** so
`/metrics?f=repo:any:acme/widgets` is the report over one repo and the
pane carries the same `NarrowingBar` every other narrowed view does. It
is a *second* narrowing, held by App beside the one every task view
shares and parsed out of the URL as `paths.js`'s `metricsNarrowing`.
Sharing the one would have been a line of code and the wrong behaviour:
opening this pane from the rail over a list narrowed to "the failed
tasks I filed" would silently scope the deployment's own report to it,
and a link to a scoped report would narrow the list waiting behind the
pane. So the rail's entry clears it — that entry is the deployment's
whole report, whatever is on screen behind it — and only a link or the
pane's own toolbar sets one. The toolbar is what makes a scope that
arrived in a link a control rather than an invisible state: it is on
screen, it says what was ignored, and `Clear` puts the whole report
back. It rides in the URL rather than staying pane state, for the reason
everything else here does — a report somebody scoped is the thing they
paste into that standup note.

That is also what collapsed two components into one. With a scope, a
window picker, a "not in force" line and a toolbar, this pane *is* a
report board with no board row behind it, so `ReportBoard.jsx` draws
both and `MetricsPage.jsx` is gone: a board names its sections and its
scope in the store, the pane takes its scope from the URL, and a board
that names no sections already fell back to the whole report. The pane's
sections are therefore in `report.js`'s own order now rather than the
slightly different one that page had.

What this still does not have is a history of its own: because nothing
is stored, a report can only ever be computed from rows that still
exist, so a task deleted from the store takes its own past contribution
with it.

## Measuring the daemon's own tick

The section above ends with the pair worth reading together — idle
capacity next to a deep queue is a scheduling problem — and leaves the
next question unanswered. `queue_wait` (approved -> the first attempt
starting) is the one latency stage that is grain's own scheduling rather
than anyone's work, and two entirely different causes produce the same
number:

1. the deployment was at `max_concurrent` and the task genuinely waited
   for headroom, which `runs.utilization` near 1.0 already shows; or
2. there was headroom the whole time, and the task waited on the tick —
   `-poll-interval`, plus however long a `RunCycle` pass itself takes
   before it reaches the dispatch decision.

Nothing measured the second, so a tick that had quietly grown to minutes
under a large store looked exactly like a busy deployment. `GET
/api/metrics` now carries a `cycles` section beside `runs`, and `grain
metrics` prints it right after capacity, so both causes are on screen
before the `queue_wait` row is:

```console
reconcile tick (this daemon, since it started -- not stored, so not over the window)
  ticks measured              720  (of 5304 run; older ones forgotten)
                                    p50        p90        max
  tick duration                    83.4ms      1.42s      4.9s
  tick to tick                        30s        30s     34.9s
  cycle start -> dispatch          21.1ms     34.6ms    212.7ms
  scheduling floor: 30.02s  (tick-to-tick p50 + dispatch p50 -- the queue wait a task pays
    for grain's own scheduling with no contention at all)

  reconciler         wait p50        p50        p90   failed
  schedule             1.1ms      2.4ms      8.9ms        0
  dispatch            21.1ms     11.2ms     48.0ms        0
  sync                32.4ms     47.1ms      1.31s        3
```

**The number the section builds to is the scheduling floor.** Ticks do
not overlap (`cmd/grain`'s `reconcile` waits for one to return before the
next interval starts), so tick-to-tick is the loop's real period, which
is the `-poll-interval` only while a tick is fast compared to it. Adding
the dispatch wait to it gives what a task pays for grain's own scheduling
with no contention involved at all. A `queue_wait` p50 near that floor is
the tick; a `queue_wait` p50 far above it is the deployment being full.
They are opposite problems with opposite fixes — more concurrency for one,
a faster or better-ordered cycle for the other — and until now the report
could not tell them apart.

**A per-reconciler breakdown, not one number for the tick.** The
reconcilers run in order ("Reconcilers, not a pipeline"), so a
pull-request sync that has grown to a minute is a minute every decision
behind it did not get to spend, and a single tick duration cannot say
which one grew. Each reconciler reports how far into the cycle it
started, how long it took, and how many of those cycles it ended in an
error — that last one because a reconciler that is fast *because* it
fails immediately is not a fast reconciler, and a duration alone cannot
tell the two apart.

**The dispatch wait is recorded by the cycle, not picked out of the list
by name.** `pkg/orchestrator` is the package that knows which reconciler
is the decision a queued task is actually waiting for — it names them —
so it reports that offset as its own field (`CycleTiming.DispatchWait`)
rather than leaving every consumer to hardcode the string `"dispatch"`.

### Why this one measurement is in memory

Everything else in `pkg/metrics` is derived from rows that already exist,
and holds to `docs/data-model.md`'s "anything derivable is derived, never
stored." A tick is the one thing that leaves no row at all: it reads the
store, decides, and returns. That left two options.

A **row per cycle** would be durable across restarts and queryable over
any window. It costs a new table, a write on every single tick forever
(2,880 a day at the default 30s `-poll-interval`) and a growth curve
nothing prunes — to measure something whose whole purpose is to say
whether *this process, right now* is dispatching promptly. It would also
make the measurement change what it measures: a tick that writes a row is
a tick with a store write in it.

A **ring in the process** — `orchestrator.CycleTimes`, 720 cycles, six
hours at the default interval — costs bounded memory, no schema, no
write, and stores nothing, which keeps the doctrine intact rather than
carving an exception into it. That is what this is. The honest cost is
that it is lost on restart, and the report says so rather than hiding it:
the section is scoped to "this daemon, since it started", carries
`observed` alongside `n` so a truncated ring is visible, and reports
`first`/`last` as the span it really covers, which is however long the
ring is rather than however long a window was asked for. Tick history
belongs to the process that produced it anyway — a daemon that has just
restarted has a fresh tick, with none of the accumulated store the slow
tick this exists to catch would have been slow because of.

The wiring follows the same seam the sandbox-health pane already uses:
`pkg/ui` does not import `pkg/orchestrator`, so `cmd/grain`'s own
`cycleTimesAdapter` is the one place both types are in scope, and the
ring is package-level in `cmd/grain` because the UI/API server starts
before the reconcile loop that writes into it (the same ordering
`reconcilerDown` and `livePullRequests` already straddle). A UI with no
reconcile loop behind it reports `"enabled": false` rather than a tick of
zero: "nobody measured it" and "the tick costs nothing" are opposite
answers, and only one of them is ever true.

`tests/e2e/loadtest_test.go` had measured `RunCycle` tick duration with
instrumentation of its own since it was written ("RunCycle tick duration:
n=… p50=… p95=…"), and no longer does. The harness passes a `CycleTimes`
into the `Deps` it ticks and reports out of that instead, so the load
test and a deployment read one measurement taken by one piece of code,
rather than two that agree only for as long as nobody changes either. It
is also the more useful of the two: the harness now reports the dispatch
wait and the per-reconciler breakdown alongside the tick, and fails on
what a stopwatch around `RunCycle` could not see at all — a cycle that did
not run every reconciler, and a p95 dispatch wait past a third of the
per-tick budget, which is a queued task waiting on the tick itself rather
than on a deployment that was full. A tick growing under a large store is
the thing a load test is best placed to catch, and that is the shape it
now catches it in.

## Measuring what a run does with its tools

The two sections above measure the outside of a run: when it started, how
long it took, how it was recorded. Everything that makes a run *hard* is
on the inside of it — a tool that answers unhelpfully, a search-and-edit
loop that keeps missing, a command that gets killed by a bound nobody
chose, a CI wait that never resolves — and none of it was measured
anywhere. `docs/agent-ergonomics.md` is a whole review of that surface
argued entirely from code-reading and single transcripts, because there
was no aggregate to argue from.

The counting was already happening. `orchestrator.toolCallSummary` has
always tallied every tool a run called and how many of those calls came
back as errors, for every run including the successful ones — and then
rendered it into English in `task_run.detail`, a column a human reads one
row at a time. Nothing could aggregate it, because it was prose.

So the census is stored as data, and `grain metrics` prints it under the
latency table:

```console
tool use (37 run(s) in the window recorded what they called)
  calls                      4127  (98 per run at the median, 212 at p90)
  errored calls               372  (9.0% of them -- a handful is the ordinary shape of this work)
  cut answers                  46  (1.1% of them -- calls whose answer grain shortened to fit the cap)
  tool                 runs    calls   errors timed out  mean bytes   p95 bytes       cut     cut p50
  run_command            37     2894       7%    12 (0%)        1841     <=16383   21 (1%)     <=32767
  edit_file              31      704      22%         -          118       <=511         -           -
  read_file              29      402       4%         -        4210     <=16383   25 (6%)     <=65535
  wait_for_checks        18       84       0%         -        1024      <=2047         -           -
  (p95 bytes is an upper bound: sizes are kept in base-2 buckets, so the real
   number is inside the octave below it. Read it with the cut columns rather than
   on its own -- the cap bounds these sizes, so a p95 under the cap means a tool
   whose answers fit or one whose answers are being cut down to fit, and only
   "cut" tells the two apart. cut p50 is how much the median cut dropped, taken
   from what each elision notice said it was dropping.)

CI waits (84 wait(s) across 18 run(s))
  verdicts                 passed=41 failed=28 timed_out=13 no_checks=2
  blocked                  p50 3m20s, p90 14m0s, max 15m0s
  pushes before green      2.4 on average, 7 at worst (over 16 run(s) that went green)

mid-run pull requests (34 run(s) in the window could have opened one)
  opened one themselves        21  (62% of them, 48 call(s) in all)
  repaired by the queue after  10% of the 21 that did, 31% of the 13 that did not
  (a repair is the merge queue cleaning up a red build the run left behind.
   It is recorded on the task, not the attempt: read the difference, not either rate.)
```

**This is the one measurement that had to be stored,** and it is stored
because it is not derivable from anything that survives the run.
`agent.Result` carries every call and every answer, and is discarded when
`RunDispatch` returns; the transcript is per-framework prose that a
tool's own output can forge (`orchestrator.outcomeOf` says why counting
calls out of it would be unsound); `task_run.detail` is a sentence. Two
tables, written once per run after its outcome, best-effort and logged
rather than surfaced on failure — a measurement that cannot be taken is
not a reason to fail the run being measured. `task_run_tool` is the
census, one row per run per tool; `task_run_check_wait` is one row per
`wait_for_checks` call, because the CI loop is a sequence rather than a
total. Neither needed a `SchemaVersion` bump: `CREATE TABLE IF NOT
EXISTS` creates a *missing* table on an existing store perfectly well,
and an older store simply starts filling them.

**Counts and sizes only.** No argument, no result and no fragment of
output crosses into a measurement table. What a run's commands said stays
in the transcript, which has its own bounds and its own reasons to exist.

**A result-size percentile is a bound, and says so.** An exact one needs
every sample, which means a stored row per tool *call* — hundreds a run,
read whole on every report. Each census row instead carries a base-2
histogram of its result sizes, so `p95 <=65535` means "95% of those
answers were at most 64 KB", with the real number inside the octave
below. That is precise enough for the question it exists to answer: what
should `mcp.maxToolResultBytes` be — a question it has now answered, and
the 64 KB guess it was left at is 16 KB because of what it said (see "No
single answer may eat the run's context" for the window it was read from). It cannot answer that question twice, though: these are
the sizes of answers as runs received them, so a cap in force truncates
the distribution at itself. The `cut` columns beside them are what
survives that, and are the half to read when the question is whether the
cap is sized right.

**Three facts had to be read back out of a tool's own text,** because
nothing else carries them: whether a `run_command` was ended by its bound
rather than by the command (a bounded-out call is an error like any
other), which of its four verdicts a `wait_for_checks` reached (every
wait_for_checks answer is a success), and whether grain shortened the
answer to fit the result cap (the size recorded for a call is the size
after any cut, so nothing else in the row can tell). `mcp.RunCommandTimedOut`,
`mcp.ReadCheckWait` and `mcp.ResultElision` live beside the code that
writes those sentences and match markers that the sentences are *built*
from, which is the only arrangement where rewording one cannot silently
zero the other. Only grain's own trailing notices are searched for the
first, so a command whose output quotes the notice is not a command that
timed out; the hedged `exit=137` notice (which may be the OOM killer) and
the stalled-transport notice are counted as neither, since neither is a
bound running out. An elision notice can only be in the middle of an
answer rather than at the end of it, so the third anchors on the notice
starting a line of its own instead — see "A cap censors the measurement
that sized it".

**Attempt outcomes are also split by what they mean.** `task_run.outcome`
is coarse enough that `cancelled` is both "a human closed the task" and
"the run hit its two-hour wall", and `failed` is both "the CLI died" and
"the run exhausted `-max-agent-turns`" — pairs with different fixes,
distinguishable only by the sentence recorded beside them. `grain
metrics` prints a second line under the outcomes for how those attempts
actually ended, `no_action` among them: a run that had tools, used them
and produced nothing is the purest measure of this surface failing, and
it used to be one key in a map beside `succeeded`. The sentences are
built in `pkg/model` and read back there (`model.EndingOf`), so the
writer and the reader cannot drift apart.

**The CI loop is measured end to end** because the prompt sends every run
around it: push, `wait_for_checks`, fix, push again. A deployment where
most waits end `timed_out` has `mcp.DefaultWaitForChecksTimeout` set
wrong for its CI; one where most end `no_checks` is sending runs to wait
for CI that does not exist; and "pushes before green" is what the loop
costs in rework — 1.0 is CI right first time. A push is counted from the
`git push` in a `run_command`'s own arguments, and only from a call that
did not error, because a rejected push is not a push: it under-counts
rather than over-counts, which is the right direction for a number whose
point is how much rework there was.

**The last stretch of that loop is `open_pull_request`,** and it gets a
section of its own because its two questions are different shapes. The
first is a share: of the runs that were offered the loop at all, how many
took it. "Offered" is the whole of what makes that number mean anything,
so the denominator is stated beside the rate and is narrow — a run that
finished inside the window, recorded a census, and belonged to a task
with a repo to push to, since `BuildPrompt` puts the push/check/repair
paragraph and the sentence naming the tool inside `task.Target != nil`
and a task with no target was never asked.

The second is a comparison and is deliberately not reported as a rate.
"A run opened its pull request and the merge queue still had to repair
it" means nothing alone: some share of branches go red for reasons no
amount of watching would have caught. So both cohorts are printed with
their own denominators — the runs that called the tool and the runs that
did not, each with the share whose task the merge queue later had to
repair (`Observation.MergeQueueRepairAt`, or the older `model.LinkFixTask`
for a task repaired before grain/task-271; both are counted, so a report
spanning that change does not show the rate falling to zero on the day
the recording moved), which is the recorded form of a red build outliving
the run that pushed it. Read the difference, not either number. The
signal is coarse in two known ways, both stated where the number is read:
it is recorded on the task rather than the attempt, so every finished
attempt of a task that ever went red counts as having gone red; and a
repair can only happen to a task that got as far as a pull request, which
flatters any cohort holding runs that pushed nothing.

**The fine-grained version of that question is not counted in bulk, on
purpose.** "Did a push follow the last failing report" is answerable by
eye from one run's persisted transcript, which is ordered — but a
transcript renders a call as a `> name(args)` line that a tool's own
*output* can contain verbatim (`agent/claude/transcript.go`), so a count
taken over transcripts would measure forgeries alongside calls. Both
numbers above come from the census rows instead, which are written by
grain from `agent.Result` and are not text an agent can author. Nothing
new is stored for either: `model.TaskTiming` reads two derived columns it
did not before — whether the task had a target, and whether it carries a
fix-task link — because a run's own row says nothing about the task it
was for and both questions are about the task.

**Everything else about it follows this package's existing rules.** A
census row has no moment of its own, so it belongs to a window when its
*run* finished inside it. A run that recorded none contributes to nothing
rather than to a zero — which is why `tool use` states how many runs are
behind it, and why none of the three sections renders at all, in the CLI
or the UI, until something has recorded one. A deployment upgraded into this reports
no tool use for its older runs, and that is the honest answer: nobody was
measuring.

## Merge capacity is its own number

Concurrency was one number: `max_concurrent`, the count of runs
`dispatch.Cycle` would let be in flight. Every kind of run drew on it
equally, which put the two least alike kinds in direct competition. Most
runs are new work, at the start of its life. A few are the merge queue's
own repairs of a pull request that will not land — the last step of work
that is already committed, pushed and reviewed. A saturated deployment
starved exactly the second kind, and starving it is expensive twice over:
the branch a repair targets keeps moving while the repair waits, so one
delayed long enough has to start over, and the queue behind it waits
too.

What counts as a merger is `Store.mergerTaskSQL`, written once and read
by all three places that decide it. It has two arms: a task the queue has
sent back to work on its own branch (`Observation.MergeQueueRepairAt`
with no `completed_at`, which is what a repair is since grain/task-271),
or one of the separate fix tasks the queue used to file for that
(`Origin.Reason == ReasonFix`), which a database may still hold one of.

`model.Limits` is that one number split in two — `MaxWorkers` and
`MaxMergers`, in the store as `grain_config.max_workers`/`max_mergers`,
on the daemon as `-max-workers`/`-max-mergers`, in Settings as "Max
worker agents" and "Max merge agents". The rule they make is
deliberately asymmetric:

- no more than `MaxWorkers` runs of ordinary work are ever live;
- no more than `Limits.AgentRuns` ordinary worker and merger runs are live
  together, which is `MaxWorkers + MaxMergers`;
- console sessions (the director and every other configured session, on
  any team) are outside both counts: each is admitted whenever it is
  ready, one live run per session.

A merger is bounded only by the second, so it may take a worker's free
slot; a worker is bounded by both, so it can never take a merger's. With
3 workers and 2 mergers a deployment can be running five mergers, or
three workers and two mergers, but never four workers and never six
ordinary runs. Capacity kept back for finishing work is reachable by work
that is nearly finished, and by nothing else.

`MaxWorkers + MaxMergers` is `Limits.Total`, and since grain CI runs its
jobs in this deployment's own sandboxes it is a count of *sandboxes*
rather than of runs: `Limits.CIJobs` — `grain_config.max_ci_jobs`, “Max
CI jobs” in Settings, one by default — is how much of that total is CI's and no run's, which is why the second
rule is `AgentRuns` and not the sum. That is a static split rather than
a borrowing one; "Grain's own CI" above has the whole of why, and what
it costs.

The split lands in the two places the old count did, and nowhere new.
`Limits.Admits` is the ordinary rule, written once: `dispatch.Cycle` asks
it before spending capacity it can see (`Store.LiveRunCounts`, the live
count split the same way, and `Store.ReadyMergers` to say which ready task
is which kind), and `Store.StartRun` asks it again inside the transaction
that records the run, which is where the limit is actually enforced — two
overlapping cycles cannot both spend the last slot. A
candidate whose own half is full is passed over rather than ending the
cycle, the same skip a task still backing off gets, so a queue of
ordinary work at the head of the backlog no longer hides the repair
behind it from the capacity kept for it.

Console sessions are the control-plane exception, not a third
configurable worker kind. `Store.directorTaskSQL` requires the identity
automation writes — `ReasonConsoleSession`, `Interactive`, and a
`console-session:<id>` tag — rather than matching a title or trusting an
arbitrary interactive task. `Store.ReadyDirectors` returns every ready
session task, the director's and every other configured session's on any
team, and each is admitted whether or not the ordinary pool, or its
team's own counts, are full; `StartRun` holds no count against one
either. A session neither cancels nor preempts a worker, so total agent
runs may exceed `MaxWorkers + MaxMergers` by however many sessions are
live. Its sandbox is still charged to the ledger
(`Limits.ChargeDirectorSandbox`) for as long as its run lasts, so every
other admission sees the machine it uses; only the budget check is
skipped.

This used to be one reserved bypass for the whole deployment
(`Limits.AdmitsDirector`, `DirectorBypass = 1`). Because a session's run
can live for hours — `chat` blocks for up to an hour per call — one live
session on any team held every other team's and user's session in the
queue, logging "director capacity full" every cycle until somebody pressed
Run now (grain/task-2323). A task has at most one live run anyway, so
each session is already limited to one; the shared slot bought nothing
but the wait. Settings host commitment and Metrics accordingly count only
`max_workers + max_mergers` (and CI jobs); sessions have no slot of their
own to report.

`-max-concurrent` still parses, as the former spelling of
`-max-workers`: a deployment's unit file is written once by
`scripts/setup.sh` and the Upgrade button then replaces only the binary,
so dropping the old flag would stop the daemon at the moment nobody is
watching. The stored column is migrated rather than reinterpreted
(`ensureConfigWorkerMergerColumns`): `max_workers` is backfilled from
`max_concurrent`, which is then dropped, and `max_mergers` starts at
`model.DefaultMaxMergers` — one — so an upgraded deployment keeps the
ordinary concurrency it had and gains a single slot the merge queue
cannot be shut out of. Setting it to 0 puts a deployment back exactly
where it was: the merge queue's own repairs contending for worker
capacity like anything else.

## A review, before the merge

A task can carry a review: `Task.ReviewTemplateID`, the id of a
`model.Template` whose title, body and grants are what a *second* agent
is dispatched with once the first one's work is done. The "reviews"
reconciler files it (`orchestrator.SyncReviews`), the merge queue waits
for it, and everything else about it is machinery that already existed.

The shape is the separate fix task the merge queue used to file before
grain/task-271, reused deliberately: a repair now runs as another attempt
of the task itself, but stacking a second agent on a first one's branch
is still exactly what a review needs. A
review task's `Base` is the reviewed task's branch (`model.BranchName`,
derived, so nothing has to agree with anything), its `AutoMerge` is set,
and it is filed already approved at the head of the backlog. So it is a
stacked branch: the reviewing agent reads the diff on the branch under
review, commits its fixes onto its own branch off that one, and
`syncEntry` merges its pull request straight back into the branch it
reviewed the moment it reads clean. That is as close to "a new agent on
the same branch" as grain can be, given that a run's branch is a function
of its task id and always will be. Like one of those fix tasks, a review
is never a
merge queue entry in its own right (`isQueueMember`): it merges into
another task's branch, not into the repo's base, so it neither takes a
head position nor waits for one.

What is new is the wait. A reviewed task does not merge while its review
is outstanding, so the order is work, review, merge — not work, merge,
and a review of something that has already landed. The wait is on the
*declaration* rather than on the review task existing, which matters more
than it looks: filing the review and advancing the merge queue are two
reconcilers in one cycle, and if the gate were "has a review task been
filed" then whether a change merged before its review existed would come
down to which of them ran first. `Task.ReviewTemplateID` alone holds the
merge; filing the review starts the clock rather than starting the wait.

And the wait is bounded, for the reason the wait on an automatic repair
is (`defaultRepairDeadline`): a task holding its merge for a review reads
PrClean, not PrPending, so the CI stall clock never times it, and the
review's own pull request is never a queue head, so nothing times that
either. A review neither finished nor abandoned after six hours is said
so on the task, which is then blocked in the merge queue's own sense —
it stops being anyone's head, so the tasks behind it move, and it merges
as soon as it reads clean like any other task the queue has given up
driving. That is the deliberate choice between the two ways to be wrong:
merging a change whose review never arrived, having said so, is
recoverable; holding a finished change out of the repo forever on a
review that is not coming is not.

A template rather than a body typed onto the task, for the same reason
`Schedule.TemplateID` is one: "read this branch and fix what you find" is
the same paragraph on every task it is attached to, and the instructions
worth improving once. Nothing about a template says it is a review; what
makes it one is being named as a task's own. Grain appends the subject
the template cannot know — which task, which branch, which pull request —
and supplies nothing else, so what the reviewing agent is told is what
somebody wrote in Templates.

It is attachable from the new-task form, from a task's own edit form (the
usual case: a task is filed, and somewhere before it finishes somebody
decides its change wants a second pass), from `PATCH /api/tasks/{id}`,
and from `grain create -review-template`/`grain update -review-template`.
An edit reaches any review not yet filed, since the template is resolved
when the work is done rather than when the task is created — so a review
can be attached to a task that is queued, running, or already finished
and waiting to merge. Once the review task exists, changing it changes
nothing: exactly one review is ever filed per task (`LinkReviewTask` is
both the record of that and what the merge queue waits on), and the
picker locks and says which task is carrying it out. A review task
carries no review of its own, which is what stops reviews nesting.

### What a review does with what it finds

The policy (owner, 10-22; task 5008) is that **the reviewer fixes
everything it can, and holds only on what needs the owner.** Every
review prompt says it: the declared-review body `fileReviewTask`
appends, the security-review system template, and the
`add_review_comment` tool's own description.

- **Fix, then go through.** Bugs, missing tests, docs that no longer
  match, an unsigned or unpinned image: the reviewer commits the fix on
  its stacked branch and pushes. The fix merges back into the reviewed
  branch, grain CI runs on the new head, and the change goes through. A
  declared review never withdrew auto-merge for this. A security hold or
  an `on-findings` gating trigger is now released by a review whose fixes
  have *merged back* and which left no findings, exactly as a review that
  read the change clean releases it (`reviewOutcome`, `settleSecurityHold`,
  `settlePathTriggerHold`). Fixes still open release nothing yet, and fixes
  closed without merging leave the change for a human. A security clearance
  stays pinned to the head it was read at, so a head that the fixes moved
  is classified again before it merges (`clearedForHead`). If the fixes
  touched the trust boundary themselves, they are held and reviewed in
  turn.
- **The security review fixes on the change's own branch** (owner,
  10-26; task 984). Stacked security-review pull requests were costing a
  full CI suite, repair cycles and a merge-queue entry each, and were
  stranded when the change merged first. So the security review is now
  filed onto the held change's branch itself
  (`model.LinkPushesReviewedBranch`, `putSecurityReview`): its checkout is
  that branch, the git proxy lets it push that branch and nothing else
  (`Store.GitPushBranch`) -- and only fast-forward it, never create,
  delete or force-move it (`Store.GitPushFastForwardOnly`, gitproxy's
  `refuseBorrowedBranchRewrite`), so it cannot replace the commits under
  review with ones it then clears as its own fixes -- and it never opens a
  pull request, so its fixes land in the change's own. It fetches and rebases before pushing, retries
  a rejected push once, and otherwise asks the owner. At its finish grain
  records the head it left (`model.LinkReviewerHead`, `recordReviewerHead`)
  -- unless the reviewed task has run since the review was filed, in which
  case that run's own finish files a fresh review. Fixes alone need no
  human: a review that finished with no open finding or question releases
  the hold and clears the change *at the head it left*, since that is what
  it read, its own fixes included; anything pushed after that head is
  classified again before it merges. That holds only for fixes off the
  trust boundary: no agent's trust-boundary edits are cleared on its own
  say-so (operator, 10-26, on this change's own security review). Fixes
  that touch a trust-boundary path, on grain's list or the repository's,
  leave a new head that is held afresh and given a second review
  (`reviewerFixesTouchBoundary`); that review's clean finish releases it,
  still with no Submit. The rule may be loosened later. A superseded or closed review can no longer
  push the branch, records no head and releases nothing. Security reviews
  already open with a branch of their own keep the stacked flow until they
  settle. Declared reviews and gating path-trigger reviews keep it too:
  they hold their change at the head of the merge queue (or under a
  path-trigger hold with several gating tasks) rather than releasing one
  security hold, so moving them is a separate change.
- **An in-place security review owns no CI** (task 1484). Sharing the
  branch did not stop the review from asking for CI as itself: its
  `wait_for_checks` started a full suite on the head the held task's own
  run was already judging, and the held task then started another on the
  head the review had pushed (bwsalmon/grain#5011 ran three commits
  twice each). Now the reviewed task owns the branch's CI
  (`model.Task.CIOwner`). `reconcileTaskCI` skips an in-place review, so it
  never starts, retries or flake-retries a run of its own. Its task-scoped
  CI calls (`wait_for_checks`, `run_ci_job`, `retrigger_ci`) are asked as
  the reviewed task and recorded on that task (`ui.Client.StartTaskCIRunOpt`).
  What it reads back (`pull_request_status`, `wait_for_checks`, its task
  page) is the reviewed task's verdict. One push, whoever made it, is one
  run, which `ci.Service.Start` hands to whichever task asks second. A
  closed in-place review cancels nothing on the branch. Stacked and
  declared reviews keep their own CI on their own branches.
- **Ask only what the owner must decide.** A design decision, a
  trade-off, or a behaviour change the brief does not settle goes in an
  `add_review_comment` call, written as a question with the reviewer's
  recommended answer. Any such call holds the change.
  `noteFindingsOnReviewedTask` withdraws auto-merge and records
  `model.LinkReviewQuestions`, which holds the review task, the comment
  that put the questions to the owner, and whether the change was merging
  itself before the questions held it. The task stays `awaiting_submit`.
  The inbox groups it under "Review needs your decision", with Reply and
  "Ship as is", and the task pane says the same and links the review.
- **The owner's reply is the decision.** The `review-questions`
  reconciler (`SyncReviewQuestions`) looks for a human comment newer than
  the questions, on the held task or on the review. When it finds one, it
  copies a reply left on the review onto the held task and sends that task
  back to the queue. Its conversation (the questions, the reply, and a
  note saying to carry the decision out) is in the next run's prompt.
  Auto-merge comes back when the change had it, so that run follows the
  same rule: it fixes what was decided, then goes through. Grain's own
  notes and agents' comments answer nothing. Submit is "ship as is": the
  change merges with the questions left open, and the hold is dropped.
- **Trust-boundary changes stay gated.** A change caught by a `human:
  required` trigger (in this repository `.grain/triggers/grain-declarations.yml`
  covers `.grain/**`, `sensitive: true`), or touching a path grain's own
  list says only a human may release, waits for its owner's Submit
  however clean its review was. The reviewer still fixes what it finds
  there; it just never releases the hold. Agents never self-release
  changes to CI, settings or declarations.

### Review threads on GitHub

New unresolved review threads on a grain-owned pull request, whether a
bot's (gemini-code-assist) or a person's on github.com, get the same
handling. The `review-threads` reconciler (`SyncReviewThreads`) reads the
pull request's review comments once the task's run is over (completed and
on the queue, or awaiting Submit). For threads nobody has sent a run for
yet, it sends the task one more run. That run's note lists each thread
and says to fix it or answer it with a reason
(`reply_to_pull_request_comment`), then resolve it
(`resolve_review_thread`). Every thread it was sent for is recorded on
the task (`model.LinkReviewThread`), so it sends one run per new batch of
threads and never loops: a reply in a handled thread, or a bot answering
the run's reply, sends nothing. A thread that was already resolved or
outdated when grain first saw it sends nothing either. Grain's own draft
reviews (`model.LinkDraftReview`) are left out, since those are the
owner's questions and not a run's to fix. Review and fix tasks stacked on
another task's branch are left out too. A change held on its review's
questions waits for its owner first.

The review task itself nests under the task it reviews, the way an
automatic fix nests under the one it repairs, and says which of the two
it is rather than borrowing the other's name: a "review" chip in the task
list, and `grain list -origin review` beside `-origin fix`. Both are
stacked on another task's branch; only one of them is a repair of a red
build.

## Pausing when the agent runs out of budget

A coding agent's credential has a budget, and it runs out: Claude Code
reports `Claude AI usage limit reached|<epoch>` for an OAuth account
whose five-hour window is spent, the Anthropic API answers `429` with a
`rate_limit_error`, and Gemini answers `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED` with a
`retryDelay`. None of that is a fact about the run that met it.

Read as an ordinary framework failure, though, that is exactly what it
became. The run was recorded `failed`, with the provider's refusal as its
diagnosis; the task took a place in its own failure streak for it and
backed off; every other run in flight kept going until it met the same
wall and did the same; and the next tick dispatched the next queued task
straight into it. A single window's exhaustion could walk the whole
backlog — each task spending an attempt, a sandbox and a VM boot to
discover something the deployment already knew — and take tasks to
`model.MaxConsecutiveFailures` and out of the queue for good, on the
strength of an outage none of them caused.

So a limit is now its own kind of failure, end to end.

`agent.UsageLimitError` is the type. Every framework recognises its own
provider's refusal and returns one instead of a plain error
(`pkg/agent/claude/usagelimit.go`, `pkg/agent/antigravity/usagelimit.go`,
`pkg/agent/codex/usagelimit.go`),
carrying what the provider said and, where it named one, when it will
serve again — an absolute instant (Claude's epoch) or a delay (Gemini's
`retryDelay`). What each package matches on is deliberately narrow, and
narrower still where a *successful* run is being read: `claude` reports
an account limit as readily in a run's final answer as in a failure, and
an agent that greps its own sandbox for the phrase must not be able to
put the deployment to sleep, so the successful path insists on the CLI's
own machine-readable `|<epoch>` form and reads only the terminal result
event, never tool output.

One of the three does not, in fact, recognise anything, and it is worth
knowing which: `agy` never repeats the provider's words. Measured on
1.1.27 against a stub of Gemini's endpoint refusing everything
(`docs/hand-runs/2026-09-08-agy-retry.md`), a `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED` with a
`retryDelay` reaches grain's stream as `Agent execution terminated due to
error.` — the sentence every other kind of agy failure ends with — and so
does an overload. So an antigravity run that meets a quota wall is
recorded as an ordinary failure and the gate below is never closed, and
one refused for capacity costs the task a place in its failure streak.
The marker lists in `pkg/agent/antigravity/usagelimit.go` and
`capacity.go` are not what is wrong; there is no text for them to match,
and the fix — read agy's own `--log-file`, or read "exit 1 with no
response" as a soft refusal — is a design decision filed as work of its
own. Both files carry the warning at the top, and a nightly probe says
when an agy release makes the question go away.

`orchestrator.Pause` is what the deployment does about it. The run that
meets a limit closes the gate on the credential it was spending until the
window resets, and every run in flight on that credential is cancelled on
the spot rather than left to grind through the same refusal — that is what the registry of live runs in there is for,
each `RunDispatch` parking its own cancel func for as long as its agent
is running. dispatch passes over what the gate covers -- the connection pool skips
a paused connection, and `reconcileDispatch` holds tasks a pause on no
connection covers; every other reconciler runs
as usual, since syncing pull requests, advancing the merge queue and
cutting releases cost no agent tokens and are exactly what should keep
working. The gate opens again on its own: it is level-triggered like
everything else in a cycle, so the first tick to find the instant passed
clears it and dispatches. If the window has not really reopened, the run
that finds out pauses it again, and no further traffic follows.

What the provider says is bounded rather than trusted: a refusal naming
no reset waits 15 minutes, one naming seconds waits a minute, and one
naming a reset days out (or an epoch this code misread) waits at most six
hours. A deployment idling for a wrong quarter of an hour is recoverable;
one idling until 2286 is not something anybody would think to look for.

Runs ended either way record `model.PausedOutcome` — "paused", its own
word beside "setup-failed" and "finish-failed", with the provider's own
sentence and the resume time in the run's detail. Both implementations of
the failure streak skip that word (`Store.FailureStreak` in Go,
`task_streak` in SQL), so an outage costs a task nothing: no backoff, no
progress toward `MaxConsecutiveFailures`, and dispatch offers it again
the moment the gate opens. Whatever such a run pushed before it was cut
off is still salvaged into a pull request the way any other interrupted
run's branch is.

The gate is in-process state, not a row — the same reasoning
`CycleTimes` is (see "Why this one measurement is in memory"). A daemon
restarted inside a paused window dispatches one run, meets the same
limit, and pauses again: one wasted attempt, against a durable row that
would have to be reconciled with a credential that may by then have been
changed by the very operator doing the restarting.

### Whose credential a pause covers

A pause was first per deployment, then per agent framework
(grain/task-104), when a deployment held one credential per framework.
Model connections are a team's own now, so a framework-wide pause let
one team exhausting its key stop dispatch for every team on that
framework, cancel their runs, and show them a banner about it.

So a pause is keyed by `orchestrator.PauseScope`: the model connection
that owns the credential a run spends -- the connection it borrows a key
from (`credentialBackendId`), else its own id
(`model.AgentBackend.CredentialOwnerID`). The daemon's pooled frameworks
say which (`orchestrator.CredentialConnection`); remote executors'
`executor-*` connections are keyed the same way. A pause on one covers
every connection borrowing its key and nothing else, and since a
connection may only borrow from its own team (both `PUT /api/settings`
and the team endpoint refuse anything else), never another team. The
refusal-burst detector counts by the same key. A run on no connection --
the legacy deployment-level credentials -- has nothing narrower than its
team and framework, and that is what its pause covers; a pause naming no
framework either covers its whole team, never the deployment.

Dispatch meets a connection's pause in the pool (`daemon.AgentPool`),
which passes a paused connection over the way it passes a busy one, so
the team's work rotates onto its other connections; `Availability`
holds a task only when nothing the team has could run it, or it is
pinned to the paused connection. The pool keeps no cool-off of its own
for a usage limit once the `Pause` is wired, so a lift takes effect at
once.

### Saying so, and lifting it by hand

None of that was visible from the UI. An operator opening grain in the
middle of a five-hour window saw a queue of ready tasks and nothing
running, and the only places that said why were the daemon's journal and
the detail of the attempts the pause had ended — which you have to know
to open, on a task you have to know to pick.

So the gate is wired to the UI as `ui.Config.AgentPause`, the way
`Config.Cycles` is wired to the metrics report: an interface named in
`pkg/ui`, satisfied by `*orchestrator.Pause` itself, handed over by
`cmd/grain/daemon.go` — which now allocates the one `Pause` at process
start, package-level beside `cycleTimes`, so the UI/API server and the
reconcile loop that comes up after it are talking about the same gate.
`GET /api/config` carries it as `agentPause` and a standing banner says,
for each pause, which connection of which team it is on, what the
provider said, when dispatch resumes, and how long that is from now;
`GET /api/pause` is the same reading on its own for anything else
polling. Each viewer is shown only the pauses of teams they can read --
a system admin, in Admin mode, sees them all.

Every read goes through `Pause.Pauses`, never `Pause.Blocked`: `Blocked`
is what *clears* an expired pause, as the reconcile loop's own read, and
a browser poll must not be able to open the gate out from under the loop
that owns it. A window whose instant has passed simply reads as not
paused.

It is deliberately not a section of `GET /api/metrics`. That report is
computed over rows for a window that has ended; a pause is a gauge of
what this process is doing right now, with nothing in any table behind
it. The `cycles` section is in that report because it is an *input* to
the same `metrics.Compute` call the rest of it comes from — a pause is
not, and filing it there would mean learning to look for "why is nothing
dispatching?" in a latency report.

`DELETE /api/pause` — the banner's own "Resume now" — lifts a pause
early: `?connection=<id>` that connection's, and a bare DELETE every pause
the caller may lift. A team's admins may lift its pauses, and a system
admin any of them (a bare DELETE from one is "lift all"); anybody else is
refused before anything is looked up. An operator who has just topped a
plan up is holding information this process cannot
have: the credential behind the refusal is not the credential the next
run would spend, and there is no reason to sit out the rest of a window
that no longer applies. A lift opens the gate and nothing more — the runs
the pause cancelled are over, recorded as `model.PausedOutcome`, which no
streak counts — so what it buys is the next tick dispatching rather than
skipping. If the limit is in fact still in force, that run meets it and
pauses again, which is the same self-correcting shape as a window that
expires without having really reset.

Both halves are on the CLI too (`cmd/grain/pause.go`), since an operator
ssh'd into the deployment, or driving it with `grain -server`, has no
banner to read. `grain pause` prints the reading — what the provider
said, when dispatch resumes and how long that is from now — and `grain
pause -lift` is the same DELETE the button sends. It is spelled as a noun
with a flag, the way `grain settings` is, rather than as a `grain resume`
verb: every verb in this CLI acts on the task its argument names
(`approve`, `retry`, `reopen`), so a bare `grain resume` would read as
one of those with the id left off. A deployment whose UI was handed no
gate at all (`enabled: false` — a UI served without a reconcile loop
behind it) says exactly that rather than "nothing is paused", which is
the one wrong answer here: it is what an operator would act on to rule
the usage limit out. `grain metrics` still says nothing about any of
this, for the reason above.

### When the provider is merely overloaded

A budget running out is not the only refusal that says nothing about the
run that met it. Gemini answers an overloaded model with a `503` and "The
model is overloaded. Please try again later."; Anthropic answers with a
`529` whose error type is `overloaded_error`; OpenAI answers with a
sentence of its own. None of that matches a quota marker, so all of it
used to fall through to `agent.RunFailure` and be recorded as a plain
`failed` run — which meant a provider having a bad minute took a place in
the failure streak of every task that happened to be running through it,
and five such minutes in a row retired a task for good. The damage
outlived the outage, and an operator could not even tell those attempts
apart from real failures without reading `task_run.detail` by hand.

`agent.CapacityError` is that refusal's own type, and deliberately not a
`UsageLimitError`. The response a usage limit earns — close the gate,
cancel every run in flight, wait out the window — is right for something
that reopens in hours and much too much for something that is over in
seconds, and it would cancel runs on *other* frameworks whose providers
are perfectly happy. So nothing is paused. The run is recorded
`model.CapacityOutcome` — "capacity", its own word beside "paused" — with
the provider's own sentence in its detail, both implementations of the
failure streak skip that word the way they skip "paused", and
`model.EndingOf` reads it back as `capacity` so `grain get`, the UI's
attempt timeline and `metrics.Runs.Endings` all show it as itself.

The retry is dispatch's ordinary backoff, and that is the one place this
differs from a pause. Nothing stops dispatch while a provider is
overloaded, so a run the streak ignored entirely would be fired at the
same refusal on the next poll, rebuilding a sandbox each time.
`model.FailureStreak` therefore carries two counts: `Count`, the failures
that are evidence about the task, which is what `StateOf` caps at
`MaxConsecutiveFailures`, and `BackoffCount`, the wider one that includes
these refusals, which is what `dispatch.retryEligible` spaces attempts
by. A paused run counts toward neither — there is no retry to space while
the whole deployment is stopped.

The classification is shared in `pkg/agent` with per-framework marker
lists (`pkg/agent/capacity.go`, and a `capacity.go` in each framework),
since an outage at any of the three providers costs a task the same
thing. The markers are as narrow as the quota ones are, for the same
reason: the text they are matched against is a run's own transcript,
which has spent an hour carrying a repository's files, diffs and test
output. A bare `503` or a bare "overloaded" is something a repository
says; "503 Service Unavailable" and `overloaded_error` are things a
provider says. A stream that simply stops mid-run stays an ordinary
failure, because nothing in it distinguishes a refused run from a CLI
that crashed.

### Retrying in the sandbox instead of paying for it twice

Classifying the refusal keeps the task's streak intact; it does not keep
the *run*. The dispatch is over either way, so the sandbox is released,
and the next attempt pays for a granule VM boot and a fresh clone before
it can begin — and whatever the agent had written but not pushed went
with the old sandbox, along with every model turn it spent getting there.
For a refusal that was over in seconds, all of that is spent for nothing.

None of it has to be spent at the moment the refusal arrives, because at
that moment everything the run needs is still there: `Framework.Run` is
still holding the sandbox, and still holding the private configuration
directory it built for the CLI. So it backs off and execs the CLI again
against that same sandbox, inside the deadline the run already had. Two
extra attempts, 30s then 60s, and only for a capacity refusal: a quota
refusal is hours from clearing and belongs to the pause above, an
ordinary failure would only be repeated, and a tripped turn cap is grain
stopping the run on purpose. A retry that would not fit in what is left
of the run's runtime is not started.

That policy is shared — `pkg/agent/retry.go`, beside the `capacity.go`
whose verdict it acts on, with `agent.RetryPolicy` as the only seam (how
many extra execs, and the sleep a test replaces so the loop costs the
suite no wall clock). All three frameworks run it. A refusal is only
ever read off an attempt that actually *failed*, which is the guard that
makes substring matching safe at all here: a run that finished has spent
an hour quoting CI logs and HTTP statuses into the same stream the
markers are matched against, and codex emits one error event per attempt
of a transport reconnect — "Reconnecting… 1/5 (unexpected status 503
Service Unavailable)" — on its way to succeeding. Without that guard a
successful run reads as a refusal, and the retry loop starts a finished
run over.

What differs between the three is how much of the *conversation* the
retry keeps. agy is asked to resume: `Run` hands back the
`conversation_id` agy puts on its own stream, and the resumed attempt
sends a short "you were interrupted, carry on" turn rather than the
prompt again, since the conversation it joins already has the prompt and
repeating it reads as "start over" to a model that had got half way.
**claude is now asked the same way**, through the `session_id` every
event of a `--output-format stream-json` run carries and `--resume
<session-id>` on the next exec. What makes that possible is where the
session lives: unlike agy, claude is not given a private HOME per run —
it is exec'd with the controller's own environment and working directory,
so the session store it has always written into is the same one on every
attempt and is still there when the retry starts.

**And so is codex**, through the `thread_id` on `thread.started` — the
first line of every exec's stream, emitted before codex authenticates —
and `codex exec resume <thread> -` on the next exec. The private
`CODEX_HOME` that looked like the obstacle turns out to be the answer:
`writeConfig` builds one per run and deletes it when `Run` returns, which
is exactly the lifetime a retry needs, since the only thread it wants is
the one its own earlier attempt opened in that directory. The rest was
measured with it (`docs/hand-runs/2026-09-07-codex-resume.md`): the
subcommand takes every flag a grain run passes, it resolves a thread out
of `CODEX_HOME` and not out of the working directory, and the resumed
exec replays the earlier conversation to the model — including the prompt
of a turn the provider *refused*, which is the only case the retry loop
ever resumes after.

All three keep the cheap variant as the fallback: the same sandbox, the
task's prompt again, and `agent.RestartPreamble` in front of it saying
that an earlier attempt's work is already in the checkout — otherwise the agent meets a dirty tree
it has no memory of making and most likely reads it as somebody else's.
That keeps the sandbox and everything in it; only the model turns already
spent are lost.

What the fallback is triggered by is the same shape in all three: an
attempt that asked to resume, died, and never opened a conversation at
all. For codex that is a stream with no `thread.started` in it, which
covers both a binary that does not know the subcommand (a clap error,
exit 2, nothing on stdout) and a thread it has no rollout for ("no
rollout found for thread id …", exit 1) — both measured. The run then
drops the resume for good, restarts in place, and says so in the
transcript, because the person reading it has to decide whether the
package should stop asking.

Four details of that were easy to get wrong, and each has a test in
every `retry_test.go`. Every attempt gets a cancellable context of its
own, since the turn cap works by cancelling the run it is watching and a
cap still holding the first attempt's cancel would stop nothing on the
second. The cap itself is cumulative, so `MaxTurns` still means what it
says for the run rather than for each exec — which for claude, whose
`--max-turns` is enforced by the binary, means each attempt is passed
what is *left* of the run's budget, counted off the turns the earlier
ones spent. The transcript mirror is opened `O_TRUNC` once and the same
sink is reused across attempts, so a retry appends to the capture
instead of erasing it — and each parser now lets the *last* attempt's
terminal event decide how a run ended, a capture holding one per
attempt.

That last rule now covers the attempt that wrote *no* terminal event,
which is a different thing from covering the one that wrote a later one.
A capture parsed whole still holds the previous attempt's ending at that
point — claude's parser overwrites the terminal event, antigravity's
clears it on a *successful* result and nowhere else — so a run refused
for capacity, resumed, and then killed for some unrelated reason was
handed back to `RunDispatch` as a capacity refusal: recorded as
`model.CapacityOutcome`, which no failure streak counts, so a task
failing that way would never retire. Both now classify from the last
attempt's own events, carried out of the retry loop that already parsed
them per attempt to make its own decisions (`attemptsResult.events`),
which is what codex's parser already gave its caller by starting a fresh
reading at each `thread.started`. Evidence the last attempt *did* leave
is untouched either way: its exit error and, for agy, its private
diagnostic are still read, so a refusal that killed the CLI before it
could report one is still a refusal.

And agy's HOME is rewritten
between attempts (`refreshAgyHome`), because agy rewrites
`settings.json` as it starts and drops the permissions block grain wrote:
a second launch reading what the first left behind would run with none of
this run's own rules and say nothing about it.

What each resume rests on is a measurement of the flag itself. Every
vendor documents that its flag exists; none documents whether it composes
with the exact argv a grain run builds — `--conversation` with
`--input-format stream-json` and a fresh user turn on stdin for agy,
`--resume` with `-p --tools '' --mcp-config <file> --strict-mcp-config
--allowedTools … --output-format stream-json --verbose` and the prompt on
stdin for claude, `exec resume <thread> -` with `--json
--skip-git-repo-check --model` and a per-run `CODEX_HOME` for codex — and
a stub CLI answers whatever the test told it to. The probes are the
proof, and they come in two shapes.

`TestLiveAgyResumesAConversationAcrossExecs` (`tests/e2e`, taken by
`live-agent.yml`) and `TestLiveClaudeResumesASessionAcrossExecs`
(`pkg/agent/claude`, taken by `live-frameworks.yml`) are the same three
short model turns against the real provider, one of them the control that
makes the other two mean anything. The claude one reads its capture with
`parseEvents`, the package's own parser, so what production reads off a
resumed run is measured against a real stream rather than against a
fixture this repository wrote. Both want a credential, and neither has
ever had one.

The other shape needs no credential, and is why all three claims are
measured rather than merely written down: point the real CLI at a
stub of the model API inside the test process, and read the request
bodies. That is the only place the answer to "was the earlier
conversation replayed?" is written — the CLI's own event stream looks the
same either way — so a stubbed model proves *more* here than a real key
would, not less.

`TestLiveCodexResumesAThreadAcrossExecs` (`pkg/agent/codex`) does it for
codex against a stub of the responses API: the second exec's request
carries the first exec's prompt, the assistant's reply to it, and the new
turn from stdin. `TestLiveCodexRefusesAThreadItDoesNotHave` is its twin
for the fallback, and reads the same stub for the opposite fact: asked to
resume a thread no `CODEX_HOME` holds, codex exits non-zero having
announced no thread and sent the model nothing at all — which is what
makes "died with no `thread.started`" a sound read of "the binary
refused this argv", and what makes the fallback free.
`docs/hand-runs/2026-09-07-codex-resume.md` records the run both were
written from, refused first turn and all; the second of them is that
run's section 4, moved somewhere a codex release has to walk past it.

`pkg/agent/codex/live_retry_loop_test.go` takes the same stub one layer
up, to the loop that uses those two facts rather than the facts
themselves: `TestLiveCodexRetryResumesTheRunAfterARefusal` drives
`Framework.Run` through a turn the stub refuses and reads the retry's own
request — the task's prompt still in the thread, `agent.ResumePrompt` on
top of it — and `TestLiveCodexFallsBackWhenAResumeIsRefused` gives the
loop an invocation this codex will not perform and checks it restarts the
task in place. Both are the codex twins of claude's own
`TestLiveClaudeRetryResumesTheRunAfterARefusal` below, and what they
needed that claude's did not is `Framework.extraConfig`: claude takes a
base URL from its environment, and codex takes a provider only from the
`config.toml` that `Framework.Run` writes itself.

`pkg/agent/claude/live_resume_stub_test.go` does it for claude against a
stub of `/v1/messages`, in four probes
(`docs/hand-runs/2026-09-08-claude-resume.md`, `claude-code 2.1.197`):
that `--resume` composes with a dispatch's whole argv and replays the
conversation; that a session whose turn the provider *refused* is written
to disk anyway, is resumable, and still carries that turn's prompt — the
only case the loop ever resumes after; that a session claude does not
have fails before it opens one and before it reaches the API, which is
what the fallback is keyed on; and, driving `Framework.Run` itself rather
than a hand-built argv, that grain's own loop reads claude's `API Error:
529 Overloaded` as a refusal, execs again with the session id off the
first attempt's stream, and sends `agent.ResumePrompt` into a
conversation that still has the task in it. Deleting the `--resume` from
`attemptArgs` fails that last one, which is what makes it a measurement.
Both packages' probes run ahead of their job's credential gate, so the
nightly measures this whether or not anybody has minted a key.

`pkg/agent/antigravity/live_resume_stub_test.go` does it for agy against
a stub of Gemini's `streamGenerateContent`, pointed at through
`GOOGLE_GEMINI_BASE_URL` — the seam `live_retry_stub_test.go` already
refuses every request through, used here to answer them, so a
conversation is written to disk and can be resumed
(`docs/hand-runs/2026-09-17-agy-resume.md`, agy `1.1.27` and `1.2.5`).
Three probes, and they cover the *cross-dispatch* resume the credentialed
one does not: that `--conversation` composes with `--input-format
stream-json` and the rest of a dispatch's argv, and replays the earlier
turn and the model's reply to it, where a control passing no
`--conversation` gets none of it; that the conversation is resolved out
of the HOME by id with the working directory of the run that wrote it
*deleted*, which is what every dispatch after the first faces; and that
nothing beside `conversations/<id>.db` has to travel with it — not
`conversation_summaries.db`, which agy rebuilds, and not the `brain/<id>/`
tree — so `pkg/agent/sessionstore` keeping everything the CLI wrote is
more than enough rather than a gamble.

**A probe asserting a vendor's numbers has to name the vendor's release,
and be held to the pin.** `live_retry_stub_test.go`'s retry schedule is
not a fact about agy; it is a fact about agy 1.2.2, and the two are the
same thing only for as long as `ARG AGY_CLI_VERSION` says so. They came
apart for a week: the probes were rewritten around 1.2.2's ladder,
measured through the vendor's unpinned installer, while the image still
pinned 1.1.27 — a release that does not retry an HTTP refusal at all — and
since the nightly installs the pin, it failed every firing, reporting the
disagreement as "its retry schedule changed". So the version lives in one
constant, `measuredAgyVersion`, with a guard at each end:
`TestMeasuredAgyIsTheAgyTheImagePins` compares it with the Dockerfile ARG
and needs no agy, which puts the failure in the ordinary `go` suite on the
commit that bumps the pin, and `requireMeasuredAgy` compares it with the
binary the live probes are about to exec, which is the half a unit test
cannot see — a self-updated agy, a `GRAIN_AGY_PATH` pointing elsewhere. It
reports through `skipUnlessLiveRequired`, so the nightly fails naming both
versions and a developer with a different agy gets a skip that says which.
The resume probes above need none of this: their findings held on 1.1.27
and 1.2.5 alike, and a probe measuring a *shape* rather than a schedule is
one a version bump does not invalidate.

The third of those probes is the one that changed code rather than
confirming it. **A conversation agy cannot find is not refused**: it
warns on stderr, opens a new conversation with a new id, runs the turn
and exits 0. So for agy alone the fallback below — "died without opening
a session" — never fires for a conversation grain's own pruning removed,
and `runAttempts` compares the conversation on the stream with the one it
asked for instead, leaving `suspendedResumeLostNote` in the transcript
when they differ. Nothing is lost when it happens: a dispatch resuming a
previous one sends the whole prompt behind `agent.SuspendedPreamble`
anyway.

What no stub covers is a CLI that stopped replaying from its own on-disk
store and started resuming server-side; none of `codex 0.153.0`, `claude
2.1` or agy `1.1.27`/`1.2.5` does, and the credentialed probes are what
would notice any of them changing. That is now the whole of what the two
missing credentials would add. `live-agent.yml` has still never been
given a `GEMINI_API_KEY` — it fired on 2026-09-04, -05, -06 and -07 and
died four steps in at `Require a credential` every time, because the
environment secret below has never been created — and
`live-frameworks.yml`'s `live-claude` job is still waiting on a
`CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` nobody has minted. Neither job is waiting to
measure the flags themselves anymore; both stub probes run ahead of their
job's credential gate.

Whoever wants any of it settled by hand can, and only the first needs a
key:

```
GRAIN_LIVE_AGENT_TEST=1 GEMINI_API_KEY=... \
  go test ./tests/e2e/ -run TestLiveAgyResumesAConversationAcrossExecs -count=1 -v
GRAIN_LIVE_AGENT_TEST=1 go test ./pkg/agent/antigravity/ -count=1 -v \
```
