```
  -run '^TestLiveAgy(Resumes|OpensANewConversation)'
GRAIN_LIVE_AGENT_TEST=1 go test ./pkg/agent/codex/ -count=1 -v \
  -run '^(TestLiveCodexResumesAThreadAcrossExecs|TestLiveCodexRefusesAThreadItDoesNotHave|TestLiveCodexRetryResumesTheRunAfterARefusal|TestLiveCodexFallsBackWhenAResumeIsRefused)$'
GRAIN_LIVE_AGENT_TEST=1 go test ./pkg/agent/claude/ -count=1 -v \
  -run '^(TestLiveClaudeResumeReplaysTheEarlierConversation|TestLiveClaudeResumesASessionTheProviderRefused|TestLiveClaudeRefusesASessionItDoesNotHave|TestLiveClaudeRetryResumesTheRunAfterARefusal)$'
```

Until the other two are taken, the fallback is what carries their claims,
and it is the same fallback in all three packages: an exec that asked to
resume and died without the CLI opening a session at all — no `init`
event for agy and claude, no `thread.started` for codex, each of which
its CLI writes before it so much as authenticates — is read as the binary
refusing the argv, and the run drops the resume for good and retries from
scratch in the same sandbox instead, leaving a note in the transcript
saying so. It spends neither a retry nor (for claude, whose budget is
enforced by the binary) a turn of the run's budget, since an exec that
opened no session ran no model turn. That cheap variant — same sandbox,
prompt again, no conversation plumbing — is most of the saving on its
own; resuming is what keeps the model turns already spent as well.

### Noticing when the wording changes

Everything in the two sections above rests on phrases: `overloaded_error`,
`api error: 529`, `503 Service Unavailable`, "Claude AI usage limit
reached". Every one of them is a token somebody else's product writes,
and somebody else's product is free to reword it in a release nobody here
reads.

That failure is silent by construction. No marker matches, the run is
recorded as an ordinary `failed`, and *every test still passes* — a test
can only assert the wording it was written against, so a fixture is worth
nothing here and a nightly against a real credential (`live-agent.yml`)
exercises a served run rather than a refused one. What an operator sees
is tasks failing normally. Five in a row retire one
(`MaxConsecutiveFailures`), and the first evidence of the rewording is a
fortnight of tasks quietly in state `failed`.

So the instrument is a record of what grain *could not* classify. When a
run fails and matches neither marker list, `orchestrator.RunDispatch`
keeps the tail of what it said — bounded, since it is model output, by
`agent.MaxUnmatchedFailureText` — as one row in
`task_run_unmatched_failure` (`model.UnmatchedFailure`): the text, which
run and task it was, which framework, and grain's own loose read of it.
`GET /api/unmatched-failures?window=7d` serves it and `grain failures`
prints it, because an instrument you can only consult over SSH with a
sqlite client is consulted after the damage rather than before it.

The loose read is `agent.ResemblesRefusal`, and it is deliberately
everything `capacity.go` refuses to be: a bare `429`, the word
"overload", "retry", "quota", "gateway". The difference is not the words
but what they are matched against and what the answer costs.
`mentionsCapacity` reads a whole run's stream — an hour of a repository's
files, diffs and test output, where "unavailable" is something a source
file says — and its verdict spares the task a failure. This reads one
failure's own error text, a kilobyte at most, and its verdict only draws
an eye to a line in a log. A false positive there is a wrong outcome; a
false positive here is a `*` in a report.

Reading a week of it is the whole point, and the report is shaped for
exactly one question: several failures saying the same unfamiliar thing
is a refusal grain has no marker for, and the fix is a marker in
`pkg/agent`, not a looser test. `grain failures -suspect` is the narrow
read for whoever already suspects one.

The same judgement is said once more where the other kind of reader is.
A run whose failure reads like a refusal gets a hedged sentence appended
to its own `task_run.detail` — "this reads like the provider refusing the
run rather than the run failing, but it matched none of grain's known
refusals" — so the person looking at one failed task, who has the context
to recognise a provider's new wording, is not left reading a bare
`failed` with the answer three layers down. It is a sentence and nothing
more: the outcome is unchanged, `model.EndingOf` reads the outcome, and
the failure streak counts the outcome. Recognising a refusal properly is
still `capacity.go`'s job.

## Two ways a deployment stops dispatching

The pause above is involuntary: a provider said there is no budget left
in this window, and grain waits it out. The other one is a decision —
somebody, or grain itself, has stopped this deployment picking new work
up — and almost everything about it follows from that one difference.

A decision has to survive a restart. `orchestrator.Pause` is a field on a
struct in one process's memory, and that is right for a window a provider
named: a daemon that comes back up inside one dispatches a run, meets the
same refusal, and pauses again, at a cost of one attempt, against a
durable row that would have to be reconciled with a credential that may
by then have changed. A deliberate pause cannot work that way — the whole
case it exists for is an *upgrade*, which restarts the process on purpose
— so `model.PipelinePause` is a row: `pipeline_pause`, at most one, its
existence being what "paused" means rather than a flag somebody has to
remember to clear.

A table of its own, and not two more `grain_config` columns, even though
the policy that decides when grain pauses itself does live over there.
`grain_config` is a settings table (`staterepo.SettingsTables`): a merged
pull request against the state repository is imported into a running
daemon wholesale, and the rule that keeps that safe is that the daemon
does not write settings for itself. This row the daemon does write for
itself, so it belongs on the other side of that line — otherwise a merge
landing mid-pause could resume a deployment nobody meant to resume, or
re-pause one somebody had just let go.

And it stops *dispatch*, not work. Runs already in flight are left to
finish, unlike the usage-limit pause, which cancels them: there is no
refusal for them to walk into, and an operator taking a deployment out of
service wants a queue that stops growing shorter rather than an hour of
agent time thrown away. Whoever needs a run stopped closes its task,
which is what that has always meant.

`dispatch.Cycle` grows one option for it, `Paused(exempt...)`, and the
exemption is the whole reason it is expressed there rather than as an
early return in the caller: a pause taken to check an upgrade has to let
that one check through, and the ready list is read inside `Cycle`. A task
passed over there is passed over and nothing else — no capacity spent, no
attempt burned, no place in its own backoff — so a pause costs a
deployment time and nothing more.

`GET/POST/DELETE /api/pipeline-pause` are the three routes, `grain pause
-set`/`-resume` the terminal's own halves, and `GET /api/config` carries
the reading so a banner can stand on every page beside the usage-limit
one. `grain pause` with no flags prints both gates: "why is nothing being
dispatched?" is one question, and an operator should not have to know
which of two mechanisms to suspect before they can ask it.

### Checking the upgrade that just landed

`pkg/upgrade` builds a new binary, runs it once to prove it is not
broken outright, installs it and restarts the service. What it cannot do
is look at the deployment that came back up. A binary that starts fine
and misbehaves only once it is serving real traffic — a reconciler
failing every tick, a dispatch path that no longer dispatches, a state
repository that stopped syncing — is exactly the class of failure that
survives every check that package makes, and it was nobody's job to
notice.

So it is a task now. The cycle's `upgrade-check` reconciler reads the
status file `pkg/upgrade` wrote just before the restart — the only thing
that crosses that restart, since the process that performed the upgrade
is gone — and files one task per successful upgrade, at the head of the
backlog. No write target: it reports what it found through
`comment_on_issue`, and a task with somewhere to push is a task that will
push. The `self-debug` grant, which is read-only tools onto this host's
own source checkout and the four task readers over the daemon's API, i.e.
the code the upgrade actually installed and the runs since it — which is
where "did the queue resume?" is answered. Read access to the state
repository, which is this deployment's editable configuration and memory
as text (`tables/grain_config.json` and the settings beside it, not
`tables/task.json`, which no export has written since `ExportConfig`), and
so is where "did anything change about what this deployment is configured
to do?" is answered. And a body carrying the upgrade's own details: the branch,
what the upgrade reported, when it started and finished, and the build
now running, none of which anything in a sandbox could find out for
itself.

Two settings decide the rest. `upgradeCheckMode` is `off`, `approve` or
`auto`, defaulting to `auto`: whether the check is filed at all, and
whether it lands queued or as a proposal for somebody to approve. An
empty column — a row written before the setting existed — reads as the
default rather than as `off`, because an upgrade nobody checked is the
failure this exists to catch. `upgradeCheckPausesPipeline` is the
expensive half and is off by default: it holds the queue until the check
is done, which is what an operator who does not trust an upgrade to be
harmless wants and what an operator who would rather not notice an
upgrade at all does not.

The pause it takes names the check, which is what lets the check run at
all while everything else waits, and the `pause` reconciler is what lets
go — when the check completes, when it is closed, when it no longer
exists, or when six hours have passed whatever it is doing. That deadline
is not a detail: a check that parks on a question nobody answers
overnight would otherwise leave a deployment doing nothing until somebody
noticed. An operator's own pause names no task and has no deadline —
nothing in the cycle may decide that one is over.

The check is filed once per upgrade, keyed by branch and start instant in
a tag, read with `Store.HasTaskWithTag` rather than the
`HasOpenTaskWithTag` a schedule uses: a schedule's next firing is meant
to happen eventually, and an upgrade checked last week is a reason not to
check it again now. An upgrade older than a day is not checked at all,
which is what keeps a daemon restarted for its own reasons a month later
from filing a report on a deployment that has been up the whole time.

## Every sandbox is built at a size grain chose

All three dimensions of a sandbox VM were opt-in: `sandbox-cpus`,
`sandbox-memory-mb` and `sandbox-disk-gb` each defaulted to zero, and
zero meant "leave the flag off the create". A deployment that configured
none of them — which is every deployment until somebody opens the
Sandbox tab — got whatever `granule vm create` decides on its own: 2
vCPU and 2048 MiB from `internal/staticpod.Defaults`, and a root disk
exactly as large as the guest image behind it, which
`scripts/granule/build-guest.sh` packs to the rootfs plus 20% headroom.

Those are real numbers a run lives inside, and nothing chose them for the
job an agent's sandbox actually does. 2 GiB of memory is a small VM for
something that clones a repo, installs a toolchain, builds it and runs
its tests; a few hundred megabytes of disk slack is what a build-heavy
checkout spends before failing part way through with no space left,
on a VM with CPUs and memory to spare. Worse, two of the three were not
grain's answers at all — one belonged to whichever `granule` is
vendored under `third_party/`, the other to whichever guest image a
deployment last built — so the size of a sandbox could move under a
resync or an image rebuild without anything in this repo changing.

`pkg/granule`'s `DefaultCPUs`/`DefaultMemoryMB`/`DefaultDiskGB` are
grain's own answer now — 2 vCPU, 8 GiB of memory, 30 GiB of disk — and
`orchestrator.GranuleConfig.createArgs` passes all three on every create,
unconditionally. The resolution order is unchanged and still per
dimension: the task's own `SandboxCPUs`/`SandboxMemoryMB`/`SandboxDiskGB`
first, then the deployment-wide setting
(`GranuleSandboxes.SetDefaultShape`, re-read each reconcile tick), then
`orchestrator.DefaultShape()`. What changed is the bottom of that chain:
it is a number rather than a missing flag, so `granule` is never asked
to pick a size and no VM's shape depends on which image or which vendored
granule a host happens to have.

The 30 GiB is a floor rather than a ceiling, and `granule` is the one
enforcing that: it refuses a `-disk-size-mb` below the guest image the
overlay reads through to instead of truncating the guest's filesystem.
This repo's own guest is nowhere near it, but a deployment booting an
image larger than 30 GiB has to raise the setting to match — which fails
at create time, naming both sizes, rather than quietly building a VM the
guest does not fit in.

Zero still means "unset" everywhere it is stored and typed — in
`model.Config`, in `model.Task`, in the CLI flags and in an empty box on
the Sandbox tab — it just resolves to grain's default rather than to
granule's. The visible consequence is that disk finally has a default to
show: `ui.Settings.SandboxDiskGBDefault` sits beside the two that already
existed, so the pane's disk field gets the same faint placeholder as
vCPUs and memory instead of a sentence explaining why it could not have
one, and `grain settings` prints `sandbox disk gb: 30 (grain default,
unset)` where it used to print `unset`. The memory placeholder moved with
the constant behind it, from 2048 to 8192.

A deployment that wants something else sets it, exactly as before: 8 GiB
and 30 GiB are a default chosen for a build-and-test agent, not a claim
about anyone's host. A per-task override is still the escape hatch for
the one job that needs more, and still the only way to ask for *less*
than the deployment's own shape.

## `top`, in the System pane

Sandbox health can say the daemon's machine is under pressure. It has
never been able to say by what. Load average, memory and disk are
aggregates by construction — `pkg/sysstat` reads `/proc/loadavg` and
`/proc/meminfo`, neither of which knows a process from another — so the
pane could show a load of 12 and leave the only question anybody actually
has at that point ("which process?") to an SSH session and a terminal.

The System pane has a Top tab now: `GET /api/host/top`, `pkg/hosttop`,
`top` itself. Shelling out rather than walking `/proc/[pid]/stat` and
reimplementing its accounting is the same call `pkg/systemlog.Journalctl`
already made for `journalctl` — `procps` is a package, the output is what
an operator already knows how to read, and there is nothing to keep in
step with the kernel. `Dockerfile` lists it among the binaries the image
carries for exactly this reason, and `tests/container` fails the image if
it is missing.

Three details that are not the obvious spelling:

- **Two iterations, not one.** `top -b -n 1` prints, for every process, its
  share of CPU time *since that process started* — there is no earlier
  sample to difference against. For a daemon up for a week that is a
  number about the week, and the busiest thing on the machine right now
  can sit at the bottom of it. `pkg/hosttop` asks for two samples half a
  second apart and returns only the second, which is a real delta;
  `lastSample` finds it by the `top - ` header that opens each iteration.
- **Cut from the end.** The sort is `%CPU`, descending, so truncating to
  the requested line count drops the idle processes and keeps the summary
  block and the rows worth reading. A caller that asks for nothing gets
  `hosttop.DefaultLines`; `?lines=` is capped at 500, the same guard
  `GET /api/logs` gives its own.
- **Auto-refresh is a checkbox.** Logs needs no such thing: a log is
  append-only, and a poll only adds lines below whatever is being read.
  Every poll here re-sorts the whole table under the cursor, which is
  exactly what one does not want while reading a row — and it costs a
  `top` run on the daemon's machine each time. So the poll can be stopped
  without leaving the tab, and stops on its own when the tab is not open.

What it lists is the daemon's own PID namespace, which in a container
deployment is the container's: `scripts/setup.sh` passes no `--pid=host`,
so this is `grain` and everything it forked, which is where daemon-side
load comes from. A sandbox's processes live in that sandbox's own VM and
are not here — the per-sandbox rows in the panel next door are what
report those. A deployment with no reader wired in (`grain demo`, an
image without `procps`) gets the same "not available" note every other
optional panel already shows, rather than a pane that could only ever
error.

## The kernel log, in the System pane

Top says which process is wearing the machine out. The failure it cannot
describe is the one where the process is *gone*: an agent CLI picked off
by the OOM killer mid-run, a disk erroring under a sandbox's checkout, an
interface dropping the git proxy's traffic. None of those write a word to
the daemon's own journal — the thing that would have written it is what
the kernel stopped — so the Logs pane could show three sources that all
went quiet at the same second and no way to ask why.

`dmesg` is a fourth source in that same dropdown now
(`GET /api/logs/dmesg`, `pkg/systemlog.Dmesg`). It is a `LogSource` like
the other three rather than a tab of its own: the kernel ring buffer is
lines of text with timestamps, which is exactly what the Logs pane
already is, and putting it beside `daemon` means comparing the two is a
change of dropdown rather than a change of pane.

It reads that log with `journalctl --dmesg`, not `dmesg(1)`. The two
print the same messages for the same boot — `--dmesg` implies
`journalctl`'s own `-b` — but only one of them is reachable from where
the daemon runs. `dmesg(1)` goes to the ring buffer through `/dev/kmsg`
or `syslog(2)`, and the daemon's container is given neither: it runs
unprivileged as `$GRAIN_USER`, with no `CAP_SYSLOG` and no such device
(`scripts/setup.sh`'s `docker_run_args`). Getting it working would mean
adding `util-linux` to the image *and* handing the container a capability
it has no other use for. journald has already collected those same
kernel messages into the host journal that `docker_run_args` bind-mounts
in read-only for `Journalctl`, `systemd-journal` group and all — so the
kernel log arrives through a mount and a group the deployment already
has, and `Dockerfile` needs nothing it does not already carry. Both
sources are one `journalctl` helper now, differing in the matcher they
pass and the name their errors carry.

The consequence worth knowing: this is the *host's* kernel log, not a
sandbox's. Every granule guest runs its own kernel, and an OOM inside one
of those is that guest's business. What shows up here is what happened
to the machine the daemon and every sandbox share — which is the level
the questions that reach this pane are asked at.

## The root shell, and why it is gone

For a while the System pane had a fifth tab: one box, one command at a
time, run as root on the machine the daemon runs on, with its output read
back in the browser (`POST /api/host/shell`, `pkg/rootshell`,
`ui.Config.RootShell`). The argument for it was a good one. Every other
panel in that pane answers one fixed question — Logs says what the daemon,
the proxy, config-sync and the kernel wrote down, Top says which process is
spending the machine, Sandbox health says how loaded it is — and the
failure that reaches an operator anyway is the one none of them has a
column for. The answer to that has always been "get a shell on the host and
look", and the deployments worth opening such a pane for are exactly the
ones where the usual way of getting one is missing: a host that stopped
accepting SSH, a VM in a cloud project whose console is three support
tickets away.

It is gone (grain/task-193), and what removed it is the paragraph that
always sat beside it. The daemon could not run the command itself — it is
an unprivileged container process with no `sudo` and no `systemctl` that
reaches a systemd that matters — so the pane went over the same control
channel the reboot button uses: the daemon wrote the command to
`$GRAIN_DATA_DIR/control/shell`, a systemd `.path` unit on the host
noticed, and `grain-shell.service` ran it as root. The three units beside
that one each run one fixed command (`systemctl reboot`, `systemctl
poweroff`, `systemctl restart grain-daemon.service`), and that narrowness
was the whole argument for replacing the `NOPASSWD` sudoers drop-ins they
came from. This one ran whatever it was handed: unrestricted root on the
host, held by whatever could reach a UI that carries no auth of its own —
loopback on a default deployment, and everyone the tailnet ACL lets in on a
tailnet one. There is no way to make a debug hatch narrower than the
failures it is for, which is why it could not be narrowed instead of
removed. The convenience of not having to find another way onto the host
does not buy that much reach.

What that means in practice: there is no `/api/host/shell` route, no
`ui.Config.RootShell`, no `pkg/rootshell` and no `-root-shell-control-dir`
flag; `scripts/setup.sh` writes no `grain-shell.path`/`.service` and no
responder script, and — since a host deployed before this still has them
installed and armed — a re-run of `setup.sh` removes any it finds, along
with whatever the last exchange left in the control directory. That
removal is the part worth remembering: taking a feature out of the code
does not take an enabled systemd unit off the machines that already ran
the old installer, and a `.path` unit watching for a command to run as
root is not a thing to leave lying about because nothing is supposed to
write to it any more.

An operator who needs a shell on a deployed host uses whatever they
deployed it with. The control channel keeps its three fixed commands, and
the System pane keeps the panels that report rather than act.

## Nested virtualization, and saying whether a sandbox has it

A sandbox is a cloud-hypervisor guest, so a VM started *inside* one is a
nested VM: `kind create cluster`, a docker runtime that wants `/dev/kvm`,
a second cloud-hypervisor for a task working on granule itself. The
question "can a dispatched task do that here?" had no answer anywhere in
this repository, and it is a question with three separate ways of being
no, in three different layers, each of which looks identical from inside
a task.

The three, top to bottom:

- **The host's KVM has to have nesting on.** `kvm_intel` and `kvm_amd`
  both default to `nested=Y`, so a physical machine has this without
  anyone asking. A cloud VM has it only if its own hypervisor gave this
  kernel hardware virtualization to pass on — `terraform/gcp`'s
  `enable_nested_virtualization` is what buys that, and buys it once:
  a GCE VM's guests do not in turn get VMX to hand to *their* guests.
- **cloud-hypervisor has to leave `vmx`/`svm` in the guest's CPUID.** It
  does. `--cpus nested=` defaults to *on* in v53.0, the version
  `third_party/granule`'s `Dockerfile` pins, and `nested=off` is the
  setting that masks the flag (`arch/src/x86_64`'s `configure_vcpu`).
  Nothing here passes it, so nothing had to change to get this — and
  nothing in the vendored granule had to be patched, which is the outcome
  `third_party/granule/VENDORED.md` asks for.
- **The guest has to load its `kvm` module and let the sandbox account
  open `/dev/kvm`.** udev autoloads `kvm_intel`/`kvm_amd` off the CPU's
  own feature bits, so the module half happens by itself. The device it
  creates is `root:kvm 0660`, and the `debian` account every tool call
  arrives as was in no such group.

That last one was the only thing actually wrong, and it was wrong
invisibly: a real sandbox on the physical deployment has `vmx` in
`/proc/cpuinfo`, has `kvm_intel` loaded, and will run a VM built with
`KVM_CREATE_VM`/`KVM_CREATE_VCPU`/`KVM_RUN` as root — while refusing the
same device to the account the agent is. `scripts/granule/guest-setup.sh`
adds that account to the `kvm` group, so the next guest image CI
publishes has nested virtualization usable rather than merely present.

The rest of the change is the reporting, because a guest image is built
and published on its own schedule: a deployment can be running the old
image or the new one, and the sandbox health pane is where an operator
finds out which. `GranuleSandboxes.Health` asks the guest one more
question inside the single command it already runs there — no extra
round trip against its 5-second budget — and reports one of four states
rather than a boolean, because the three failures want different fixes:

| state | means | fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ready` | `/dev/kvm` is there and the sandbox account can open it | — |
| `denied` | the device is there, the account cannot open it | a guest image from before the `kvm` group grant |
| `no-device` | the CPU offers `vmx`/`svm`, nothing loaded the module | a guest image without `kvm_intel`/`kvm_amd` |
| `unsupported` | no `vmx`/`svm` in the guest's CPU at all | the layer below: the host's own nesting |

The host's own half is read separately — `pkg/sysstat`'s
`NestedVirtualization`, straight off
`/sys/module/kvm_{intel,amd}/parameters/nested` — and shown on the same
pane beside the load average, because it is what tells an `unsupported`
sandbox from a host that was never going to give it one. `scripts/setup.sh`'s
`ensure_granule_nested_virt` logs the same reading at install time and, on
a host where something turned nesting off, writes the modprobe drop-in
that turns it back on, reloading the module only if nothing is using it
— never pulling KVM out from under a running sandbox, since that script
is the updater as well as the installer.

## A sandbox shape the backend ignores says so

`grain settings` and the Settings pane's Sandbox tab print three numbers
on every deployment — `sandbox cpus`, `sandbox memory mb`, `sandbox disk
gb` — because they are stored on every deployment. Only one kind of
deployment builds anything to them. Without `-granule-sandboxes` a run
gets an `orchestrator.HostSandboxes` directory on the daemon's own
machine: `liveConfig.refresh` offers a changed shape to whatever
implements `defaultShaper`, that backend deliberately does not, and the
three settings size nothing. Read from inside such a sandbox, `cpu.max`
and `memory.max` are both `max` and `nproc` reports every core the host
has.

Shown unannotated, that is worse than showing nothing. "2 vCPUs, 2048
MiB" is a sentence about a cap, and it was describing a deployment whose
runs have no cap at all — an operator reading the pane would have
concluded the opposite of the truth, and would have gone looking for the
throttle when a run ate the machine. The per-task half of the same
setting was already honest about it: `HostSandboxes.Acquire` *refuses* a
non-zero shape rather than ignoring it, naming both what was asked for
and why a host directory has none of its own. The deployment-wide
default was the one number still being dropped in silence.

`ui.Config.SandboxShapeIgnored`, reported onward as
`ui.Settings.SandboxShapeIgnored`, is that fact where the numbers are
shown: the Sandbox tab carries a warning above the three fields, and
`grain settings` ends each of the three lines with `-- not in effect:
host-directory sandboxes have no shape`. Per line rather than once
underneath them, since whoever is misled here reads one line and stops.

The daemon works it out from the backend it built rather than from the
flag that chose it — `sandboxShapeIgnored` asks whether `sandboxes` is a
`defaultShaper`, which is exactly the test `refresh` applies before
handing a changed shape on — so what the pane calls "not in effect"
cannot drift from what is really applied. A backend that grew a
`SetDefaultShape` would stop being annotated on the same commit that
made the annotation false.

The fields stay editable and the values stay stored. They are what this
deployment would build VMs at the day it is pointed at granule, and
configuring a shape ahead of that switch is a reasonable thing to do:
what was wrong was the silence, not the numbers. `false` is the quiet
answer, so a UI with no backend to speak for (`grain demo`'s throwaway
one) and an older daemon that predates the field both render the pane
exactly as it was.

## Host mode is a choice now, and says so

`scripts/setup.sh` used to install an unisolated deployment by default.
`GRAIN_KONTUR_ENABLE` was off unless something turned it on, so the
`sudo ./setup.sh` that file's own header recommends produced a daemon
dispatching every agent into a plain directory on the host
(`orchestrator.HostSandboxes`) — as `$GRAIN_USER`, with that host's
filesystem, its network, its git proxy and whatever credentials either
can reach, and with nothing it wrote thrown away at the end of the run.
Nothing said so: not the installer's summary, not the daemon's journal,
not a single screen of the UI, which drew a deployment giving every run
a VM of its own and a deployment giving every run the machine grain
itself is on exactly alike.

Two ways to arrive there, and neither of them was a decision. The
default was one. The other was the fallback every granule prerequisite
took when it was not ready — no `/dev/kvm`, a sandbox image that would
not pull, no gateway address a guest could reach the git proxy through:
each logged a line and set `GRAIN_KONTUR_ENABLE=0` for the rest of the
run, on the "converge with what's ready, don't fail the whole install"
principle `mint_gemini_operating_key` still follows for a missing Gemini
key. That principle is right where what's ready is a subset of what was
asked for. It is wrong here, because the thing it converges on is not a
lesser deployment — it is a different security posture, reached because
a registry was briefly unreachable, on a host nobody was watching.

So the installer asks. `GRAIN_KONTUR_ENABLE` defaults to 1, and
`GRAIN_HOST_SANDBOXES=1` is the only way to get host mode: without it,
`setup.sh` exits before it touches this host at all rather than
installing a shape nobody named, and a granule prerequisite that is not
ready fails the run instead of falling back (`granule_unavailable`). With
it, the fallback is exactly what it always was — an operator who has said
host mode is acceptable is not told twice — and the installer's own
readiness report ends by naming what that deployment is. `terraform/gcp`
needs no new variable: `enable_granule_sandboxes = false` is the asking,
and `files/deploy.sh` passes the matching `GRAIN_HOST_SANDBOXES=1`
through.

The daemon and the UI say it too, because an install is a moment and a
deployment is not. `grain daemon` logs a warning on every start when it
builds `HostSandboxes`, and `-host-sandboxes` — a flag that selects
nothing, since leaving both sandbox flags off already runs that backend —
is how a unit file records that the shape was chosen, so the startup line
can tell a choice from an accident. The UI carries
`ui.Config.HostSandboxes` from the same field `run()` branches on, out
through `GET /api/config`, onto a standing banner that stacks above the
reconciler-down and agent-pause banners rather than taking turns with
them: those two describe an incident that will end, and this describes
what the deployment is for as long as it runs.

What this deliberately does not do is make the daemon refuse to start in
host mode without the flag. A deployment installed before any of this
existed has a unit file with neither sandbox flag in it, and the UI's own
Upgrade button replaces the binary without rewriting that unit — so a
binary that insisted would turn an upgrade into an outage, at the moment
nobody is watching a terminal. The installer is where the refusal
belongs; the daemon's job is to be loud.

## The new-task form stops offering a shape that would fail the run

The Sandbox tab now says when the deployment-wide numbers shape nothing
(above). The per-task half of the same setting stayed generic: the
new-task form's "Sandbox shape override" fieldset was legended *optional,
granule-managed deployments only* — true, and no help at all in deciding
whether this deployment is one of them, since the form was identical on
both kinds.

Here the consequence is worse than a number that sizes nothing. The
deployment-wide shape is stored and dropped; a per-task shape is
*refused*. `HostSandboxes.Acquire` fails with "a host-directory sandbox
has no shape of its own" rather than silently handing the run the host's,
so a task filed with an override on such a deployment is queued,
dispatched, and then dies at sandbox setup — the run killed by a number
typed into a form days earlier, under a legend that read as an
invitation. The one field on that page that can guarantee a task never
runs was the one saying least about where it applies.

So `GET /api/config` now carries `sandboxShapeIgnored` beside
`hostSandboxes`. The form has no other way to see it: `App.jsx` fetches
`/api/config` before its first paint and on every poll, and
`/api/settings` only when somebody opens the pane, so the flag
`grain/task-9` added to the settings response reaches the Settings tab
and nowhere else. Same source either way —
`ui.Config.SandboxShapeIgnored`, asked of the backend that was actually
built rather than of the flag that chose it. It is deliberately not the
same field as `hostSandboxes` beside it, which today always agrees with
it: that one is what the daemon was *asked* for, and this one is what
would refuse the shape.

Where it is set the three fields are disabled and the fieldset says why —
this deployment's sandboxes are directories on the daemon's own machine,
an override is refused rather than ignored, and the task would fail at
sandbox setup. Disabled, not merely annotated, which is the opposite of
what the Settings pane does with the same fact and for a reason: a stored
deployment-wide value is worth setting the day before a deployment is
pointed at granule, and a per-task override has no such day. It is applied
to this task's next dispatch or it is nothing, so there is nothing to
preserve by leaving it typeable. A disabled field is left out of the
submitted form entirely, which is already the `0` the request means by
"no override".

The detail pane carries the same sentence under the three shape rows,
because the form only stops the *next* task: a task filed through the
API, or filed before the deployment moved onto host directories, arrives
on that page with an override and nothing else there explains why every
attempt at it dies. At first the note ended by saying to file the task
again without one, since nothing on the page could clear an override; it
carries a button that does now, two sections below.

## And the API refuses one too

Disabling three fields in the form (above) is a fix for the people who
file tasks through the form. `POST /api/tasks` went on accepting
`sandboxCpus`/`sandboxMemoryMb`/`sandboxDiskGb` on a deployment whose
sandboxes have no shape of their own, so a task filed by an
`ui.HTTPClient` caller, by a script, or by anything else posting JSON at
that endpoint was still queued, still dispatched, and still died at
sandbox setup with "a host-directory sandbox has no shape of its own" —
the exact failure the form now prevents, reached by every other door.
(`grain task create` has no flags for the three, so the CLI was never one
of those doors; `grain task update` has none either.)

`HostSandboxes.Acquire` refuses in the right place for correctness and
the wrong place for the person filing the task. By the time it speaks the
task exists, has waited its turn in the backlog and has burned a
dispatch, and its answer is a line in a run's log rather than a failed
create. So `ui.Client.CreateTask` now gives the same answer at the moment
the shape is stated: a `ValidationError` — a 400 over HTTP — naming the
shape asked for, saying the sandboxes have none of their own, and saying
to file the task with the three fields unset.

Refused rather than accepted-and-cleared, which was the other way this
could have gone. Clearing never fails a filing, but it discards a stated
intent in silence: somebody who asks for 8 vCPUs and gets a run on an
unshaped directory is told nothing at all, and is worse off than the
person whose create was rejected. `Acquire` was deliberately written not
to do that, and moving the refusal earlier is no reason to start.

`PATCH /api/tasks/{id}` carries the same three fields — the detail pane
has no editor for them, but the endpoint does — so the same rule applies
there. It is asked of the numbers a request *states*, not of the shape
the task would end up with: an unstated field is a zero whatever the
store holds, so a task filed with an override before the deployment moved
onto host directories can still be edited back to no override, one field
at a time, instead of being frozen by its own stored numbers. Nothing
that passes leaves a non-zero shape behind that was not already there.

The deployment-wide default is still stored, still editable and still
merely annotated (the Sandbox tab, above). That asymmetry is the whole
distinction this pair of changes rests on: a stored default is worth
setting the day before a deployment is pointed at granule, and only a
per-task shape ever reaches `Acquire` and kills a run.

## And the detail pane can clear one

The warning the detail pane shows over a refused shape (two sections
above) ended with "Nothing here can clear the override; file the task
again without one". True of the pane, and needlessly true: `PATCH
/api/tasks/{id}` had carried the three fields all along, and the section
just above made the endpoint *allow* clearing them on exactly this
deployment while refusing any non-zero shape. So the fix for a task filed
with an override before the deployment moved onto host directories was
one request the pane could have sent and didn't, and the note was
apologising for a missing button rather than for a missing endpoint.

The button is in the warning itself: "Clear sandbox shape", which PATCHes
`sandboxCpus`, `sandboxMemoryMb` and `sandboxDiskGb` to `0` in a single
request and re-reads the task, at which point the three rows and the
warning above it are gone and the task runs like any other here. All
three go in one request because the override is one thing — a task left
with two of the three set still dies at `Acquire` — and because
`UpdateTask` is asked about the shape a request *states*: three zeroes
state no shape, so nothing about clearing them needs the fields sent one
at a time.

The alternative was telling people to file the task again, which is what
the note used to say, and it is a poor trade: a task carries its comment
history, its dependency links, its capabilities, its attachments and
whatever a run has already said on it, and refiling discards all of that
to unset three numbers.

Scoped to the warning rather than offered beside the rows generally. The
three rows in `Declared` are read-only display, not an editor, and this
is not the beginning of one: where the deployment's sandboxes do take the
shape they are given, an override is a working setting somebody chose,
and a one-click "clear it" next to it would be a control for undoing a
decision nobody has complained about. Where it appears, it is the way out
of the one case where what those rows display stops the task running at
all.

## Release branches on a cadence, and two names that do not move

A release branch grain could cut was one somebody asked for, one at a
time: `POST .../releases`, then a candidate, then a promotion. That is
the right shape for a release somebody is steering, and the wrong shape
for a train. A weekly release cut by hand is a weekly reminder, and
everything downstream of it — a qualification suite, a soak job, a
customer pinned to "the current release" — has to be re-pointed at
whatever this week's branch is called.

So a repo can now carry **release trains** (`model.ReleaseSchedule`): a
branch prefix, a cadence, and the names of two branches the train
publishes. Every period it cuts one iteration — `rel.1.0.1`, then
`rel.1.0.2`, and so on — from the source branch's tip, and then moves
`rel.previous` onto the release before it and `rel.latest` onto the new
one. The numbered branch is the release and never moves again; the two
named ones are what anything downstream targets, which is the whole
point: a suite pointed at `rel.latest` is pointed at the release under
test forever, without anybody re-pointing it.

The cadence is `model.Recurrence` — the same "every N hours, or daily,
weekly or monthly at a time" a task schedule already fires on, read
against the deployment's own clock — so there is one cadence vocabulary
here and not two, and a weekly release train is described in the same
words a weekly task schedule is. It is the same catch-up rule too: a
deployment that was down for a month cuts one release when it comes back
and resyncs, rather than one per week it missed.

`rel.latest` and `rel.previous` are registered as ordinary `branch` rows
on the repo the first time they are published (`Store.EnsureBranch`),
which is what makes them *fixed target branches in grain* rather than
names only GitHub has heard of: they appear on the repo page, and a
suite or a task can be pointed at one the same way it is pointed at any
other branch. Written once, however many times a train republishes them.

### What lands on `rel.latest` does not stay there

The reason a train has a moving branch at all is that things get fixed
on it: a qualification run finds something, an agent fixes it against
the release under test, and that fix has to reach the default branch too
— and, while the previous release is still supported, that as well.

So a pull request grain is watching that merges into a train's own
`latest` branch files backport tasks: one against the repo's default
branch, one against the train's `previous` branch, approved already and
with auto-merge on. All four of those are switchable per train
(`model.BackportPolicy`), because whether the previous release still
takes fixes is a fact about one release line and not about a deployment.

Three choices in that sentence are worth stating outright.

**On the merge, not on the open.** A backport of a change nobody
accepted is a task to port something that was rejected, and grain
already watches every pull request it opened through to its ending, so
the merge is a moment it observes anyway rather than a new thing to
poll for.

**Before the merge is recorded, not after.** Recording the merge is what
closes the task out and takes it off the list `syncEntry` walks, so it is
the last cycle that ever runs for it. Filing the backports first means a
cycle that could not file one leaves the task open and tries again next
cycle; the other order would lose a fix quietly, which is the one
failure mode a backport feature must not have.

**Off grain's own pull requests.** A pull request a human opened by hand
against `rel.latest` is not one grain has a task for, so nothing here
sees it merge — the same limit everything else in this package that
reacts to a merge already has ("Input is a model update, not a GitHub
issue", above). The fixes this exists to carry arrive as grain's own
tasks, which is what makes that limit affordable rather than merely
true.

### And from a terminal, not only a browser

Trains were UI-and-REST-only to begin with, which is the wrong shape for
this particular pane. A train's failures are *per iteration*: the
reconciler records why it could not cut or publish against the release it
was cutting, and the question somebody actually asks — "why has
`rel.1.0.7` not appeared" — is asked from a shell on the host, by
whoever is already reading the daemon's journal. The only answers were a
browser and `curl /api/release-schedules/{id}/releases`.

So `grain repo` carries them (`cmd/grain/releasetrains.go`): `grain repo
release-trains <owner/name>` prints one line per train — id, branch
family, cadence, source, the two moving names, the next cut or `paused`,
the backport policy and the reconciler's last error — and `create`,
`update`, `pause`, `resume`, `delete` and `releases <id>` are the rest.
The listing needs no verb in front of it because a repo is `owner/name`
and no subcommand here contains a slash, so a mistyped verb prints the
usage instead of being sent to the server as a repo name.

**Under `grain repo`, and it does not make schedules next.** The doc
comment on `cmd/grain/repo.go` argues that the CLI covers *deployment
configuration* and not *authored content* — which is why `grain settings`
and `grain secrets` exist here and templates, suites and schedules do
not. A release train is the first of these; it is a cadence and a pair of
branch names left running, standing configuration of one repo in exactly
the way its own setup command is, and it sits on the repo page for the
same reason (`RepoReleaseTrains.jsx`). A schedule fires *content*, and
there is still nothing in this CLI that could name the template or suite
it would fire.

**Two flags replace a whole value, and say so.** `ui.
UpdateReleaseScheduleRequest` carries `Recurrence` and `Backport` as
whole structs, because neither has a stored id a PATCH could address a
half of. The CLI keeps that shape rather than papering over it.
`-cadence` and the four flags under it are a sum type keyed on the kind,
so `-at 10:00` on its own could only be applied by reading the train back
and guessing which of the other fields to keep; naming one without
`-cadence` is refused locally, where the error can say what to type,
rather than sent as a kind of `""` and returned as a puzzling complaint
about the kind. `-backport` takes the policy as one string — `off`, or a
comma-separated list of `default`, `previous` and `auto-merge`, the same
words the listing prints back — rather than as four booleans over a
struct that is replaced wholesale, which is how
`-backport-auto-merge=false` would otherwise quietly turn backporting off
altogether. Everything else keeps the read/write distinction the rest of
`grain repo` makes: a flag omitted leaves its field alone, and `-source
""` puts a train back on the repo's default branch.

### Two trains, one prefix, from the other direction

Two trains on one repo sharing a prefix would hand out the same iteration
branch names from two independent counters, which is why
`CreateReleaseSchedule` refuses the second one. A prefix is *editable*
though — `grain repo release-trains update -prefix`, and, since a train
got a page of its own (below), a text box in a browser — so an edit was
the other way into exactly that state, and it went unchecked.

`Store.UpdateReleaseSchedule` now makes the same check inside its own
transaction, returning the same `ErrReleaseSchedulePrefixInUse` and so
the same 400 rather than a collision discovered later on GitHub. The row
being edited is excluded from it, so re-saving a train under the prefix
it already has — which is what a form that sends every field on every
save does — stays an ordinary edit rather than a collision with itself.

### Not on the settings tables

`release_schedule` looks like settings — it is a cadence and a set of
branch names, which is what `schedule` is — and it is deliberately not on
`staterepo.SettingsTables`. `release_iteration` rows point at
`release_schedule`'s own autoincrement id, and `Apply` is a wholesale
replacement, so importing the parent table underneath a running
deployment would orphan every release cut since the dump was made: a
branch on GitHub with nothing left in the store that knows why it is
there. A train proposed in a pull request against the state repository is
imported at startup like every other row there, and is live on the
restart rather than on the next tick.

That is not an argument against declaring a train in a file, and `grain
sync`'s `"repos"` section (above) does exactly that without inheriting
the problem. What the settings tables cannot do is *import* this one: the
danger is `Apply`'s wholesale replacement of a parent table whose
autoincrement ids `release_iteration` rows point at, under a deployment
that is running. A sync reaches the REST API instead — one `POST` for a
train that is new and one `PATCH` for a train that drifted, each against
the id the store already assigned — so no table is replaced, nothing is
renumbered, and no cut release loses the train it belongs to. The two
answers are about two different mechanisms: "not importable as a table"
and "declarable as configuration" are both true of `release_schedule` at
once.

## A schedule says what to do about its own unfinished firing

A schedule that comes due while the last thing it filed is still open
does not file another one. That rule is as old as the feature — v1
checked GitHub for an open issue carrying the job's marker label, and
this checks the store for an unclosed task carrying the schedule's own
firing tag (`schedule:<id>`, `Store.HasOpenTaskWithTag`), or for an
unfinished run when the schedule runs a suite instead
(`Store.HasActiveRunForSchedule`). It is the right rule: a chore that
takes longer than its own cadence would otherwise put a second copy of
itself on the queue every tick, and then a third, with nobody watching.

It was also the only rule there was, which is the part that needed
fixing. `model.Schedule.Overlap` is now a two-valued policy — `skip`,
the zero value and the default, or `allow` — on its own `schedule.overlap`
column, and `fireTaskSchedule`/`fireSuiteSchedule` ask the question only
when the policy says to. Nothing else about a firing changed: a
suppressed one still leaves `NextRunAt` exactly where it was, so it is
*delayed* rather than dropped and happens as soon as the previous firing
closes, and the schedule stays on its own cadence rather than catching up
one firing per missed occurrence.

The default is what makes this safe to have at all. A database written
before the column gets it filled with `skip`
(`ensureScheduleOverlapColumn`), a `POST /api/schedules` that says
nothing about overlapping gets `skip`, and the zero `OverlapPolicy` reads
as `skip` everywhere — so the only way to end up with two unfinished
firings of one schedule is for somebody to have asked for it. Where it
earns its keep is a schedule whose firings genuinely do not collide: one
whose task parks on a question for a day while the cadence is the point,
or one filing independent work against separate branches each time.

In the UI the choice sits with the cadence in the schedule's own pane —
"If the last run has not finished: Skip this run / Start it anyway" —
because it is the other half of the same question, and it is a picker
rather than a checkbox so that skipping reads as a decision somebody made
rather than as the absence of one. The list chips only the non-default
answer: "Can overlap" on the rows that can, and nothing on the rest,
since a badge every row carries says nothing.

## A schedule can be run now

Everything about a schedule was about *when*: a cadence, a next run, a
pause. The one thing it could not do was run — somebody who wanted
tonight's dependency bump to happen this morning filed the task by hand,
which meant copying the template's title and body into the new-task form
and remembering which capabilities, read-only repos, write targets and
custom fields that schedule carries. That is a chore about a chore, and
every part of it is already written down on the schedule itself.

"Run now" sits beside Pause and Delete in a schedule's own pane, over
`POST /api/schedules/{id}/run`, and it fires the schedule rather than
imitating it: the same code the reconciler fires through, so the
template is resolved fresh (an edit since the last firing is what runs),
the firing tag is attached, the task lands already approved and
attributed to the schedule principal, and a suite-backed schedule starts
a run of its suite exactly as its cadence would have. The response
carries the filed task's id — or the started run's — and the schedule as
it now stands.

It is an extra firing, not a rescheduling, and the three rules that
follow from that are the whole design:

- **`NextRunAt` does not move.** The occurrence this schedule was
  already going to have still happens when it was going to. Running a
  chore by hand at four in the afternoon does not move the 09:00 it also
  runs at, the same way pausing and resuming keeps a schedule's firing
  time rather than resetting it. `LastRunAt` does move: it really did
  fire.
- **A paused schedule fires anyway.** `Enabled` stops the *cadence* —
  `Store.DueSchedules` never returns a disabled schedule — and a human
  asking for this one run is not the cadence. It stays paused
  afterwards.
- **The overlap policy still applies.** A schedule set to skip is
  refused while its previous firing is still open, with a 409 saying so
  and what to do about it, rather than filing a second task. The gate
  exists so a chore cannot have two copies of itself running, and a
  button is no reason to walk round it — but unlike the cadence's own
  suppressed firing, which is silent because nobody is waiting on it,
  this one is reported, because somebody is.

Firing moved from `pkg/orchestrator` into `pkg/model` to make this one
firing rather than two: `Store.FireSchedule` is what the reconciler
calls when a cadence comes due, `Store.FireScheduleNow` is what the
button reaches, and everything below them is shared. It moved rather
than being called across because `pkg/ui` does not import
`pkg/orchestrator` — a presentation-layer package importing core
dispatch logic runs the wrong way — and the alternative, a second
implementation of filing a firing in `pkg/ui`, is exactly the drift that
would have a schedule's template stop being re-read, or its custom
fields stop being sifted, on the path a human uses and not on the other.
`orchestrator.reconcileSchedule` keeps its own job: read the due
schedules, resolve the deployment's clock, fire each one, and let one
schedule's failure cost no other schedule its turn.

## grain's own CI

Every check a branch got until now was GitHub's. That is fine for this
repository and useless for the thing grain is: a deployment works in
repositories it does not own the CI of, gets no answer at all for the
ones with no workflows, and cannot ask "does this branch pass" of
anything without a GitHub Actions runner behind it -- while the
sandboxes it already builds, on a machine it already pays for, sit idle
between runs. `pkg/ci` is grain answering that question itself.

Checks are declared in `.grain/workflows`, one YAML file per workflow,
and the format is GitHub Actions' wherever GitHub has a
word for the thing: `name`, `on`, `jobs`, `needs`, `steps`, `run`,
`env`, `runs-on`, `timeout-minutes`, `working-directory`,
`continue-on-error`, spelled the same, nested the same, meaning the
same. Everybody who will ever write one of these has already written the
other kind, and the resemblance is the whole point of the design.

Grain adds one event and one job switch for releases. `on: release` runs
against a destination branch after Grain observes a pull request merge; it
cannot be requested through the API or CLI. `cache: false` makes a job execute
on every matching run, which is required for publishing or any other external
side effect. The merge reconciler starts the release run before it closes its
task, so a transient start failure is retried on the next cycle.

Where those files live is the other half of it, because a repository
grain does not control cannot carry them: a grain-specific CI directory
in somebody else's tree is a pull request they have to accept, and most
of the repositories a deployment works in are somebody else's. So a
workflow can be declared on grain's own side instead, against the repo
(`model.RepoWorkflow`), and read back through the same interface the
in-repo files come through (`ci.Source`) -- the same format, the same
parse, the same jobs, with nothing in the engine or the plan knowing
which side a workflow arrived from. They are edited on the repo's own
page, or proposed in a pull request against this deployment's state
repository, and the save runs the parser so a file that could never run
is refused at the form rather than at the run. Where a repository has
both, `ci.Layered` takes the union by path and lets the declared one win
a path the repository also declares -- which is what lets an operator
replace a check in a repository they cannot edit, rather than only add
to it.

That difference in *provenance* is real: a workflow declared on grain's
side is operator config and an in-repo one is not. It is deliberately
not a difference in *power*, which is the subject of the next paragraph
and is "none" for both.

What the format does *not* implement it refuses by name rather than
ignoring -- `uses:` above all. An `actions/checkout@v4` that silently
did nothing would be a green tick over a job that never checked anything
out, which is worse than a format that never claimed the resemblance. A
job's sandbox instead arrives with the commit already checked out,
because that is what grain's sandboxes already do for an agent run; that
also keeps a workflow free of anything that could reach a credential to
do it with. `runs-on` names grain's own sandbox rather than a runner
pool, and `sandbox: {cpus, memory-mb, disk-gb}` is the question actually
worth asking -- how big, in the same three dimensions
`orchestrator.Shape` already carries. There are no `${{ }}` expressions
and no `secrets` context.

**`needs:` in a borrowed `.github/workflows` file orders the jobs and
carries nothing between them.** A repository with no `.grain/workflows`
has its Actions workflows read instead, each job run as one `act --job`
invocation in a sandbox of its own -- and for a year a job that declared
`needs` was refused, which took the whole file with it. On
`gke-labs/granule` that read as a run of no jobs concluding success in
0s: a green tick nobody could tell from a pass, and several merges went
through behind it before somebody deleted the key from `ci.yml`. So
`needs` is honoured as far as separate machines allow. The ordering and
the skip are the engine's own, the ones every native job already gets.
What cannot cross is refused *by job* rather than by file: a job that
reads `${{ needs.<job>.outputs.… }}`, or downloads an artifact another
job uploaded, is a workflow definition error naming the file, the job
and the key. The other thing standing in the way is that act resolves
`needs` itself -- `act --job image` runs everything `image` needs before
it -- so a job that needs another is handed a copy of its workflow with
its own `needs:` commented out, written into the sandbox rather than
into the checkout. Commented rather than deleted, so that every line
keeps the number act will report an error on, and verified against the
original document node for node before it is used (`pkg/ci/actions_needs.go`).

**A failing job's files outlive its sandbox, and only a failing one's.**
A job's machine is destroyed the moment the job ends, so for a year the
suite's own log was the whole of what a red job left behind. That cost
`grain/task-182` an afternoon: two `ui e2e` runs red on two different
chromium specs, both reports saying only "element(s) not found, 5000ms",
and the cause — a `TypeError` that unmounted the React tree — sitting in
the Playwright trace both times, inside a machine nobody could reach.
So a job may declare `artifacts:` with `actions/upload-artifact`'s own
`name` and `path`, and grain copies those paths out before releasing the
sandbox. Only for a job that did not succeed: that is the `if:
failure()` GitHub puts on the upload step, which this format has no way
to spell and — being the only case anybody wants — has no key for
either. A green job runs one command fewer than it did before this
existed, namely none.

The copy goes through the one seam a `ci.Sandbox` has. The paths are
tarred and gzipped *inside* the job's sandbox, the size is checked there
against the store's own per-artifact bound, and what comes back comes
back as base64 in the output of an ordinary `Exec` — so an oversized
artifact is refused before a byte of it moves, and no backend, adapter
or test fake needs a new method. A transport that grows a real file
transfer can be reached through an optional interface exactly as
`StreamingSandbox` is.

Where they live is `DirArtifacts`: a directory of the daemon's own, one
subdirectory per run, and deliberately not `model.Store` — a trace
bundle is megabytes of binary and everything in the store is exported to
the state repository as text, which git never forgets a version of. It
is bounded the way the job cache is and for the same reason, with one
bound the cache does not need: an age, a ceiling on the directory, a
ceiling on a single artifact, and a ceiling per *run*, because one push
of a workflow whose dozen jobs all fail is the shape that surprises a
host. Eviction drops whole runs, oldest first, since half a run's
artifacts is a reader finding one of the two traces they came for. A
cached job result carries none: these belong to the run that produced
them, and a hit would be advertising a download from a run nobody is
looking at.

`JobRun.Artifacts` is the one field of a result that is not written
down. What a reader can actually download is whatever that directory
holds *now*, not what was true when the run finished, so the answer is
read at the moment a run is served (`ci.Service.WithArtifacts`) — which
also means a run read back after a restart is right rather than empty.
`GET /api/ci/runs/{id}/artifacts` lists them, `.../artifacts/{job}/{name}`
serves the bytes as a download, the CI pane draws a link above the job's
steps, and `grain ci artifact <run> <job> <name>` fetches one from a
terminal.

One deployment property worth knowing before adding a key to
`.grain/workflows`: these files are parsed by the *daemon's* build, not
by the checkout's, and an unknown key is a refusal (the decoder runs
with `KnownFields` set). So a new key cannot appear in a workflow file
until the deployment runs a build that knows it — which makes every new
key two commits, one for `pkg/ci` and a later one for the file that uses
it.

**A workflow file is trusted with nothing, deliberately.**
`docs/data-model.md`'s "the tree is operator config, and in v1 there is
no in-repo file at all" is the rule this has to live under: a `.grain/`
file in a target repository is a file every agent grain dispatches can
rewrite, so it must never widen what anything may do. A workflow widens
nothing -- it spends compute in a sandbox, which is exactly where the
agent that could have edited it was already running arbitrary commands.
CI jobs receive only capabilities explicitly configured by an operator for
that repository under **Repos → repo → CI capabilities**. Agent task defaults
are independent. The service snapshots this set before planning, includes it
in cache keys, and provisions and revokes each job's own material. Workflow
files and CI requests cannot add grants. See [CI capabilities](ci-capabilities.md).

### The `grain-ci` capability is the switch

`pkg/capability/grainci` is how this is turned on selectively while it
is new. A capability is already the thing this deployment enables at
exactly the three granularities this needs, with no new column, no new
pane and no new vocabulary: per task in the picker
(`ui.OfferedCapabilities`), per repo in
`model.RepoConfig.DefaultCapabilities`, and deployment-wide in
`model.Config.DefaultCapabilities`. A GRANT provider in `selfdebug`'s
shape -- it mints nothing, places nothing, and what it grants is not
material in a sandbox. `POST /api/ci/runs` refuses a repository none of
those name, and the refusal says which two clicks turn it on.

### Something starts a run, and the answer lands where the task is read

`wait_for_checks` is the trigger. It starts the requested jobs against
the task branch's current head with `ci.EventPush` and waits for the
answer. Nothing starts merely because a task finishes or a reconciler
ticks: this keeps sandboxes idle until the agent asks for feedback and
lets a focused selected run be useful during iteration.

Only an unselected call records the task's required run. The call may
time out or the agent may exit before a multi-minute run ends, so
`orchestrator.reconcileCI` remains as the collector: every cycle it reads
an already-recorded full run and copies its eventual verdict to the task.
If a push moves the branch while one is running, the collector cancels
the stale work but starts nothing; another explicit unselected call is
required for the new head.

**The verdict is copied, not linked to.** A `ci.Run` lives in a bounded,
in-memory `ci.RunStore` that keeps the last hundred finished runs and
forgets all of them across a restart, so a task carrying "grain CI run
3f2a1c" would be carrying a dangling pointer within the day — and the
question it was meant to answer is the one asked *after* the run is
over. `model.Observation.CI` holds the conclusion and a one-line account
of it instead, on six nullable columns of `task_observation`, and it is
overwritten in place: a task pushes one branch, so a redispatch replaces
the answer about it rather than adding a second one, and a task
dispatched ten times carries one current verdict rather than ten stale
ones. `GET /api/tasks/{id}` serves it as `ci`, `grain get` prints it,
and the task pane shows it.

The words go two places on different terms. The task's own conversation
gets one comment per concluded run, green or red — which is also how the
next agent dispatched onto this branch is told that the last thing it
pushed went red and which job said so, since a run reads the comment
thread back in its prompt. The pull request gets one only when the run
did not pass, with a bounded tail of the first failing step's output: a
reviewer wants to be told about red, and a green comment on every push
is exactly the noise GitHub's own checks UI avoids by reporting a pass
in a badge and saying nothing.

**A red grain CI run holds the merge.** It did not, at first — the
report was built before the policy was decided — and the decision it was
waiting on is `orchestrator.withGrainCI`: the verdict on a task is one
more check, judged where GitHub's own checks are judged and by the same
rules. A run that failed makes the pull request `FAILING`, which earns it
the one automatic repair any broken head gets, with grain CI named among
the failing checks and its verdict quoted in the repair's own brief; a
run still going makes it `PENDING`, which waits, bounded by the same
stall deadline an unfinished GitHub check is waited on with. Nothing
posts a commit status or a check run even so: the merge queue reads the
verdict off the task, so reporting it to GitHub would only add a second,
slower path to the same decision.

The capability means one successful full-suite verdict is required for
the exact head. A repository that declares no workflows satisfies it,
because an empty plan is a success (`ci.PlanRun`). A verdict about an
older commit, a cancelled or skipped run, a CI service that is down, or
a daemon that forgot an in-flight run does not satisfy it. Those cases
remain `PENDING`, not `FAILING`: no repair is filed against an untested
tree, and the existing stall deadline eventually hands an infrastructure
problem to a person. The switch is the `grain-ci` capability and stays
that one switch:
"run the workflows but ignore what they say" would be a setting meaning
nobody trusts the runner, and the answer to that is to take the
capability off the repository.

**A run grain could not *do* is not a red build.** A job whose sandbox
could not be built used to conclude `failure`, the same word a job that
compiled the tree and found it broken gets, and the first CI runs on a
granule-backed deployment showed what that costs: every job died
acquiring a sandbox — the name was longer than a VM name may be — and
every open pull request was told its checks were failing, with a repair
dispatched to fix code that had never been compiled. `ci` has a word for
it now. `ConclusionErrored` is a job that never ran at all: no machine
to run it in, no permit for one, no sandbox backend wired. It is a
verdict on the deployment rather than on the commit, so a run is errored
only when nothing in it found anything wrong with the tree — a genuine
failure beside it still concludes `failure` — and a job whose sandbox
died *mid-run* is still a failure, because by then the tree had been
running in it. `withGrainCI` holds such a verdict `PENDING`: merging
would land a tree nothing has tested, exactly as under a run still
going, but nothing is filed against a branch with nothing wrong with it,
and the wait leaves by the same stalled-checks door — at the stall
deadline a person is told that grain CI could not run and what stopped
it, which is where a deployment-wide breakage belongs. Nothing re-runs an
errored verdict on its own; that wants a rule for staying quiet across
attempts and is a decision of its own.

### One commit is tested once

The point of CI on a task queue is that one commit is tested once, and
every decision is made against a key a result can be looked up by:
`ci.Fingerprint` hashes the repository, the commit, the job's own
declaration, the sandbox it asked for and the environment grain itself
supplies the job with; the engine consults `ci.Cache` before it acquires
a sandbox and writes back to it after; each result carries the key it was
produced under and says whether it was remembered rather than run
(`cached` on the job).

`ci.DirCache` is that cache: one JSON file per key under
`<data-dir>/state/ci-cache`. A directory rather than a table, because
everything in the store is committed to the state repository as text and
an entry holds a job's whole output -- and because a cache is disposable
by definition, so nothing backs it up and a fresh data directory simply
starts cold. Its bounds are about disk rather than correctness (a key is
a promise that the work is identical, so there is nothing to
invalidate): entries past 30 days go, one result over 4MB is never
stored, and the directory is held under 256MB and 4096 entries by
evicting the oldest. A cache can never fail a build -- anything it
cannot read or trust is a miss, and an error from it makes the engine
run the job -- and only a self-contained conclusion is ever kept: never
`skipped`, never `cancelled`, and never a failure whose cause was the
deployment rather than the job.

**That cache is visible and clearable from outside the daemon**, which
it was not when it was first written: its size was a `du(1)` on the host
and emptying it was an `rm -rf`. `GET /api/ci/cache` says what it holds
-- entries, bytes against the ceiling, the age span of them, when the
bounds were last enforced, and the hits and misses since this daemon
started (they live in memory, so a full cache with no hits against it is
usually a daemon that came up a minute ago). `DELETE /api/ci/cache`
empties it. The CI pane draws that as a line under its heading with a
"Clear cache" beside it, and `grain ci cache` / `grain ci cache clear`
are the same two from a terminal. Clearing is gated on the `grain-ci`
capability, read deployment-wide, because one directory serves every
repository -- and the gate is about cost rather than damage: an entry is
a promise that identical work was already done, never a fact only the
cache holds, so an emptied cache costs the re-runs it was saving and
nothing else. Three answers, not two: no CI wired at all, CI running
with no cache behind it (every job runs, every time), and a cache to
describe -- because "there is no cache" and "the cache is empty" send a
reader to different places.

**The bounds themselves are settings, and the flags are their seeds**:
`-ci-cache-max-age`, `-ci-cache-max-bytes` and `-ci-cache-max-entries`
are written to the config row the first time a deployment starts and
read out of it from then on (`model.Config.CICacheMB` and its
neighbours), alongside the artifact store's four next door. The
`-ci-artifact-max-*` group is the same; `-ci-cache-max-entry-bytes` is
the one that is still only a flag, because it refuses a single oversized
result rather than sizing the directory and the System pane shows no
reading against it.

They were flags alone until grain/task-317, on two arguments worth
recording because this is where they were answered. The first was that
what they bound is a property of the machine grain is installed on --
how big the `-data-dir` disk is -- rather than of how this deployment
works: nothing here can change an answer, so the whole of what a tighter
bound buys is disk at the price of jobs running again. What changed is
that the System pane's Storage section now reports what each of them is
*holding* (grain/task-276). An operator reading "200 MiB of 256 MiB" is
being shown a ceiling and asked to act on it, and "edit the systemd unit
and restart" is the wrong next step -- it is the one that put this
deployment into a 52-restart loop once.

The second was that live editing would be a promise the cache could not
keep, since `DirCache` read its bounds once at `OpenDirCache` and making
them live meant a store read on the sweep path. It does not. Both stores
take a `func() ci.StorageBounds` -- one closure over `cmd/grain`'s
`liveConfig`, which already holds a copy of the config row refreshed
once a reconcile tick, so reading it is a mutex rather than a query --
and call it on every sweep, every `Save`, every `Lookup` and every
`Stats`. One provider for both directories, because they are one
decision about one volume. What remains true is that a *lowered* ceiling
frees nothing until the next sweep, five minutes out at most, which is
why "Clear cache" and `grain ci cache clear` are still the answer for an
operator who needs the disk back now: the pane keeps the verb, and the
row now keeps the sizing.

None of the seven has a "keep it all" reading, unlike the CI history's
four, which take a negative number for "keep every run forever". A
positive number is the bound and 0 is grain's own default, and
`ui.UpdateSettings` refuses anything below that: what these bound is a
directory on the volume the deployment dispatches out of, and a data
disk with no ceiling stops it admitting work at all, which is the
failure the bounds exist to prevent rather than a trade anyone can
usefully make.

What keeps that honest is `fingerprintVersion`. Anything that changes
what a job does has to be in the key or in that number, and the
environment grain hands a step counts: because a workflow may read
`GRAIN_CI_REF` and `GRAIN_CI_EVENT`, the key covers them, which means
two branches at one commit no longer share an answer. The cheap half of
the same idea sits above it: `ci.Service.Start` answers a second request
for work already in flight with the run doing it, rather than doing it
twice.

### What runs a job, and what lets it read the repository

The API is `POST /api/ci/runs` (a repo and a branch, answered with a run
id and the jobs it is about to run), `GET /api/ci/runs`,
`GET /api/ci/runs/{id}` and `DELETE /api/ci/runs/{id}`, plus
`GET /api/ci/cache` and `DELETE /api/ci/cache` for the job cache behind
them, and a daemon started with `-ci` (the default) answers all six for
real.

`cmd/grain/ci.go` is where the engine meets the machines, because it is
the one place `pkg/ci`'s types and the orchestrator's are both in scope
-- the argument `sandboxHealthAdapter` and `cycleTimesAdapter` already
make. Acquiring a job's sandbox builds one out of whichever backend this
deployment runs, clones the repository at the commit under test, and
answers only once a step could run; a step is that sandbox's own
`run_command`, which is already the right call for a host directory and
for a granule VM alike; releasing it destroys it. A job's sandbox is
acquired straight from the backend rather than through `RunDispatch`, so
only the repo's explicit CI capabilities are resolved and placed in it
-- which is how "a workflow file is trusted with nothing" stays
checkable by reading the wiring. `-ci=false` turns the whole engine off
for an operator who wants none, without touching any capability set:
`ui.Config.CI` is then nil and the API says this deployment has no CI,
the same nil-means-unavailable contract `Sandboxes`, `Cycles` and
`AgentPause` already give.

A job's sandbox is another sandbox this deployment's host has to find
room for (grain/task-296). `max_workers` plus `max_mergers` caps agent
runs, while `max_ci_jobs` independently caps CI jobs. The values are
additive: raising `max_ci_jobs` can raise CI parallelism without silently
reducing agent capacity. The sandbox commitment shown in Settings counts
all three, so the machine load implied by the independent limits remains
visible.

Each side enforces its own limit where it already could: the agent limit
inside the transaction that records a run (`Limits.Admits`, from
`StartRun`), the CI half in a `ci.Gate` every job takes a permit from
before it asks for a machine, so several CI runs at once cannot between
them exceed `max_ci_jobs`. The gate reads the limit through `liveConfig`,
so a deployment resized in Settings is honoured by the next job rather
than at the next restart. `ConcurrencyLimit` reads the same value; this
avoids the engine's fallback default of four becoming an accidental cap
on a single run.

The part that had to be designed rather than adapted is what lets that
sandbox read anything at all. Every scope the git proxy has ever
answered with came from the live task model -- a sandbox resolves to the
run on it, the run to its task, and the task's `Target` and `Reads` are
what it may touch (`gitproxy.ModelAuthorizer` over
`model.Store.GitScope`). A CI job's sandbox has no task, so that
resolves to nothing and every fetch it makes is refused, its own
checkout included. `gitproxy.ReadScopes` is the scope it gets instead:
this sandbox, this one repository, fetch only. The CI service registers
the pair as a job starts and drops it as the job ends, and
`ReadOnlyScopeAuthorizer` consults the registry before falling through
to the model. Three things are code rather than convention --
`git-receive-pack` is refused whatever is registered, a second grant for
a sandbox replaces the first rather than adding to it, and a released
job authorizes nothing at all -- and the forbidden set (grain's own
state repository, where it holds the encrypted secrets file) is still
checked ahead of the registry, so a read scope can never be what gets a
job into it. The live tests drive exactly that against a real git
server: a job may fetch the repository under test, may not push it, may
not reach a second repository, and may not fetch anything once its job
is over.

Workflows themselves are read by a shallow clone the daemon makes with
its own credential and deletes again, because a run's workflows are
parsed synchronously on the request that asked for the run and building
a sandbox to read one directory would turn an HTTP request into a VM
boot. Nothing it reads reaches a job's sandbox: the job clones the
repository itself, through the proxy, under the read-only scope above.

A step's script goes over `orchestrator.SandboxShell` rather than over
