the `run_command` tool an agent's own commands go over. The two do the
same thing; what differs is what they do to a long step. `run_command`'s
bounds exist to protect a model's turn -- every call clamped to ten
minutes, every answer cut to a few tens of kilobytes -- and neither is
survivable for CI. This repository's own `go` job is `go test -race
-timeout 30m` under `timeout-minutes: 45`, which `run_command` would
kill at ten and report as a failure the workflow file plainly did not
ask for, and the log somebody opens a failed job to read is exactly what
the output cap throws away. Both real backends implement the shell over
the transport they already have -- a subprocess for a host directory,
the guest's own bash for a granule VM -- and a `Sandbox` that has no
shell still runs its steps over `run_command`.

Proving that a job can actually be given a machine, a checkout and a
shell is `cmd/grain/ci_e2e_test.go`: one real run of this repository's
own `.grain/workflows/tests.yml`, planned from the commit under test and
run to a verdict, gated on `GRAIN_TEST_CI_E2E=host` or `=granule` the way
the container and live suites gate themselves. Given
`GRAIN_TEST_GITHUB_TOKEN` it also holds its own verdict up against what
`.github/workflows/tests.yml` concluded about the same commit, because
two CIs disagreeing about one commit is the finding the exercise exists
to look for and asserting only that grain's own is green would find a
grain that is wrong in the same direction twice.

### Reading a run

Those four routes were served and read by nobody for a while: watching a
run meant curling the daemon and paging its JSON. There are two readers
now, over the same API.

`grain ci` is the terminal one (`cmd/grain/cicmd.go`): `run` against a
repo and a branch, `list` what has run, `show` one run, `cancel` one
still going, and a bare `grain ci` lists the way a bare `grain pause`
reads. The CI section of the nav rail
(`ui/src/components/CIPage.jsx`) is the other: the sandboxes CI is
holding right now, recent runs newest-first, and one run's jobs and
steps when you open it -- at `/ci` and `/ci/<run>`, so a run is a link
somebody can send. It was a tab inside the System pane until
grain/task-354.

Both are shaped around the two questions anybody actually has -- which
job failed, and what the step that failed printed -- so both put a run's
jobs failures-first (`ci.SortJobRuns` owns that rule, so they cannot
disagree about it) and show the failing step's output without being
asked: expanded in the pane, printed by `show` unless `-output none`
says otherwise, with `-output all` for every step's. A step's output is
already truncated in the middle past 256KB where it is produced
(`ci.maxStepOutput`), and neither reader truncates it further -- a view
that quietly dropped the tail of a failing test's output would be hiding
the one thing it was opened for.

A run is readable while it is still going, because the engine reports
each job to the service's store twice -- once as it gets its sandbox and
again as it finishes -- rather than reporting the lot at the end. So
the pane polls and fills in job by job, and `grain ci run
-watch` waits for the run and exits non-zero naming the conclusion. The
polling is bounded in both directions: an open run stops the listing
polling, and a run that has reached a conclusion stops polling
altogether, since nothing further will happen to it. `GET /api/ci/runs`
leaves each step's own output out of the runs it lists for the same
reason -- a hundred remembered runs' worth of 256KB steps, re-sent every
few seconds, to draw a table with no output column in it. Everything
else about a job and a step it keeps, because how far a run has got is
what a listing is for while it is still going.

`grain ci watch <id>` (equivalently `grain ci show -follow <id>`) is that
same poll pointed at a run somebody else started: every five seconds it
asks after the run and writes only the text no poll before it carried,
under a header line whenever the writing moves from one step to another,
and when the run concludes it prints the run and exits with its verdict.
It compares the whole of what it has already written rather than
remembering a byte offset, because a step's live output is bounded the
way a finished one's is -- past `ci.maxStepOutput` the buffer keeps its
head and its newest lines and drops the middle, so the text is
*rewritten* and an offset into the old text points at the middle of some
other line. When that happens the follower resumes from the newest thing
the reader was actually shown and says the middle was dropped, rather
than silently printing nothing for the rest of a job that has just got
interesting. Under `-json` it streams nothing at all and prints the
finished run as one document, since a document per poll would be a
stream of half-written runs rather than a run.

The first of those two reports is what makes the pane's top section
possible: a job carries the name of the sandbox it is running in
(`ci.JobRun.Sandbox`) from the moment it has one, so "which of this
deployment's machines is CI holding right now, and for how long" is
answered out of the runs the listing already fetches rather than by a
route of its own. A job queueing for a CI slot has no sandbox yet and a
job answered from the cache never gets one, so neither appears there --
which is the point: every row is a machine that exists.

The pane was a tab of System until grain/task-354, on the argument that
a deployment can be running no CI at all (`-ci=false`, and
`ui.CIRunsResponse.Enabled` says so, which is what the pane shows
instead of an empty table) and that a rail entry mostly reading "not
available" is one nobody opens. What moved it is that a red branch is
something people come looking for on purpose, several times a day, and
it is a fact about a repository rather than about the host -- which is
all the System pane is otherwise for. It has a figure of its own now,
cut from the same plate as the rest (`ui/src/brand/item-glyphs.js`,
`docs/brand.md`).

### A repo's runs, on that repo's page

There is a third reader now, and it is not a third view: a repo's own
page lists that repo's runs (`ui/src/components/RepoRuns.jsx`), under
the form where this deployment's workflows for it are written.

It is there because those two things are one sitting. The repo page is
where a workflow is edited for a repository grain does not own the tree
of, and it is the one place in the UI where somebody is thinking about
one repo's CI -- and it said nothing at all about what those workflows
had done. Seeing that meant leaving the page, opening System, picking CI
and narrowing a hundred deployment-wide runs back down to the repo you
had just been looking at. Now it is the five most recent, newest first,
each row's conclusion, branch, commit and job summary, with the rest a
button away.

Almost none of it is new machinery, which is the point. `GET
/api/ci/runs?repo=` already narrows at the daemon, so this page asks for
its own repo's runs and no others; the rows are the pane's own `RunList`
with the repo column dropped (a column repeating the page's title in
every row is noise, so the link that opens a run moves to the branch);
and `StartRunForm` is the pane's, with its repo picker fixed to the page
-- the repo is not a question here, so the form is a branch and a button.

What a row opens is where the decision was. Run detail -- the jobs, the
steps, the output, cancelling -- lives in the System pane, and there were
two ways to reach it: lift `RunDetail` into an overlay both pages could
draw, or send the reader to the CI tab the way a task's verdict already
does (`App.openCIRun`). This does the second. `openCIRun` now takes a
repo as well as a run, so it serves both callers: a task's verdict names
a run and no repo, "all runs for this repo" names a repo and no run and
opens the listing narrowed to it, and a row from this list names both --
so "← All runs" out of that run lands on the repo you came from rather
than on the deployment's hundred. The overlay is the better page and is
worth doing on its own; folding it into placing this list would have
grown a second copy of the run view to keep in step with the first.

The deployment that runs no CI at all is worth saying out loud here
rather than leaving to an empty table, precisely because the workflows
form is directly above: `-ci=false` will store every workflow written
there and run none of them, which is worth knowing before writing
another.

## What the whole deployment commits its sandbox host to

Every check grain made about a sandbox shape asked the same question:
can *one* sandbox of this shape exist? A per-task shape a backend cannot
honour is refused before the task is filed; a deployment-wide shape a
backend ignores is annotated where it is shown. Nothing asked whether
`max_workers` of them could exist at once on the machine they are built
on -- and that is the question this deployment got wrong. The Settings
pane accepted `max_workers` 5 x `sandbox_cpus` 3 x `sandbox_memory_mb`
3072 on a 4 vCPU / 15.8 GiB host: 15 vCPU committed against 4 cores, and
15 GiB of 15.8 before the daemon, the container runtime and the page
cache got any. It had been at 6 workers the day before, where the sum is
more memory than the machine has -- stated in two fields that never met,
on two different tabs, with the host's own size on a third.

It cost what you would expect. Over 36.9 hours of one deployment's
`task_run` history (185 runs), bucketed on each run's own time-weighted
mean concurrency, the rate at which a run's test suite hit "Test timed
out" went 0/3 below 3 concurrent, 3/16 at 3-4.5, 13/43 at 4.5-6 and
18/34 at 6 and above; median wall time went 24.5m, 35.3m, 41.5m, 58.1m
across the same buckets.

`ui.SandboxCommitment` is that arithmetic, reported on `GET
/api/settings` and shown on both tabs that set a term of it. Both kinds
of ordinary run are counted -- `max_workers + max_mergers`,
`model.Limits.Total` -- because every admitted run acquires a sandbox of
its own. Console sessions are not a term of it: no count bounds them, so
there is no slot to multiply (grain/task-2323).

It says the numbers, never a verdict: "5 workers + 2 mergers x 3 vCPU =
21 vCPU committed against the 4 this host has (5.2x); 21.0 of 15.7 GiB
memory (133%)". A bare "oversubscribed" would be no use, because
overcommitment is often the right call here -- an agent run spends most
of its wall time waiting on a model rather than on a core, and a strict
`workers x cpus <= cores` rule would have held that deployment to 2-3
concurrent runs at a real throughput cost. The three levels it computes
(`ok`, `caution`, `warning`, drawn where the figures above put the knee)
only decide how loudly to say it: an Alert on the pane past the
thresholds, plain helper text below them, so an operator can see where
they are before they get somewhere bad.

Once a deployment has a budget (`model.Budget`, above), the sentence
changes shape: the two pools are said separately, because only one of
them is a count times a shape. The agent pool's reservation is
`max_workers + max_mergers` at the deployment-wide
shape, exactly as before; CI's is not a product at all, and pretending it
was is what made this understate the commitment by half on a deployment
whose CI jobs ask for 16 GiB against an 8 GiB agent sandbox. A CI job
names its own `sandbox:` in the workflow file, so `max_ci_jobs` bounds
how many jobs there may be and not how much machine they take -- what
takes machine is bounded by `Limits.CIBudget`, the budget less the agent
pool's reservation, which is the figure that job's own gate admits it
against. So the note reads "3 workers + 1 merger x
2 vCPU = 8 vCPU reserved for agent runs, and 15 CI jobs share the 54
vCPU left of this deployment's 64 vCPU budget", with the memory clause
naming the reserve the budget is taken off the top of. The three fields
that set it are on the same tab, right under it (grain/task-197).

Memory warns rather than refuses too, and that is a finding rather than
a preference. A granule sandbox is a qemu guest given `-memory-mb` inside
a docker container created with no memory limit of its own
(`GranuleConfig.createArgs`), so guest memory is committed rather than
allocated and becomes resident only as the guest touches it. A
deployment whose slots are rarely all full genuinely runs this way, and
grain refusing the sixth sandbox on arithmetic done at save time would
be inventing a limit the backend does not have.

Where the host figures come from is asserted, not assumed. The capacity
reading is a seam of its own (`ui.Config.SandboxHostCapacity`) rather
than the `HostStats` the System pane already has, because those are
answers about two different machines and only the daemon knows when they
coincide: `HostStats` is *this process's* host, and this is the host a
*sandbox* is built on. The daemon wires it for the two backends whose
sandboxes are on this machine -- `GranuleSandboxes`, whose VMs are docker
containers created by a `granule` this process execs on its own
machine, and `HostSandboxes`, whose sandbox is a directory on this
filesystem -- so `/proc` here really is the sandbox host's `/proc`, and a
backend that built sandboxes anywhere else has to come and say so rather
than inherit a claim nobody made for it. Reporting the daemon's own
figures for one of those would have an operator sizing a deployment
against a machine that runs none of its work, which is worse than the
`nil` it gets instead.

The deployment with no shape at all is the one that commits the most.
Under host sandboxing the three shape settings are stored, shown and
annotated as sizing nothing, and it is `max_workers` that puts runs on
the machine: each of them an agent, a clone, a build and a test suite
with no cpu or memory limit of any kind, so five workers and two mergers
on a 4 vCPU host is seven of those at once. The first version of this
computed nothing there, on the grounds that a product of two numbers
that size nothing is arithmetic about a fiction. It is -- but
`max_workers` is not a fiction on any backend, and "sandbox cpus: 2 --
not in effect" is a true sentence that reads as reassurance. So that
deployment gets the same arithmetic with the shape taken out of it
(`ui.NewUncappedSandboxCommitment`): "5 workers + 2 mergers = 7
concurrent runs, each with no cpu or memory limit at all, on a host with
4 vCPU and 15.7 GiB (1.8 runs per core)". Runs per core is the only
ratio left, and the thresholds it is read against are the same evidence
divided by the same host's 4 cores -- caution at 0.75 runs per core,
where that deployment's test timeouts started appearing, and a warning at
1.5, the bucket where they were the ordinary outcome. Memory is not read
at all there rather than read leniently: what an unlimited run takes is
what it touches, which is not a share that can be added up in advance,
so the host's own total is printed as context and nothing is claimed to
be committed out of it.

Said in three places, because a pane only helps whoever used the pane.
On a deployment configured by merging a pull request against its state
repository, nobody edits those fields at all, and the first moment the
new numbers exist anywhere is when the daemon reads the merged row -- so
`grain settings` prints the same line, and the daemon logs it at startup
and again from `liveConfig.refresh` whenever one of the four settings it
is made of changes under a running daemon.

## An agent you can sit in front of

Every run grain has ever dispatched has been headless: a prompt goes in,
a transcript comes out, and the only thing anybody can say to a run in
flight is a comment on the task that the next poll may or may not fold
in. That is the right shape for work handed off, and the wrong one for
work being figured out -- pairing on a bug, walking a repository nobody
here knows, or driving an agent through a change whose next step depends
on what the last one printed.

There are two answers to that here, and they are not versions of each
other. A task holding the `console` capability gets the framework's own
CLI on a terminal in the browser, which is this section. A task filed as
*interactive* gets a chat window over the conversation the task already
has, which is "The other way to sit in front of one" at the end of it --
no PTY, no session manager, no per-framework command line, and nothing
dispatched differently.

A task holding the `console` capability is driven the other way. It is
dispatched by `dispatch.Cycle` like any other task, it gets a sandbox of
its own with its repository already cloned into it, and then
`consoleDispatch` wraps the framework `runOne` built in
`console.Framework` instead of calling it directly. That wrapper starts
the framework's own CLI on a pseudo-terminal (`agent.TerminalFramework`,
which `pkg/agent/claude` implements), registers the session with the
deployment's `console.Manager`, and blocks -- for as long as somebody
wants it. The session ends when they close it, when the CLI exits because
they typed `/exit`, or when `MaxConsoleRuntime` (a day, by default) runs
out on a session somebody forgot.

Everything else about the run is untouched, which is the whole design.
`RunDispatch` cannot tell a console framework from any other, so the run
gets the same clone, the same capability placements, the same branch
name, the same deadline machinery and the same ending: whatever the
session pushed becomes a pull request in the merge queue exactly as an
unattended run's would, and the terminal's own output is the attempt's
transcript in the task pane.

### The tool roster is the same one, and that is what makes it safe

The agent CLI runs on the controller, not in the sandbox -- the same
place `claude -p` has always run, reaching the sandbox through the forked
`grain mcpserver` its config names. So an interactive session gets
exactly what an unattended run of the same task gets, and what is dropped
is only ever the flags that make a run headless. A session without that
roster would be a person typing into an agent whose file tools point at
the daemon's own filesystem.

All three CLI frameworks implement it, and each keeps its own fence in
its own way -- which is the point: `TerminalCommand` sits beside `Run` in
the same package and reuses the same setup, rather than restating it.

  claude   keeps `--tools ""`, `--strict-mcp-config`, `--allowedTools`
           and `--mcp-config` naming this run's sandbox; drops `-p` and
           the `--output-format`/`--verbose` that make print mode
           parseable.
  codex    reads its whole configuration out of a private `CODEX_HOME`
           written per run, so there is nothing to repeat on the command
           line: the MCP server, `approval_policy = "never"` and
           `sandbox_mode = "read-only"` are all in that file either way.
           Drops the `exec` subcommand, `--json`, and
           `--skip-git-repo-check` -- the last of which is not a flag a
           session has no use for but a flag `codex` does not have:
           it belongs to `codex exec`, and passing it to the interactive
           CLI is "error: unexpected argument" and a dead session.
  agy      keeps `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, `--add-dir` and the
           model and effort; its denials of agy's own filesystem tools
           live in the settings file inside the private `HOME`, written
           the same way `Run` writes it. Drops the two stream-json
           formats and `--print-timeout`.

`agy` is the one that also drops something a headless run passes on
purpose: `--disable-slash-commands`. The slash commands are half of what
somebody sits down at that CLI for, and `/exit` is one of the three ways
a session ends at all.

Each of those three lists was derived by reading the framework's own
`Run` and removing what makes it headless, which is the right derivation
and not a measurement: a flag that survives it is asserted against
nothing, and the failure is not subtle -- it is "unexpected flag" on the
terminal of whoever first opens a session, on whichever deployment tries
it. `docs/agy-surface.md`, `docs/codex-surface.md` and
`docs/claude-surface.md` are those three binaries' own answers, captured
off the installed CLI by a workflow (`agy-surface`, `codex-surface`,
`claude-surface`) and committed so that a test can read
them: every flag each `TerminalCommand` passes has a row in a capture
saying the binary takes it, in that position. That check is what found
codex being handed `exec`'s repository flag at the top level.

The codex capture also says what happens instead of that flag. `codex
exec` refuses to start outside a git repository, which is the whole
reason an unattended run passes `--skip-git-repo-check` -- a granule run
has no local directory at all. The interactive half does not refuse: it
asks, "You are in ... an untrusted directory ... 1. Yes, continue", and a
session, unlike a run, has somebody there to answer.

The prompt is not passed by any of them. An unattended run's prompt
travels over stdin, and a session's stdin is a keyboard; its first
message is typed by whoever opened it. One thing goes with it for agy,
and is worth naming rather than leaving to be found: an unattended run's
prompt opens with the paragraph telling the model to treat agy's native
run/read/write/search tools as unavailable, and a session has no prompt
to carry it. The model is still *stopped* from using them -- the settings
file denies them by name and the hook blocks the call -- so what is lost
is the warning rather than the enforcement.

### A capability, not a column

`console` is a GRANT capability in `grain-ci`'s shape -- it mints
nothing, places nothing, and adds no prompt section. What that buys is
the three granularities this needs while it is new: per task by ticking
it in the new-task form, per repo in `RepoConfig.DefaultCapabilities`,
and deployment-wide in `Config.DefaultCapabilities`. It is deliberately
not `Task.Interactive`, which marks a task filed as a live chat -- filed
ahead of the backlog and opened in the chat view -- and changes nothing
about how its run is driven.

Both ways a console dispatch can fail say so rather than falling back: a
deployment holding no session manager, and a framework whose CLI cannot
be driven by hand, each end the dispatch as a `setup-failed` run naming
what was missing. The fallback would be to run the task unattended, which
is not a smaller version of what was asked for -- it is an agent working
alone through a task somebody meant to sit with, and they would find out
afterwards.

### The API the pane is built on

Five routes, all under `/api/console`:

    GET    /api/console                which sessions are live
    GET    /api/console/{task}/output  ?offset=N -- everything since N
    POST   /api/console/{task}/input   base64 bytes, as typed
    POST   /api/console/{task}/resize  {"rows": R, "cols": C}
    DELETE /api/console/{task}         close it, and end the run

Output and input are base64 because a terminal carries bytes rather than
characters: escape sequences, `^C`, and whatever half of a UTF-8 rune
happened to be at the end of a read. Output is a ring with an offset, and
a read that has fallen behind it is told `dropped: true` rather than
handed a hole -- a terminal emulator recovers from that by redrawing.
Polling rather than streaming because that is the transport this API has
everywhere else; a websocket would buy a terminal fewer round trips and
nothing else.

### The rail is where a session is found

A live session gets a section of its own in the sidebar, beside Boards,
listing one entry per session with a marker saying whether its CLI is
still running. That is not decoration: it is the only place a console is
findable. The task behind it looks like any other running task in the
list, and the whole value of an interactive run is being one click away
from the terminal somebody left open. It is also the one section of that
rail whose contents nobody saved -- a console exists while it is being
sat in front of, and stops existing when it is closed. A deployment that
serves none grows no section at all, on `enabled: false` rather than on
a guess.

Clicking one opens `ConsolePage`: the task's title, the repo and
framework it is working in, a link to the task itself, one button that
closes the session, and the terminal under all of it. `/consoles` is the
list and `/consoles/42` is one session's terminal, so a console is a link
somebody can send or reload back into -- which matters more here than
anywhere else in `paths.js`, because reloading is the ordinary way a
terminal pane is recovered, and landing back on the task list instead
would put the session three clicks away.

Closing is the one control on that pane that acts on the run rather than
on the view, so it asks first. Navigating away leaves a session exactly
where it was; closing ends the CLI, finishes the run, and sends whatever
it pushed to the merge queue.

### Why the front end takes a dependency

The terminal is xterm.js, and it is the only new package this whole
feature adds. What is on the other end is a full-screen TUI: it moves the
cursor, repaints regions, opens the alternate screen and colours half of
what it prints, all in escape sequences. Rendered as plain text those are
line noise; rendered with the escapes stripped they are a pile of
half-drawn frames. The tool is only legible if something interprets them.
`LogsPage` next door prints log lines into a `<pre>` and is right to --
lines somebody scans and copies a fragment out of -- and this is the
other thing.

Everything else about the pane is this repository's own conventions.
`ConsoleTerminal` polls, like every live pane here, but on a clock that
moves: a poll that returned output is followed in 60ms, because a busy
terminal is one somebody is watching; an idle one backs off to 400ms, so
an agent thinking for a minute does not cost seventeen requests a second;
and a keystroke kicks the loop directly, so the echo never waits on the
idle timer. A fixed three seconds -- `POLL_INTERVAL_MS`, what the rest of
the UI runs on -- would have been the delay between pressing a key and
seeing it. Keystrokes are serialized rather than fired in parallel,
because two POSTs racing would arrive at the PTY in the other order and
transpose what somebody typed.

### Filing one

"New console" opens the ordinary new-task form with the `console`
capability already ticked. There is no second form and it would be wrong
to write one: a console is a task, and everything else that form asks --
which repo, which agent, what it may read, what it may write -- is as
much a question for an interactive task as for any other.

Ticked rather than forced. The capability appears in the picker like any
other and can be un-ticked before the task is filed, which keeps the
form's own rule that what it says it is about to file is what it files.

### The other way to sit in front of one: a chat

The terminal above is one answer to "an agent you can sit in front of",
and it is the expensive one. A task filed as a *chat* -- `Interactive` on
the task, the flag `grain new -interactive` and the new-task form's own
"Interactive session" tick already set -- is the other, and it is served
by the frontend alone (grain/task-414).

Nothing is dispatched differently for it, which is the point. grain
already carries a conversation in both directions: a comment posted while
a run is in flight reaches the agent mid-run (`agent.RunConfig.Addenda`,
`orchestrator.addendaPoller`), and what a run says back -- a relayed
`ask_question`, a closing `comment_on_issue` -- is posted as a comment on
the same task. An interactive session is that exchange. What was missing
was never a transport; it was that the exchange was drawn as a task's
timeline, which is a history of something that happened rather than a
conversation somebody is having.

So an interactive task's pane opens as a chat window
(`ui/src/components/TaskChat.jsx`, with `ui/src/chat.js` deciding what a
chat says): the messages in bubbles oldest-first, the task's own body as
the message that started it, a composer under them, and -- while an agent
is working -- an indicator carrying whatever the run last said it was
doing (`ui.Task.Activity`, written by `update_status` and by every
`run_command`'s own description). The timeline that pane used to borrow
folds up underneath it, so an attempt's transcript and its pull request
events are one click away rather than gone. Every other task is
untouched: its timeline is still the whole of its conversation.

Two things the chat says that a bare feed of comments would not. A run
that ended without answering -- failed, cancelled, setup-failed -- gets a
line of its own, because it is why the conversation went quiet, and a
chat that simply stops is the one thing a person cannot diagnose from the
window they are looking at. A successful run gets nothing: every turn of
a chat is a run, and "Succeeded" between each pair of messages would be
one separator per message saying what the reply under it already says.

What a chat gives up against the terminal is the CLI's own interface: a
slash command typed here is text in a message rather than a command, and
an agent wanting a decision asks for it in words. What it costs is one
frontend dependency and no backend at all -- against a PTY per session, a
session manager, five routes, a byte ring with an offset, a second
command line per framework and a captured surface per binary to check
those flags against. That is why both exist rather than one replacing the
other: a task that really needs the CLI holds the `console` capability
and gets the terminal.

The dependency is `@chatscope/chat-ui-kit-react` (MIT), on the same
reasoning that took xterm.js next door -- a chat window is a solved shape
with a dozen details in it (pinning the view to the newest message unless
the reader has scrolled up, growing the input with what is typed, Enter
to send and Shift+Enter for a newline), and none of them are this
repository's problem. What stays grain's own is what is grain's rather
than the chat's: message bodies go through `Markdown.jsx` like every
other relayed answer, and a file on a message is a task attachment
(`AttachmentPicker`/`AttachmentLinks`) rather than a chat upload, so the
library's own attach button is off.

One environment gap comes with it, shimmed in `ui/src/setupTests.js`
beside the two already there for xterm: jsdom's selector engine (nwsapi,
including the newest release) mis-parses a selector *list* whose
alternatives are attribute selectors, which is exactly the line the
library asks on every update of a message list. Every browser accepts it,
so without the shim any re-render of a chat throws under test and passes
in production -- the worst shape a test-environment gap can take. The
shim only ever rescues: the native call is tried first, and the fallback
re-asks each alternative and returns whichever match comes first in
document order.

### What typing in it costs

An operator reported that typing in a long-running session's chat was
"very very slow" (grain/task-174), and the shape of the report was the
diagnosis: nothing is sent to the daemon between one character and the
next -- a comment goes out on Enter or on Send and at no other moment --
and it showed up on an old conversation rather than a fresh one. So it
was main-thread work that grew with the transcript.

It was. The composer is controlled by state on `TaskChat`, and
`TaskChat`'s render body *was* the transcript: `chatEntries(t)` with its
sort, then a `<Message>` per entry, each one a `<Markdown>` -- remark and
rehype over kilobytes of an agent's prose -- with no `memo` anywhere on
the path. Every character typed re-parsed every message in the
conversation. Measured at 2.7ms of script per message per keystroke:
112ms on a 41-message chat, 186ms on 81, which is what a Director
session looks like after an hour and after two
(`docs/hand-runs/2026-09-17-chat-keystroke.md`, with its harness).

Two changes, and the second is the one that needed a decision.
`Markdown` is `memo`'d, which is worth doing on its own merits
everywhere -- its props are a body string and a className, so the
comparison is two `===` against the most expensive component in this UI,
and the task timeline and the inbox render many of them at once under an
overlay that polls. And the transcript is held as one memoised element
keyed on the entries rather than built in the render body, so the
keystroke re-renders the composer and React bails out of the subtree
under it. Per-keystroke script time is now flat in the length of the
conversation: 2.8-3.8ms at every size measured, against 25ms-186ms
before.

The tidier fix is the one the library forbids. Moving the draft into a
small child that renders only the `MessageInput` would put the list out
of `setDraft`'s reach structurally rather than by memoisation --
but `ChatContainer` picks its children *by component type*
(`getChildren(children, [ConversationHeader, MessageList, MessageInput,
InputToolbox])`) and silently drops everything else, so a `<Composer>`
wrapping a `MessageInput` renders nothing at all. There is an `as`
escape hatch, and it would still leave the draft out of reach of the
Send button and `AttachmentPicker`, which sit outside the chat window in
a different parent and read `draft.text`. The component says so where
somebody would otherwise try it.

What is pinned, in `TaskChat.renders.test.jsx` and
`Markdown.memo.test.jsx`, is the *property* rather than a duration: the
number of message bodies rendered per keystroke is zero, and it is the
same number on a 41-message conversation as on a three-message one. A
millisecond threshold would have been a red build about a busy CI
sandbox; what broke here was never a constant, it was the constant's
dependence on N.

One cost this leaves is the poll's, and it is filed rather than widened
into: on a task whose `activity` moves every tick, `keepIfSame` cannot
bail out, `t` is a new object, so the entries are recomputed and every
`Message`, header and `AttachmentLinks` re-renders three seconds apart.
The `Markdown` memo takes ~88% of that with it -- 108ms to 12ms at 41
messages -- but what is left is still linear in the conversation, and
fixing it properly is a change to what a poll hands the chat rather than
to the composer.

### A turn of the chat happens inside one run

A live turn used to *be* a run. A message posted while a run was in
flight was folded into it -- but only `agent/claude` polls addenda at all
-- and everything a run said back was recovered from `agent.Result` once
the process had exited (`orchestrator.ProcessResult` relaying
`ask_question` and `comment_on_issue`), so a two-line exchange cost two
dispatches, two sandboxes and a cold prompt each way. A message that
landed after a run finished waited for the next dispatch to be read at
all (grain/task-421).

The tool that closes that is `chat`. It posts what the run has to say
into the task's own conversation, points
`Observation.PendingQuestionCommentID` at it so the row reads
*awaiting reply* the instant the run pauses, and blocks until a person
answers -- their words come back as that same tool call's result, with
the run's sandbox, its reading of the code and the whole conversation
still in front of it. It is the shape `pkg/capability/selfrepair`'s
`Confirm` has described since before anything could call it; what makes
it callable is that the waiting now happens over the daemon's REST API
(`POST`/`GET /api/tasks/{id}/messages`, modelled on `activity.go`) rather
than against a `*model.Store` no forked `mcpserver` has.
`cmd/grain/mcpserver.go`'s `daemonChat` posts and then polls that
conversation once a second, which is not a tuning knob: this is a session
somebody is sitting in, and a reply that takes a minute to arrive is not
a conversation.

It is registered only for a task filed as `Interactive`
(`agent.RunConfig.Interactive`, one `-interactive` flag that all three
frameworks pass on the way `GrantArgs` passes grants). A background run
is not offered a tool whose whole promise is that somebody is there:
every call would stand still for an hour before finding out nobody was.

Three things this had to decide, and the answers are the interesting part
of it.

**What a chat turn costs the run's budget: nothing.** `MaxRunRuntime` is
two hours of *working*, and a run blocked waiting for somebody to type is
spending nothing at all -- an agent inside a tool call asks its provider
for nothing, exactly as an idle console session does. One turn can wait
up to an hour (`mcp.ChatWait`), which is most of an ordinary run's whole
budget, so an interactive dispatch gets a clock of its own
(`DefaultMaxInteractiveRuntime`, eight hours) the way a console session
gets a day, rather than a chat wait being credited back one turn at a
time against a budget for work. Eight hours rather than the console's day
because the two differ in one way: a console session costs a sandbox and
no tokens, and this one has an agent in it that can also *work* between
turns, so the wall has to be close enough to bound a session that stops
chatting and starts looping. Both agent CLIs' own per-tool-call caps are
now sized from `mcp.MaxBlockingToolWait`, the longer of a chat turn and a
`wait_for_checks`, so a second blocking tool cannot quietly outlive a
number that was set for the first.

**What `codex` and `agy` do: the same thing `claude` does.** Neither
polls addenda, so "a reply reaches a live run" was a claude-only property
of the old arrangement. A blocking tool call asks nothing of a framework
except that it lets the call block, which all three do -- so this is a
property of the tool rather than something to discover per framework.
(`codex` is the one to watch: grain writes its whole configuration and
sets no per-tool-call timeout there, so a build of `codex` that enforces
one of its own would cut a long turn short.)

**What happens when a wait ends with nobody there: the task stays
parked**, which is the honest state. The message is in the conversation,
the task reads *awaiting reply*, and their next message un-parks it
through the same `Client.AddComment` every other awaiting-reply task is
answered by and dispatches a fresh run with the whole thread in front of
it. Nothing is lost by a session ending; the conversation simply goes
back to costing a run per turn. `ProcessResult` now reads that park
before it decides an ending (`parkedOnAQuestion`) -- without it, a chat
run that also left a closing note would mark the task *complete*, since
`CompletedAt` outranks a pending question in `model.StateOf`, and a
completed task is not dispatched by a reply, so the conversation would
have died there with nothing saying why.

## A proxy per model vendor, and a token per run

A run that wants to call a model *for itself* -- a script it writes, a
second `claude` or `codex` started inside its own checkout, an
evaluation harness that has to score a hundred answers -- had two
options here, and neither was one to reach for. It could be handed this
deployment's own credential for that vendor
(`secrets.ClaudeOAuthTokenSecret`, `secrets.OpenAIAPIKeySecret`,
`secrets.GeminiAPIKeySecret`), which is the credential every other run
and the daemon itself authenticate as: a run that leaks it into a log, a
transcript or a commit leaks all of it, and there is nothing to revoke
short of rotating the thing the whole deployment runs on. Or it could do
without.

`pkg/modelproxy` is the third option, and it is the same shape
`pkg/gitproxy` already is for GitHub: the credential stays on the
controller, and what crosses into the sandbox is a token that is worth
nothing anywhere else. The proxy authenticates a request against a
registry of tokens this deployment minted, swaps the caller's own
credentials for the deployment's, and forwards upstream. A token is
minted per run, as its capability is materialized, and dropped when the
run's lease is revoked -- so the credential a finished run's sandbox
holds authorizes exactly as much as that run's git token does, which is
nothing.

**Past the token check, nothing is grain's.** The path, the method, the
body, the status and the stream are the vendor's own, which is what
makes `export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=...` (or `OPENAI_BASE_URL`, or
`GOOGLE_GEMINI_BASE_URL`) enough for any client that reads it -- the
SDKs, the `claude` and `codex` CLIs, plain `curl` -- and what stops this
build from breaking a run on the day a vendor ships something it has not
heard of. It is an `httputil.ReverseProxy` rather than the
read-body/decide/write-body shape the git proxy uses, because a model
reply is a server-sent-event stream a human is watching arrive: the git
proxy can buffer a pack it has already decided about, and buffering this
would turn a streaming API into a batch one.

**One package, three vendors.** It began as `pkg/claudeproxy`, one
vendor's proxy, deliberately not generalized until there was a second
caller to generalize against; codex and Gemini were that caller, and the
seam the generalization found is the one that was already visible. The
token registry, the endpoint a capability provider mints from, the
handler, the bind-and-advertise and the whole of the capability --
placement, prompt, lease, credential check -- know nothing about any
vendor and are written once. Everything that does know is a
`modelproxy.Vendor` value:

- **the upstream**, and the base URL a client of that vendor expects to
  be given (`OPENAI_BASE_URL` carries the `/v1` an `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`
  does not, so the file placed in the sandbox carries it too);
- **the credential rule** -- which is not decided here either.
  `credcheck.AuthorizeAnthropic` and its `AuthorizeOpenAI` and
  `AuthorizeGemini` siblings are the same rules Settings' own "test this
  credential" button follows (a Claude Code OAuth token as a bearer with
  the beta it is paired with and anything else as an `x-api-key`; an
  OpenAI key as a bearer; a Gemini key as a `key=` query parameter),
  exported so that the pane testing a credential and the proxy spending
  it cannot disagree about one secret;
- **the error shape a refusal is written in**, which stays each vendor's
  own on purpose: Anthropic's `{"type":"error",...}`, OpenAI's
  `{"error":{...,"code":"invalid_api_key"}}` and Google's
  `{"error":{"code":401,"status":"UNAUTHENTICATED"}}`, so a client
  library refused by grain raises the error it already knows how to
  raise, with a message naming grain.

**Gemini's key is not a header**, and that is the one place the
generalization is more than a base URL. That API takes its key as a
`key=` query parameter, so swapping a credential means rewriting the
outbound URL: the caller's own key is stripped from the query before
anything leaves, this deployment's is put in its place, and the rest of
the query (`alt=sse` and whatever else) is the client's own. Everything
downstream of that follows from a credential living in a URL. An audit
entry records a method and a path and never a query string. A transport
error is redacted against the deployment credential before it is written
back into the sandbox, because an error naming the URL it failed on
would otherwise hand a run the very credential this exists to keep from
it.

**It needs no routing.** A granule guest can already reach the docker
bridge gateway -- that is how a `git clone` from the git proxy works at
all -- so more listeners on the same address, advertised at the same
`-granule-git-proxy-host`, are visible from inside the guest with no
DNAT, no second flag and no change to any sandbox image. Loopback for a
deployment whose sandboxes are directories on this host, every interface
for one whose sandboxes are VMs, exactly as `startGitProxy` decides it.
One listener per vendor rather than one multiplexing them on a path
prefix: the whole promise here is that what is behind the address is the
vendor's own API at the vendor's own paths, and a socket is cheaper than
a base URL that is not quite right. A failure to bind is logged rather
than fatal, unlike the git proxy's -- and it is per vendor, so a port
that will not bind costs that one capability rather than the other two:
nothing dispatched needs these to start, and the capability that does
refuses cleanly for as long as its endpoint has no address to hand
anybody, where a deployment with no git proxy cannot check anything out
at all.

That last claim is the one nothing on the controller can check, so it has
a test of its own inside a guest:
`pkg/orchestrator/model_proxy_real_test.go` boots a real
cloud-hypervisor VM in the `real-vm` job and, for each of the three
vendors, binds a real proxy in front of a local stand-in upstream (no
vendor call, no spend), advertises it at the gateway docker reports for
that VM's own network namespace, materializes that vendor's capability
for a run whose sandbox is that VM, and then runs `curl` in the guest
against the two placed files -- once for the stand-in's answer, and once
after the lease is revoked for the 401. All three rather than one because
the routing claim is vendor-blind but the rest of what the guest is
handed is not: this is the only place the exports the prompt tells a run
to paste are executed rather than asserted, `/v1` and `?key=` included.
The git proxy made the same claim and had it wrong for months
(bwsalmon/agents#567), because every test that could have caught it ran
on the host, where `127.0.0.1` is the right answer.

**A token is two halves**, `<id>.<secret>`, and only the id is ever
written down. `pkg/capability/modelproxy` is a MINT provider, so what
it mints is recorded as a `model.Lease` -- and a lease is a row in
grain's store, which is a file in the state repository grain exports
itself to every 30 seconds (`pkg/staterepo`). A lease naming the token
would publish a live credential to a git repository on the next sync; a
lease naming its id revokes exactly as well and says nothing. The
registry itself is in memory rather than a `sandbox-tokens.json` of its
own: the git proxy's file exists because a restarted proxy must not
break a sandbox that is still cloning, and nothing here has that shape
-- a token is minted mid-run, for a run a restarted daemon has already
lost. So this deployment's disk never holds a credential whose only
purpose is to be handed to a sandbox, and the one copy that exists is
the file inside the sandbox.

**Three grants, not one with a vendor argument.** `claude-proxy`,
`openai-proxy` and `gemini-proxy` are separate capabilities, so a task
is granted the vendor it needs and gets a token for that proxy alone,
and Settings reports each one ready off its own secret -- a deployment
holding an Anthropic credential and no OpenAI one has one capability
ready and one not, which is two rows rather than one hedged sentence.
They cost one provider registration each and no duplicated code, since
the provider is written once and built three times. `claude-proxy` keeps
the name it was born with, so a deployment that already defaults it is
untouched.

Each grant is ordinary in every other way: ticked in the picker or
defaulted per repo like any other capability, and the "test credential"
button beside it asks that vendor to list the models the credential can
see -- the same call the Agents tab makes for the framework, because it
is the same secret. What a run holding one is told is two lines:

```sh
export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL="$(cat /home/debian/.claude-proxy-url)"
export ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN="$(cat /home/debian/.claude-proxy-token)"
```

```sh
export OPENAI_BASE_URL="$(cat /home/debian/.openai-proxy-url)"
export OPENAI_API_KEY="$(cat /home/debian/.openai-proxy-token)"
```

```sh
export GOOGLE_GEMINI_BASE_URL="$(cat /home/debian/.gemini-proxy-url)"
export GEMINI_API_KEY="$(cat /home/debian/.gemini-proxy-token)"
```

## Apache 2.0, in one file at the root

`LICENSE` is the Apache License, Version 2.0, verbatim -- the text
Debian ships as `/usr/share/common-licenses/Apache-2.0`, byte for byte,
so a checksum matches the canonical file rather than a retyping of it.
Until it landed there was no license in this repository at all, which is
not the same as "do what you like": code published without one carries
no permission to use, copy or modify it, whatever the repository's
visibility suggests. Apache 2.0 rather than MIT for the two things MIT
does not say -- an explicit patent grant from every contributor, and a
termination clause if someone sues over one.

The holder is one person, and `NOTICE` is where the repository says so:
`Copyright 2026 Brandon Salmon`, and nothing else. A NOTICE file is a
commitment rather than a decoration -- §4(d) makes its contents
something every downstream redistribution has to carry along -- which is
exactly why it is one copyright line and not a paragraph about the
project. The history looks like several authors at a glance, since
commits land under `grain agent`, `Claude`, `Brandon Agent` and plain
`grain` as well as `bwsalmon`, but each of those is a run of this
deployment's own agents rather than a contribution from outside, and
every commit with a human behind it carries the same address. One holder
is the reading that matches what happened.

`LICENSE` itself stays verbatim, appendix and all. Its
`Copyright [yyyy] [name of copyright owner]` is the boilerplate the
appendix tells you to paste into your own files, not a blank the license
file is waiting to have filled in, and filling it in would cost the
byte-for-byte match that makes checksumming it worth anything. This is
what Kubernetes and most large Go projects do too. The name lives in
`NOTICE`, which is the file Apache 2.0 already points every
redistributor at.

There are no per-file copyright headers, deliberately: a banner on every
file is a line every file then has to keep correct, and nothing here
reads one. Naming a holder does not change that -- `NOTICE` names it
once. The license lives in the one file at the root, and
`SPDX-License-Identifier` lines can be added on top of that later
without any of it moving.

The image needs no change to carry either file: the runtime stage copies
the whole tree to `/usr/local/share/grain/src` for the self-debug
capability (Dockerfile, "The source the runtime stage carries"), so
`LICENSE` and `NOTICE` ship wherever the binary does, and
`read_grain_source` can quote them.

`third_party/granule` is the one directory this does not speak for. It is
a source snapshot of [bwsalmon/granule](https://github.com/bwsalmon/granule),
kept byte-for-byte upstream on purpose -- its `VENDORED.md` is the file
that says why, and what a local patch costs -- so it is that project's
code on that project's own terms, and a license for it belongs on
granule's `main` and arrives here by a resync, like everything else in
that directory. `NOTICE` reaches it no further than `LICENSE` does: it
is the same author's repository, so the copyright line is not wrong
about it, but the terms it is offered under are still granule's to
state.

## A sandbox with no network

A task can say how much of the internet its sandbox reaches
(`model.Task.NetworkAccess`, grain/task-269): `open`, which is what every
sandbox grain has ever built had, or `none`. A template can fix it for
everything it files, and a deployment sets the default every task that
names nothing falls back to (`model.Config.NetworkAccess`, the Sandbox
tab, `grain settings -network-access`). Empty means "no override" on a
task and on a template, and means `open` on the deployment -- the same
"zero means unset" ladder the agent framework and the sandbox shape
already climb, resolved per dimension in `orchestrator.Shape.orDefault`,
because the network a sandbox has is decided exactly when the sandbox is
created and there is nothing to change afterwards.

**What `none` means is "this deployment and nothing else".** A sandbox
still has to reach two things or no run can happen at all: the control
link `granule exec` arrives on, and the git proxy every checkout clones
through. Both are directly connected -- the proxy is advertised at the
host-side docker gateway (`GRAIN_KONTUR_GIT_PROXY_HOST`), which under
netshim's flat mode is the guest's own subnet, and the Claude proxy is on
that same address. So the mechanism is the guest's **default route**:
`GranuleSandboxes.enforceGuestNetwork` deletes it (looped, for a guest
with more than one, plus the v6 flush), then reads `/proc/net/route` and
`ip -6 route show default` back to check. No packet filter, nothing that
has to be installed in the guest image, and the check is in the same
command as the change.

It fails the acquire when it does not take, which is the difference
between this and `ensureGuestKVMAccess` beside it: that one repairs a
guest image's oversight and logs whatever it could not fix, because a
sandbox that cannot run nested VMs is still a sandbox nearly every task
can use. This is a promise, and a run dispatched into a sandbox that
quietly kept its route is worse than a run that never started. The same
goes for the other half of the promise: with the route gone, the git
proxy has to still be reachable *on-link* (`ip route get`, refusing an
answer that goes via a gateway), or the sandbox is one where every clone
would fail for a reason nothing would explain. A `recreate_sandbox`
rebuild re-applies both, since the replacement guest boots with its
routing table intact.

The honest caveat, which is also in `docs/design.md`: dropping the
default route leaves the guest's own directly-connected segment
reachable, and that segment is the host's docker bridge. The git proxy
is the point of that; a sibling sandbox's container is on it too, which
is already true today with the network on. This is `egress_policy(
allowlist)` narrowed to one destination, not a hypervisor-level cut.

`orchestrator.HostSandboxes` -- the default, a directory on the daemon's
own machine -- can enforce none of this: a run there uses the host's own
network stack, so the only way to withhold it would be to withhold it
from the daemon. It refuses to acquire for a task asking for `none`,
naming the backend, and the API refuses such a task at the moment
somebody files it (`Config.SandboxShapeIgnored`, the same flag that
disables the sandbox-shape fields, because it is the same question about
the same backend). The new-task form disables the picker there for the
same reason it disables those.

## The System pane's load average has a denominator now

The host reading on Sandbox health said "Load average (1/5/15 min): 8.00
/ 6.20 / 5.10" and stopped there. That is not a reading anybody can act
on: 8.0 is a quarter of an idle 32-core machine and twice what a 4-core
one can run at once, and the pane exists to answer "is this host starved
right now" -- which is the same number over two different denominators.
The count was already being read on every poll (`pkg/sysstat.Snapshot`
gained `CPUs` for the commitment arithmetic, counted from `/proc/stat`'s
per-CPU lines), and simply was not carried past `hostStats`.

`ui.HostPressure.CPUs` carries it now, and the pane says "8.00 / 6.20 /
5.10 of 4 vCPU" with each figure past the core count coloured: amber
from one runnable process per core, red from two. Two levels because
they are different news. As much runnable work as there are cores is a
fully committed machine with nothing waiting yet, which is the ordinary
state of a deployment running the number of sandboxes it was sized for.
Twice that is a machine where the average runnable process waits about
as long as it runs, which is what a sandbox that looks stuck looks like
from underneath. The number itself is never replaced by a word -- the
figure is what an operator decides on, and the colour is only what makes
them look -- and the per-core figure is on each coloured number's
tooltip.

Zero `cpus` means no count, and the pane then reads exactly as it did
before: a daemon not on Linux has no `/proc` to count, and one older
than the field sends nothing, neither of which is a reason to divide by
zero or to claim a single core.

It stays a colour on a live figure rather than the banner the
overcommitment warning gets, because these are two different questions
and conflating them would make both harder to read. This is a reading
that crosses back over on its own as runs finish; `ui.SandboxCommitment`
is about settings that stay wrong until somebody changes them, and it is
not always even about this machine (`Config.SandboxHostCapacity` is the
sandbox host, `HostStats` is this process's). The caution/warning
vocabulary is shared with it deliberately, so an operator reading both
panes reads one scale.

## The agent's own memory is not offered to a run that cannot reach it

`claude` ships a persistent memory of its own: a directory under the
CLI's `$HOME`, a system-prompt preamble describing the file format to
save facts in and the `MEMORY.md` index to point at them from, and that
index's contents injected into every session's context as "user's
auto-memory, persists across conversations". For an engineer running the
CLI on their laptop that is a feature. For a grain run it is two lies.

The agent process runs on the controller, because its credential must
never enter the sandbox ("The agent runtime is a CLI now" above), so the
`$HOME` that preamble names is the controller's — `$GRAIN_DATA_DIR/home`,
laid out by `scripts/setup.sh` — while `read_file`, `write_file` and
`edit_file` all act in the sandbox at the other end of the MCP
connection, where that path does not exist. A run that follows the index
to one of its own files gets `ENOENT`; a run that tries to save a memory
finds `--tools ""` has already emptied the native roster the preamble
tells it to use, and would be writing into a sandbox that is destroyed
when it ends. In grain's own deployment seven runs each spent a turn
discovering the first of those, following the one pointer in an index
that described a deployment two sandbox backends ago.

So `agent/claude` sets `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY=1` for every run
it dispatches, alongside the `MCP_TOOL_TIMEOUT` it already sets, and both
halves stop arriving: no preamble, no index. An operator who set that
variable themselves is left alone on exactly the same terms
`mcpToolTimeout` leaves theirs — including the `=0` of a deployment that
has found a way to give its runs a memory directory they really can
reach, which is the option this deliberately does not foreclose.

Two things this does not do. It does not delete
`$GRAIN_DATA_DIR/home/.claude/projects/-/memory` on a host that already
has one: nothing reads that directory into a prompt any more, and
removing files from a running deployment's home is an operator's `rm`
rather than a setup script's. And it does not touch the standing note a
deployment may have put in its own `prompt_extension` telling runs to
ignore the preamble — that lives in the state repository, and is a
pull request there rather than a change here.

## A sub-tab per capability

The Capabilities tab drew one card per capability, stacked. That was a
readable shape when the stack was `gcp-key`, `gemini-key`, `self-debug`
and `github-sandbox`; the catalog is fourteen now, plus one row per
named GitHub token a deployment has configured (`github-credential:*`),
and the stack had stopped answering the two questions it exists for.
"Which capabilities is this deployment configured for" was only
answerable by scrolling the whole list and reading fourteen badges, and
the fields for the one an operator actually came to fix — its own
write-only credential boxes, "Test credential" beside them — were
somewhere down that scroll with nothing above to say which way.

So `CapabilitiesPanel` is a strip of sub-tabs now, one per capability,
and each label carries a dot: filled where this deployment is configured
for that one, a hollow ring where it is not. The dot is the information
rather than decoration, so unlike `ItemGlyph` it is named for a screen
reader — the tab announces "GCP key, not configured" — and the strip is
both the summary and the way in. Opening one shows exactly what its card
showed: the readiness, grantability and default chips, every "needs" and
"missing" line, its secret fields, and the credential check where this
deployment can make the call.

The strip stays in the API's own catalog order and is deliberately not
sorted with the unconfigured ones first. Setting a secret is what makes
a capability ready, and a strip that re-sorted on readiness would move
every other tab under the cursor of whoever had just fixed one. The
count that ordering would have given — how many are configured, and the
names of the ones that are not — sits on the deployment-wide sub-tab
instead, where nothing moves.

That sub-tab is the other half of the tab: the GCP project and service
account fields `gcp-key`/`gemini-key` need, the picker choosing which
capabilities every new task is filed holding
(`model.Config.DefaultCapabilities`), and "Other secrets". It leads the
strip and opens first, so the tab still lands on what it always landed
on, and it stays `SettingsOverlay`'s own `<form>` — passed to the panel
as a node, with that pane's save, preview and payload behind it
untouched. Switching sub-tab clears any change preview for the same
reason switching tab does: a plan belongs to the form it was asked
about.
## A cluster is a third host adapter

grain has had two places to put a sandbox: a directory on the machine the
daemon runs on (`orchestrator.HostSandboxes`, no isolation at all) and a
bwsalmon/granule VM on that same machine (`orchestrator.GranuleSandboxes`).
Both assume the deployment owns a machine. `orchestrator.K8sSandboxes`
(grain/task-358) is the third: one Kubernetes pod per run, created by
`Acquire` and deleted by `Release`, reached with `kubectl exec` instead
of over SSH.

The seam it plugs into is the one that was already there. `Deps.Sandboxes`
is an interface, and everything above it — the checkout, the git
credential write, the capability placements, the four sandbox tools, the
health pane, the startup sweep for what a killed process left behind —
goes through `Sandbox` and its optional interfaces rather than through
anything backend-specific. So the whole of the new backend is a
`Sandboxes` implementation, a transport (`mcp.KubectlExecRunner`,
answering the same unexported `remoteRunner` contract
`mcp.DockerExecRunner` does, so `NewSSHSandboxTools`,
`ConfigureGitCredentialsOverSSH` and `PlaceFileOverSSH` all work over it
unchanged), and a driver for the verbs it needs (`pkg/k8s`).

`pkg/k8s` shells out to `kubectl` rather than linking client-go, which is
the same choice `pkg/granule` makes about `granule` and for the same two
reasons: client-go is an enormous dependency whose version has to be kept
in step with the cluster's, for about eight verbs' worth of use; and
`kubectl` is what an operator debugging a stuck sandbox reaches for
anyway, so every call grain makes is one they can paste into a shell and
watch fail identically.

### What a pod is and is not

Worth saying plainly, because it is not the trade the granule backend
makes. A pod is a container, so a run shares its node's kernel with every
other pod scheduled there; a granule VM shares a kernel with nothing.
Against a task's own agent that is a real difference. Against what
grain's sandboxing is mostly for — one task not inheriting the next
task's checkout, credentials or leftover processes — it is the same
guarantee, from the same place: the sandbox exists for one run and is
deleted with it.

What it buys is that scheduling, sizing, placement and teardown are the
cluster's primitives. A sandbox's `Shape` becomes a pod's resource
requests and limits — equal to each other on purpose, so a task that
asked for a size is not throttled or evicted for using it — and the
cluster's scheduler is what refuses to overcommit, rather than an
operator doing arithmetic against one machine's cores. That is why
`sandboxHostCapacity` declines to answer for this backend: there is no
single machine whose capacity the deployment's concurrency is spent
against, so the pane that multiplies shape by concurrency has nothing
true to say and shows nothing instead of something plausible.

### Saying no rather than saying nothing

Two refusals carry most of this backend's honesty.

A task that asks for no network access is refused unless the deployment
has passed `-k8s-network-policy`. Taking a pod's network away means a
`NetworkPolicy`, which every cluster accepts and only some enforce — a
cluster running kubenet, or a managed one with its plugin off, stores the
object and ignores it. Applying one and hoping would hand a task that was
promised an air-gapped sandbox a fully networked one with nothing
anywhere saying so. So the flag exists for an operator to assert
something about their cluster that grain cannot check from inside a pod,
`deploy/kubernetes/networkpolicy.yaml` says what to verify and in what
order, and until then the dispatch fails naming the flag. It is the same
refusal `HostSandboxes.Acquire` already gives, for the same reason.

The other is `k8s.Client.Manifest` writing all three dimensions of a pod's
shape on every create, even the ones nobody named. An absent request is
filled by whatever the namespace's `LimitRange` happens to say, which
makes a sandbox's size a property of the cluster rather than of grain;
passing grain's own `DefaultShape` through instead is the property
`GranuleConfig.createArgs` already gives a VM.

### The git proxy, and how a pod finds it

A sandbox has always had to reach this process's git proxy to clone
anything, and a pod's `127.0.0.1` is its own — the same problem a granule
guest has, which `-granule-git-proxy-host` solves by naming the docker
bridge gateway. Here the answer is grain's own pod IP: sandbox pods route
to it directly, so `startGitProxy` binds every interface and advertises
that address, and nothing has to pin the proxy's ephemeral port or put a
Service in front of it.

The address is not something a manifest can write down — a Deployment's
args are a literal list, and the address is assigned at scheduling time —
so `deploy/kubernetes/grain.yaml` asks Kubernetes for it through the
downward API (`fieldRef: status.podIP`) and `-k8s-git-proxy-host` reads it
back out of `$GRAIN_POD_IP` when the flag names nothing.

### Upgrading is a rollout

`upgrade.ModeKube` is the third pipeline beside `ModeImage` and
`ModeSource`, and it is the shortest of the three: run the branch's
published image once as a throwaway pod, carry the schema across if it
moved, then repoint the Deployment and let Kubernetes do the restart.
There is no pull step, because the cluster pulls — as part of the health
check, which is the first thing that asks a node for the image — and no
restart step, because repointing the Deployment has already started one.

The health check earns its place here more than on either other path.
`deploy/kubernetes/grain.yaml` runs one replica with `strategy: Recreate`,
because two grain processes against one SQLite store is data loss — so the
old pod is stopped before its replacement is created, and an image that
cannot be pulled or cannot start is an outage rather than a rollout that
stalls with the old pod still serving. Proving it runs *before* the spec
changes is what keeps that from being how an operator finds out. Nothing
needs rolling back on failure, for `ModeImage`'s own reason: the
Deployment is untouched until the last step.

**It also checks the Deployment's own args against the image it is about
to roll out** (grain/task-244), which is the `unit flags` step the image
path gained after the outage of 2026-09-18. A cluster deployment's
command line is the `args:` list of a Deployment an operator applied
once, and the Upgrade button rewrites only the image in that same spec —
so the args are frozen at whoever applied them while the build behind
them moves with every upgrade and every rollback, which is exactly the
drift that crash-looped the host deployment, with `kubectl` in systemd's
place and a `CrashLoopBackOff` of the single replica in place of a
restart loop. So `stageKube` asks the candidate image for its flag list
(`grain daemon -flag-names`, in the same kind of throwaway pod the health
check uses) and names the args the new build would ignore, before the
spec changes. Reported, not refused, for `checkImageFlags`'s own reason:
the upgrade that *removes* a flag is the one every already-applied
Deployment needs. A build too old to answer is "not checked" — and on
this path that matters more than on the other one, because the answer
arrives through `kubectl logs`, which merges the usage dump such a build
writes to stderr into the same stream. `flagsNotDefined` takes only lines
shaped like an answer, so a dump is "no answer" rather than a
reassuring-looking flag list. The pod it asks in runs under the
Deployment's own `securityContext`, like every other pod here that runs
the candidate image — see the paragraph below. The same list for the
build running *now*, and the count of how many times this pod has
restarted around it, are on the Sandboxes pane's Daemon line — see "The
restart count, on a shape with no journal".

**The check pod runs as the uid the Deployment does** (grain/task-242).
It used to run with no `securityContext` at all — as root, whichever uid
the Deployment it was a candidate for runs as — and since the daemon
became uid 1000 with an `fsGroup` and no capabilities (grain/task-209)
that stopped being the same question the rollout asks. An image that only
works as root (a future base image whose entrypoint writes somewhere
root-owned, a CLI installed where only root can read it) would pass the
check and then fail on the pod that replaces the running daemon, which is
precisely the outcome a check before a `Recreate` cut-over exists to
prevent. So `stageKube` reads the `securityContext` off the Deployment it
holds in `-k8s-deployment` — pod-level and that container's own, verbatim
(`k8s.Client.DeploymentSecurity`, `k8s.PodSecurity`) — and every
throwaway pod running the *candidate grain image* is created under it,
the health check and `kubeRunner.ask` alike. Read rather than configured:
the manifest's `securityContext` is the one place that answer lives, and
a uid named a second time in this deployment's flags is a uid free to
drift from the one the rollout uses. Verbatim rather than a typed subset
of the fields in use today, because a field a future manifest grows and
this code drops would put the check quietly back to being weaker than the
rollout. Two things deliberately do not follow: a sandbox pod still names
no uid (`k8s.PodOptions.Security` is empty for every sandbox — which one
it runs as is its image's own declaration, and pinning a number here
would override images this package has never seen), and neither does the
throwaway pod that pull-checks the *sandbox* image, since that image runs
unconstrained in production too.

One thing it genuinely does less of. When the new build knows a different
schema, the rows are still exported and the new build's first start still
rebuilds the store from them, but the *rehearsal* of that import is
skipped — it works by handing the new build the export directory
read-only at the same path, which needs a shared filesystem a pod does
not have, and the directory is on a claim only grain's own pod can mount.
`upgrade.kubeRunner.rehearse` refuses rather than pretending, and
`cmd/grain` leaves that check unconfigured on this path so the step says
so in the log.

### The controls that assume a host

`-k8s-sandboxes` is also what tells the daemon it has no machine of its
own, and five things go unwired with that (`cmd/grain`'s
`kubernetesMode`): reboot, power off, restart, the `top` snapshot, and
the host's own load and disk figures. Each is `nil`
rather than broken, which is the contract `ui.Config` already has for
"unavailable here" — the same one `grain demo` uses — so the pane reports
them as unavailable instead of offering buttons that would take out a
node full of other people's workloads, restart something that is the
Deployment controller's to restart, or report a shared node's pressure as
this deployment's own.

Sandbox health stays, because those are pods this deployment really does
own. Two of its figures mean something slightly different: load average
and memory come from the node's `/proc` rather than the pod's cgroup, so
they report the pressure a sandbox is contending with rather than its own
share of it.

### The restart count, on a shape with no journal

The Daemon line on that pane answers "is this deployment restarting
rather than running?", which is the one question none of the other
figures can answer — they are all taken by a process that is up, and
every one of them looks healthy in the four seconds between two crashes.
On a host it is a count of `Started` lines for `grain-daemon.service` in
the last 30 minutes of the journal. A pod has no journal and no unit, so
that half was left unwired at first: the pane reported the uptime and
the ignored flags and then "this deployment has no journal to count
starts in", which is exactly the shape where the loop it exists to make
visible is a `CrashLoopBackOff` of the single replica
`deploy/kubernetes/grain.yaml` runs.

The kubelet has the number — `.status.containerStatuses[].restartCount`
on this deployment's own pod — and `k8s.Client.ContainerRestarts` reads
it with the `pods get` the Role already grants (grain/task-367). What it
needs that a pod does not otherwise know is *which* pod it is, so
`GRAIN_POD_NAME` joins `GRAIN_POD_IP` as a downward-API `fieldRef`
(`metadata.name`); a deployment whose manifest predates it reports no
count and says why, the same fallback a machine with no journal already
had. Nothing goes looking for the pod by label or by hostname instead: a
wrong pod's restart count is worse than none.

**The two numbers do not mean the same thing, and that is the whole of
the design here.** The journal count is starts within a window; a
`restartCount` is restarts since this *pod* was created, with no window
at all, and it returns to zero whenever the pod is replaced — which
every rollout does. Reported as each other they would make the pane lie
in both directions, so `ui.DaemonHealth` carries `StartsScope`: the
words the count is a count *of*, filled by the daemon that took it
("in the last 30 minutes", "since this pod was created") and printed by
the pane rather than composed there. `WindowMinutes` stays, and is
absent on the reading that has no window. The count itself is converted
to starts (`restarts + 1`) so `Starts` means one thing on both shapes,
including its floor: a container that has never restarted has started
once, which is what a healthy journal reading also says.

The same reasoning moved the pane's *advice* to the server. It used to
tell whoever was reading it that "this host's grain-daemon.service
passes" the flags the build is ignoring and that "re-running
scripts/setup.sh on the host rewrites the unit", and pointed a restart
alert at `journalctl -u grain-daemon.service` — three sentences that are
all wrong in a cluster, where the flags are a Deployment's `args`, the
fix is an edit and an apply, and the log is `kubectl logs`. The daemon
knows which shape it is and the browser does not, so `DaemonHealth` now
carries `FlagSource`, `FlagFix` and `LogCommand` and the JSX branches on
nothing. `cmd/grain`'s `daemonShape` is the pair of answers, and its
Kubernetes half is deliberately the same wording `upgrade.KubeConfig.
flagFix` already uses for the same disagreement found one step earlier —
naming the objects rather than the manifest, because the args are on a
Deployment somebody applied and a cluster edited in place has drifted
from the file in this repository.

### What ships and what does not

`deploy/kubernetes/grain.yaml` is the whole deployment in one file, with
the values that cannot have a default marked `CHANGEME` so that applying
it unedited fails on something obvious. The single-node docker
deployment (`scripts/setup.sh`) is untouched and remains the right answer
for a machine one operator owns.

What this did not include was a sandbox image. `-k8s-sandbox-image` was
required and had no default, because the image is the whole of what a
dispatched agent finds when it lands, and the artifact CI publishes as
`guest` is a VM disk rather than a container. Building and publishing a
container sandbox image was its own piece of work.

**Since then it ships** (grain/task-452), so that paragraph is history
and this is what an operator gets today. `Dockerfile.k8s-sandbox` is the
image: bookworm-slim, all three agent CLIs, `git`/`bash`/`curl`, the OCR
tools a run needs to read an attached screenshot rather than a wall of
binary, a non-root `agent` user with a writable home — and deliberately
no docker and no kind, because the *published* default must not be one
that only works as a privileged pod.
`.github/workflows/build-artifacts.yml` and `scripts/release-images.sh`
publish it as `k8s-sandbox` beside `grain` and `guest`, `cmd/ghcr-prune`
retains it with them, and its same-commit reference is stamped into the
binary exactly the way the guest's is (`defaultK8sSandboxImage`, the
`Makefile`'s `-X`, and `grain k8s-sandbox-image` to ask a build which one
it expects). The flag therefore has a default now, and it is the image
that goes with the build rather than whatever an operator last pinned —
which is the drift argument "An installation's own sandbox image" below
makes about the guest, applied to the container. It is also why the
manifest is down to two `CHANGEME` values from three: the grain image to
run and the default target repo, with the sandbox image no longer among
them.

Two consequences worth naming here rather than leaving to be rediscovered.
The same image is the local Docker backend's default too
(`-container-sandbox-image`), since a container sandbox is the same
user-space either way and only its creator differs. And the rollout above
grew a step: `stageKube` asks the candidate grain image which sandbox
image *it* names and pull-checks that in a throwaway pod as well
(`stepSandbox`, between the health check and the schema export), because
an upgrade whose grain image the cluster can pull and whose sandbox image
it cannot is a deployment that comes up healthy and then fails every
dispatch.

**And it carries the same CLIs the daemon's image does** (grain/task-208).
`Dockerfile.k8s-sandbox` installed agy and claude through their vendors'
`install.sh`, each of which serves the current release, so two builds of
the same grain commit could hand a task two different CLIs with nothing
in the tree saying which — agy pinned at 1.1.27 in the daemon's image
against the 1.2.5 `antigravity.google/cli/install.sh` was serving that
week. The skew is invisible until it is expensive: `pkg/agent/*` builds
argv for the CLI this repository *measured* (`docs/agy-surface.md` and
its two siblings are captures of exactly the versions `Dockerfile` pins,
and their tests fail stale against those `ARG`s), and the sandbox's own
binary is what runs that argv, so a flag one version takes and another
rejects surfaces mid-run rather than at build or dispatch. Both files now
carry the same `ARG` defaults — agy by immutable release artifact and
sha256, for both architectures, claude by version argument to its
installer, codex as before — copied into the second file rather than
passed as `--build-arg`, since every build of either image is a bare
`docker build`. `TestBothImagesPinTheSameAgentCLIs` is what makes a bump
of one a bump of both. This is the other half of the self-update switch
(`AGY_CLI_DISABLE_AUTO_UPDATE`, above): that one stops the binary
changing under a running task, this one settles which binary it started
as.
