### The daemon does not run as root

That manifest set no `securityContext` at all until grain/task-209, and
what a manifest does not say about uids it gets uid 0. The image cannot
settle it either: the main `Dockerfile` declares no `USER` on purpose,
because the systemd unit `scripts/setup.sh` writes passes `--user` with
the host's own grain uid so that a bind-mounted store comes out owned by
the account that owns it. So the single-node deployment was unprivileged
by decision and the Kubernetes one was root by omission.

What that omission was worth is not abstract. The agent CLIs a dispatch
runs — `claude`, `agy`, `codex` — run **in the daemon's own container**,
beside it; only their tool calls are relayed into a sandbox pod. So the
least trusted process in the deployment had root over the image it was
started from, and agy was using it: replacing the Dockerfile's pinned,
sha256-verified 1.1.27 with whatever its updater served, on the first
dispatch of every fresh pod (`docs/hand-runs/2026-09-17-agy-self-update.md`
§3, and "agy may not update its own binary" above). That specific hole is
held by an environment variable rather than by permissions, because no
permission could cover `GRAIN_AGY_PATH` — but nothing at all was holding
the other two pinned CLIs.

So: `runAsNonRoot` with uid/gid 1000, `fsGroup: 1000`, `seccompProfile:
RuntimeDefault`, and `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` with every
capability dropped on the container. Three things that decision drags
behind it, each of which is the reason this is a task rather than a line:

- **An existing volume is full of uid-0 files.** `fsGroup` repairs that
  at mount time on any CSI driver that implements it, recursively, which
  is why the policy is `OnRootMismatch` rather than a walk over every
  checkout on every pod start. On a driver that does not implement it the
  init container fails before the daemon starts — deliberately, over a
  daemon that comes up and cannot write its store — and
  `deploy/kubernetes/README.md` carries the one-off `chown` Job for that
  case and says to take it before applying.
- **`HOME` had to be named.** There is no passwd entry for uid 1000 in
  that image (nor for the host uid `--user` names on the other path), so
  the daemon would inherit `HOME=/`, and `claude` runs on the controller
  and writes its state under the controller's `$HOME`. `setup.sh` solves
  this with `install -d $GRAIN_DATA_DIR/home` and an `--env HOME=`; the
  manifest does the same two things, an init container and an `env`
  entry, and puts it on the volume for the same reason — that state
  belongs on the disk the deployment keeps rather than in a pod
  filesystem a rollout throws away.
- **`readOnlyRootFilesystem` is not set.** An agent CLI writes in more
  places than a manifest can enumerate, and that is a change to measure
  rather than to assert. Running as a uid that owns nothing in the image
  already makes every binary in it unwritable, which was what was at
  stake.

Sandbox pods are untouched by any of it, and `pkg/k8s` sets no `runAsUser`
on them on purpose: which uid a sandbox runs as is its image's own
declaration (`USER agent`, uid 1000, in `Dockerfile.k8s-sandbox`), a
number this package would be overriding for images it has never seen and
for a `-k8s-workspace` home it cannot know exists under it. The daemon's
uid has nothing to do with it either way — the two pods share no
filesystem and meet only over `kubectl exec`.

## A release train has a page

A release train (`model.ReleaseSchedule`, above) is a branch stem, a
source branch, two published branch names, a cadence, a four-way backport
policy, a pause switch and however many releases it has cut. All of it
was one `<li>` on the repo page: a line of prose with four buttons under
it, a fold-out list of releases, and — below the list — a nine-field
form that unfolded into the same column, at the same indent, as the
trains already running.

Two things were wrong with that shape, and they are the two this changes
(grain/task-377).

Nothing on screen said where the train being created ended and the trains
already there began. The form is now a dialog over the repo page
(`ReleaseTrainOverlay.jsx`) — the centred box `Overlay` keeps for a single
action taken over the page you are already on, the same shape as "Run a
suite" — so what is part of the release train is inside the dialog and
what is not is outside it. Creating one lands on its own page, which is
both where the rest of what was just declared lives and what says the
dialog worked.

And a train could not be *changed* at all. `PATCH /api/release-schedules/
{id}` has taken every field since the trains landed, and `grain repo
release-trains update` has sent them since they reached the CLI, but the
browser had only the pause switch: editing a cadence meant deleting the
train and setting it up again, which forgets the releases it has cut.
`ReleaseTrainPage.jsx` is a train's own page, at `/repos/{owner}/{name}/
release-trains/{id}` — a destination beside the repo's page and its
releases pane, bookmarkable like both — and it carries what the row could
not: what this train is cutting and when, what it publishes, the
reconciler's own last error where somebody asking "why has `rel.1.0.7`
not appeared" is looking, every release it has cut, Pause/Resume and
Delete, and the form that edits any of it.

The row is left as what a row is for: which trains this repo has, what
each cuts and when, and whether it is running — plus the reconciler's
error, which is the one thing that has to be visible without opening
anything, since otherwise the only sign of a stopped train is a release
that never appeared.

Three smaller notes.

**One field set, asked twice.** The dialog and the page ask for the same
nine fields, so they are one component (`ReleaseTrainFields`) and one
function that reads the submitted form back into JSON
(`releaseTrainBody`) — `ui.CreateReleaseScheduleRequest` and `ui.
UpdateReleaseScheduleRequest` are the same fields, so the POST and the
PATCH take the same body. Every field goes on a save, including the ones
nobody touched: the recurrence and the backport policy are whole values
on the wire rather than a kind and four booleans, so a half of either
cannot be addressed on its own anyway.

**No route for one train.** A train is listed per repo and its releases
per train, so the page reads the repo's list and finds itself in it
rather than growing a `GET /api/release-schedules/{id}` that nothing else
wants. A train that is not in that list is a page saying so — this is a
URL somebody keeps, and the train it names may have been deleted from
another window or from a shell since.

**A cadence without an overlap policy.** `RecurrenceFields` renders the
"if the last run has not finished" Select only for a caller that has
somewhere to put the answer. A schedule fires a task that can still be
running when the cadence comes round; a train cuts a branch, and has
nothing that can overlap. On the train form that Select was rendering
empty and unread.

## An installation's own sandbox image

The guest a dispatched run lands in is one artifact for every deployment.
CI builds it from `scripts/granule/build-guest.sh`, `cmd/grain` stamps its
reference into the binary, and an upgrade pulls the guest the new build
names — which is what makes a deployment's daemon and its sandboxes
provably one commit, and what the drift warning in
`cmd/grain/sandboximage.go` exists to defend.

It is also why nothing installation-specific can be in it. What a run
needs inside its VM is not the same everywhere: a private CA, a language
toolchain grain has never heard of, a package one team uses and nobody
else does. Until now the answers were a fork of that build script, or a
`granule guest build` run by hand and pinned with `-granule-image` —
and the pin is exactly the drift the stamp was built to prevent, because
the pinned image stays where it is while grain moves.

`grain_config.sandbox_setup_script` is the answer that does not drift: a
shell script, editable in `Settings → Sandbox` or as an ordinary pull
request against the state repository, run as root *inside* the stock
guest with the result committed as an image of this host's own.
`pkg/sandboximage` is the whole of the machinery, and two properties are
what make it different from doing it by hand.

The derived image is named after its inputs. `Spec.Tag` hashes the stock
reference and the script text together, so an upgrade that moves the
stock image names an image that does not exist yet — and rebuilds — while
a restart, or an edit that puts the script back to something built
before, names one this host already has and costs a `docker image
inspect`. Nothing has to notice that an upgrade happened; the name
notices.

And nothing is dispatched into an image that is out of date.
`GranuleConfig.SandboxImage` is asked at each create which guest that VM
is built from, `Customizer.Image` blocks while a build is in flight
rather than answering with the stock guest, and a build that failed is
returned as an error that fails the `Acquire`. A run that started in a
sandbox missing exactly what this deployment said its sandboxes need is
the outcome worth refusing; a run that starts a few minutes late is not.
The failure is a line in the journal and a retry on an interval, since
half of what breaks a guest build is a package mirror rather than the
script.

The build itself is `granule guest build`: boot the guest, run the
script against a real kernel and a real systemd, scrub the per-boot
identity a cloned image must not carry, commit. That is the same
mechanism `build-guest.sh` is built on, and the one
`scripts/granule/guest-setup.sh`'s own header already pointed operators
at — *"customizing this guest is `granule guest build --from <this
image>` with a script of your own"*. What this adds is that grain now
runs it for them, keeps the result in step with the image grain
publishes, and prunes the derived images nothing boots any more, which
are gigabytes each.

What has deliberately not happened yet is any trimming of the stock
image. `guest-setup.sh` installs gcloud and terraform, kind, docker, and
warm Go and npm caches for this repository's own dependency graph, and
some of that is here because grain's own tasks need it rather than
because every deployment does. Moving one of those out is now a small
change to this repository plus a setup script in the deployment's own
state repository — but the two halves land in different repositories, so
each candidate is worth doing as its own change with the deployment's
script in place first, rather than as a removal that quietly takes a
toolchain away from tasks already relying on it.

## What a pull request is called

The description a pull request carries was the agent's own words already
("What a pull request says it does" above). Its title was not: it was the
task's, and a task's title is a request rather than an account of what
came of it. "Check the parser for bugs" is a perfectly good thing to ask
for and a poor name for the branch that answers it, and grain's own list
of open pull requests was full of them -- questions where a reviewer
scanning the list wanted answers.

So the title comes off the branch too, from the same commit the
description leads with (`orchestrator.titleFromCommits`): the summary line
of the first commit whose message has a body, which is git's own
convention for exactly this sentence and is already the line
`BuildPrompt` asks every run to write. A task called "check the parser for
bugs" now earns a pull request called "Fix the off-by-one in the header
parser". A branch that says nothing -- no commits, none with a message,
or commits grain could not read -- still falls back to the task's own
title, which is what every pull request grain opened was called before
this.

That fallback is the same three-line ladder `EnsurePullRequest` has always
ended with, one rung longer: the branch, then the task, then `grain:` and
the task id for a task with no title at all.

It is also the whole of how an agent renames its own pull request, and
deliberately so. There is no tool for it and no argument on
`open_pull_request` -- the agent already writes the name, once per branch,
in the summary line of the commit that explains its work, and a second
place to say the same thing is a second place for it to go stale.
Rewriting that commit message is the rename: the title is read back from
the branch every time grain touches the pull request, so a run that opens
one after a single `wip` commit and works out what it is doing afterwards
ends up with the name it settled on, not the name it started with
(`refreshPullRequest`, which is `refreshDescription` renamed for what it
now does -- one compare read for both lines, since two would be two
answers about a branch a run is still pushing to).

The human guard is the one that was already there, and it is a weaker fit
for a title than for a body. A description that does not end in grain's
footer belongs to a reviewer and is never overwritten; a title carries no
such marker and there is nothing to read it off. So the body is what is
consulted about both: a reviewer who renames a pull request and wants the
rename to stick should write something in the description too. That is a
judgement call rather than a discovery -- the alternative, never touching
a title after it is first written, would have cost the rename above,
which is the point of the change.

`BuildPrompt` says all of this outright, for the reason it says the rest:
a run cannot see any of it from inside its sandbox, and one that is not
told its summary line names the pull request has no reason to write that
line as a name.

## A task can name the model it runs on

A model could already be taken out of the rotation without being removed
from the deployment -- `model.AgentBackend.Disabled`, the Enable/Disable
button on Settings -> Models -- and the pool skips a disabled one when it
picks whose turn it is. What there was no way to do afterwards was send
that model any work. Nor was there any way to say "this one task on that
model" at all: a task could name a framework, and which account inside it
the run landed on was the rotation's business.

`model.Task.AgentBackendID` is the pin, beside `AgentFramework` and with
the same "zero means unset" reading: empty is the rotation, which is what
every task takes unless somebody says otherwise. `Deps.Framework` takes
both halves as one `orchestrator.AgentChoice` now rather than a bare
framework name, and `cmd/grain`'s `pinnedBackend` resolves the id against
`grain_config` as it stands at dispatch.

Three things the pinned path deliberately does not do, each of them
something the rotation does:

- **It does not skip a disabled model.** That is the whole point of the
  pair. An expensive or rate-limited account is disabled so nothing lands
  on it by accident, and named by hand for the one job worth spending it
  on. A picker that hid the disabled models, or a dispatch that refused
  one, would leave "disabled" meaning "deleted, but still on the page".
- **It does not skip a model inside a quota window.** There is nowhere
  to fall back to that would still be what was asked for. Running it and
  meeting the limit says the same thing the refusal would, and might not
  have to.
- **It does not advance the rotation's cursor.** A pinned run is not
  anyone's turn, so it neither takes nor skips one.

It refuses in exactly two cases, both of which mean the pool was edited
underneath a queued task: an id that names nothing, and a task that names
a model *and* a framework that model does not run on. Both end the run at
setup saying so, rather than quietly dispatching onto some other model of
ours -- which is the one moment where guessing would be worst.

The framework and the pin travel together, so `ui.CreateTask` fills the
task's `AgentFramework` in from the model it names: `frameworkFor` is
what decides which usage pause a run counts against, and it reads the
name rather than resolving the pool. Naming both is an error only when
they disagree. An edit that states a framework *on its own*, over a task
pinned to a model of another kind, drops the pin instead of failing --
otherwise a bulk "move these onto Claude" would break on whichever task
in the selection happened to be pinned.

`GET /api/config` carries the pool for the pickers that file tasks --
`ui.AgentBackendOption`: id, name, framework, model, effort, disabled.
Deliberately not the stored `AgentBackend`, since anyone who can see the
board reads this response while Settings is not open to everyone, and a
picker needs to label a choice rather than to know how it authenticates.
The New task form, the task pane's edit form and the bulk-edit pane each
offer it; the task pane's detail column says which model a task runs on,
naming the pinned one or saying "Rotation". `grain create -model <id>`
is the same choice from a shell, validated at the same end and against
the same pool.

## A CI result's missing timestamps are missing

`ci.Run`, `ci.JobRun` and `ci.StepRun` tagged their `StartedAt` and
`FinishedAt` with `json:",omitempty"` and then sent them anyway.
`omitempty` has never applied to a struct, and `time.Time` is one: a job
that never started went out as `"startedAt":"0001-01-01T00:00:00Z"`, and
every reader of that field had to know to disbelieve what it said. The
readers that did not subtracted it from now. That is how a job which
spent four minutes queueing for a `gcp-key` grant and then errored came
to be drawn on the CI page as having taken 17756979h 39m, the span from
the year 1 to that afternoon.

That one was patched at both ends first -- the engine gave such a job a
real `StartedAt`, and `CIPage`'s `instantOf` learned to read the year-1
instant as no time -- which fixed the symptom and left the trap set for
the next reader of those fields. So the fields are `*time.Time` now, and
`nil` is the whole point of them: a time nobody has is a field that is
not there. It is the idiom the rest of grain already uses for exactly
this (`upgrade.Step`, `ui.Task`, model's optional columns), and it lets a
job that never got a machine keep its `FinishedAt` and have no
`StartedAt` at all -- which is the honest record of something that is
over and never started. Every printer of a duration already reads "no
start" as no duration rather than as two thousand years:
`ci.Run.Duration`, `cicmd`'s `ciJobDuration`, `CIPage`'s `spanOf`.

Neither store moved a column. `model.CIRun` keeps plain `time.Time`, so
`storedRun` writes `nil` down as the zero time and `runOf` reads the zero
time back as `nil` -- a row written before this round-trips exactly like
one written after, which is what keeps the state repository's
`tables/ci_*.json` and the schema version out of it. `DirCache`'s
on-disk envelope cannot be normalized the same way, because a year-1
instant decodes into a pointer that is *not* nil and would go back onto
the wire on the next cache hit, so `cacheEntryVersion` is 2 and entries
written under the old shape are a miss: one re-run each, on a cache that
is disposable by definition.

`instantOf` keeps its refusal of the year-1 instant even though grain no
longer sends one. It costs one comparison, and nothing this UI draws
happened before the Gregorian calendar; what changed is that the pane
relies on an absent field again, and the comment no longer claims the API
sends something it does not.

## Run now

Nothing in grain could say "work on this one next". The queue decides
what runs, from `task_ready` and the backlog's order, and a person who
knew what they wanted done had only the blunt end of that: drag a row to
the top, then wait out whatever was already in front of it. Worse, a task
whose work was *over* could not be handed back to an agent at all.
Completed, awaiting submit, sitting on the merge queue — the only thing
in the whole daemon that ever sends a task back for more work is the
merge queue's own repair, which is automatic, granted once per pull
request, and not something anyone can ask for. So an operator who read a
merging change and wanted one more commit on it had nowhere to click.

The **Run now** button is one stamp on the task — `Observation.RunNowAt`,
written by `ui.Client.RunNow` over `POST /api/tasks/{id}/run-now`, with
`grain run-now <id>` as the same ask from a shell. `dispatch.Cycle` reads
it before it looks at the ready list at all, and *without* consulting
`task_ready` about those tasks: `Store.RunNow` shares almost no SQL with
`Store.Ready` on purpose, since a request is precisely the operator
saying they do not want that query's answer. Blocked, deferred,
unapproved, failed, finished with a pull request already open — started
all the same.

What a request does not override is anything that is not the state
machine's opinion. Capacity still applies (a run needs a sandbox, and a
request waits for one exactly as ready work does), so do both pauses and
the caller's own `Busy` guard; a request the cycle cannot honour stays
outstanding for the next one rather than being dropped. A capacity
refusal passes that entry over rather than ending the cycle, because this
list is in the order the requests were made and not the order capacity is
spent in — the next entry may well be of the kind there is still room
for. Two tasks are refused outright at the button instead: a closed one,
whose run `orchestrator.runOne` would cancel on the spot, and one already
running, which has an agent on it and for which a second run is a store
invariant away (`task_run_open_task`).

The request is spent by the run it asks for. `model.startRun` clears it
in the same transaction that records the run, the way it already clears a
task's grant wait — so a request is worth exactly one run, a request an
ordinary dispatch happens to satisfy first costs nothing extra, and a
task whose run-now run ends is not started again on the very next cycle
forever.

Asking for a run also tells the state machine the truth about a task that
is about to be worked on again, which is what makes the second case work
at all: `CompletedAt` goes back to nil, `RetryRequestedAt` clears the
failure streak, and a parked question (with the `PendingSecret` that may
sit beside it) is un-parked. That is exactly what `requeueForRepair`
already does, for the same reason. An unapproved task is approved and a
deferred one picked back up rather than run in spite of either — a task
that ran while still reading `proposed` would go back to being a proposal
the moment its run ended. The whole action leaves a comment on the task,
which is both its record and what the run's own agent reads: for a task
with a pull request open it names the branch the work belongs on, since
otherwise the agent has no way to know it is continuing somebody's change
rather than starting one.

The merge queue learns one fact to go with it: a task with an agent run
in flight does not merge, and does not get its head refreshed or sent for
repair, *whoever* asked for that run. It only knew about repairs it had
asked for itself (`Observation.RepairInFlight`), which was enough while
that was the only way a finished task went back to an agent. Mostly such
a task is not a queue entry at all now — clearing `CompletedAt` takes it
out of `Store.OpenPullRequestLinks` — but the one that still is, is the
one this button is most for: a change the queue tried, gave up on, and
left for a person, whose repair stamp keeps it in that list and which
merges the moment it reads clean, whoever made it clean. Merging a branch
out from under a live run is the exact thing run-now exists to make
possible to avoid. The entry is passed over rather than held, so the
queue behind it keeps moving. The deadline on an unfinished repair is
deliberately *not* gated on the same fact: that deadline exists for a run
that is never going to end, and waiting for one to end before enforcing
it would be a wait with nothing left to end it.

## Cancelling a CI run can say why

Stopping a run recorded the word "cancelled", and so did three things
nobody chose: a supersede when the branch moved under a run, a daemon
that stopped mid-run, and a run that hit its own ceiling. The reader who
most needs those told apart is not in front of the person who stopped it
-- it is the agent whose branch the run was judging, which calls
`wait_for_checks`, is told "cancelled", and has nothing to go on when
deciding whether to start another run, push a fix, or wait for somebody.

So a cancellation carries an optional note. `DELETE /api/ci/runs/{id}`
takes a `reason` in an optional body -- `readOptionalJSON`, the idiom
`handleClose` uses for its own late-arriving field, so a request with no
body at all is still the cancellation this route has always answered --
`grain ci cancel -reason "..."` sends one, and the run pane asks for it
in the `prompt` that replaced the `confirm` already guarding the button.
Dismissing that prompt is still "leave the run alone"; an empty answer is
still a cancellation, with nothing to say.

`ci.Service.Cancel` records it in two places on purpose. On the run's
record straight away, so a pane polling a run whose jobs are still giving
up is told why rather than waiting for the conclusion to catch up; and in
a map on the service, because `Start`'s goroutine replaces the record
wholesale with the finished article when the engine unwinds, and a note
written only on the record would go with it. `ci_run.cancel_reason`
carries it to disk, `TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT ''` and added by `ensureColumn`
rather than a schema version bump: a run recorded before the column
existed reads back as one nobody cancelled by hand, which it is.

From there it reaches whoever arrives afterwards. `orchestrator.ciDetail`
makes the note the task's stored verdict rather than the names of jobs
that were told to give up -- those say nothing a reader of the word
"cancelled" did not already know -- and the task's own comment carries it
into the prompt of the next run of that task. `wait_for_checks` says
"This run was cancelled by hand" with the note under it. `grain ci show`
and the CI page print it. grain's own two internal cancellations (a run
superseded by a newer head, and one superseded by a run an agent started
for the same task) now leave the same kind of note a person would,
because a run stopped by grain is one somebody will meet later with no
way to ask why either.

## Upgrading after the work is finished

An upgrade ends in a restart, and a restart discards every run in flight:
`RecoverOrphanedRuns` finishes their rows as orphaned on the way back up,
the agents' work is gone, and their tasks are queued again. The pane has
warned about that since grain/task-213 -- "3 runs are in flight" above
the button -- and `orchestrator.UpgradeHold` already stops *new* runs
starting for the duration. Neither does anything for the runs that were
already going, because nothing can: what an operator of a busy
deployment actually had was a choice between paying that cost now and
watching the run count until it reached zero so they could press the
button by hand.

grain/task-156 is the third option. `POST /api/upgrade` takes
`afterTasksFinish`, and with it set the route starts nothing at all: it
validates the branch the same way `Upgrader.Start` would
(`upgrade.ValidateBranch`, exported for exactly this -- a branch name
that would be refused has to be refused while the person who typed it is
still looking at the form) and writes it down as `model.ScheduledUpgrade`,
a singleton row beside `pipeline_pause` and off `SettingsTables` for the
same reasons and one more: the daemon clears the row the instant the
upgrade begins, and a settings import landing in that window would put an
upgrade that has already started back on the books to be applied again by
the deployment the restart brings up.

`reconcileScheduledUpgrade` is what makes it happen, level-triggered like
everything else in the cycle and sitting just after `pause` so that a
hold taken this tick is a queue that does not move this tick. With a
schedule pending and no pause in force it holds the queue as
`model.ScheduledUpgradePrincipal`; with none pending it lets that hold
go, which is how cancelling takes effect without the API having to know
what a pause is. In between it asks whether there is anything left to
lose. "Busy" is `Store.BusyRunCount` plus `Store.LiveCIRunCount`: a run
an agent is working in, and a job of grain's own CI that has not
concluded. A task parked on a question, sitting in the merge queue or
already finished is not busy, because a restart costs it nothing -- and
neither is an interactive run, which is the one exclusion that makes the
wait terminate at all. A console session is a live run whose agent is
waiting for a person to type; counting it would mean a deployment with
the Director open never goes idle and a scheduled upgrade never lands.

There is deliberately no deadline on the wait, unlike the six hours
`pipelinePauseDeadline` puts under the upgrade check's own pause. That
one waits for a task that may never finish; this one waits for runs,
which are bounded by `maxRunRuntime` and by CI's own timeouts. Giving up
after some hours would mean either abandoning an upgrade somebody asked
for or restarting on top of the very work this exists to protect.

Two handovers make the hold behave. When the reconciler fires, it clears
the schedule row *before* starting anything -- the row means "still
waiting", and one left in place across the restart would have the
arriving deployment upgrade itself onto the same branch again, forever --
and puts it back if `Start` refuses, which is what an upgrade an operator
kicked off by hand looks like from here. Then it relabels the hold as the
upgrade's own, inside the same tick, so the next tick's "nothing is
scheduled" branch cannot race the upgrade's goroutine and open the queue
in front of a restart. `UpgradeHold` itself now takes over a hold of
grain's own rather than deferring to it: before, an upgrade that found
the deployment already paused took no hold and so had no release to call,
which for a scheduled upgrade that then *failed* would have left the
queue shut with nothing left to lift it. An operator's pause, and the
upgrade check's own task-scoped one, are still left exactly where they
are.

The one place this reaches outside the upgrade paths is `ResumePipeline`.
Lifting a scheduled upgrade's hold on its own would be undone by the next
tick, since the reconciler re-takes it for as long as the schedule
exists -- which is also what re-closes the queue after a restart, and
what makes `ReleaseUpgradeHold` opening it at startup harmless. So
resuming a deployment that is paused *only* because it is waiting to
upgrade calls that upgrade off too, and says which branch in
`cancelledUpgrade`. Asking for the queue back and asking to keep waiting
for an empty one are not two things somebody can want at once.

### Who asked for it

`ScheduledUpgrade.By` was `Config.Actor` -- this deployment's operator
principal -- because for a while the only thing that could schedule an
upgrade was a person pressing the button. The `self-upgrade` capability
(grain/task-335) broke that: an agent schedules one too, and the pane
went on saying "operator" about a restart no operator had asked for,
with the responsible task named only in the daemon journal.

So `POST /api/upgrade` carries a requester -- `requestedBy` and
`requestedByKind`, validated by `requestPrincipal` -- and
`cmd/grain`'s `daemonUpgrade` fills them with `{agent, <task id>}` off
the run it is serving, the same way `daemonMemory` already attributes an
`update_memory` write. A body that names nobody, which is what the pane's
own button sends, still records the actor. It is a claim and not a proof,
exactly as a memory's author is: the API is unauthenticated, so it buys
attribution for the honest caller and nothing else -- which is all that
is wanted, since anything that can reach that port can schedule the
upgrade under its own name anyway.

The reading carries `byKind` beside `byId` (as `pipelinePause` already
did), and both readers spell an agent out as its task: the pane says
"asked for by task 353" in the waiting banner, and
`deployment_upgrade_status` says the same in prose, so an agent looking
at a schedule it did not make can go and read why. Only a *scheduled*
upgrade is attributed -- an immediate one writes no row for anyone to be
recorded in, and the journal line the capability writes before it calls
is the only account of that one there can be, since the restart it
triggers may well destroy the process that would have written anything
after.

Which leaves one surprise to head off, and `PipelinePauseBanner` is where
it would land: an operator who presses Resume now on that banner has
pressed a button about tasks and lost an upgrade, and the schedule that
would have told them is two clicks away in Settings. So the banner
recognises the hold by its principal -- `upgrade-schedule`, not by the
reason, which is prose -- says that Resume now cancels it, and asks
before it does. Every other pause still resumes on one click, on the same
reasoning the upgrade pane only confirms when runs are in flight: a
dialog that appears every time is one nobody reads by the time it
matters.

The pane grew a checkbox beside the button and an alert for a pending
schedule: what it is still waiting for, counted from the two numbers
`GET /api/upgrade` now carries, and a Cancel button on
`DELETE /api/upgrade/scheduled`. Those counts are deliberately not the
`inFlightRuns` above them, which stays every live run including sessions,
because the two answer different questions -- "what would pressing
Upgrade right now throw away" and "what is this still waiting for".

## Who invalidates a derived admission fact

`task_grant_wait` is the one row grain writes about a task that has not
been dispatched and is not going to be this tick: the capability and the
finite resource that held it up, and since when. The UI reads it as a
queued task's activity ("waiting for repository CI for acme/widgets
(grain-ci grant)"), which is the only place an operator finds out that a
task is sitting still because of something they can fix.

It is a *derived* fact. Its inputs are the task's own grants, the
repository it targets -- which is what decides whether Grain CI is
required of it at all -- and whatever the scarce capability pools held at
the instant the admitter looked. Three things write it, and before this
change only two of them could make it stop being true:

- `orchestrator.grantAdmitter` derives it, on the admission probe
  `dispatch.Cycle` makes for a candidate.
- `Store.StartRun` clears it, in the same transaction that records the
  attempt it was waiting for.
- and the reconcilers that park a task for the same reason outside
  dispatch -- `reconcileTaskCI` for a missing repository-required
  `grain-ci` grant -- write and clear their own.

The gap was the fourth thing that changes an admission fact and is none
of those: an operator editing the task. A task parked for a missing
`grain-ci` grant kept displaying that reason after the grant was added,
because the only code that would have noticed runs inside an admission
probe, and a probe only runs for a candidate a cycle still has worker
capacity for. On a busy deployment that is never, so the task went on
telling everyone who looked at it that it was missing a capability it
now held. Tasks 21 and 22 sat in exactly that state.

So the rule, and it is the general one rather than a patch for
`grain-ci`: **the mutation that changes an admission fact's inputs
invalidates that fact, and the next admission probe derives it again.**
`putTask` -- which every task write goes through, `UpdateTask` and the
UI's own `SetCapability` included -- compares the stored grants and
target against the ones being written, and deletes the wait when either
moved (`invalidateStaleGrantWait`). That is deliberately the whole of
what the store knows how to decide: it does not know what `grain-ci`
means, or whether a key pool has a key free, and it does not try to
work out whether the *new* grants would admit the task. It knows only
that the evidence is no longer evidence.

Invalidation is therefore not a claim that the task can run. It is a
claim that grain no longer knows why it cannot, which is the honest
thing to display and the thing the next probe replaces within a tick of
capacity existing. Removing the grant again, or editing a task whose key
pool is genuinely empty, produces the same wait once more on
reconciliation -- the orchestrator tests walk both round trips.

The other half of the rule is what is *not* invalidated. A write that
leaves the grants and the target alone -- a retitle, a reorder, a
state-repository import of an unchanged task -- keeps the row, because
nothing it was derived from moved, and an exhausted pool is still
exhausted after somebody renames a different task. Dropping the wait on
every write would have been a line shorter and would have made the UI
claim a scarce resource was available every time anything nearby was
touched.

One smaller fix came with it, of the same shape. `grantAdmitter`
returned "admitted" for a task with no scarce grants without clearing
any wait it might still carry, so a probe that found nothing wrong left
the row behind for `StartRun` to deal with -- and `StartRun` is exactly
the step that does not happen when the dispatch it was admitted for
fails for some other reason. Every path out of the admitter that admits
a candidate now clears the row, since reaching one is the statement that
nothing is holding the task up.

## Sandboxes are admitted against a budget, not only a count

Every limit this deployment schedules by was a count. `max_workers` plus
`max_mergers` say how many agent runs may be live, `max_ci_jobs` how many
CI jobs, and the startup line says all three back as though they were the
whole answer. None of them knows what a sandbox is made of. Agent
sandboxes here are 4 vCPU / 8 GiB and CI jobs ask for 16 GiB apiece, so a
host configured for "15 CI jobs alongside 5 agent runs" had committed
about 136 GiB of a 128 GiB machine: at the reading that prompted this,
twelve sandboxes were live, 80 GiB of memory was in use, 12 GiB of swap
with it, and the load average sat at the core count. The UI is served
from that machine, which is how it was noticed -- an operator reported
that typing into it had become slow (grain/task-173).

Nothing was wrong with any individual limit. Fifteen concurrent CI jobs
is defensible *if* the jobs are small, and at 16 GiB a job it is 240 GiB
of commitment that nothing was in a position to notice, because the
scheduler had no total to hold the shapes against.

`model.Budget` is that total:

    memory budget = (host memory - reserve) x memory overcommit
    cpu budget    =  host cpus             x cpu overcommit

The reserve is what is kept back for everything on the host that is not a
sandbox -- the daemon, the container runtime, each VM's own qemu
overhead, and the page cache all of them read through -- and it defaults
to an eighth of the machine, never less than 2 GiB. It is subtracted
before the ratio rather than after, so raising the ratio can never eat
into it. The ratios are separate per dimension because the two failures
are different, which is the same distinction `ui.SandboxCommitment`'s
thresholds are drawn on: contention for a core costs a run time, while
memory the host does not have costs it the run, or costs every run on the
box once the kernel starts swapping to find it. vCPU is promised at 2x by
default and memory at 1x.

All three are settings -- `grain_config.sandbox_cpu_overcommit`,
`sandbox_memory_overcommit` and `sandbox_memory_reserve_mb`, on Settings
-> Sandbox, in `grain settings` and in a config repository's settings
file -- read against one host reading taken at startup, since the size of
the machine is a fact about the hardware and `sysstat.Read` costs a
sampling interval. They were daemon flags when the budget was introduced,
and the flags remain as the seed for a fresh database, but a limit an
operator can only move by editing a systemd unit is one they work around
by raising a count instead, which is the very thing the budget exists to
stop meaning more machine (grain/task-197). `config.withModelConfig`
copies them off the row each reconcile tick and `config.budget()` is
rebuilt from them, so a budget widened in the pane binds the next job
rather than the next process. Narrowing one binds the next job and
nothing else: a sandbox is held against a budget only on its way in
(`model.Budget.Admits`), so runs and CI jobs admitted under the larger
figure keep their sandboxes and finish, and what the smaller figure does
is refuse the next admission until enough of them have drained below it.
Nothing is killed to make a new number true, and the "runs alone" rule
keeps even a shrink past one sandbox's shape from wedging the
deployment. A negative reserve means "grain's own", an
eighth of whatever machine this turns out to be; a negative ratio is
refused on the way in, since the budget reads anything at or below zero
as unbounded and a row saying -2 would quietly take a bound off a
dimension somebody believes is bounded. Zero itself is accepted, and is
the deliberate "bound this by the run counts alone".

`ui.SandboxCommitment` shows that budget beside the fields that set it:
what is promised, what is reserved for the host itself, what the agent
pool's standing reservation takes and what that leaves CI. The same
reading fixed what the pane said about CI, which used to be `max_ci_jobs`
times the *agent* shape -- a product that bounds nothing, since a CI job
names its own `sandbox:` in the workflow file and this repository's ask
for 16 GiB against an 8 GiB agent sandbox. What CI is actually held to is
`Limits.CIBudget`, the figure its own gate admits each job against.

`model.Limits` carries the budget and the deployment-wide agent shape, so
the one rule both admission paths already shared now has both halves of
it in one place. An agent run is admitted while the budget has room for
another sandbox of that shape (`Limits.BudgetAdmitsAgent`, checked inside
the same `Limits.Admits` that `StartRun` enforces transactionally, so the
look-before-you-leap check and the enforcing one still cannot drift). CI
is admitted against the budget *less* the agent pool's standing
reservation -- `max_workers + max_mergers + the Director bypass`, each of
the deployment-wide shape -- which is the coupling the two settings were
missing: raising `max_workers` now takes capacity away from CI rather
than from the host. On the host above that is 112 GiB of budget, 48 GiB
reserved for agents, and four 16 GiB CI jobs where the count allowed
fifteen.

`ci.SharedGate` holds each job's own shape against that share alongside
the count it already enforced, so a 16 GiB job on a full host waits for
memory while a 4 GiB one behind it still starts -- the budget is a bound
on the machine, not a queue. Which of the two bounds is holding a job
reaches `JobRun.Activity`, where a job waiting for a capability grant
already says what it is waiting for, so a slow check reads as held rather
than as merely late. One case is deliberately not a wait: a sandbox
larger than the whole budget is admitted when nothing else holds the
budget, because no amount of waiting makes room that was never going to
arrive. A budget too small for one job costs a deployment its
parallelism, which an operator can see and fix; refusing outright would
cost it its CI, silently.

Counts still apply, first and unchanged. They are a coarse limit an
operator recognises and they have simply stopped being the only one: a
deployment whose host cannot be read is bounded by them exactly as
before, and the daemon says so at startup in place of the budget it would
otherwise have printed.

Disk is deliberately not budgeted this way. A sandbox's disk is a qcow2
overlay that grows as it is written rather than a slice taken out of the
volume when the VM is made, so summing declared sizes would refuse work
on a host with plenty of room -- `/var/lib/grain` going from 70 GiB to
181 GiB of 443 GiB in an hour is a question about what the runs write,
and bounding it wants a free-space floor rather than an admission sum.

## Saying which budget refused the job, and what the rest of it is going on

The split above is invisible from inside a refusal, and that cost a night
(grain/task-506). At 03:48 on 21 Sep this deployment had six agent
sandboxes and five CI jobs live against a 56 vCPU budget -- 28 host vCPU
at 2.0x -- with `max_ci_jobs` at 7, so CI was not short of job slots. The
agent pool's standing reservation was seven slots at 4 vCPU (four
workers, two mergers, the Director bypass) and the five CI jobs held all
28 vCPU of what that left. An eight-vCPU `go` job therefore queued for
30-45 minutes at a stretch, a one-job dispatch took 51m26s of wall clock
to do 4m53s of work, and merge-queue batches went from 32 minutes to
50-58. The host itself was not saturated: load 20.07 on 28 cores, 42 GB
of 128 GB in use. The binding constraint was the accounting.

What every queued job was told, on every attempt, was:

    cpu: 56 vCPU is committed of this deployment's 56 vCPU sandbox
    budget (28 host vCPU at 2.0x), and this one wants 8

True, and no help. The 56 that is full is not the 28 that refused this
job; neither pool is named; and the six agent sandboxes holding half the
budget were at load averages of 0.00, 0.00, 0.00, 0.03, 0.00 and 0.21.
Establishing that took reading the sandbox health pane sandbox by
sandbox. Meanwhile the only number in that sentence an operator can move
is the overcommit ratio, so that is the lever that got reached for.

Four ways out were weighed. **Separate budgets** is the one taken, and
the reason is that grain already has them: `Limits.CIBudget` has been the
deployment's budget less `Limits.AgentReserve` for as long as the budget
has existed, and CI has been admitted against that share and no more. The
two pools could not crowd each other out by accident. What they could do
is refuse a job without being able to say which pool's budget did it.

So nothing about admission changed and the reporting did.
`model.Budget.HeldFor` sits beside `Held`, `Budget.Reserve` is `Less`
with the reservation named, and a refusal against a budget with something
held out of it now reports the asking pool's own occupancy against the
asking pool's own budget before naming the deployment-wide total and what
the rest of it is being kept for:

    cpu: 28 vCPU is committed of the 28 vCPU left to this pool, and this
    one wants 8 -- of this deployment's 56 vCPU sandbox budget (28 host
    vCPU at 2.0x), 28 vCPU is held back for this deployment's agent pool:
    7 sandbox slots at 4 vCPU / 8.0 GiB each, 6 of them live and each
    holding its whole declared shape for as long as it exists, however
    idle it is

The live count is a reading rather than a setting, and it reaches the
budget the way the disk reading does -- `limitsWithAgentPool` wrapping
`liveConfig.limits` beside `limitsWithDisk`, over a backend that can
count its own agent sandboxes without probing them
(`orchestrator.HostSandboxes.AgentSandboxCount` and its siblings, which
separate the two kinds by the leading "c" of `ci.sandboxName`). It bounds
nothing: a backend that cannot answer says so and the sentence falls back
to describing the configured pool. With nothing held at all -- the agent
side's own verdicts, where the pool *is* the deployment -- the original
single sentence is shorter and exactly as true, so it is still what is
said.

The three that were not taken, and why:

**Admitting long-lived sandboxes on observed load** rather than on their
declaration would use the machine better and is the hardest of the four
to make safe. An agent admitted while idle wakes up the moment its tool
call starts; the reservation is the only thing stopping the agent side
-- which is admitted against the whole budget without counting CI's usage
at all -- from promising a core CI has just been given; and there is no
continuous per-sandbox load reading to admit on, since
`orchestrator.Sandboxes.Health` probes each guest over its own transport
and exists to serve a pane. The failure mode is a thrashing host rather
than a slow queue, which is the trade the budget was built to refuse.

**Declaring agent sandboxes smaller** is cheap, may well be right -- they
sat at load 0.00 with 4 vCPU each -- and does nothing about the
structural question. It is also a `grain_config` change rather than a
code one. The message above is what tells an operator whether it is
warranted, because it now names the slot count and the shape the
reservation is made of, which are exactly the two numbers that would
move.

**Raising `sandbox_cpu_overcommit`** is what was reached for on the
night, and it works. It is also a workaround that makes the accounting
less honest rather than more, and it was reached for because it was the
only number the refusal mentioned. Naming the reservation is what makes
the honest levers visible beside it.

## A floor under free disk, rather than a budget over it

That floor is `model.DiskFloor` (grain/task-196), and it is the third
bound on an admission alongside the counts and the budget. It holds new
CI jobs and defers agent dispatch while the volume this deployment writes
to has less free space than it keeps:

    floor = min(max(share x volume, minimum), quarter of the volume)

A share with an absolute minimum for the reason the memory reserve has
one -- a constant is wrong on both a 100 GB volume and a 4 TB one -- and
a cap on top, which the memory reserve has no need of: a floor bigger
than the volume it is on would hold every job for ever, and a deployment
wedged by its own safety margin is a worse day than the full disk it was
avoiding. A tenth, never under 5 GiB, never over a quarter. On the 443
GB volume this was filed about that is 44 GiB; on a 20 GB store disk it
is the 5 GiB minimum; on a 10 GB one the quarter caps it at 2.5.

Both halves of it are stored settings, `grain_config`'s
`sandbox_disk_floor_share` and `sandbox_disk_floor_min_mb`
(grain/task-372), on exactly the terms the budget's three ratios are: a
limit an operator can only move by editing a systemd unit is one they
work around, and this is the one they want to move at the worst possible
moment -- a filling volume has already stopped every dispatch, and a
daemon restart is the last thing that deployment needs. `Settings ->
Sandbox` shows both, with what the share comes to on each of this
deployment's own volumes under them, since a share is not a quantity of
disk until it meets a disk. `-sandbox-disk-floor-share` and
`-sandbox-disk-floor-min-mb` remain as first-boot seeds and are ignored
once a row exists, like `-max-workers` beside them.

Live in the same sense the ratios are, and it took one thing more to be:
`diskWatch` used to resolve the floor once at construction and hold it on
a field, so a lowered floor would have bound nothing until the next
restart. It asks `liveConfig.diskFloor` per reading now -- as do the
reclaim sweep's own target and the host pane's per-volume figures -- and
`config.withModelConfig` copies both columns off the row each reconcile
tick. A watcher is built wherever there is a volume to read rather than
only where a floor was configured at startup, so turning the floor back
on from nothing is live in that direction too.

The reading is live, and that is the whole difference between this and
the memory half. Host memory is a fact about the hardware, read once at
startup; free disk is what the runs have written since, so it is read at
each admission. `cmd/grain`'s `diskWatch` takes one `statfs` per volume
grain writes to -- the same list the host status pane draws a row for,
resolved once per process by `hostDisks` (`-data-dir`, `-sandbox-dir`, and
docker's data root, whether `-docker-root-dir` named it or the pane's one
`docker info` discovered it) -- folds the paths that turn out to be a
single filesystem, and keeps the one with least room over its own floor
-- these are separate volumes and a job cannot spend one's free space on
another. `ci.SharedGate` reads it per attempt, so a job held on a filling
disk starts as soon as space is freed rather than at the next restart,
and `orchestrator.Deps.DiskSpace` reads it once per cycle, so a dispatch
is deferred on the tick the disk fills.

Two asymmetries with the memory rule are deliberate. A shape of nothing
is still held: a backend that applies no sandbox shape commits no memory
anything can add up, and its runs write to the volume exactly the same.
And there is no counterpart to the "admitted because nothing else holds
the budget" escape hatch, because it does not carry: a sandbox larger
than the whole memory budget runs alone since waiting cannot make room
that was never coming, but a volume with nothing left has nothing to give
whoever is alone on it either -- running anyway is how the store ends up
on a full disk.

Which leaves the wedge this trades for. A deployment under its floor with
nothing reclaiming space stops admitting work rather than filling up
slowly, so the floor is worth exactly as much as what stands behind it.
The crossing is said out loud either way -- one journal line when the
deployment starts holding work back and one when it stops, and the
refusal's own words on every held job (`model.BudgetVerdict.Reason`,
through `JobRun.Activity`), so a job held for disk reads as held for disk
rather than as merely slow -- and what stands behind it is below.

The screen says it as well as the journal, which is the half grain/task-214
was about. Each disk row on the System pane carries the floor for its own
volume (`ui.DiskUsage.FloorMB`), resolved in Go rather than sent as a
share for the pane to apply -- the arithmetic has a minimum and a cap in
it, and a second implementation of it in JavaScript would be a second
answer to "why is this deployment holding work". The row reads "44.3 GB
kept free, 16.7 GB spare" rather than leaving the subtraction to whoever
is looking, and it speaks at the two levels `ui.SandboxCommitment` already
uses for the host's other dimensions: a caution on a volume with less free
space than a sweep of it aims to leave (`ui.DiskUsage.ReclaimMB`, so the
row is read before the deployment goes quiet rather than after), and on a
volume under its floor the journal's own sentence in prose, naming the
volume. A journal line is not where anybody looks when a deployment has
merely stopped starting things.

## What actually fills the volume, measured

grain/task-213 went looking before it deleted anything, because the
honest outcome was allowed to be "nothing here can be reclaimed
automatically". Four things live on the volumes a deployment writes to,
and they are not the same size as each other by three orders of
magnitude.

**Released sandbox overlays are reclaimed correctly.** This was the
suspect -- 60-80 GB apiece for a CI sandbox, and the only thing on the
host big enough to account for `/var/lib/grain` going from 70 GB to 181
GB in an hour -- and it is not leaking. A VM's writable root is a qcow2
overlay at `/var/lib/granule/overlay/disk.qcow2` *inside its own
container* (`third_party/granule`'s `internal/config.PrepareOverlay`;
bwsalmon/granule#37), which is why nothing grain writes ever passes
through a path grain names. The granule image declares no `VOLUME` for it,
so it is in the container's ordinary writable layer, and `granule vm
delete` force-removes both of a VM's containers (`internal/dockervm`'s
`Delete` -> `stopAndRemove` -> `docker rm -f`, on the VM container and
the netns holder). `PrepareOverlay`'s own comment says the same from the
other end: "Discarding the overlay (removing the container)".

Measured against a real docker daemon rather than read off: a container
that writes 800 MB into its own filesystem shows as 838.9 MB of
`Containers` in `docker system df`, reclaimable 0 while it runs, 100%
reclaimable the moment it exits, and the 800 MB comes back to `df` on
`docker rm`. So the growth that hour was live sandboxes doing what
sandboxes do, and that answer changes what the floor is for: it is not
guarding against a leak, it is guarding against a dozen runs legitimately
writing more than the volume has.

**What is left behind is exactly what a delete that never ran left.** A
daemon killed mid-run, a `granule vm delete` that failed, an `Acquire`
interrupted between creating the VM and registering it. Each of those is
a whole overlay held by nobody, and until now they waited for the next
restart: `GranuleSandboxes.ReapOrphans` runs once, at startup, when
nothing can be live. That was enough while a deployment restarted often
and had no floor to be wedged under. `SweepOrphans` is the same pass with
the daemon up -- every VM under this deployment's prefix that neither a
live sandbox nor an `Acquire` in flight is using -- and it is the only
thing behind the floor that can return tens of gigabytes. `Acquire` now
claims its VM name for the whole call, because a VM is real from the
moment `granule` creates it and does not reach the live map until its
guest has answered, minutes later on a deployment building a guest
inline; a sweep in that window would cost a run rather than reclaim
anything.

**The CI job cache and the artifact store are too small to be the
answer, and are swept anyway.** 256 MiB and 2 GiB by default, 2.25 GiB
together, against a 44 GiB floor on a 443 GB volume -- five per cent of
the floor, and nothing like what filled it. They are in the sweep because
doing it is nearly free and because the floor is a better trigger than
the bound: a bound asks "is this cache too big", and the question here is
"is this volume too full", which a cache well inside its own bound can
still be part of the answer to.

**Nothing else under `-data-dir` grows the way a sandbox does.** The
store and the secrets are megabytes, the state-repo clone is a text
export of this deployment's settings, transcripts are one JSONL per run.
Worth watching, not worth sweeping.

**One unbounded accumulator was found and deliberately not swept**, and
it is in docker's data root rather than under `-data-dir`:
`lifecycle.DockerImages.Prepare` pulls a repository's guest image and
`docker build`s an assembled `grain-lifecycle-guest:<tag>` from it, one
per (stock guest, repository digest) pair, and nothing ever removes
either -- where `sandboximage.Customizer` does prune its own derived
images (`pruneOthers`, for precisely this reason: "guest images are
gigabytes each"). An upgrade moves the stock guest, so every serving
repository's assembled image is replaced and the old one stays. That is
gigabytes per repository per upgrade, plus the build cache behind it. It
is a bound the lifecycle images want for themselves rather than something
a disk sweep should discover, so it is filed separately.

**That bound now exists, and it is in the images rather than in the
sweep.** `DockerImages.Prepare` labels every assembled image with the
lifecycle image and the digest it was assembled from
(`grain.lifecycle.image`, `grain.lifecycle.digest`) and, after a
successful assembly, removes the other assemblies carrying that same
label -- `sandboximage.Customizer.pruneOthers`' shape, keyed on the label
because `grain-lifecycle-guest` holds every serving repository's guest
while an assembly knows only about its own, and because the tag is a hash
of (stock guest, digest) and so says nothing about whose it is. Removing
what a repository no longer serves is safe rather than merely tidy:
`Registry.start` refuses any version but the one its repository has
resolved, so a superseded assembly is already unservable rather than
merely unused. Best effort in the sense sandboximage means it -- docker
refuses to remove an image a container was created from, which is exactly
right for one a sandbox is still serving from, and that refusal is a line
in the journal rather than a failed assembly.

Two pieces of the same accumulation are deliberately still there. The
pulled repository image is somebody else's name rather than grain's and
is removable only by digest, so it wants more care than a tag in grain's
own local repository does. And the `docker build` behind the assembly
leaves buildkit another copy of the guest disk as a local-source cache
record, which is buildkit's own GC to bound: `--no-cache` would not help
-- it stops the build *reading* cache, not writing it, so it costs a
rebuild and saves nothing -- and a `docker builder prune` here would
throw away build cache belonging to everything else on the host. The
assembly has no `RUN` in it, so the way out of the builder is to stop
using it: `docker create`, `docker cp` into the container, `docker
commit`, which executes no more of the repository's image than the
extraction beside it already does.

## What the floor reclaims, and what it deliberately will not

`cmd/grain`'s `diskReclaim` hangs off the crossing `diskWatch` already
logs: found under the floor, it sets a sweep going in a goroutine --
`report` runs inside an admission check, and a sweep execs a `granule
vm delete` per orphan, which no dispatch should wait on. Single-flighted
and paced at ten minutes, so the gate polls and reconcile ticks that go
on arriving under the floor do not pile sweeps on each other.

Three steps, ordered by what each costs if it turns out not to have been
needed:

    orphaned sandbox VMs   nothing: no run can reach one
    the CI job cache       re-runs, which is `grain ci cache clear`'s
                           own price
    a failing job's        the only copy of the evidence; nothing will
    artifacts              make them again

It sweeps to a target rather than to the floor -- the floor and half as
much again (`model.DiskFloor.ReclaimTargetMB`) -- because stopping on the
floor is stopping at the reading the next write undoes, and the whole
reason the deployment is here is that something is writing hard. It stops
at the first reading over that target, so an ordinary crossing never
reaches the artifacts.

What the journal gets is the volume's own readings before and after,
never a sum of what the steps removed. The runs that filled the volume
are still writing while this sweeps, so those two figures differ --
sometimes by more than the sweep reclaimed, and that difference is itself
the answer to "why is it still holding work back". A sweep that found
nothing says so in as many words, with the lever the operator has left --
the disk floor in `Settings -> Sandbox`, which binds the next admission
rather than the next restart (grain/task-372).

The off switch is the floor. A deployment that has set no floor is still
watched, since the floor is a setting it can turn back on without a
restart, but nothing is held back and so nothing is swept: there is
nothing for a reclaim to be reclaiming *for* where no work is being held
back, and sweeping one would be deleting against a threshold nobody set.

Nothing here runs `docker system prune`, and that is a decision rather
than an omission. grain does not own docker's data root: a blanket prune
takes the sandbox image a live VM was created from, the guest images a
repository's lifecycle boots, and the build cache the next inline guest
build reads -- on a host where an inline guest build already costs 50-110
minutes because nothing has published a guest image since 2026-09-16.
Every step above deletes something grain itself made and can name, which
is the property that makes running it unattended, on a deployment already
in trouble, a safe thing to do.

And the case none of this helps: a volume genuinely full of live
sandboxes. The sweep finds nothing, says nothing was found, and the
deployment goes on holding new work until the runs in flight finish --
which is the floor working as intended rather than a gap in the reclaim.
The levers there are the floor's own settings and the sandbox budget, not
anything that deletes.

## Publishing the sandbox guest without an Actions budget

`ghcr.io/bwsalmon/grain/guest:inputs-<key>` is the content-addressed
cache the whole guest arrangement rests on: the tag is a hash of `git
rev-parse` over the paths `scripts/granule/guest-inputs.sh` names, so a
commit that changes none of them pulls the image an earlier commit built
instead of booting a VM to produce a byte-for-byte equivalent one. For a
year the only thing that ever wrote that tag was the `sandbox-guest` job
in `.github/workflows/build-artifacts.yml`.

On 17 September 2026 this account's Actions began being refused before
their first step -- "The job was not started because an Actions budget is
preventing further use" -- and nothing has published a guest since
2026-09-16T15:22Z. The cost of that is not a missing tag on a shelf. Any
commit touching a guest input misses the cache *for ever*, so every job
that resolves a guest from then on builds one inline: ~10 minutes and
~500MB of downloads inside a nested VM, on a host routinely running a
dozen other sandboxes. That is where grain/task-72's three failures
happened -- 68.7MB at 393kB/s before a timeout, with `Acquire::Retries`
already set, which is a throughput collapse under contention rather than
the blocked route it was first read as.

What answers it is the release job, and it is worth saying why that is
the right *shape* rather than a second workflow that publishes guests.
`.grain/workflows/release.yml` runs `scripts/release-images.sh` on every
merge into `main`, in a Grain CI sandbox: same `build-guest.sh`, same
content-addressed key, same four names out the other end
(`guest:inputs-<key>`, `guest:sha-<short>`, `guest:<branch>`,
`guest:latest`), bounded push retries for the `unknown blob` race GHCR
loses on its own, and a 100GB sandbox because a cache miss puts the base
image, the VM's container and the commit's own layer on one disk. The
guest cache is therefore already independent of one vendor's billing, and
is so without anything in `.grain/workflows` being trusted with a
credential that the file it lives beside is not.

Three shapes that look like they would improve on it, and do not:

  - a second grain workflow publishing the guest on push to `main`.
    That is the same event and the same images as the release job, one
    workflow later; `needs:` does not cross workflows, so the second
    publisher would race the gate the release job puts in front of its
    own push.
  - the same thing on a schedule. The key is the content of the inputs,
    not the date, so a nightly rebuild with unchanged inputs republishes
    the identical image. What actually goes stale under a fixed key --
    Debian's archive, the module and npm caches -- is a *drift*
    question, and `nightly.yml`'s `guest-cache-drift` job is what asks
    it, by building the long way and diffing a probe of both guests. It
    deliberately publishes nothing, for the reason any second publisher
    of `guest:latest` is a bad idea: that name is
    `cmd/grain/sandboximage.go`'s default for a build stamped with none,
    so a deployment does resolve it.
  - publishing from a branch *on every push*, so that a branch changing
    a guest input warms the cache without anyone asking. That is a
    package-write credential handed to a job running unreviewed branch
    code, which is exactly what `package-publish` refuses to place on an
    ordinary push run (`docs/ci-capabilities.md`), and an agent's
    task-scoped CI request is an ordinary push.

What closes the residual hole without that is the third thing
`package-publish` is placed for: an *operator-triggered*
`workflow_dispatch`. `.grain/workflows/image.yml`'s `guest-cache` job
(grain/task-222) runs `scripts/release-images.sh guest-cache` -- the
guest half of the release build, split out as a phase so there is still
one derivation of the key and one pull-and-skip -- and a branch that
changes a guest input warms its own cache by being dispatched once:

```sh
grain ci run -repo bwsalmon/grain -branch <branch> \
  -job .grain/workflows/image.yml:guest-cache -watch
```

Two things keep that from being the bullet above under another name.
Grain decides who may run it, not the workflow file: a task-scoped
request is still an ordinary push and is granted no credential, so the
job stops on its first step rather than building for twenty-five
minutes and being refused at the push. And the phase publishes only
`guest:inputs-<key>` and, on a base miss, `guest-base:<key>` -- names
derived from the content of the inputs, which nothing resolves but the
jobs that derive the same key from the same tree. The moving tags stay
in `publish_images`, which only `push` and `all` run, because
`guest:latest` is `cmd/grain/sandboximage.go`'s default for a build
stamped with no image and a deployment does resolve it.

What is left of the hole is a judgement rather than a mechanism: an
operator dispatching this vouches for the branch's guest inputs, since
the image published under that key is the image `main` will pull after
the branch merges instead of building one. That is the same trust a
reviewer gives those files when the branch merges, moved a few hours
earlier, and it is the reason this is opt-in and stays opt-in. A branch
that is never dispatched behaves exactly as before: the first run that
needs a guest builds one inline, and the first merge after the input
changes pays the guest build inside the release job.

What is outstanding is the credential, and no file in this repository can
supply it. Publishing needs the `package-publish` CI capability on
`bwsalmon/grain` -- operator-owned repository configuration, so a change
to this deployment's own settings (grain/config) rather than to a
workflow here. Until it is granted every release run stops on its first
step and says which grant it is missing (4db248e43 made it stop there
rather than an hour later at the push, where merges from 199b85bcd
onwards died in ghcr.io's `unauthenticated: User cannot be authenticated
with the token provided`). Grain CI run 47952a4f2c8ff19d, on a6bf4ff, is
the newest of them.

The one thing the two publishers must agree on is the key, and they
cannot see each other. `build-artifacts.yml` and the three GitHub jobs
that read the cache spell the derivation as the same literal three lines;
`release-images.sh` cannot, because it names the registry from its own
variables and calls its array `guest_inputs` to leave room for the base
key beside it. A key derived even slightly differently does not fail --
it misses, on every commit, for ever, and reads as a release that is
merely slow. So `tests/deploy`'s
`TestEveryGuestCacheKeyIsDerivedTheSameWay` finds every file that
performs a derivation, rather than holding a list of them, and compares
what each one computes with the local names and the registry normalised
away.

## The daemon log says which CLI it just started

Every run here ends in an exec of somebody else's CLI, and until now the
journal never said which one. `orchestrator` logged the dispatch, the CLI
logged whatever it logs, and the line in between -- which binary, which
model, which `--mcp-config`, which directory, which variables were set --
existed nowhere. That is the first thing anybody reaches for when a
framework upgrade moves a flag, when two deployments disagree about a
model name, or when a run dies before its CLI has written a byte of its
own.

`agent.LocalHost.Run` now writes it, as `agent: running: <command>`,
*before* starting the process rather than after waiting for it: the
failures this line is most wanted for are the ones where the process
never comes back, and a CLI that hangs to its deadline or a daemon killed
mid-run would otherwise leave the journal with nothing to say. The same
line covers the paths that do not go through a `Host`: `pkg/console`
logs the interactive invocation it is about to put on a PTY, and
`agent/custom` logs the backend command it execs, both through the same
renderer.

That renderer is `agent.CommandLine`, and it is the whole of the care
this took, because the line most worth printing is also the one most
likely to carry a credential -- a credential is exactly what a CLI is
handed to log in with, and `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`
and `GEMINI_API_KEY` are all in the environment a framework builds. So
nothing is printed unexamined, two ways at once, the same pairing
`pkg/capability/grainlog`'s `Redactor` already makes for the journal a
run reads back:

- **Shapes.** Every argument and every environment value goes through
  that `Redactor`'s patterns, so a `ghp_`, an `sk-`, a JWT or a token in
  a URL's userinfo is cut wherever it turns up, including somewhere
  nobody expected one.
- **Names.** A flag or variable *named* like a credential has its value
  cut whether or not the value looks like anything -- the shapeless
  secrets are precisely the ones no pattern can recognize. This
  over-redacts by construction: a path passed as `--exec-key` goes too.
  The trade is deliberate, because over-redacting costs a debugging
  session one value it can read out of the configuration instead, and
  under-redacting costs a credential in a journal that leaves this host.

The word list is picked for its false positives rather than for
coverage: `AUTHORIZATION` and `OAUTH` rather than a bare `AUTH`, which
would have eaten `GIT_AUTHOR_NAME`, and no `SESSION` at all, because a
resumed run's session id is the thing an operator most wants to read back
out of this line.

Three smaller decisions. Stdin is not rendered: it carries the run's
whole prompt -- untrusted issue text, kilobytes of it -- which is not
what this line is for and which the attempt transcript already keeps. An
argument holding an unprintable byte is escaped Go-style rather than
shell-quoted, so one invocation is always one journal entry and
`journalctl | grep` finds the whole of it. And the line is capped at 4KiB
with a byte count on what it cut, because `claude`'s `--allowedTools` is
the entire roster comma-separated and would otherwise cost every reader
of the journal a screenful per run.

An empty value is left visible rather than redacted (`GOOGLE_API_KEY=`):
that is `agent/antigravity` deliberately unsetting a variable, and hiding
the nothing it set would hide the fact.

## A chat that never ends is not split for you

The fourth of the four policies task 268 put on the table for a
conversation that outgrows a prompt -- offer a week-old interactive chat
a split, "start a fresh director carrying this handover", rather than
cutting its thread forever -- is decided here (grain/task-309), and the
decision is that grain builds no split mechanism and never takes one on
anybody's behalf. Three of the reasons are facts about what already
exists rather than arguments, which is why this is worth writing down at
all.

**grain never takes it.** Automatic was the one thing `conversation.go`
declined to do, and standing in front of the console-session reconciler
the refusal gets sharper than "a prompt builder may not decide this".
`reconcileConsoleSessions` is level-triggered and runs every cycle: it
reads the settings, looks at the task, and makes the difference. It knows
nothing about whether somebody is mid-thought, and it cannot be taught to
-- a person typing is not a row. The failure mode of an automatic split
is therefore not an over-long prompt; it is a chat that answers the
message before yours and has never heard of yours, and a person who has
to work out for themselves that the thing they were talking to was
replaced between two sentences. There is also no threshold that would be
honest. Age is not one (a week-old chat of eleven messages needs
nothing), and the prompt size that `model.PromptSize` and
`Store.RunPromptSizes` now record is a reason to *tell* somebody, which
is what the warning already is -- not a mandate to act for them.

**For a standing session the split already exists, and nobody had written
it down.** `reconcileConsoleSession` looks its task up by tag, and a
closed one is read as a conversation somebody ended: it is not reopened,
and the session is filed again as a fresh task with a fresh conversation,
its title, body, capabilities, network access, reads and writes rebuilt
out of the `model.ConsoleSession` row, approved with no approver, parked
on its opening line. `Store.TaskIDWithTag` orders open before closed and
newest first, so the rail's entry for the session
(`ui.Client.ListConsoleSessions`) follows to the new task the cycle it
appears, and the closed one keeps its whole record -- every message,
every run, every prompt -- readable as an ordinary task. **Closing the
director's task is the split.** Everything question two of that task
asked about inheriting is inherited already, because none of it was ever
carried from the old task: it comes from the settings row.

**What was missing is one thing, and it is the handover.** A refiled
session started on `consoleSessionOpening` and nothing else, so the
standing summary the last run wrote -- the one message written precisely
to survive a thread being cut (`model.Comment.Handover`) -- stayed on the
closed task and reached nobody. That, rather than a split feature, is
what was worth building, and it is one comment: the most recent handover
off the session's previous task, posted onto the new one as it is filed.
An operator agreed to it and it is built (grain/task-324).

The argument for wanting it at all is specific to sessions, and it is
that the bound's own premise is weakest here. `commentThreadSection`
keeps the oldest messages because a thread's terms of reference are
usually in them -- but a session's terms of reference are its *body*
(`model.DirectorSessionBody`), which is outside the conversation budget
entirely and is rewritten from settings every cycle. So the head third of
a director's budget is not the terms of reference; it is whatever was
said in week one, which after a month is the most stale text in the
prompt. A fresh session with the handover in front of it is strictly
better-informed than an old one holding a head it has outgrown.

These are its terms, which are the answers to the four questions
grain/task-309 was filed to settle:

- **Who is offered it, and where.** The person in the chat, in the pane
  the chat is in: `ConsoleSessionPage`, in the header beside the
  capabilities toggle, for the reason that pane already gives for the
  tick boxes being there rather than in a settings dialog -- a control
  you have to go and find is a control nobody uses at the moment they
  want it. Not a message from grain in the thread: grain speaks in a
  session's conversation only as punctuation (`consoleSessionResting`),
  and an offer in a message bubble reads as the agent asking to be
  restarted. Not an operator-only action somewhere else either; the chat
  belongs to whoever is looking at it. Shown when there is something to
  show, and the recorded sizes are what decide that -- the last
  dispatch's prompt past `model.PromptWarnTokens`, or a thread that was
  cut (`model.PromptThreadCutNotice`) -- never the thread's age. That
  test is `ConsoleSessionSetting.Crowded`, measured off `Store.
  LastPrompt` and reported with the measurement behind it; the button
  opens a panel saying what a fresh chat costs and what it keeps, and
  the close behind it is the ordinary `POST /api/tasks/{id}/close` --
  there is no restart endpoint, because closing the task *is* the
  split.
- **What the new task inherits.** The envelope, already, from the
  settings row; console-session standing likewise is not inherited but
  reconstructed, since the tag is the settings' and the new task has it
  by being the session's task. What the piece adds is the most recent
  handover and nothing else of the thread -- carrying more would be
