  carrying the thing the bound exists to stop carrying, and the old
  thread is not lost, it is a closed task one click away. Posted as
  `model.ConsoleSessionPrincipal`, not as the agent: the new task's run
  did not write it, and a comment attributed to a run that never happened
  is a lie in the record. It is a handover on the new task as well
  (`orchestrator.carryConsoleSessionHandover`), so the next cut goes on
  carrying it outside the head/tail budget; a session whose last
  conversation never wrote one is refiled exactly as it was.
- **What happens to the old task.** Closed, not completed. Completed says
  work was delivered and none was; `ClosedAt` is already what the
  reconciler reads as "somebody ended this", already what the UI's close
  action writes (`ui.Client.setClosed`), and already what
  `TaskIDWithTag` sorts behind an open one. The link is provenance only
  and must not be `LinkDependsOn`: `LinkKind.Blocks` is true for that
  one, so a fresh session depending on the closed one would never be
  dispatched -- the session dead the moment it is split. A new kind
  reading "continues", with `LinkProposedBy`'s shape (no blocking, the
  timeline only), so the new chat says where it came from and the old one
  is findable from it. That is `model.LinkContinues`, carried onto the
  wire as `ui.Task.Continues` and drawn in the pane as "Open the chat
  before this one".
- **Is it ever automatic.** No. See above.

**For an interactive task that is not a standing session, the answer is
no altogether, and the option is closed.** Such a task is a piece of
work, not a standing conversation: it has a branch, often a pull request,
capabilities somebody granted for *that* work and an auto-merge standing
that goes with them. A second task carrying half of that is not a
continuation, it is a duplicate with the same write targets and a worse
memory -- and the two ways to get a fresh task with a fresh thread
already exist and both have a human in them, the New Task form and
`propose_task`. The handover is the whole of what those tasks get, and it
is enough: it is carried outside the head/tail budget, it is written by
the run that had the context, and none of that weakens as the task gets
older.

What a bound has over all four policies is that it holds when nobody is
watching, which is the state this was found in. A split is the opposite
kind of thing, and the honest case for it is not that it saves context --
the bound already did that -- but that a person sometimes wants a clean
slate in front of them. That is a preference, and a preference gets a
control, not a rule.

## Reading the config repository from the UI

grain exports its whole configuration, and everything its memory agent
has written, into a git repository the controller owns -- and for as long
as that repository has existed, nobody running a deployment through a
browser could read a byte of it.

The repository is controller-local by design: it has no external remote,
its origin is grain's own local git endpoint (`pkg/gitproxy/local.go`),
and `grain backup` protects it and the database together rather than
mirroring it somewhere with a credential. That is the right arrangement
and it has one consequence nobody had answered: there is no github.com
page for it and no remote a browser can be pointed at, so the only ways
to read `tables/grain_config.json` or `memory/repos/<owner>/<name>.md`
were to be an agent in a sandbox that had it checked out, or to have a
shell on the host.

The memory files are the case that makes it urgent rather than tidy.
`memory/deployment.md` and `memory/repos/<owner>/<name>.md` are the prose
appended to the prompt of every run in that scope -- told to each agent
as fact before it starts -- and `tables/memory.json` holds only a pointer
to the sidecar file, so even reading the table dump does not give you the
text. A note that has gone stale is therefore repeated to every run
dispatched, and nothing in grain notices. Something that wrong should be
one click from the pane that already tells this repository's story.

So: `GET /api/state-repo/files` lists it, `GET /api/state-repo/file`
reads one file, and `StateRepoBrowser` hangs both off `StateRepoPanel`.
Read-only, and said on the pane -- changing any of this is a pull request
against `grain/config`, which is the deployment's own model, and an edit
box here would be one that could not work.

### The part the review turns on

**It serves an allowlist, never a directory.** `staterepo.Repo.Dir()`
holds `.git`; it has held the encrypted secrets file on older builds
(`SecretsFile`'s comment: a sandbox that may clone may read every object,
and history does not forget); and it is the surface `handleImportSecretsKey`,
`handleSetSecretsRepo` and `Repo.HasSecrets` all sit on. A file browser
over that directory is a file browser that eventually serves something
nobody allowed.

`pkg/staterepo/browse.go` therefore serves exactly the paths grain itself
writes -- `README.md`, `schema-version`, and anything under `memory/`,
`scripts/`, `tables/` and `workflows/`, named from the layout constants
in `dump.go` rather than spelled again -- and it checks them twice:

- **Lexically, before the filesystem is touched.** A path must be
  relative and already clean: any spelling that `path.Clean` would change
  -- `tables/../README.md`, `./tables/x`, `tables//x`, a trailing slash
  -- is refused rather than quietly rewritten, so that what was checked
  and what is opened cannot come apart. Absolute paths, `..`, NUL and
  backslashes are out.
- **Again on where it landed.** The path is resolved through symlinks and
  the *result* is tested against the same allowlist. That second check is
  the one that counts: a symlink at `tables/x.json` pointing at
  `../.git/config` resolves to a path still inside the repository, and
  has no `..` in the request at all. The listing never follows or names a
  symlink either -- grain writes none, so one in the tree is somebody
  else's.

A refusal names what is browsable instead of 404ing. That gives nothing
away, because the browsable set is identical on every deployment, and it
saves a reader from being unable to tell "you may not have this" from
"this is not there" -- which is the other answer, `404`, kept distinct
for exactly that reason.

Reads are bounded (256 KiB by default, 1 MiB at most) and a cut file says
it was cut, which is the lesson from the unbounded agent tools: a bound
that does not announce itself is a file that reads like the whole of it
and is not.

### Saying which commit is on screen

The working tree is written by the export loop on a timer, so a file read
here is what the last cycle left. The obvious failure of a pane like this
is somebody reading a stale file and concluding the wrong thing, so the
listing carries the head it was read at, `GET /api/state-repo` now
reports `syncedAt` -- stamped whether or not the cycle succeeded, since a
timestamp that has stopped moving is itself the symptom -- and the pane
says "showing ff335f5, exported 05:26" with the button that runs a cycle
beside it.

## A wait that is over leaves something behind

`JobRun.Activity` says what a queueing job is waiting for, and says it
well -- the count, the budget, a hole of the job's own shape, a
capability grant. What it could not do is be read afterwards. It is live
state: `runJob` clears it the moment the job is admitted, and `neverRan`
clears it on a job that never got in at all. So a job that queued for
eighteen minutes and ran for four was recorded exactly like one that ran
for twenty-two, and three `image` jobs cancelled at exactly 36m0s left
nobody able to say whether they had been running or waiting. There was
no way to ask, after the fact, whether the gate's ordering and its
reservations had done anything, or to notice that one repository's
expensive jobs wait forty minutes while its cheap ones wait none.

`JobRun.Queued` is the span between the job becoming startable -- the
instant `runJob` is entered, every `needs` of it having succeeded -- and
its `StartedAt`, which the engine can bracket because it owns both
sandbox gates and the admission in front of them. `QueuedReason` is what
held it for the longest of that span. Both are written on a job that got
a machine *and* on one that never did: a job cancelled while queueing
now has its whole wait written down where its row had no duration at all
to show. A cached job has neither, which is the one place this parts
company with the timestamps beside it -- those stay as the earlier run's
because they say what the work costs, while a wait says what this
deployment did to this job, and a job answered from the cache waited for
nothing.

**Attribution is by cause, not by sentence.** A gate's reason describes
how the deployment stands at the moment it is asked -- "2 jobs this
deployment would rather run first are queued ahead of it", "8 GiB free
and this job asks for 16 GiB" -- so it is a different string a minute
later. Bucketing the strings would turn one thirty-minute wait into three
ten-minute ones and lose the argument about what starved the job. So
`GateRequest.Wait` and `ci.Admission` report a `ci.Wait`: a `WaitCause`
that does not move, and the sentence to show. A small per-job
`queueClock` adds the time up per cause and keeps the last sentence said
about each, and what is stored is the duration plus the winning cause's
own words.

The per-run gate reports too, under `WaitForRun`. It had nothing to say
before, because it is the run's own concurrency bound rather than the
deployment's pool -- but a suite of eight jobs on a deployment that runs
three at a time holds five of them right there, which on a quiet
deployment is where nearly all of CI's queueing happens, and a wait
nobody reports goes down as time spent on nothing. It is kept apart from
`WaitForSlot` because the two limits are raised in different places: a
suite queueing behind itself is a suite wider than the deployment runs,
and a suite queueing behind other runs is a deployment with too little to
go round.

It is shown where a duration is shown, because "18m queued, 4m running"
is a different sentence from "22m" and only one of them sends an operator
to look at capacity: the CI page's job rows and its run rows, `grain ci
show` (the job line, the reason under it, the run's total), and
`wait_for_checks`, whose reader is an agent about to decide whether a
cancelled job is its own change. `ci.Run.Queued` adds a run's jobs
together, which is job-time and can exceed the run's own duration -- and
that is the figure that says whether a deployment is short of sandboxes,
since no single job's wait can.

The store keeps it as `ci_job.queued_ms`, `ci_job.queued_cause` and
`ci_job.queued_reason`, defaulted columns an existing database migrates
into, so no schema version moves and a run recorded before any of this
reads back as a run whose wait is unknown and therefore zero.
Milliseconds rather than nanoseconds because the column is one somebody
may well read by hand. (`queued_cause` came later, with the aggregate
below; the first version of this stored only the winning cause's
sentence.)

## Adding that queueing up, by cause and by repository

A wait per job answers "was this job starved or slow". It does not
answer any of the questions an operator actually has, because all of
those are additions: how much of this deployment's CI job-time went on
waiting over the last day or week, whether that share is rising, which
of the six things that can hold a job is holding them -- each sends an
operator to a different setting -- and whether one repository's
expensive jobs wait forty minutes while its cheap ones wait none, which
is the suspicion that motivated measuring any of it and which nothing
measured either way. `metrics.CIQueueing` is that addition
(grain/task-345): a section of the measurement report, beside the
latency distributions, over the report's own window and narrowed by its
own scope.

**The cause became a column.** Only the winning cause's *sentence* was
stored, so an aggregate by cause had two ways to exist: parse the
sentences, or keep the cause. Parsing was never really available -- the
argument the previous section makes for bucketing by cause rather than
by sentence is the same argument against recovering the cause from the
sentence afterwards, since the sentence is prose each gate is free to
rewrite and a deployment's own numbers would move when somebody
reworded a gate. The cause was already chosen at the source, by the
`queueClock` that picks the winner, and was simply discarded once its
sentence had been read off; so `queueClock.stop` returns it and
`ci_job.queued_cause` keeps it. Nothing anywhere matches a reason
string.

What that costs is stated rather than hidden: every job stored before
the column has a duration and no cause. Those jobs count in every total
and under no cause, and the section reports
`CIQueueing.Unattributed` -- how much of the waiting is missing from the
breakdown -- rather than guessing. It is also where a wait at a gate
with nothing to say about itself lands, so the bucket does not empty
once the history turns over.

**Cache hits are counted apart.** A job answered from the job cache
never asked for a machine, and its timestamps are the earlier run's on
purpose. Folding it in as a job that waited no time would let a
deployment improve its queueing share by caching more, which is a good
thing to do and not an answer to "am I short of sandboxes", so `Cached`
is reported beside `Jobs` and is in neither half of the share.

**Job-time, not wall clock.** `QueuedShare` is queued over queued plus
running, added across jobs, so a deployment running four jobs at once
spends four minutes of it a minute and both figures can exceed the
window. That is the figure `ci.Run.Queued` already made the same
argument for at the scale of one run: no single job's wait can say
whether a deployment is short of sandboxes.

The breakdowns are worst first: by cause, carrying the gate's own
sentence from the longest wait of each (`budget` says where to look, and
"8 GiB free and this job asks for 16 GiB" says what to set it to); by
repository; and by repository *and* job name, because two repositories
with a job called `test` are two different jobs on two different shapes
of machine, and the comparison the whole thing exists for is between one
repository's expensive jobs and its cheap ones. The same share is
sliced into the window's own buckets -- the ones `Throughput` already
uses, so the two trend lines are points over the same spans -- which is
what answers "and is it rising?".

**A scope narrows it by repository and not by author.** A CI job belongs
to a repository and a branch; nothing joins a run's ref back to the task
that pushed it, and this deployment runs CI for base branches and for
operators as well as for tasks. So `Scope.Repos` narrows this section
like every other, `Scope.Authors` does not narrow it at all, and that is
said in the section's own comment and on screen rather than left to be
discovered -- the treatment `Cycles` already gets for the same kind of
reason.

**It went on the Metrics pane, not the CI pane.** The CI pane answers a
question about one run, and already shows a job's wait beside its
duration. This is a question about the deployment over a window -- is
the share rising, which repository wears it -- and the window picker,
the scope, the report boards and the bucketed trend lines all live on
the report. It is a section of `model.ReportSections` in its own right
(`ci_queueing`), so a report board can name it alone, and `grain
metrics` prints the same numbers at a terminal.

One bound is worth knowing before reading a long window: CI history is
swept (`ci.StoredRunRetention.History`, five thousand concluded runs by
default), so ninety days asked of a busy deployment covers however much
of it is still stored. The oldest buckets go empty where that bites, and
`Jobs` is the denominator every share here is read against.

## An empty `.grain/workflows` no longer hides a repository's Actions files

Which directory a repository's workflows are read from was decided by
whether `.grain/workflows` *existed*, not by whether it said anything.
Git cannot commit an empty directory, so the way this happens is a
directory holding something that is not a workflow: a README, a
`tests.yml.disabled`, a `.yml` somebody renamed while bisecting, a
`shared/` subdirectory -- `loadWorkflowEntries` skips all four. Such a
tree answered "this repository declares no workflows", which is the one
empty plan `PlanRun` is deliberately quiet about, and a whole
`.github/workflows` suite behind it never ran. The run came back green in
fifteen seconds, which is the shape grain/task-254 took the rest of out:
a merge queue and an agent waiting on `wait_for_checks` both read it as a
tested tree.

`ci.LoadDir` falls back now when `.grain/workflows` declares no workflow
file, not only when it is absent. The rule written down in its comment is
"a directory that says something is authoritative", and the point of it
is that grain's silence again means the tree holds no workflow file
anywhere, rather than that grain looked in the wrong one of two
directories. A broken file under `.grain/workflows` is not a fallback: it
is still this repository's answer and still an error, because running
GitHub's suite because grain's own file does not parse would report a
verdict on a commit nobody's workflow tested.

The alternative was to keep the precedence and make the case loud --
`Plan.Unmatched`, an errored run, the machinery task-254 already built.
It was not taken because it leaves the repository's real CI unrun either
way, and the directory that caused it says nothing about wanting that.
The cost of falling back instead, stated so nobody is surprised by it:
emptying `.grain/workflows` no longer turns grain CI off for a repository
whose `.github/workflows` has files in it. That was never a declared way
to say "run nothing" -- there isn't one *in the tree*, since a workflow
matching no event is an errored run rather than a quiet one -- and an
opt-out that is meant belongs on the repo's own config rather than in the
shape of a directory.

Which is where it already is, and grain/task-389 was filed to add a
second one before anybody checked. The declared way for a repository to
run no grain CI is to not hold the `grain-ci` capability: every place a
run is planned asks first -- `orchestrator.reconcileTaskCI` and
`cycle`'s merge admission through `grainci.Granted`, the CI API through
`ui.Client.ciEnabledFor`, base branches through
`orchestrator.baseBranchCIWanted` -- so a repository grain CI is off for
plans nothing at all, whatever its two workflow directories hold.
`SetRepoWatchDefaultBranch`'s comment already says so in as many words,
and the switch lives in `RepoConfig.DefaultCapabilities`, on the repo's
own config, exported in grain/config beside the very flags a `RunNoCI`
would have been added next to.

A flag would also have to be a *subtraction*, which is the one shape
this composition deliberately refuses. Capability sets compose by union
across the deployment's defaults, the repo's and the task's grants --
`grainci.Enabled` is variadic and order-independent for exactly that
reason -- so a per-repo "run nothing" would have to beat a grant an
operator ticked in the picker, and `pkg/capability/grainci`'s own doc
takes the position that a second setting meaning "nobody trusts this
yet" is answered by taking the capability off the repository instead.
The case that could still force one is a deployment that has put
`grain-ci` in `Config.DefaultCapabilities` -- on for everything, no
per-repo way down -- which is where that package expects this to end up.
Nothing to do until a deployment is actually there and a repository in
it actually objects.

## A run reads its own repository's CI

The filter vocabulary above deliberately settled no policy: `repo` was a
convenience for whoever asked, and `list_ci_runs` went on answering with
every run this deployment remembers, for every repository, to every run
that holds `grain-ci`. `get_ci_log` did not even take a repository -- a
run id was enough, whoever the run belonged to.

That was the one tool on the roster with no boundary. `PullRequestScope`
fixes which branch of which repository `pull_request_status` may report
on; `GrainCIReader` answers about this run's own task and no other;
`daemonChat` can only reach the conversation on the task the run belongs
to. Each of them is fixed where the reader is built, because what a run
may see is grain's to decide rather than the agent's to ask for. CI is
now the same (`pkg/mcp/ci_repo_scope.go`, `CIRepoScope`):

- **Its own repository**, which is `-pr-repo`: the repository whose
  branch the run is pushing to, and the only one grain CI ever runs that
  branch in (`orchestrator.reconcileTaskCI` starts runs for `task.Target`
  and nothing else). Every branch of it, including the base branch the
  work has to merge into -- "is my change red, or is it red like
  everything else here" is the question these two tools exist for.
- **Every repository, for a task holding `self-debug`.** That grant
  already means "this task is here to work out what grain itself did": it
  carries `read_grain_task` and `read_grain_task_transcript` across every
  task in the deployment. "Is this job flaky everywhere" and "did the
  guest image break every repository at once" are the same question asked
  of the same record, and a deployment that wants one answered grants the
  capability that already answers the rest of it.
- **Nothing, for a task with no repository of its own**, which is a real
  shape here rather than a misconfiguration. Fail-closed is the only
  direction that fails safe: the cost of refusing is one answer a run can
  ask a person for, and the cost of the other default is that "no scope
  configured" quietly means "all of it".

That last case has one consequence worth stating plainly, because it is
this deployment's own: a standing console session has no `Target` by
design (`orchestrator.reconcileConsoleSessions` -- it answers in words
and files tasks, so giving it a repository to write to would invite a
pull request nobody asked for). A session configured with `grain-ci` and
nothing else therefore reads no CI at all now. That is the right default
-- a session with no repository has no CI of its own to be asked about
-- but a session whose *job* is to watch CI across the deployment wants
`self-debug` in its configured capability set, which is a change to the
session row in `grain/config` rather than anything in this repository.
The refusal names the grant, so the session says so itself the first
time somebody asks it.

The refusals are the point rather than the filtering. A `repo` naming a
repository outside the scope is refused with the one it may name and the
grant that would widen it, exactly as `ParseRunState` refuses `failed`
with the words the vocabulary does have -- because an unrecognized word
answered with an empty list is the single easiest way to get an answer
that reads as "nothing is wrong". `get_ci_log` takes a run id and no
repository, so it is scoped after the lookup: a run belonging to somebody
else is refused in a sentence naming both repositories, never as a
404-shaped "no such run", which would be a plain falsehood about a run
whose id a person may well have handed over.

Both tool descriptions now say which repositories they are about, and
both name `self-debug` -- a run that can see everything should know that
is why it can, and a run that cannot should be told what the boundary is
instead of reading an empty answer as a fact about CI. The scoped
repository is pinned into the filter rather than applied afterwards, so
the answer's own heading says `repo acme/widgets (this run's own, and the
only one it may read)`: the counts beside it (`3 of 40 remembered runs
match`) are deployment-wide, and without that clause a reader would try
to widen the one filter that cannot be widened.

`ci.RunFilter` itself is unchanged and stays a question rather than a
grant. Filtering is not authorization: the scope pins `Repo` before the
question reaches the store, `Matches` still has no notion of a caller,
and `GET /api/ci/runs` -- an operator's view of their own deployment --
is scoped to nothing, which is why the pane and a scoped agent can now
honestly disagree about how many runs there are.

## A CI run says which build of grain produced it

Reading a run is reading two things at once: what a commit's tests did,
and what the grain that ran them did. The first is on the record in
detail. The second was not on it at all, and a deployment upgrades on its
own schedule, so "the code is right here and it did not fire" has always
had two answers -- the implementation is wrong, or the deployment is
running a build that predates it -- with nothing on the run to tell them
apart.

grain/task-388 spent most of a run establishing the second one. The
report was that task-254's matchless-run reporting had not fired: a run
that matched no workflow still concluded `success` in 0s with no jobs,
while the code that concludes `errored` and names every workflow the
commit declares was in the tree, correct and tested. Nothing about the
run said which build made it, so the way to the answer was archaeology
over `list_ci_runs`: find a repository whose runs have the same shape
every time -- grain/config's post-merge `release` runs against a workflow
answering `push` and `workflow_dispatch` -- and bisect `since` windows
until the boundary appeared between two runs of that shape, one `success`
in 0s and the next `errored`. It worked, and it only worked because such
a repository happened to exist.

So `ci.Run` carries a `Build`: the commit the running binary was built
from, that commit's own timestamp, and whether the tree it was built in
was dirty. It is read out of the binary by `pkg/version`, the same stamp
`GET /api/config` already puts in the UI's sidebar, so there is nothing
for a deployment to configure and nothing for it to get wrong -- and it
is a pointer, absent rather than blank, for the reason
`ui.versionResponseFrom` returns nil for the same fact: a test binary and
a `-buildvcs=false` build carry no stamp, and "this record cannot say" is
a different answer from "this build has no revision".

`ci.Service` stamps it, not `ci.Engine`, though it is the engine that
does the work. They are the same process; the Service is what a daemon
wires up and hands requests to; and one writer is what keeps the stamp on
a record that `Start`'s goroutine replaces wholesale when the run unwinds
-- the same trap `cancel_reason` fell into and is carried over beside it.
A run that never reaches the engine is stamped too
(`recordWorkflowFailure`), which matters more than the ordinary case: a
matchless run and a workflow that would not parse are exactly the runs
somebody is attributing.

`ci_run` gains `build_revision`, `build_time` and `build_modified`,
defaulted and added by `ensureColumn` on `cancel_reason`'s terms, so an
existing database migrates into them and every run recorded before this
reads back as a run that cannot say what made it -- which is what it is.

The readers cost almost nothing, because the API serves `ci.Run` as it
stands: `GET /api/ci/runs` and `/api/ci/runs/{id}` carry it for free.
`grain ci show` prints a `build:` line with the whole revision, since a
reader with one run in front of them is about to hand it to `git show` or
`git merge-base --is-ancestor`. `wait_for_checks` and `list_ci_runs` put
it on each run's headline in seven characters and the commit's date,
which is what makes a build *change* visible as an agent reads down a
list of twenty runs -- the same bisection task-388 did by hand, now a
column. The CI pane says it under the run's heading, short on the line
and whole on the hover.

Two things deliberately left out. The deployment's own current build
needed nothing: `/api/config` has reported it since grain/task-50 and the
sidebar prints it on every view. And nothing here says how far behind
`main` a build is. That is a question about a remote repository -- which
commits are between this one and the head of a branch nobody here has --
and the daemon holds no clone to answer it from; the revision on the run
is what lets whoever *does* have one answer it in a single command.

## A task is superseded when its replacement is filed

Refining a task means re-filing it. A chat session cannot edit a filed
task's description, so five revisions of one merge-queue design were five
tasks -- `465 → 466 → 467 → 468 → 471`, in about forty minutes -- and
each revision left its predecessor `queued` and dispatchable. Two of them
sat there long enough that a dispatch would have spent a sandbox and a
full CI suite on a design already superseded twice; the only thing that
prevented it was an operator reaching the close button first, four times
in one sitting. The relation itself lived nowhere but in a sentence at
the top of each body ("this replaces grain/task-468, which an operator is
closing"), so "why are there five near-identical tasks?" was answerable
only by reading all five.

`propose_task` takes a `supersedes` argument now: the id of an existing
task this proposal replaces. Filing it closes that task, records the
reason as superseded by the new one, and writes both halves of the
relation as links -- `LinkSupersedes` on the replacement, pointing back,
and `LinkSupersededBy` on the task it replaced, pointing forward.

Both directions are stored rather than one being queried back, because
both are read in the same breath: a chain of revisions is walked forwards
from the first ("what replaced this?") and backwards from the last ("what
did this replace?"), and the answer has to be on the task in front of the
reader. The frontend spends them immediately -- a closed row carries a
`superseded by 471` chip, and the task pane links both halves -- which is
the whole point of recording the relation rather than prose.

**Why an argument on `propose_task` rather than a `close_task` tool.** A
supersede with no replacement is not expressible: the close only happens
in the act of filing the thing that replaces it, so there is always a
successor on the record and always a link saying which. That is what
makes it safe to hand to a run without a capability of its own. A general
close is more useful -- the same session that day also wanted to close a
proposal an operator had made redundant by ticking a setting, and a
duplicate filed by another task's run, neither of which is a supersede --
and it is also genuinely more power. If it is built it wants its own
capability, its own decision, and the same never-dispatched bound at
minimum.

**The bound is `model.SupersedeRefusal`, and it is the same in both
places a proposal is filed.** Only a task that has never been dispatched:
no attempts, not running, no pull request open, and in one of the two
states a never-dispatched task can be in (`proposed` or `queued`).
Anything else has work in it -- a sandbox spent, commits pushed, possibly
a branch -- and throwing that away stays a human's call. And only a task
in the same repository as the replacement, which is the scope
`propose_task` already enforces from the other side: a proposal could be
filed anywhere the caller may file, and pinning the two together is what
keeps a proposal in one repository from closing work in another.

A refused supersede does not refuse the proposal. The run has still said
something true and useful -- this work replaces that work -- and losing a
whole proposal over an argument nobody would ever see is the worse
failure. The task named is left exactly as it was, untouched and
uncommented-on, and the reason goes in the new task's body
(`SupersedeRefusedNote`, the treatment `unresolvedDependencyNote` and
`unknownProposalRepoNote` already get) where the human approving it
reads it. A live call is told in its own turn, too: `FiledProposal`
carries the id actually closed, read back off the filed task rather than
repeated from what was asked for, so a run cannot come away believing a
stale task has stopped being dispatchable when it has not. That belief is
the expensive one -- a run that holds it neither says so in its closing
note nor asks anybody to do the close by hand.

**Checked twice, because nothing holds the dispatch loop still.** Both
filing paths -- `ui.Client.CreateTask`, for a call the daemon relays
while the run is still going, and `orchestrator.relayProposedTasks` for
the end-of-run replay -- decide the note before the proposal is written
and do the close after it, and `Store.Supersede` asks the store again at
the moment it writes. A task that was queued when the replacement was
composed and is running by the time the close lands is left alone, which
is the one outcome this whole path promises. In that (rare) case the
replacement keeps its link, since "this was filed to replace that" is
still true, and a comment on it says what changed.

The close is recorded the way any other close is: `Observation.ClosedAt`,
plus a comment on the closed task's own conversation naming the
replacement and attributed to grain on behalf of the task whose run asked
for it. A task that vanishes from the backlog should say why on its own
thread, not only in a link.

**A supersede moves the old task's dependents onto the replacement.** A
blocking link (`depends-on`, `child-of`: `LinkKind.Blocks`) is satisfied
by its target closing for any reason, and a supersede is a close -- so
until 23 Oct 2026 every task waiting on a superseded task was released
the moment the replacement was filed, and dispatched beside the very task
that had taken over the work it was waiting for (the director's supersedes
of 22 Oct). The replacement does the old task's job, so the tasks waiting
on the old one now wait on the replacement: in the same transaction as
the close, `Store.Supersede` retargets every open task's blocking link to
the old task onto the replacement, keeping its kind, and comments on each
("Now waits on task 471, which superseded task 465."). Two are left where
they were, and their link to the closed task releases them as before: the
replacement itself, which may have been filed waiting on the task it
replaces and must not be made to wait on itself; and a dependent the
replacement already waits on, directly or through other tasks, which would
otherwise wait on the replacement while the replacement waits on it. That
one gets a comment saying why it was not moved. Closed tasks are not
touched. The live `propose_task` answer names the tasks that moved and the
ones that stayed, with why (`FiledProposal.SupersedeMoved` and
`SupersedeKept`, read off `ui.Task`'s fields of the same names on the
`CreateTask` answer). The UI has no "close as superseded" action of its
own: a person supersedes a task the same way a run does, by filing its
replacement with `supersedes`, and gets the same rule. A plain close or
cancel moves nothing. It names no task to wait on instead, so it releases
its dependents exactly as it always has.

## A guest that never hibernates must not wait for a resume device

The 21 September sandbox outage was 105 seconds of an initramfs waiting
for hardware that does not exist, and the reason it took three tasks to
find is that the only thing that ever said so was the guest's own
console:

```
[   2.140440] virtio_blk virtio0: [vda] 62914560 512-byte logical blocks (30.0 GiB)
        ... ~105 seconds, "Gave up waiting for suspend/resume device" ...
[ 107.737809] EXT4-fs (vda): mounted filesystem with ordered data mode
[ 108.335825] EXT4-fs (vda): resizing filesystem from 1062770 to 7864320 blocks
[ 122.111348] bridge: filtering via arp/ip/ip6tables ...          ← login prompt
```

That line is Debian initramfs-tools' `scripts/local-premount/resume`,
which waits for the device `RESUME=` names and eventually gives up.
Nothing in this repository set `RESUME`, so the initramfs was built with
whatever initramfs-tools inferred at build time; the guest has no swap
and no hibernation image, so the device never appeared and the guest paid
the full timeout on every boot. Take it out and the same guest reaches
its login prompt in about seventeen seconds.

**Why 105 seconds was an outage rather than a slow boot.**
`GranuleConfig.readyTimeout` is two minutes and hard-coded. The guest
reached its login prompt at ~122s. Every sandbox creation was therefore a
coin flip between a guest that got there first and a timeout that did:
254 failed creations (120 agent, 134 CI) against `failed: 0` for this
deployment's whole history before the granule migration, 87 "never
acquired a default route" journal entries in one 30-minute window, and an
operator merging twenty-odd pull requests by hand. A deadline two seconds
away from the thing it bounds does not fail like a deadline; it fails
like flakiness, which is why the daemon's own record read as a network
fault for days.

**The fix is in two places because it is about two different guests.**
`RESUME=none` in `/etc/initramfs-tools/conf.d/resume`, written by all
three Granulefiles before any package is installed, is what fixes the
guests this repository builds -- before, so that every initramfs the
build generates carries it, including the one `linux-image-amd64`'s own
install triggers. `noresume` on granule's derived kernel command line
(both spellings: `vmspec.VMSpec.Validate`'s derived one and
`pkg/config`'s `defaultCmdline` fallback) is what covers a guest built
from an image this repository does not control. A granule VM is booted
fresh from a packed image every time and never hibernates, so waiting for
a resume device is never right for one, whatever it was built from. The
cmdline half started as a local patch on the vendored tree. It is on
granule's own `main` now and arrives here by resync
(`docs/granule-local-patches.md`).

The two halves also reach a running deployment by different routes, which
matters while the deployment is the thing that is down. `RESUME=none`
only takes effect once the guest image is rebuilt and published, and
every job that would publish one needs a sandbox that currently cannot
boot. `noresume` does not: `pkg/granule` shells out to the `granule`
binary the grain image builds out of `third_party/granule` (see
`Dockerfile`), so a grain image carrying this change writes `noresume`
into the command line of every VM it creates -- including VMs booted from
the guest image already published, which has no `RESUME=none` in it and
does not need one in order to stop waiting. Upgrading the daemon is
enough to end the stall; rebuilding the guest is what makes it true for
anybody booting these images by some other route.

**What this corrects.** Two earlier tasks looked for the stall in the
disk and found real things that are not this. grain/task-588 suspected
`--disk ...disk.vmdk,image_type=raw` of being a VMDK misread: it is not,
`guestimage.DiskImage` is a raw ext4 image and `config.PrepareOverlay`
takes its non-`.vmdk` branch, so the overlay is a raw file with a
misleading name. grain/task-592 blamed `vmdk.CloneOrCopyExtent` falling
back to a full byte copy for want of reflink: that copy is real and worth
about 4.9 GB per sandbox, but it happens before cloud-hypervisor starts
and so cannot be an in-guest stall. Both tasks' other asks stand --
`ReadyTimeout` as a setting rather than a constant, `reflinkUsed` logged
by somebody, and in particular replacing the in-guest failure dump with
`docker logs`, since the guest has no dbus and every one of those 254
failures printed "Failed to connect to bus" and explained nothing.

That last one is the lesson worth keeping. The daemon said "the guest
answered but never acquired a default route" 87 times and stopped there;
the guest said what was wrong in one sentence, on a console nothing was
reading. A diagnostic that cannot reach the place the failure is
described is not a diagnostic.

## Local container sandboxes are hardened (#2413)

`-container-sandboxes` used to start each run's container with resource
limits and nothing else: Docker's default capability set (`NET_RAW`,
`SETUID`, `DAC_OVERRIDE` and the rest), setuid binaries free to elevate,
and Docker's shared default bridge, where every container can reach every
other. `ContainerSandboxes.runArgs` now adds `--cap-drop ALL`,
`--security-opt no-new-privileges`, `--pids-limit 4096` and
`--memory-swap` equal to `--memory`, and puts the container on
`grain-sandboxes`: a bridge grain creates on first use with
`com.docker.network.bridge.enable_icc=false`. Measured against Docker 29:
a container on that network still reaches a listener on the host's
`docker0` gateway (which is what `-container-git-proxy-host` normally
names) and the internet, and no longer reaches a peer container, which on
`bridge` it does.

The stock sandbox image runs as the unprivileged `agent` user and has no
`sudo`, so it needs none of what was dropped. A custom image that does can
be given capabilities back with `-container-sandbox-cap-add` (comma
separated); `no-new-privileges` has no opt-out, so an image relying on
`sudo` does not work under this backend. `-container-sandbox-network`
names a pre-existing network instead (`bridge` restores the old
behaviour), for a host whose firewall only admits `docker0` into grain's
listeners. The backend still reports `IsolatesNetwork() == false` and
still refuses `NetworkAccess none`: containers are kept apart from each
other, not from the internet. No disk quota is set -- `--storage-opt
size=` needs a storage driver most Docker installs do not run.

## Host sandboxes are removed (task 1465)

With container sandboxes available on any host with Docker, the
unisolated host-directory backend is gone as a deployment choice. The
`host` value of `model.SandboxBackend` is removed (a stored `host` reads
as an unknown backend: the daemon keeps what its flags select and says so
at startup), as are `-host-sandboxes`, the daemon's silent fallback to
host directories when no backend flag was passed, `ui.Config.HostSandboxes`
and its standing banner, and `GRAIN_HOST_SANDBOXES` in `scripts/setup.sh`
(which now refuses it). A daemon must select `-container-sandboxes`,
`-granule-sandboxes`, `-k8s-sandboxes` or `-disable-native-sandboxes`, or
be started with the plumbing for one so the stored Settings choice can
select it; `-sandbox-dir` remains, for the caches and disk figures that
live under it. `setup.sh` falls back from granule to containers, and the
cloudtop installer and terraform's `enable_granule_sandboxes = false` now
ask for containers.

`orchestrator.HostSandboxes` itself stays as the in-process stand-in
tests dispatch into (orchestrator, tests/e2e, `grain demo -observability`,
the director e2e server). A daemon reaches it only through
`cmd/grain`'s `localSandboxes` hook, which is nil in every deployment
build: this package's tests set it, and so does the `grain_e2e` build tag
the browser suite builds with for `ui/e2e/config.spec.js`.

## A burst of identical fast failures pauses the framework (task 1638)

On 2026-10-02 the Claude CLI started refusing runs with "You've hit your
session limit · resets 5:30pm (UTC)" -- a wording neither
`agent/claude/usagelimit.go` marker list knew -- and for a quarter of an
hour every Claude run failed in about 20 seconds as an ordinary failure.
Dispatch kept going, and six tasks spent all five attempts on it. The
unmatched-failure log above recorded every one, but a log is read after
the damage.

Two fixes. The marker: `usagelimit.go` now reads "hit your <session|
usage|weekly|...> limit" loosely in a failed run and strictly (the whole
short answer, opening with "You've hit your") in a successful one, and
parses its "resets 5:30pm (UTC)" / "resets Oct 5, 5pm" clause into
`ResetAt` -- the next occurrence of that time, or zero when it does not
read, which the pause turns into its default window.

And the net under the next rewording (`orchestrator/refusalburst.go`):
three runs on one framework within five minutes, each failing within a
minute of its agent starting and before any tool call, with exactly the
same error text, are read as the framework refusing every run.
`RunDispatch` begins a `Pause` for that framework with no named reset
(`defaultUsageLimitPause`), logs `level=error
condition=unrecognised_refusal_burst` with the runs and the words,
records the third run as `paused`, and re-records the first two the same
way with `Store.SetRunOutcome`, so no task's failure streak pays for it.
The counting is in-process state on `Pause`, like the windows themselves.
The words still go to the unmatched-failure log: the burst buys time, and
the fix is still a marker.

## `latest` is the last promoted release (task 1681)

On 2026-10-03 an operator upgraded a deployment to `latest` and got
7b07fd1, a 2026-09-25 build about 1,940 commits behind `main`. The git
tag `latest` had followed every promotion and was at v1.5.0. The image
tag had followed none of them. `build-artifacts.yml` moved it on main
pushes, and GitHub Actions had stopped running. `release-images.sh`
moved it only for a tag ref, and `release.yml` never lets a tag ref
through. The candidate cut only tags git.

The image tag `latest`, on `grain`, `guest` and `k8s-sandbox`, now means
the last promoted release, the commit the git `latest` tag names. It is
never main's head: that is `main`, and the current candidate is
`candidate`. Exactly one path moves it: `scripts/release-images.sh
promote`, run by `.grain/workflows/promote.yml` on every `release` of
`main` and `candidate` and by hand with `workflow_dispatch`. It finds the
`vX.Y.Z` tag at the git `latest` commit, checks that all three
`sha-<short>` images exist, and retags them registry-side as `vX.Y.Z` and
`latest`. It builds nothing, and if an image is missing it fails without
moving anything.

It cannot run inside the cut. The cut is an agent task, and
`package-publish` is CI-only. Firing on every release means the image
follows the git tag within one merge, and a run when nothing changed
re-copies three manifests onto the tags they already hold. `ghcr-prune`
used to treat `v1.5.0` as a branch tag with no branch behind it, which
would have deleted it after 48 hours. It now keeps release tags forever,
like `latest`.
